reviews.transcript_full: Everyone, did you know that there is an airport right near us that once vied for the top two spots in the world for passenger volume? Unfortunately, it is not Incheon Airport, nor is it far away in Hong Kong or Singapore. Today, we are talking about an airport in China that ranked second in the world for passenger traffic before COVID-19 but has completely collapsed since the pandemic! This is a review of my flight from Beijing Capital Airport, the capital of China, to Gimpo on Korean Air. Beijing Capital Airport, also known as PEK (or Capital Airport), was one of Asia's main airports, ranking second in the world for passenger volume with over 100 million annual passengers as of 2019. Beijing Capital International Airport is also the main hub for China's flag carrier, Air China. It is likely one of the airports you have considered for a layover at least once, as Air China offers incredibly cheap flights to Europe via Beijing. However, the situation has been gradually changing since the COVID-19 pandemic. Based on Terminal 2, which Korean Air uses, the facilities had become outdated due to continuous use without major renovations since its opening in 1999. Furthermore , as demand continued to rise, the airport reached saturation, leading to the opening of a new airport south of Beijing in 2019. That place is now PKX Beijing Daxing International Airport. Recently, it seems the Chinese government and airlines are pushing for support for Daxing Airport. For starters, China Southern Airlines has moved its hub to Daxing, and only Air China and some Star Alliance airlines... They are staying at PKX while the other airlines are moving to Daxing and investing in facilities there. Even though people say Daxing is failing, it seems the trend is to inevitably push Daxing because further upgrades to the Capital Airport are impossible. Ah, but then again, the situation at Daxing doesn't seem that great either... well, I guess they will figure it out. Anyway, today I will show you my experience flying Korean Air from Beijing Capital Airport (Shoudu Airport) to Gimpo—which used to be (and still is) China's capital airport, but has become a bit of a shady hub. Korean Air is still using the Capital Airport and operates a total of four flights to the metropolitan area : three from Incheon and one from Gimpo. Oh, they do operate one flight a week from Busan on weekdays as well, but the timing is absolutely terrible. Seeing that Asiana operates similarly, I am curious whether they will transfer the eight flights to and from Seoul alone after the merger to LCCs or foreign airlines , or if they will operate all of them themselves . I came in the day before on a China Eastern domestic flight, so oh wow, this is really ... I had a flight canceled and so many other things happened ... I have a lot to say, but I'll save that for the next video. I will try to get back to it soon. Anyway, after arriving on a domestic flight, I stayed one night at the Ibis near the airport. After sleeping there, I took Didi Taxi, the Chinese version of Kakao Taxi, to the airport . It took about 10 minutes and cost around 22 yuan. If you are flying with Korean Air, you need to come to T2, or Terminal 2. For your information, North Korea's Air Koryo also uses Terminal 2. If you fly Korean Air on Tuesday, Thursday, or Saturday, you can see the Air Koryo counter and aircraft. I didn't go out of my way to look for them, but if you are curious, I think watching them from afar at least once would be a unique experience. Let's get back to the airport. One peculiar thing about Chinese airports is that when you enter, they gather everyone in one group and block entry, then let them all in at once. So, don't panic; it's best to just wait and then come in. I also waited and entered the airport all at once. Wow , but there aren't even any decent restaurants here. I can't see very well. The airport is huge, but it feels somewhat ambiguously large. I think I'll need to check in and look around a bit more . Okay, then, I'll head to check in. Korean Air handles check-in at Counter B. They operate a total of eight check-in counters: two SKY PRIORITY counters, two Morning Calm counters, and four general counters. Since I have Elite Plus status here, I completed my check-in at the red SKY PRIORITY counter and checked in one piece of luggage. It was a small case, but I was touched that they attached a "Fragile" tag to it. I received a physical boarding pass, not a receipt, along with a lounge pass. I thought it was just an information sheet, but when I got to the lounge, they just took it away. They also checked to make sure the aircraft was arriving safely. My previous flight was so eventful... Since there doesn't seem to be much to see at the airport, I'll go straight through security and head inside. Security checks in China tend to be quite strict. They really scrutinize you thoroughly during the body search, so don't panic; just think of it as China's guidelines. I managed to get into the security area relatively quickly, so I’ll take a quick look around the duty-free shops. There are vending machines near the Chinese liquors, and a Starbucks is located here as well. Aside from that, there isn't much else worth seeing, so I’ll just skip through it and head to the lounge. As a SkyTeam Elite Plus member, I ’ve come to the lounge provided by Korean Air. It is the Air China First & Business Lounge. Although Korean Air is a SkyTeam member, it seems they are using this location because there aren't many suitable lounges at capital airports. If you look here, you can see that Air Koryo also uses this lounge . Okay, so I’ll settle down in this not-so-large lounge and show you the food first. The hot food is prepared with vegetables, mushrooms, sausages, fried eggs, boiled eggs, rice, donuts, and various kinds of porridge . True to a Chinese lounge, dim sum and steamed buns were also available. Wow, that’s a relief. Fruit, bread, and cake are also provided. There is also a dumpling soup live station; you order, they give you a bell, and you pick it up. There are snacks, which are a must-have in a Chinese lounge, as well as beverages and wine. The selection is pretty decent for a Chinese lounge, but this is a lounge provided by Korean Air. Considering the circumstances, it is a bit disappointing. Of course, if you go to places like Kumamoto or Okayama in Japan (I wish for the speedy recovery of the Kumamoto region), there are lounges that only serve tea, but I was still glad that this dumpling soup was delicious. I had a bit of a cold and struggled throughout the journey, but thanks to the dumpling soup, I was able to make it back to Korea alive. This concludes my revenge meal for yesterday evening's China Eastern Airlines in-flight meal. I brought a few snacks to eat, making sure to pick only from reputable brands. The restrooms are plastered with the kinds of things you would see if you flew with Air China. After feeling a bit under the weather in the lounge for a while, I’ll head out in time for boarding. On my way to the gate, I’ll talk briefly about the ticketing machine and the aircraft today. I’m flying on an A321neo today. Korean Air used to be a huge Boeing fan. No, no... they were actually huge Airbus fan. For a while, they kept bringing in Boeing 737s and things like that, but then suddenly, at some point, they started introducing the A321 and A350. I originally booked a business class ticket. This plane is equipped with the Prestige Sleeper 2.0 Product, and I really wanted to try Sleeper 2.0... I tried to book it using Delta mileage, but while it only takes 15,000 miles for Japan, it basically costs 30,000 miles for China... (What kind of standard is that, really?) Does that mean 40,000 miles would allow me to fly business class for about 7 hours? I felt like this wasn't quite right, so since booking with a Skying partner through Delta allows for free cancellation, I canceled and booked an economy ticket instead. There really isn't much to it now that I've come this far... (but I still wanted to fly business class), so I tried to book with Asiana. However, when I tried to book a business class ticket, it was 100,000 won for 20,000 miles, so I thought that wasn't right either. Instead, I booked a one-way ticket with Korean Air for about 140,000 won. The airfare for Korean Air is only 30,000 or 20,000 won, but the taxes are 100,000 won... I have so much business in China that I want to travel comfortably. It seems I always take Asiana or Korean Air when returning from China. When going to China, I book one-way tickets because they are cheap, but when coming back, I always end up flying Korean Air or Asiana. There is a certain comfort that national carriers provide. I really like that comfort. Boarding starts at 11:15 today , and it is currently around 11 o'clock. I will head over. This is Gate 11. I have arrived in front of Gate 11, where I will be boarding today, and I am at the gate... I was told that boarding would begin as soon as I arrived, so I lined up at SKY PRIORITY. As I entered ahead of the business class passengers, let me briefly explain today's flight. It is Flight KE 2052; the schedule is to take off from PEK at 11:45 AM, fly for two hours, and land at GMP at 2:45 PM. Today, we will be flying on Korean Air's A321neo. The registration number is HL 8557 —a two-year-old aircraft that still wears the old livery. As for the weather today, it snowed quite a bit in Beijing, so we will need to be careful during takeoff and taxiing. That was a brief explanation of the flight; a flight attendant scanned my ticket at the front, and I was able to enter. First of all, you can see the 2-2 seating arrangement with full-flat business class seats. I will try to leave a review of this soon. Although it is a relatively new aircraft, since it is a bit older now, you can see the headrests folded down. Of course, the headrests fold down well. As you continue straight in, my seat today is 54A, a window seat. Since it is a window seat, I went to the restroom first. Korean Air's trademark, The black sink flusher is button-operated, and you have to press it for the water to come out. Since it is a narrow-body restroom, it is bound to be small, but it felt like they made it larger than a 737. I will return to my seat after admiring the view from behind. Personally, I think this seat is the best among Korean Air's economy seats . Let me show you why. First, this monitor ... it is insane. It is a 13.3-inch monitor that reflects a lot of light . I want to show you various things, but the reflection is too intense and I look a mess, so I will just show you the airshow briefly. Just watching the airshow, you can understand why it is the best monitor; the picture quality is that good. Above the monitor, you can see the air vents and reading lights are well-mounted, and below the monitor, there is a slow USB-A type port. However , there are fast charging ports and Type-C ports under the seat, so it would be good to charge your devices there. The seat pitch is enough for a passport to move back and forth vertically, and the seat width is a bit awkward for a passport vertically , but wide enough to move around horizontally. According to the specs, they are 31-32 inches (I guess I felt it was as wide as 32-33 inches ㅠ) and 17.8 inches, respectively. Narrow-body seats are usually in the low 17-inch range. Compared to the 787, which is in the low 17-inch range, this is angelic. The tray table is this one-piece table, and underneath it are the duty-free catalog, the Morning Calm in-flight magazine , and the safety card. Speaking of which, let me verify the aircraft type: A321-200. There are buttons next to the seat, so you can recline it easily, and you can also open and close the window visible on the opposite side. Oh, there was a coat hanger too . Just as I finished taking pictures of everything, the flight attendant came over to greet me and confirm my special in-flight meal. If you fly with SkyTeam Elite Plus status, you always receive a greeting; ah, it feels a bit overwhelming when there is a greeting, but it feels empty without it... honestly, there is a bit of that feeling . (In- flight announcement ) (In-flight announcement) (In-flight announcement) (In-flight announcement) (In-flight announcement) They also made the in-flight announcements, and then started playing the safety video in order. Ah, I think I've memorized the Korean Air safety video by now . Still, since there are parts of the announcements that differ by aircraft type, finding those parts is part of the fun. While watching the safety video, the aircraft began pushback, and it looks like there is a slight delay today. I can see a KLM aircraft outside the window . The KLM "Blue Mackerel" looks exactly like Korean Air's new livery. Alright then, I will observe the aircraft heading to the runway both out the window and on the monitor as we take off for today's flight. We have reached cruising altitude; even though it is a short flight, I brought slippers, so I changed into these. The 321 monitor has really severe glare. I hear that they have recently been applying anti-reflective film to monitors starting with the 787-10, but this really needs to be implemented urgently. Honestly, whenever a black screen appears while they are playing things like airshows, I have to face it directly. This is a bit overwhelming. Anyway, I just had the airshow playing and worked on my script for a bit; after a few minutes, the in-flight meal came out right away. Since I requested a special Kosher meal today, it came out quickly. It was a green Kosher meal box. Personally, I tend to prefer Korean Air's Kosher meals for short-hauls , seafood meals for medium-hauls, and standard or gluten-free meals for long-hauls. Anyway, regarding the Kosher meal, although I am not Jewish, I eat it often because it is tasty. They tore open just the middle part like that and heated it up for me. Today 's Kosher meal consisted of something that looked like a fish fillet, chickpeas , a chocolate cake, a piece of fruit bread , and a chocolate roll . The fish fillet-like thing in the center wasn't bad. However, something about it —the seasoning and everything —was missing, about 20%. Eating it with the chickpeas, it really felt like I was just filling my stomach. I looked around and saw there was ketchup , so I quickly drizzled some on it. With the ketchup, the seasoning was actually pretty good. I don't dislike chickpeas, so I forced myself to finish this meal . I regretted it . Oh, and I had dumpling soup at the lounge... I should have just eaten the plate. Still, that chocolate roll was really delicious. The fruits and the chocolate dessert were tasty too. It seems like they really take the desserts seriously with the Kosher meal. I don't think the desserts on the Kosher meal have ever disappointed me. Ever since I hit the peak of short-haul Kosher meals at Narita , I haven't been able to stop eating them... I even had salmon as a Kosher meal again a few days ago, so it would be great if I could choose the Kosher meal option (Delta allows it). Ah, but anyway, for short-haul flights, the Kosher meal is better than the regular in-flight meal. I grumbled a lot, but compared to the meal next to me, the composition was substantial and I filled my stomach pretty well. I definitely filled my stomach... Since there is quite a difference between the highs and lows of Korean Air's short-haul Kosher meals, I'm debating what to do going forward. Maybe I should try the short-haul seafood meal. As I finished my meal, we were passing over Weihai. Even though I had loaded up on sugar, they gave me another can of guava juice. They saw how delicious it was and just gave it to me straight from the can. It was so nice. With this, I think I'll have a pretty intense blood sugar spike. I arrived and dozed off, and when I opened my eyes, they were making the landing announcement. Landing is now truly just around the corner. Since Korean Air is known for its great playlists, I put on a playlist to listen to some music. The playlist chosen by me today is this one. Because this is the route from Beijing to Gimpo , we are flying along a path where you can see downtown Seoul and Gimpo clearly. They say you can even see Lotte Tower if you fly Gimpo. And today's aircraft is the Korean Air Headquarters! Hanjin flew by, and we landed at Seoul Gimpo International Airport. It feels like it's been a while since I arrived at Gimpo, and I see the whole place is being torn apart. I wonder if the construction will be finished by the time this video is uploaded. Today , I decided to board my flight to Gimpo from Beijing Capital Airport, which was China's main airport and seems likely to remain so in the future . I don't have any video of the disembarkation because I was chatting small talk with the flight attendants on my way out. They asked if I had a YouTube channel, and I was a bit shy, so I just filmed with Jimmy and told them I didn't have one before leaving. (Guraping) Regarding today's flight, the Korean Air 321 is an aircraft I like more and more the more I see it. The seats are spacious for a narrow-body plane, the seat condition is comfortable, and the monitors are good, so if I were to fly a narrow-body on Korean Air, I would only want to fly this one. I think I need to give the in-flight meal a little more thought. Next time, I should try ordering something different on a short-haul flight. Lastly, it is too early to evaluate the entire airport based only on seeing the Korean Air terminal at Beijing Capital Airport , but there were a few aspects that left something to be desired for a capital airport. Personally, I think Pudong or Guangzhou had slightly better aspects. Even considering it as a typical Chinese airport, it felt pretty similar to Beijing. Personally, next time I’d like to try flying from Daxing and compare the two. Since this is a video about China, I’m sure I’ll get some hate today~ After uploading the last C919 video, I got all sorts of hate—everything you can get out of YouTube—so... I ’m going to get a bit of swearing about this China flight cancellation story . I was actually worrying about what to do because I knew I would get a bit of hate. I think I’m going to live a long time haha. Anyway , that’s all for today’s video. (Sorry about my voice as I’ve had a cold this week.) If you found this helpful, please subscribe and like. (Sorry about my voice as I have a cold this week.) If you have any questions, please leave a comment or send a DM, and I will answer to the best of my knowledge. Thank you for always watching. This has been BeFly. Thank you, and have a good flight! In China, I woke up the next day, and China really tormented me until the very last day. I couldn't catch the last taxi, so I took a metered taxi, but they casually quoted three times the normal fare. I didn't want to argue, so I got in and left. This is the Ibis Styles Beijing Capital Hotel in China . It was a bit difficult to find a hostel, so I paid a little extra to book a hotel. It didn't cost much; it was 30,000 won, but the taxi fare to get here was 15,000 won. I'm running late now because I overslept. Since I overslept, my mindset was to arrive three hours before my flight, but now I have two and a half hours left. I'll be heading off . This video will follow the Korean Air video, so please watch it. I'm not sure which one will upload first, or if this one will even get uploaded. Thank you. Thank you so much. Yes, thank you. Bye. This was B-ple.

reviews.transcript_full: Today I'm trying out ZIPAIR's incredibly cheap business class (ZIP Full Flat). I review both the good and bad points. Please enjoy. Early in the morning, I'm heading to Narita Airport on the first Narita Express. ZIPAIR operates from Narita Airport Terminal 1, so I'm taking this train to Narita Airport Terminal 1 Station. It's around 6 AM now, and I was able to see a beautiful sunrise. If you take the first Narita Express, you'll arrive at Narita Airport Terminal 1 Station at 7:19 AM. I'm heading to the departure lobby on the 4th floor. Terminal 1 is divided into the North Wing and the South Wing, and ZIPAIRs check-in area is in the North Wing. I've arrived at the North Wing on the 4th floor of Terminal 1. ZIPAIR operates flights from Tokyo/Narita to destinations in Asia, North America, and Hawaii. Today's flight departs at 8:55 AM for Manila. The basic fare for business class (ZIP Full Flat) is 55,000 JPY (337 USD). Adding the PREMIUM service package costs an additional 12,500 JPY (76.5 USD). This package includes Prior seat selection, carry-on baggage,  checked baggage, in-flight meal, and an amenity kit. Let's check in. ZIPAIR's check-in counters are C and D. ZIPAIR is a low-cost carrier (LCC) wholly owned by Japan Airlines (JAL). As it's an LCC, you're basically responsible for checking in and dropping off your own baggage. Mobile check-in via smartphone is the standard, but you can also check in using a self-service check-in machine. There's also a priority check-in service called Express Service (for a fee of 3,000 JPY). I won't be using Express Service today. I issued my boarding pass in advance using mobile check-in. Checked baggage is normally subject to a fee, but it's included in this PREMIUM package. I have checked my suitcase, and I will be taking my backpack on board with me. As it's an LCC, you're basically responsible for checking in your own baggage. Normally, you would use the self-service baggage drop-off machine over there. It's 7:42 AM now, and I have about 40 minutes until boarding begins.  I'll go through security and immigration and enter the restricted area. You can use the Narita Premier Lounge for a fee. The fee is 9,200 JPY (56.3 USD). The lounge is 930 square meters in size and has 148 seats. This lounge is uncrowded and offers an excellent selection of alcoholic beverages. You can take off your shoes and relax in a Japanese-style room. You can look out the window at parked airplanes. The seats and tables are spaced far apart, making it very comfortable. There is a buffet area in the center. Bread, desserts, cold meals, sushi, etc. There are four types of hot meals. White rice and soup are also available. There is a beer server and an automatic wine dispenser. Online reviews praise the wide selection of alcoholic beverages. There are various wines and sakes. TWININGS tea and Ito En tea are also available. There are three shower rooms, and amenities such as toothbrushes are provided. You should be able to take a comfortable shower. Now, let's move on to the boarding gate. If you don't go to the lounge, using the restaurants and shops is a good option. There's a McDonald's, and there's a queue in the early morning. It's nice that there's a 7-Eleven in the airport. Starbucks is crowded in the early morning, so I don't feel like using it. My boarding gate is number 21. It's about 7:55 AM now, so I still have plenty of time. My flight to Manila is scheduled for 8:55 AM, a 5-hour and 5-minute flight. The aircraft is a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner. The registration number is JA825J, and it was operated by its parent company JAL from 2012 to 2019, and has been operated by ZIPAIR since January 2020. ZIPAIR uses the Boeing 787 to  efficiently operate medium- and long-haul routes and achieve low fares. There are three reasons for this: long range, excellent fuel efficiency, and the ability to utilize aircraft from its parent company JAL. The exterior of the aircraft is characterized by green lines and the ZIPAIR logo. Green is the corporate color that shows a strong commitment to "safe operation". Boarding begins 30 minutes before departure, at 8:25 AM. All passengers board through the same door. There are two classes: ZIP Full Flat (Business Class) and Standard (Economy Class). Standard (Economy Class) has 272 seats with a 3-3-3 seating arrangement. ZIP Full Flat (Business Class) has 18 seats with a 1-2-1 seating arrangement. The 1-2-1 arrangement is herringbone-style, and all seats have aisle access. There are no doors on the seats. The green headrest covers feature Santa Claus? There is a movable partition between the two center seats. When the partition is closed, you shouldn't be bothered by the person in the next seat. The seats are made of high-quality black genuine leather. There is a luggage rack above each seat. The seat width is 20 inches (51 cm), and the seat pitch is 42 inches (107 cm). The seats recline completely to a full flat position of 180 degrees. My seat is 5A. Headrest. Genuine leather seat, nice to the touch. No personal screen. Reading light. Storage space. Lighting switch, attendant call button. Universal power outlet, USB-A port. A switch to return the seat to its original position. There seems to be a mesh pocket for small items. Seat and lighting control panel. The mesh pocket contains a disposal bag, Boeing 787-8 safety card, and information on in-flight Wi-Fi service. Free internet, in-flight shopping, in-flight entertainment, and flight map. Information on the use of electronic devices on board. Actions that endanger the safety of the aircraft are prohibited by aviation law. Dining table. Can also be used as a laptop desk. There is ample legroom. Fortunately, there was no passenger next to me. The white partition wall around the seat looks cool. You can place your backpacks and bags on the overhead racks. The floor is carpeted. The windows are electronically dimmable windows (EDW). The electronically dimmable windows have a structure where  gel is sandwiched between two panes of glass. You can view the flight map on your smartphone. I feel a little strange because I'm used to viewing the flight map on the screen. The flight from Tokyo to Manila is 3263km and takes about 5 hours. I'll try out the in-flight entertainment during the flight. For some reason, the windows are yellow. I can see the engine from the window of my seat, 5A. It is equipped with a General Electric (GE) GEnx-1B70 engine. There are no shared screens in the cabin, and the cabin crew demonstrates the in-flight safety procedures. In-flight safety instructions are also played in both Japanese and English. For some reason, the windows are yellow, so the images are also slightly yellow. When I looked up the reason for the yellow windows online, it said that it is mainly due to the aging deterioration of the gel in the electronically dimmable windows. Originally, this was an aircraft that JAL had been operating since 2012. Compared to the latest aircraft,  the electronically dimmable windows seem to be showing signs of aging. Normally, electronically dimmable windows change from transparent to a dark indigo color that is almost black, so these yellow windows are apparently not normal. Finally, takeoff. Successful takeoff. Let's check the flight map. After takeoff, you can see the current flight information on the flight map. I'm used to seeing it on the screen, so  it's refreshing to see the flight map on my smartphone. The ceiling has a seatbelt sign, lights, and air nozzles. The scenery is also yellow due to the yellow windows, making it look like an area with heavy yellow dust. The plane is gaining altitude and we are now flying over the sea again. From here to Manila, we will be flying over the sea for a while. There is an item called "Views". It seems you can see various things just like on a normal flight map. You can also see the current speed of the plane. We are already going about 800 km/h (500 mph). Let's try the free internet. Free internet access for all passengers is a great service. Currently, all ZIPAIR aircraft (8 planes) are equipped with Starlink Wi-Fi. When I boarded, Starlink hadn't been introduced yet. Wow... beautiful clouds. I feel like I want to jump into them. The window color has turned blue-green. The blue-green color is due to the effect of the electronically dimmable window. After takeoff and reaching cruising altitude, an amenity kit is handed out (for a fee). I'm excited to see what's inside. Fleece blanket. It's a large blanket and feels nice to the touch. An tote bag. This is... an air neck pillow. I'm not sure how to use it. It seems I have to inflate this myself. The travel goods set of three includes in-flight slippers, an eye mask, and earplugs. You can place your shoes here. The amenity kit was comprehensive, but there were no cosmetics. There are lavatories at the back that are shared with Economy Class. It's a normal lavatory in terms of size and interior. Only hand soap is provided, and there are no amenities such as toothbrushes. There is a full-length mirror and a changing table. I tried inflating the neck pillow. It has a simple design. Let's try making the seat fully flat. With the press of a single switch, the seat reclines to a fully flat position. The fully flat bed is 76 inches (193 cm) long. The black genuine leather bed has a luxurious feel. What I noticed was the lack of a pillow. The headrest is small and doesn't serve as a pillow. The neck pillow moves around easily and is also not very useful as a pillow. With no pillow and a narrow bed width, it felt a little uncomfortable to sleep. This is a matter of personal preference, of course. But the fare is cheap, so I can't really complain. It's good enough just to be able to lie down on a fully flat bed. There are no doors on the seats, but the person next to you doesn't bother you too much,  so I think there's a certain degree of privacy. I moved my seat to the dining position and extended the table. After takeoff, in-flight meals are served (for a fee). Diet Coke and mineral water. I ordered a beef bowl. It looks like a beef short rib bento box that you can buy at a convenience store. It was a very tasty beef bowl. It tasted like convenience store food. I had a Coke. It was a Coke that I bought for an additional 270 JPY (1.65 USD). You can view the meal menu on ZIPAIR's official website. Beef bowl 1,500 JPY (9.2 USD). Does it look different from the picture? Butter chicken curry 1,500 JPY (9.2 USD). ZIP original curry rice 1,800 JPY (11 USD). Tempura soba 1,600 JPY (9.8 USD). Pork cutlet sandwich 1,600 JPY (9.8 USD). Eel rice bowl 3,000 JPY (18.4 USD). ZIP original Wagyu beef curry rice 3,000 JPY (18.4 USD). Teriyaki burger 1,800 JPY (11 USD). Pork cutlet bowl 1,800 JPY (11 USD). Soft drinks, tea, mineral water. I'll take a look on my laptop since I have the chance. Just like with my smartphone, I can connect to Wi-Fi for free on my laptop. The content I can see on my smartphone and laptop is the same. There is a section called Seat Options. You can also watch in-flight entertainment such as movies. Light meals such as cup noodles and snacks. Alcoholic beverages such as sake and beer. Red wine, sparkling wine, and white wine are also available. Paid amenities can be purchased on board. Electronic products such as USB ports are also sold. Let's take a look at the in-flight entertainment. You can watch the latest movies and classic films. A tablet or laptop makes watching movies easier. You can also watch videos and e-books. Music, live TV, and games are not available. The in-flight entertainment doesn't seem to be very extensive. My seat today was a bit of a drawback as it was close to the lavatory. The lavatory, which is shared with economy class, is very busy. My seat today is in row 5, but rows 2-4 might be better. Time flies, and the plane is already beginning its descent. I put my seat back to its original position and prepare for landing. There are in-flight announcements in Japanese and English, but apparently only about 30% of the passengers are Japanese, and the remaining 70% are foreign nationals, so it seems to be popular with foreigners visiting Japan. Especially on the North American route, there are apparently many American passengers. The scenery of Manila, Philippines. Because the window is yellow, the sea looks like a desert. Actually, ZIPAIR's Narita-Manila route has been suspended since the summer 2026 schedule. The reason for the service suspension is low demand on the Narita–Manila route in recent years. Indeed, when I was on board, there were many empty seats. Landing. There was significant shaking during the landing. Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila, Philippines. There was no delay, and we arrived on time. ZIPAIR's on-time arrival rate is 80.31% (delay rate is 19.69%), and its on-time performance rate is 99.75%. ZIPAIR's on-time arrival and on-time performance rates are said to be relatively high among low-cost carriers. I'd like to reflect on the flight. The biggest advantage was the low fare, which was 71,930 JPY (440 USD) for a flight of about 5 hours. Other advantages included high-speed Wi-Fi and free internet access, and seats that could be reclined to a full flat position. Amenities are available for a fee, and there are no cosmetics or amenity pouches. Personally, I felt that the lack of a pillow was a disadvantage. It might be tiring on a long-haul flight from Narita to North America. The lack of personal screens is also a slight concern. On long-haul flights, you might get bored with nothing to do. In-flight meals are extra and may not be of the highest quality. Wine and beer are available, but champagne is not. Overall, it didn't feel luxurious, and I felt it was a business class experience commensurate with the price. That being said, I thought ZIPAIR's low fares were very attractive. For people who want to keep travel expenses down, ZIPAIR is the best option. Thank you for watching.

reviews.transcript_full:
Cathay Pacific business class has one 
of the best reputations in the sky.   But this regional version is no Aria 
Suite — and might be one of the worst   business class seats I've flown. Today's 
flight takes us from Taipei to Hong Kong,   on the oldest Boeing 777-300 in existence.
Stay tuned for the full review,   and how you can look out and perhaps 
avoid this product for yourself. Our journey begins at Taipei’s main station. I've previously made a full video 
on the in-town check-in service at   Taipei Main Station, which made life so 
much easier — link's in the description.  We were able to complete almost 
the entire check-in process right   at this train station before we took 
the 40 minute train to the airport. My backpack though couldn’t be checked in 
at the train station due to its odd shape.  Cathay has a piece based luggage 
allowance of 2 pieces up to 32kg   each in Business Class. I prefer 
weight based allowances to be honest. Immigration and security were super efficient   and soon we were airside walking 
towards the lounge for the day. Cathay has a huge presence in Taipei So it is no surprise that they operate 
their own lounge at this airport.  The lounge pretty much retains the same 
DNA as Cathays lounges around the world.  First stop, the bar… to get our favourite 
non-alcoholic airline drink - Cathay delight. The centre piece of the lounge is the noodle 
bar offering a good selection of hot dishes   prepared fresh and served minutes later. With our flight almost about to land, 
I headed to our gate to catch a glimpse   of this piece of history. This is 
B-HNE, our aircraft taking us to   Hong Kong today. The cool part? It is 
the original Boeing 777-300 prototype,   the first one ever made and now 28 years old. 
It is impressive that it still flies today. The gate featured cool semiconductor artwork, an 
ode to Taiwan as the leader in global chip supply. Anyway, it is time to board and here is 
a quick look at the seat map for today. Cathay Pacific has a fleet of 
52 Boeing 777 family aircraft,   but 17 of them are the original Boeing 777-300 
non-ER variants. These are a 2 class product with   438 passenger seating. The business class 
consists of 42 seats in a 2-3-2 layout. And, this is it.
As you can see, this is no Aria suite. In fact,   it feels like Cathay’s old Premium economy seat. 
It is a recliner style seat though for its part   comes with decent legroom with three windows. 
It was enough to get this little guy excited. The screen in the distance came 
with a USB socket and there was   an old school power outlet next to the window. In terms of amenities, a pillow and 
paper menus were provided at the seat.   There was a pre-departure drink service and 
soon after that it was time for pushback. (Takeoff roll with pilot commentary) It was a short 1 hour and 15 minute service to 
Hong Kong. Inflight entertainment came in the   form of TV that had to be controlled using a 
remote which was slow and barely responsive.   The entertainment outside was better anyway 
with this view of the Taiwan’s offshore wind   farms appearing to float in the sky.
Despite its age, the aircraft was   equipped with WiFi. And it was 
free for business class passengers. An inflight magazine was available. I 
found the fleet page very interesting   as Cathay lists its future aircraft as 
well as ground service equipment in this. Here is a look at the menu for today’s flight. It 
was pretty impressive for a flight this length.   Two options for main complete with dessert. And 
a decent range of beverages to go with that.   The tray table comes out and here is what the meal   looks like in reality. A proper 
single tray service with proper   crockery and cutlery. The chicken meal 
was served hot and tasted good as well. Here is a quick look at one of 2 lavatories 
serving the business class cabin. All pretty   standard, although this one had a baby change 
table which came in handy. And it was equipped   with Bamford amenities that you will find 
on long haul amenity kits. I've previously   made a full video on Cathay's long-haul 
Business class product. The link's in   the description if you want to see what the 
good version of this experience looks like. Returning back to my seat, it was already time 
for the descent. As Hong Kong came into view,   here are my partying thoughts. Starting with 
the start product, it is top notch and the   Cathay that I have come to love, whether 
it is the meals or the onboard hospitality.  But it is the hard product that is the let down 
here. Only because Asian airlines including Cathay   themselves set such high standards. That said, 
it does come with its warnings. As I mentioned   before there are up to 15 flights per day and 
all I had to do was book an alternative Airbus   A330 or A350 service if I really wanted the 
lie-flat experience. But, hey it is a 2 hour   flight at best and as an aviation nerd, I got 
to experience a piece of aviation history.   What do you think about Cathay’s regional 777 
business class? Let me know in the comments.

reviews.transcript_full:
When most people think of 
Spanish long-distance trains,   the iconic AVE high-speed 
sets usually come to mind. But today we'll be on the last classic loco-hauled   service operating around the country, where 
the high-speed lines have yet to reach. We'll be in First Class from Madrid down 
to Almería, on Spain's sunny south coast. This is one of my favourite routes in the country,   as there's plenty of stunning scenery 
on this relaxed 6 and a half hour ride. So come along with me and let's check it 
all out on another epic Nonstop Eurotrip. Today's journey starts in the 
vibrant Spanish capital, Madrid. This city has a population of 3.5 million people, 
expanding to 7 million in the metropolitan area. It is packed with history, stunning 
architecture and beautiful green spaces. OK, let's head to the station. Well, after a quick coffee :) All Spanish long-distance and 
high-speed trains include a   free transfer - just scan the barcode 
on your main ticket at the gate line. This is valid at both ends of your 
journey, and is a great perk to have. It can be used on Cercanías 
or Rodalies local trains and   the Alicante tram, but not on metro systems. It's a quick hop from where 
I was staying in the north of   the city down to Madrid Chamartín 
where today's journey starts from. There has been a huge €560 million 
(£474m, $642m) redevelopment going   on at the station for the past 4 years. Building work was ongoing at the time of filming,   but the new station concourse has since opened 
in June 2026, and it's a massive improvement. The station has many automatic ticket 
machines spread around the main lobby,   and also a staffed ticket office. Vending machines are available 
for snacks and drinks purchases. My train is departing from one of the platforms 
not guarded by the airport-style security checks,   so I have got time to head to one 
of the cafés to grab some breakfast. Let's check out today's route! We depart Madrid Chamartín and head basically 
due south, making 8 intermediate stops on the   direct line to Almería, on Spain's south coast. Step-free access to all platforms 
is available by lift. Well, usually. And also by escalators. The tracks are 
one level down from the main concourse. Our train today will be hauled by two of these 
Renfe Class 334 diesel-electric locomotives. This is almost identical to the UK Class 68. They have a top speed of 200km/h 
(125mph), and a power output of   2,500kW (3,300hp). The fastest speed will 
we achieve today though is 160km/h (100mph). Trailing is a 9-coach rake 
of Talgo VI coaches. We'll   talk about these a bit later on in the video. After a ticket check at the 
door, I am allowed to board. This is level with the platform,   but there's a decent gap to cross. 
Ramps are available on request. I will be in the Elige Confort seating 
for today, which is basically First Class. This is laid out in a 2+1 configuration. Luggage can be stored on the 
stacks in the vestibules,   or on the overhead racks above the seats. Let's get settled down as 
departure time is fast approaching. If you've watched my channel for a while,   you'll know I'm constantly travelling - 
on overnight trains, buses and ferries,   or sleeping in airport lounges - and getting 
decent sleep on the road isn't always easy. That's why I've been using Manta Sleep 
and their excellent selection of high   quality sleep masks for the past few years now,   and I was very excited when they reached 
out to partner with me on this video. What I love about Manta Sleep masks is 
that they completely block out all light   thanks to their adjustable eye cups 
- which put no pressure on your face,   allowing you to keep the mask on 
all night, and in total comfort. They have a range of masks for different 
situations too, including the 'Cool Mask',   which calms your eyes and sinuses, 
the 'Sound Mask', which has built-in,   ultra-thin Bluetooth headphones, and the Sleep 
Mask Pro, which gives unbeatable zero-pressure,   side-sleep comfort, ventilation and breathability. I am currently using the incredibly soft Manta 
Silk Mask, which feels great against your skin,   and is perfect for long journeys 
when comfort really matters. If you want to improve your sleep either at home, 
or while travelling, check out Manta Sleep using   the link in the description below, and get 
10% OFF all products using my code: NONSTOP. Now back to the video! We depart Madrid Chamartín right on-time,   at 7.58am. Since filming the departure 
time for this train has changed to 8.20am. The route down to Almería covers 
a distance of 562km (349mi) which   is scheduled to take us 6 hours 
and 29 minutes of travel time. Compared to AVE high-speed tickets 
over the same sort of distance,   tickets onboard this loco-hauled 
train are excellent value. They are dynamically priced due to demand,   but start from just €29 (£25, $33) in Elige 
Confort, and just €24 (£25, $33) in Básico. You can then tweak them to your desire 
by choosing to pay for seat selection,   flexibility and food options - the latter 
of which we will look in more detail soon. Immediately after leaving Chamartín, we dive in to 
the Madrid cross-city tunnel which takes us 7.3km   (4.5mi) under the Spanish capital, passing 
through some Cercanías stations en-route,   and popping out at Atocha, the main 
station in the city for our first stop. As we are on the Iberian gauge (1,668mm) through 
tracks, we stop at the commuter train platforms. The Atocha high-speed terminus can be 
seen high up to the right as we depart. The main Renfe depot is off to the left 
shortly after where you will be able to   spot many of the different types of high-speed 
and regular trains in operation in Spain today. [ANNOUNCEMENT] Renfe welcomes you 
onboard this train bound for Almería. [ANNOUNCEMENT] During the journey, we will 
be announcing the stops along the way. [ANNOUNCEMENT] You will find earphones at 
your seat to listen to music, or watch a film. [ANNOUNCEMENT] We inform you that a 
caféteria service is at your disposal. [ANNOUNCEMENT] The crew 
will be happy to assist you. [ANNOUNCEMENT] On behalf of Renfe, 
we wish you a pleasant journey. All onboard announcements are 
made in both Spanish and English. After about 15 minutes, tickets are checked 
and my pre-ordered meal is delivered. I went for the 'Fresh Box' which consisted of 
a cold smoked salmon salad, some bread sticks,   crackers, Greek yoghurt and an orange juice. The price was €12.55 (£10.67, $14.35) and it 
was all pretty nice! Here are the other choices. My only real complaint about 
this train is the ride quality.   It's not as bad as some of their faster trains, 
but still bumpy, noisy and very noticeable. This will come as no surprise to regular 
viewers of the channel, but Talgo's highly   irregular one-wheel arrangement between coaches, 
and no proper bogies is the root cause of this. OK, moving on to the seats. I have no complaints here. The ones in Elige Confort are large leather 
recliners which have excellent padding,   a good shape and slightly winged headrests. There are adjustable armrests and 
they can be reclined using this lever. Next to this is the headphone jack and 
controls for the shared onboard entertainment. Legroom is absolutely huge, and I can barely reach 
the footrest on the back of the seat in front! There is also a large and sturdy tray 
table there, along with a small litter bin. Under your own seat you will find 
one European-style power socket. Up above you will find coat hooks on the walls,   reading light on the under side of the 
luggage racks, and sun blinds on the windows. No WiFi is available onboard these trains. Overall though, a pretty 
good First Class products! It's not very busy on this service today, 
with only 4 other people in my coach. Our first stop outside of Madrid is at Alcázar 
de San Juan, a small city of 30,000 people. It is located 120km (75mi) to the 
south-east of the Spanish capital. OK, time to check out the toilets. As these Talgo coaches are much 
shorter than on a regular train,   there is one in every couple of coaches. The water and soap both worked as expected. There was a bin, plenty of toilet 
paper and a functional hand dryer. They were also pretty clean! The two wheelchair spaces are located adjacent 
to where I was sitting, with two companion seats. The accessible toilet being in 
the vestibule just behind these. We will shortly be coming up to start 
traversing the most scenic parts of the   trip and some of the best #TrainWindowViews 
anywhere in Spain, in my opinion. This is the Despeñaperros Natural Park, 
which translates as 'The Falling Dog Cliffs'. This 76km² (29m²) natural canyon was 
carved out my the Despeñaperros River   and has steep walls, some more 
that 500m (1,600ft) in height. We now make a short stop at Vilches, where 
the north-bound service is waiting in the   station's passing loop, as the majority of this 
classic line is single track due to the terrain. [ANNOUNCEMENT] Ladies and Gentlemen, 
next station: Linares-Baeza. Our next calling point in at Linares-Baeza 
- a important junction station where the   line from Madrid diverges west to Sevilla 
and Cadíz, or continues south to Almería. A high-speed line should have already been 
in operation to our destination today,   on a route via Alicante and Murcia. The opening date for this has now been pushed back 
to early 2027, but once in operation, it will cut   the journey time from Marid to Almería nearly in 
half, down from 6 and a half hours, to just under   3 and a half, and improve the service frequency 
from twice per day, up to a planned 5 times. I am not going to lie though, 
yes it will save a lot of time,   but the trade off is losing spectacular scenery 
such as this, and the magic of slow train travel. OK, let's pop down and have a 
look at the Second Class seats. Honestly, they are still really 
good - probably the best in Spain! You certainly lose some legroom 
and width, but they are still very   comfortable reclining leather seats, with 
power sockets and tray tables available. The price difference isn't so much 
though, so I guess that makes sense! Food options onboard, if you don't order 
yours while booking are pretty good too. There is a roaming trolley service. And also a dining car.
 
They have a pretty good   selection of sandwiches, snacks, sweets 
and drinks and even some meal deals. This impressive Anchurón Viaduct 
carries the single track railway   line at a height of 45m (150ft) over the valley. The original bridge here opened in 1893,   but this current one was modernised 
and rebuilt in the late 1970s. We now call at Guadix, the final 
intermediate stop on today's journey. This historic Andalucían town is known 
as the cave house capital of Europe,   with around a quarter of 18,000 
residents actually living in them! We are now passing through the Tabernas 
desert, one of the driest places in Europe,   with an average annual rainfall 
of just 20-24cm (8-9.5"). This covers a total area of 280km² (110mi²) 
and due to its near identical landscapes to   the south-western USA and northern Mexico, it 
is a popular area to shoot spaghetti westerns,   and other films and TV series, with 
three dedicated film studios based here. There are a few abandoned 
stations on the line here too. I love this part of Spain. It's such 
a different vibe to the bustling big   cities, the temperate north, 
or the Mediterranean resorts. Due to high-speed line preparation works at 
Almería's main station, trains currently terminate   here at Huércal-Viator, with a free onwards 
bus connection to the city centre provided. This had not started when this video was 
filmed, so as we continue all the way to   the end of the line, let me summarise 
this six and a half journey from Madrid   down to Almería onboard this loco-hauled, 
Renfe Intercity service in First Class. This is, without doubt, one of my favourite 
routes in Spain, and I had a great trip today. I love the slow and super scenic southern section,   the seats are super comfortable and the train had 
all the amenities you could need for this trip. It's also EXCELLENT value and lovely throwback to 
when not everything was about high-speed travel. The only moot points are the worse than 
average ride quality and lack of WiFi,   but overall I really enjoyed it! We arrive at Almería' s main 
intermodal train and bus hub   a couple of minutes late, at just before 2.30pm. Honestly, if you want a much more 
relaxed Spanish seaside holiday,   I can't recommend this area enough. I have 
been 5 or 6 times now and really love it! Have you been on any Spanish 
classic trains before? If so,   which ones? How did you find them? 
Let me know in the comments below! I'm always open to new video ideas, so if you 
have something you'd like to see on the channel,   then drop me DM on Instagram, BlueSky or Twitter. Don't forget to subscribe, thanks for watching 
to the end, and I'll see you in the next video!

reviews.transcript_full: I don't think I've ever heard anyone boast about flying Sri Lankan Airlines, even in business class. And yet, this is a country with culture full of detail, warmth, and a coastline that would make the Moldes blush. Having just flown the regional business class, this is the long haul product. A proper life flat seat and a noticeable step up from what we've experienced before. So, the question is whether this is an overlooked long haul experience that deserves more credit or just a reasonably comfort way to get home without sitting upright in economy. because sometimes an airline surprises you and sometimes it just quietly gets the job done. So, we are hoping to be impressed, but is [music] there a chance of being underwhelmed? Sometimes I feel a little bit like a test subject flying these airlines so you can sit comfortably at home and decide whether it's actually worth clicking book. And who am I? I'm Alex. Someone who really should have had a nap in the lounge, but was far too worried about missing my flight. Throw in some heavy dose of jet lag and I'm probably not operating at peak performance today. And in today's review, we've flung an airline that's doing everything it can to impress. And the question is, if it's trying this hard, why was the ticket such a bargain? I've just come off a flight with Sri Lankan on the A320. What a nice experience that was. But now we're having a bit of an upgrade as we fly on the A330. In many ways, paying just over £900 for business class all the way from Tokyo back to Europe sounds like an absolute bargain. The ticket even included a 7-hour flight with Japan Airlines, a genuine five-star carrier down to Singapore, followed by a rather basic lounge, and my regional flight down to Columbbo, which was originally meant to be a widebody with a flatbed before getting swapped out. Then a real problem came before I'd even left home. Booking this ticket turned into surprisingly difficult experience with various technical issues preventing me from booking directly with the airline on their website. In the end, I had to use a third party travel website, which isn't something I normally recommend because if your flight changes or something goes wrong, the airline will usually send you back to the travel agent, and getting a hold of them can sometimes be a challenge. Still, I've made it and my expectations are fairly low. And with a 6-hour connection ahead of me, I'm now on the hunt for Sri Lankan Airlines business class lounge. There's only so many hours the human can spend eating, drinking, and scrolling through Instagram before the novelty wears off. With my next flight not departing until the following morning, I'm genuinely relieved to have lounge access. After long day flights, that suddenly feels less like a luxury and more like a survival tool. It's sort of how I expected. There's a lot of brown and leather chairs. Um, it's not the most exciting lounge in the world, but is open 24 hours and that's beneficial. My flight is not till 2:30 in the morning. All I really want is a comfortable bed and a full night's sleep. When you're running on empty, reving an airline isn't exactly easy. Still, the food looks rather good, and the chicken curry is far too tempting to ignore. And after a quick sandwich, some fruit, and a muchneeded cup of tea, I managed to find a cozy corner. It's not completely quiet because it's connected to the main lounge. We just have a row of black leather recliners where I can at least close my eyes for the next few hours. Hopefully, a little nap will leave me feeling humid again before today's journey really begins. According to my boarding pass, we'll be departing at 2:30 in the morning for an 11-hour journey down to Paris. From there, we're taking a bit of a gamble with just a 3-hour connection booked back to the UK on separate tickets. I'm already praying for an empty immigration queue and a flight that arrives on time. And with today's route firmly in my mind, I think it's time to head down to the gate. Partly because the departure board is suddenly saying final call despite making absolutely no sense. and partly because I've just spotted a cockroach. Either way, I think that's my cue to leave. At the gate, there's a separate boarding area behind the barrier for certain frequent flyers and business class passengers, but for some reason, I'm directed to the right, and I can only assume this is where I'll get a nice view of the aircraft while waiting. How wrong I was. Instead of find myself surrounded by a sea of passengers waiting to board an economy and luckily enough to explain the situation to member staff, I'm eventually allowed through. Although the response was less, let me fix this for you and more, fine if you insist. But at least I made it through to the right side of the barrier. Sri Lankan Airlines operates two different business class configurations on its Airbus A330 fleet. And thankfully on the longhaul routes, it tends to be the more desirable one. It features a onetoone layout across seven rows, giving every passenger direct aisles access. The seats I probably avoid are to the front right purely because the proximity to the galley and the bathroom. The seat itself is a Zodiac Cirrus, a product that was once very popular with the airlines, but now it's starting to show its age. There are still things I like. The headrest cover is pretty, and the teal green color scheme gives the cabin some personality. But the reality is that seats evolve quickly in aviation and newer versions of this exact product such as the one found on Kathy Pacific's Airbus A350 feel like a significant step forward. It left me wondering why Sri Lankan Airlines hasn't been able to introduce new aircraft or a more modern business class seat especially when so many competitors have moved on. And then I found this article which explains the situation Sri Lankan Airlines is currently in. So, first impressions, this product is looking just a touch dated, but it's kind of the same product as Cathy Pacific. And I can see why they upgraded. I don't think Sri Lankan's got the money, which is why they're still mainly with flagship fleet of A330 products. Um, I do like the green, though. It's kind of a bit like Vietnam Airlines. There kind of like that warm, bubbly side to it, and the cabin crew seem really good. There's a lesson to be learned here. You could have one of the best hard products in the sky. But if the service, food, and overall cabin experience feel a little flat, it can completely change how you remember the flight. Looking around this cabin in 2027, it feels close to a premium regional product than a true longhaul business class experience. That being said, the seat still delivers the things you'd expect from a liflat seat. Space, privacy, and a comfortable way to travel long distances. The question is whether it's enough anymore with so much competition offering them a polished and consistent experience elsewhere. I'm not sure this is a product I could confidently recommend to a friend. At least not without knowing exactly what they value most from their business class experience. So let's check out the amenities. There is quite a lot and I really like the pillow. For an airline that's faced its fair share of financial challenges, the Benning was actually a pleasant surprise. The pillow felt plush and has an attractive design that's right on brand. and the green blanket was wonderfully warm and together they made for a very comfortable night's sleep. If you already noticed I'm still wearing my jacket. Don't worry, I'll explain why later. And I won't even attempt to pronounce the name of the munity kit, but inside this rather understated beige pouch was everything you'd expect. A toothbrush, earplugs, lip balm, body lotion, and a rather thoughtful pack of tissues. The headphones don't exactly scream premium. In fact, they look fairly expensive, but appearances can be deceiving. The sound quality was perfectly respectable and more than good enough for the entertainment system. What impressed me far more was this little detail. The double-sided wait me do not disturb and I'd like my meal option card. It's a simple idea, but one that's genuinely useful. I was also rather taken by the beautifully designed menu. Did I keep it? I was tempted. But we'll take a close look at the food once we're in the air. And before departure, the crew came around with a welcome drink. At this point in the morning, I'm perfectly happy with a glass of still water. It was served alongside a refreshing towel and a small but always welcome touch. Even the safe video offers a glimpse into the airlines identity. Although it's already a couple of years old, it leans heavily into showcasing the natural beauty and culture of Sri Lanka. Make it feel as much as a tourism film as it is a traditional safety demonstration. >> But before we get started and set you on [music] your trip, please buckle up and hear out these safety tips. [music] Now store your bags overhead or under the seat. Keep the exits and aisles clear. Then tuck in your feet. >> Cabin's lights dimmed. It's clear this aircraft has been fitted with the optional LED mood lighting package. Bathing cabin in a calming shade of red and purple. It's also become very dark for the takeoff. Well, it is 3:00 in the morning and to make matters worse, the window has completely steamed up. things. >> I was originally intending to go straight to sleep because honestly I have never been so exhausted. But I'm also hungry unfortunately. So I'm just going to have a main course lamb of potatoes and then go to sleep and hopefully I'll wake up for breakfast. If that doesn't sound appetizing to you, here are some of the other options that are available on the menu. And after spending two weeks traveling around Asia, I found myself craving something that felt a little bit more familiar, something that reminds me of home. And in all honesty, if I wasn't reviewing this flight, I'd have probably enjoyed a proper meal in the lounge before boarding and then gone straight to sleep, just as many of the other passengers seem to be doing. The soft blue mood lighting is certainly doing me some favors. My eyes are probably looking a little red after such an early start, but thankfully the cabin crew already in full flow and despite the late hour, they're working efficiently to get everyone served while remaining warm, professional, and genuinely engaging. Even the head person stopped by to welcome me on board personally, which I always think is a lovely touch. And then the service begins with a bowl of cashews and a drink from the bar. And unsurprisingly, I'm sticking with still water. Yes, it's boring, but staying hydrated especially important on these older aircraft where the cabin humidity tends to be much lower. reviews.transcript_full: Business class is supposed to be the best way to fly. But paying thousands of dollars doesn't always guarantee a premium experience. In 2026, some airlines still operate business class cabins that feel more than a decade behind modern standards. This isn't a ranking of individual seats. It's a ranking of airlines based on how much of their long-haul fleet still exposes passengers to a weak business class product today. Many of the airlines on this list also fly genuinely excellent cabins. [music] What puts them here is scale. The outdated product isn't a rare exception. It's a meaningful share of what you could actually be assigned. So today, we're ranking the 10 weakest long-haul business class products still flying in 2026. Number 10, China Eastern. We start with an airline where the problem isn't really about the bed. China Eastern operates more than 50 Airbus A330s, and the majority [music] still fly the outdated 2-2-2 layout that's been in service since the early 2000s. The beds themselves are fully flat. That's not the issue. The issue is that 2-2-2 still means window passengers have no direct aisle access on an aircraft type that dominates the airline's long-haul network. The rest of the experience doesn't help. >> [music] >> Reviewers describe entertainment libraries with barely 20 international titles, most of them old, and content [music] overwhelmingly in Chinese with limited subtitle options. Wi-Fi has been called terrible when you can even connect. Catering is inconsistent, too. Chinese dishes fare better than Western options, >> [music] >> and multiple passengers report flights with no wine, tea, or coffee at all, just water, juice, cola, and canned beer. The newer aircraft, the A350-900 and 787-9, do offer a real 1-2-1 product, and a small number of retrofitted A330s have been upgraded as well. If you're booking China Eastern, confirm you're on one of those before you commit. Number nine, Air India. If China Eastern shows what fleet-wide neglect [music] looks like, Air India shows the opposite problem. An airline caught mid-transformation. This is one of the fastest-improving carriers in the world right now, but that improvement is still in progress and the aircraft you're assigned matters enormously. [music] Air India's own website confirms that its Boeing 777-200LR still flies a 2-3-2 business class layout with 35 seats, one of the densest configurations [music] still in the sky. Older 787s carry a similar risk with legacy cabins that feel dated next to newer competitors. The turnaround, though, is real. Under Tata Group ownership since 2022, Air India has been aggressively renewing its fleet. The A350-900 now flies genuinely excellent 1-2-1 suites with sliding doors and modern screens. A new 787-9 with a bespoke interior entered service in January 2026. Three 787-8s have already been retrofitted with 1-2-1 seating and roughly 25 more are scheduled by 2027 >> [music] >> with an A350-1000 also on order. Air India is on its way out of this [music] list. Until the retrofit finishes, though, the aircraft type is everything. Number eight, LOT Polish Airlines. The seats are genuinely lie-flat at 180° and the pitch is generous, but there's no direct aisle access for window passengers and currently no Wi-Fi at all on these Dreamliners. Unlike almost every other airline on this list, there's no better aircraft to hope for. No modern alternative anywhere in LOT's current fleet. Relief is coming, eventually. New Recaro seating in a proper 1-2-1 layout with sliding doors starts rolling out on the 787-8 fleet in the third quarter of 2026. But by LOT's own published timeline, the full roll out across the fleet won't finish until 2030. For the next several years, every LOT long-haul passenger is flying the same outdated product. The airline also has a large modern fleet, more than 30 A350-900s and over 26 787-9s, all with proper 121 direct aisle access suites. In front of you is the in-flight entertainment system, which is about three Aviation With Chris Hands long, and beneath that you'll find another storage cubby, USB-A outlet, and bifold tray table. Knowing that this was Polaris after all, you get plenty of amenities, including a cooling memory foam gel pillow and standard day blanket. Rather than the old United headphones, which were absolutely buns, you get these brand new Meridian audio headphones. High-quality stuff as well. As for the amenity kit, it's made in partnership with Brooks Brothers and it was the laughing stock of the show of all the amenities we have today. This iconic blue cup probably came from a high school cafeteria. And it comes to show how much United does not care with the smallest, simplest things. I don't mean to complain, but when you pay thousands of dollars for a transatlantic business class ticket, these small things matter. Taking a look at United's entertainment system, I was impressed by the variety of content, including movies, TV shows, audiobooks, and podcasts you'll find on the screen available on demand. The IFE on this 767 didn't really leave me that impressed, especially when compared with the other entertainment software you'll find on the 777 or 787 aircraft. Soon, flight attendants came through the aisle to confirm our meal orders for lunch. And here's a pro tip, always pre-order your meal so that you get your preferred choice when on board. It was small and cramped, but I still appreciated the Perricone MD skin care products. I didn't really find the bathroom to be that clean, either, and noticed a piece of trash on the floor. And shortly after we reached our cruising altitude, hot towels were passed around. The hot towel service was immediately followed by warm nuts and a round of drinks. Finally, here's one thing United and other US airlines do right, and I love how they give you the full can of your beverage of choice. Okay, maybe the drink service made a great impression to the start of the meal service, but what was not so impressive? This appetizer presentation. I opted for the torn mozzarella with balsamic and grapes, which had way too much balsamic. Very acidic. Provided on the appetizer tray was a side salad and bread roll, both of which were fine, just your typical United Airlines food. The presentation definitely doesn't scream business class, though. As you can tell by my reaction, I was not impressed with the appetizer at all. Was this pasta dish even cooked properly? I had pre-ordered the orecchiette with sun-dried tomatoes, fava bean paste, and green beans and Parmesan. I went for a slice of mango cream cake, as well as the fruit and cheese plate. And if you're going to provide crackers, at least provide proper artisan crackers, or even better, bread. And the brownie, [music] don't even get me started on dessert. That thing had the structural integrity of a brick. What a meal this was, absolutely buns. Now, time to share my thoughts on United Polaris business class. Over these past 2 years, I've had the chance to fly Polaris quite a few times. For starters, what leaves me impressed is the ground experience and the seat. Particularly, when departing Zurich Airport, the ground experience is efficient and the Swiss lounge will sure not be a disappointment. I also love how the Polaris business class seat is consistent across the fleet compared to Delta One and American Flagship business who have multiple seat types across their aircraft, especially Delta One. The Polaris product has held up great over the years and if you're lucky enough, like I was, to get an odd-numbered window seat, you'll still be treated to plenty of privacy. While the seat can be nice, I will say that the 767 airframe is old and dated with an airframe from the 1980s and 1990s. Considering the small overhead bin size, narrow fuselage, and loud cabin, I would do almost anything to avoid flying this aircraft. Sure, it might be special to fly such a classic wide-body aircraft like the 767. But really, when you consider the wear and tear around the seat as well as an older version of the IFE system, it's really not that fun to fly 8 and 1/2 hours on this aircraft. As for the food and drink, talk about fine dining. Think a frozen salad, rock-hard brownie, microwaved couscous, and a dry pasta dish. The food almost never leaves me impressed when I fly with United, really. And when it comes to the service, the crew were friendly and efficient, but not super engaging or memorable. The interactions with the crew felt more transactional rather than personal. Even small things like serving pre-departure beverages in a plastic cup As for booking and pricing, one-way cash fares on the Zurich to Newark route in Polaris business class typically start from $2,500 to $3,000. And depending on your reward availability, you can also book saver awards using United MileagePlus miles. These typically cost 60,000 to 90,000 miles plus taxes and fees of about $5.60. If you have a credit card such as the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Preferred, you can easily transfer your Chase points to United at a one-to-one ratio. So, would I fly Polaris again? The answer is yes, on an overnight flight if I'm desperate to get some sleep. Otherwise, on a daytime flight, there's really no point in flying United business class if you have better options like Swiss or British Airways. Thank you guys so much for watching and sticking around. Please be sure to leave a like, subscribe, and follow us on Instagram at Aviation with Krish, which I've linked in the description below. Bye for now, and I hope all of you enjoyed the trip report. But until then, cheers and safe travels.
