reviews.transcript_full: Imagine you're planning the trip of a lifetime. You've decided where you're going, you've picked your dates. Now, there's just one decision left to make. Which airline should you fly? If you're looking for one of the best experiences in the sky, two names almost always rise to the top. Emirates and Singapore Airlines. Both are known around the world for luxury, outstanding service, and some of the most advanced aircraft ever built. But while they may compete for the same passengers, they couldn't be more different. One has built its empire around Dubai, connecting the world through one of the busiest airports on Earth. The other has spent decades perfecting every detail of the passenger experience, earning a reputation that many airlines still try to match. Today, we're putting Emirates and Singapore Airlines head-to-head. Let's get started. Every airline's reputation begins with its fleet, and this is one of the biggest differences between Emirates and Singapore Airlines. Emirates has kept things surprisingly simple. For years, the airline has relied almost entirely on just two aircraft families, the Airbus A380 and the Boeing 777. At first, that might seem like a limitation, but in reality, it's become one of Emirates' biggest strengths. Operating fewer aircraft types makes pilot training, maintenance, and day-to-day operations far more efficient. It also creates a more familiar experience for passengers. If you've flown Emirates before, there's a good chance you'll already know what to expect on your next flight. And then, there's the Airbus A380. No airline has embraced the superjumbo quite like Emirates. With the largest Airbus A380 fleet in the world, the aircraft has become almost inseparable from the Emirates brand. Singapore Airlines has chosen a very different strategy. Rather than relying on just a couple of aircraft, it operates a much more varied fleet. Alongside the Airbus A380, you'll also find the Airbus A350, Boeing 777, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and Boeing 737 on regional routes. This gives Singapore Airlines far greater flexibility. Smaller aircraft can be used where demand is lower, while larger aircraft operate the airline's busiest long-haul routes. Looking ahead, both airlines are investing billions in the future. Emirates is preparing for the arrival of the Boeing 777X, while introducing the Airbus A350 into its fleet. Singapore Airlines continues expanding with additional Airbus A350s and Boeing 787 Dreamliners as older aircraft are gradually retired. Neither strategy is necessarily better. Emirates focuses on simplicity and consistency. Singapore Airlines prioritizes flexibility and modernization. Having an incredible aircraft means very little if the airline can't take you where you need to go. Fortunately, that isn't a problem for either of these airlines. Emirates has built one of the largest international networks in the world. Nearly every journey passes through one place, Dubai International Airport. Dubai has become one of the world's most important connecting hubs. Singapore Airlines follows a similar model through Singapore Changi Airport. Although its network isn't quite as large as Emirates' is, it connects many of the world's major cities while serving as one of Asia's most important gateways. Singapore Airlines also operates some of the longest non-stop flights ever scheduled, including routes linking Singapore with New York. For passengers, both airlines make long-distance travel remarkably convenient. The difference simply comes down to where you're going. For some destinations, Emirates offers more options. For others, Singapore Airlines provides the more direct route. This is where the vast majority of passengers will spend their journey. And despite the premium reputations of both airlines, the competition here is surprisingly close. Both offer generous baggage allowances on many routes, complimentary meals, seatback entertainment, and friendly cabin crews. Emirates' biggest advantage is its ICE entertainment system with thousands of movies, television shows, music albums, documentaries, podcasts, and even live television on some flights. It's widely considered one of the best entertainment systems in aviation. On ultra-long-haul flights, having that much content can make a huge difference. Singapore Airlines' KrisWorld entertainment system may not offer quite as many titles, but it remains intuitive, responsive, and packed with high-quality content. Food is another area where both airlines perform exceptionally well. Meals are inspired by destinations across their networks, giving passengers a wide variety of international dishes. Where Singapore Airlines often receives praise is consistency. Whether you're flying on an Airbus A350, Airbus A380, or Boeing 777, the experience remains remarkably similar. With Emirates, your experience can sometimes vary depending on whether you're flying on the Airbus A380 or one of the Boeing 777 aircraft. Neither experience is disappointing. They simply feel a little different. For travelers choosing between the two, it really comes down to what matters most. Do you value the massive entertainment library offered by Emirates, or do you prefer the consistency that Singapore Airlines is known for? For years, premium economy was something Emirates simply didn't offer. Singapore Airlines had already established itself as one of the leaders in the cabin, while Emirates focused entirely on economy and business class. That changed in 2022. Emirates introduced an entirely new premium economy product. First on its newest Airbus A380s before gradually expanding it across more aircraft. The difference from economy is immediately noticeable. Passengers get wider seats, significantly more legroom, greater recline, larger entertainment screens, and upgraded dining. The cabin itself also feels quieter and far more spacious. Singapore Airlines has had years to refine its premium economy experience. Its seats are equally spacious, offering generous recline, adjustable leg rests, and thoughtful storage for personal items. Passengers also receive enhanced meals, priority services on many routes, and additional baggage allowances depending on the fare. Perhaps the biggest difference isn't the seat itself. It's availability. Singapore Airlines offers premium economy on a much larger portion of its long-haul fleet. With Emirates, you'll need to check carefully before booking because not every aircraft currently features the cabin. Neither airline disappoints here. Instead, the better choice often depends on which aircraft is operating your flight. Business class has become one of the biggest reasons passengers choose one airline over another. And both Emirates and Singapore Airlines offer products that consistently rank among the best in the world. Let's start with Emirates. If you're lucky enough to board one of the airline's Airbus A380s, you'll immediately notice something very few airlines offer. An onboard lounge. Located at the rear of the upper deck, it's a space where business and first-class passengers can enjoy drinks, light snacks, and stretch their legs while cruising at 37,000 ft. It's become one of Emirates' signature experiences. The seats themselves convert into fully flat beds and include direct aisle access on the Airbus A380. However, not every Emirates business class cabin is identical. Many Boeing 777 aircraft still feature a 2-3-2 seating layout. That means passengers seated by the window may need to step over another passenger to reach the aisle. While Emirates has begun refurbishing these aircraft with a much more modern cabin, it's something travelers should still pay attention to when booking. Singapore Airlines takes a different approach. Rather than offering dramatically different cabins depending on the aircraft, it focuses on consistency. Passengers can generally expect a spacious seat, direct aisle access, and plenty of privacy. The seats are among the widest in commercial aviation, and convert into fully flat beds designed for long-haul comfort. Another feature that frequently receives praise is Singapore Airlines' Book the Cook service. Instead of choosing from only the meals loaded onto the aircraft, eligible passengers can pre-order from an expanded menu before departure. For many frequent flyers, it's one of the airline's standout features. When it comes to onboard dining, both airlines deliver premium multi-course meals, quality beverages, and attentive service. The difference lies in the experience. Emirates creates a sense of luxury through features like the onboard lounge and glamorous cabin design. Singapore Airlines focuses on comfort, privacy, and delivering an experience that's remarkably consistent across its fleet. Neither approach is necessarily better. They're simply designed with different priorities in mind. So, which business class would you rather fly? If business class is impressive, first class is where both airlines showcase everything they're capable of. Emirates has built one of the most recognizable first class products in aviation. On selected Boeing 777 aircraft, passengers are welcomed into fully enclosed private suites featuring floor-to-ceiling doors, virtual windows for the middle seats, personal climate controls, and video call technology that allows passengers to request cabin crew assistance without leaving their suite. It's one of the most technologically advanced first class cabins ever introduced. Then there's the Airbus A380. Alongside spacious private suites, first class passengers also have access to one feature that's become almost legendary, the shower spa. Being able to take a shower while flying at 37,000 ft is something very few people ever experience, and it remains one of Emirates' biggest selling points. Singapore Airlines has taken a different approach. Instead of focusing on technology and unique features, it focuses on space. Its suites aboard the Airbus A380 are among the largest in commercial aviation. Each passenger gets a separate leather armchair and a full-size bed, eliminating the need to convert the seat into a bed before sleeping. For couples traveling together, the center suites can even be combined into a genuine double bed. Combined with exceptional dining and attentive service, it creates an experience that's often described as more like a luxury hotel than an airplane. Emirates impresses with innovation and unforgettable features. Singapore Airlines impresses with comfort, elegance, and space. Both represent the very best of commercial aviation. The question is, which experience would you choose? After comparing every major category, one thing becomes very clear. There isn't a simple answer. Emirates and Singapore Airlines are considered two of the world's best airlines for a reason, but they've reached that position in very different ways. Emirates has built its reputation around bold ideas, the world's largest Airbus A380 fleet, an onboard lounge, a first class shower spa, one of the biggest entertainment libraries in aviation, and a global network that connects almost every corner of the world through Dubai. Singapore Airlines has taken a different path. Rather than focusing on headline-grabbing features, it has built its reputation on consistency, attention to detail, and delivering an exceptional passenger experience across almost every aircraft in its fleet. From economy class to first class, the experience feels refined, polished, and remarkably dependable. So, which airline is actually better? The truth is, that depends entirely on what you value. If unique onboard experiences and iconic features matter most to you, you may find yourself leaning toward Emirates. If consistency, comfort, and understated luxury are your priorities, Singapore Airlines might be the better fit. And that's what makes this comparison so interesting. Neither airline is objectively better than the other. They're simply exceptional in different ways. Now, I'd like to hear from you. If someone handed you two tickets right now, one for Emirates and one for Singapore Airlines, which airline would you choose and why? Let me know in the comments below. If you enjoyed this comparison, don't forget to like the video, subscribe for more aviation content, and I'll see you in the next one.

reviews.transcript_full: Today, I flew on an Airbus 380 operated by Emirates, the world's premier luxury airline , for just $120 Even those with no interest in airplanes or airlines have likely heard of it at least once. Emirates is considered the undisputed best among the "oil money" Middle Eastern "Big Three " and is the world's largest operator of the A380. Emirates owns 120 of the 251 aircraft produced by Airbus, accounting for nearly half of the total. From the luxury in the skies featuring onboard showers and bars to the ultra-fast in-flight Wi-Fi "Starlink ," Emirates' A380 has a lot to show you today. Let's get started! Hello, this is Manager Woo. This is Bangkok Suvarnabhumi Airport. Since Bangkok is a top global travel destination, Emirates operates five flights daily; one of them is dedicated to the "Fifth Freedom" route between Bangkok and Hong Kong. EK384 and EK385 depart from Bangkok at 2:15 PM and from Hong Kong at 9:30 PM. I am off to my destination. I booked a one-way economy ticket to Hong Kong on Agoda for $120. Since the lowest fare for this route is in the 110,000 won range on Hong Kong Express, adding 50,000 won to book Emirates is by no means a bad deal. I will proceed with check-in at the S counter. Although there are self-check-in kiosks, I will check in at the counter because the line isn't long. Actually, one of the reasons I checked in at the counter was that I wanted to receive a ticket with this red logo on it. It is convenient because there is an escalator right next to the counter that goes up to the departure hall. Since I have to take a train to get to Gate S today , I will visit the lounge in the main terminal first. This is the Coral Business Lounge located near Gate D1. It has been open for about two years, so I heard the facilities are relatively clean and nice. You can enter using both a PP card and a The Lounge card. There is a shower room here, but it is not free, so if you need a shower, it might be better to go to the Miracle Lounge near Gate D5. Inside, the area is divided into a group space and individual tables. They have a good selection of drinks here, and the bar offers a variety of cocktails. I think this place would be good for people who like to drink, but the food here didn't really suit my taste. Should I say it tasted a bit like stainless steel? It had a slightly strong taste, so since I prioritize food over alcohol, I probably won't visit again. I then came to the Miracle Lounge near Gate D5. Many smokers visit here; you can grab a Zero Coke from the refrigerator right after entering and exit through the side door to smoke on the outdoor terrace. I noticed many people just come here and leave. Now, I will head to the gate. Gates starting with 'S' are located in the satellite terminal, so you have to take a train from the main terminal to get there, just like at Incheon Airport Terminal 1. This is my second time using this place; unlike the Incheon terminal, it is quite large enough to accommodate A380s, and since it hasn't been long since it opened, it is very pleasant. Today's boarding gate is S113. Since this is my first time flying on an Emirates A380, I took some photos of the plane from various angles. It has a sturdy front view with a width of 80 meters, the starboard side on the right where you can feel the height, and the port side on the left where the jet bridge connects. The jet bridge connects first to the upper deck where First and Business Class are located, and then to the main deck on the lower level where Economy is located. Two additional aircraft are being connected. With a wingspan of 36 meters alone, you can immediately feel how massive it is when standing next to a B737, which has a total width of this size. A Qatar Airways A380 had just pulled in at the opposite gate, so I went over to take a picture. Perhaps because its livery is split between gray and white, the all-white Emirates seems to look somehow larger. I have returned to the gate, and the flight attendants are giving a pre-flight briefing. This is a jumbo jet carrying over 20 crew members. Higher classes and membership tiers board first, and economy boarding begins on the lower main deck. That path on the right leads to the upper jet bridge for First and Business, while the Economy main deck is downstairs. Emirates is an airline I have a love-hate relationship with; I applied here several times when I was flying. With the resolve that "I will fly if I get accepted," I used Etihad and Qatar but never flew here, and here I am finally getting to fly it... The A380 is extraordinary starting with its door size, and heading upstairs... I’ll go past the stairs and head to my seat. This is the main deck, filled entirely with economy seats, and the seating arrangement is 3-4-3. The seats are made of fabric in bright pastel tones; to me, they reminded me a bit of the color of a Little Mermaid's fin . My seat today is 50C, an aisle seat in the very back row of the front cabin. The seat width is 18 inches, which is spacious and comfortable. The legroom is ample, even with the pockets packed full . When you recline the seat, the lower seat slides out to create a full recline, yet there is enough room for my knees not to touch the seat. The angle of the backrest is about this much, and the headrest is thick and adjustable up and down. I usually find leather headrests a bit uncomfortable, but since this is fabric, I used it comfortably . Even though it is a flight of less than three hours , headsets, cushions, and blankets are provided as standard. The cabin was so cold that I covered myself with it as soon as I boarded, and the temperature was just right. Now, an announcement is coming on saying, "We are closing the doors, so ground staff, please disembark." I will now verify the aircraft type using the safety card. The safety announcement plays along with the pushback. Over there. The male flight attendant who appeared reminded me a bit of the male lead from the Netflix series 'You.' All the flight attendants here looked like movie stars. 'I guess that's why I didn't make the cut' :(( I briefly had a metacognitive moment. Then an announcement came on saying that Starlink is available. After takeoff, I will check the Starlink speed. Power ports are located next to the monitors in each of the three window seats, excluding the aisle seat. The seat next to me was empty, so I just used it; you can consider there to be two ports for every three seats. Also, there is a USB-A charging port at every seat. Below the monitor is a remote control with a touch screen, and below that is the tray table... no, let's look at the cup holder first. The cup holder here is gimbal-style; the inner holder rotates, so they say it maintains a level position even if you recline the seat in front of you. But when I actually used it, it looked a bit scary. I'll show you later when I get my coffee. Returning to the tray table, it is semi-foldable and adjustable forward and backward. Even though it is a 13-year-old aircraft, the cabin environment and seats are generally clean. We have arrived at the runway, and we will take a look at the A380's heavy takeoff via the tail camera. Because the wings are so big, the landing gear retracting is obscured and hard to see. The overhead control panel is a bit high, so it is difficult to operate while sitting; you have to stand up to operate it, especially on the aisle side. Seat and flight information is displayed at the top of the monitor, and if you press 'I' in the bottom left, you can check the flight details and the aircraft you are currently on. Since the flight is only two hours long, I will diligently capture various things. First, if you go to the in-flight entertainment language settings, you can select from a whopping 14 languages, including Korean. This is the entertainment section, which boasts a vast amount of content that is considered the best in the world. There are sections by genre, and I will go into the latest movies to check for Korean subtitles. I checked 'Project Hale Mary,' but there are no Korean subtitles. Not all content has subtitles, and the content that does have Korean subtitles is... If you go back to the previous step and enter the Korean Movies section at the top, you will find a list. It seems they have separately categorized and stored content that offers Korean dubbing or subtitles. The headset for watching videos is good because it has cushions inside. Now, I will try connecting to Starlink. This is my first time using it, too. If you connect to Emirates Wi-Fi while in airplane mode, the window changes, and once you enter the main screen, the connection is complete. First, let's go into Netflix. I clicked on the "Manager Kim" video, and it loads almost immediately. The playback starting speed is wow... At this rate, it doesn't seem much different from doing it on the ground. Also, when I travel abroad, I usually use A.T. Baro Call; I wonder if it uses data for calls, because it connects as well. Let's check how fast Starlink speeds are at 39,000 feet. Wow , it keeps going up. Let's speed it up a bit. The download speed was 260 megabits per second, and the upload speed was 3.7 megabits per second . You can expect it to take about 30 seconds to download a 1GB video. I also tried connecting with my MacBook. I can watch live broadcasts of CNN, BBC News, and sports matches on the laptop's large screen. However... If I had to point out a downside, since it allows for work, it seems difficult to use the excuse that I can't check emails when flying on a business trip. I was sitting and replying to some emails when the meal cart arrived, so I turned it off immediately. I removed the cushion from my back, adjusted my posture, and will now reverently receive the meal. It is a flight of less than three hours, but the tray is overflowing. A flight attendant at the back even brought me a separate Zero Coke. The main course is chicken, served with cucumber salad for appetizer, blueberry chocolate cake for dessert, and bread. It comes with boiled carrots and mashed potatoes. I was a little disappointed that it wasn't rice, but everything tasted really good. The cabin is tidied up, and now I will go check the restroom. It is decorated luxiously with white and wood patterns, and the space is decent enough not to feel cramped. Even the lid has a wood pattern, and there are disposable toilet seat covers, so you can use it cleanly. Feminine toiletries are also placed under the mirror next to it, but I won't bother opening them. Above the sink, there is an air vent and a call light for the flight attendant, and the faucet below dispenses water automatically with just a touch of the temperature control, keeping it clean. It is set up so you can just wash your hands. Paper towels are right above it, making it convenient to use. Next to the sink, there is hand lotion and an Eau de Toilette spray; these are products from the Noir line by the British lifestyle brand 'The White Company'. The 500ml hand lotion was selling for 30 pounds, which is about 60,000 won in Korean currency. You can tell a lot of money was invested in various details. I came back to my seat and asked for a cup of coffee, but the flight attendant told me not to put it in the cup holder. As I showed you earlier, this holder rotates inward, right? If you insert the coffee, it adjusts the horizontal level like a gimbal, but I was a bit afraid to let go of it. So I just placed it on the table to drink . The monitor tilt works well so you can see the screen when you move over to the seat in front. With about 30 minutes left, the captain's announcement regarding the destination is coming on. The seat next to me is empty, and the legroom is spacious, so I was able to fold my legs and travel comfortably. I didn't show you the remote control; the touch sensitivity of the screen isn't exactly fast, but since I don't really need to use it much, I think it's fine. It is quite large, so when I held my iPhone up to it, [there is] a case It looks like it would be boiling if I took it off. Just like the captain's announcement, it has been raining continuously in Hong Kong , so I can see water passing outside the window. Since we are descending , the water is rising. Seeing the tail camera fog up due to the rain, I thought the rain was really intense. But then, just as the city of Hong Kong started to come into view, the rain stopped again. We are landing at Hong Kong International Airport. An announcement comes on telling us to stand up when the seatbelt lights go off, but everyone is in a hurry . We have about 500 people to disembark from this plane alone, so we really need to get going fast. Today was my first time flying on an Emirates A380, and it was also my first experience with Starlink, so I boarded with a lot of excitement. I have a lot to show you, but time is short, so the three hours seem to have passed in a rush. Actually, for the viewers to enjoy Emirates, you would need to fly Business or First Class to really appreciate it , but this is a small channel that hasn't been around for long, and it’s only fun to start from Economy and work your way up step by step, right?! However, I found Economy class to be excellent as well. I heard that they are currently upgrading the seats on all their aircraft as they add Premium Economy class . I don't know when it will happen, but for my next Emirates review, I plan to move up one class at a time on a retrofitted aircraft. I will not be entering Hong Kong; instead, I will be transferring to Incheon via Hong Kong Express. I will organize the review of the next section well and upload it as well. Thank you for watching the long video until the end.

reviews.transcript_full: Join me as I fly United Polaris from San Francisco to Taipei. At SFO, Polaris passengers do get their own dedicated check-in lane, which they share with Global Services and United 1K flyers. United also amazingly had the QR codes for the different countries arrival cards, just in case you're irresponsible like me and forgot to do it beforehand. Make sure you leave enough time for the United Polaris Lounge, which is just located to the right side of security and occupies two entire floors. And my golden rule for the first thing you should always do is check the dining room waitlist, check the shower waitlist. Once you're in the Polaris Lounge, you can enjoy a wide range of seating depending on what your social vibe is. Make sure you stop at the bar to get a drink or two or three or until you can't count anymore. The dining room has an excellent selection of food options to choose from like the ones that you see here, but if you don't have enough time or you spent too long at the bar, the buffet will do just fine. >> [music] >> And please make sure to leave time for a shower where my normal 5-minute showers turn into 30-minute therapy session. Once you get to the gate, as a Polaris passenger, you can board with group one, but if you have United's top-tier 1K or Global Services status, then you can pre-board as they call it. On board the 777-200, we have eight rows of Polaris in the forward cabin and five rows in the rear cabin. My seat is 9L, which is a bulkhead seat in the rear cabin on the right-hand side of the aircraft. In my opinion, the best seat on this aircraft. Waiting for you at your seat is, in my opinion, the best bedding in business class, an amenity kit that's really well stocked with creams and eye masks and pajamas and slippers if you move fast enough. And after getting a feel for my seat, having a little bit of pre-departure champagne, and making sure that my shoulder strap was securely fastened, off we go to Taipei. As far as Wi-Fi goes, United currently charges for Wi-Fi, but Starlink is very much on the way and should be much faster and free once it's here. Once we reach cruising altitude, service began with the hot towels followed by me changing into pajamas and then champagne [music] and warm nuts and a delicious meal consisting of smoked salmon and a very flavorful stir-fried chicken main course. [music] This main course needs to be there on every flight. And our dessert this evening was supposed to be a special 4th of July edition ice cream sundae, but with the blueberry compote missing, it was only red and white on my plate. So, apparently, we were going to be honoring Poland this evening instead of the United States. After the meal finished, I reclined my seat into flatbed mode and fell asleep while watching one of my favorite childhood movies. This is truly a bed in the sky, just with more seat belts. And after getting some quality sleep, I woke up to us flying through a thunderstorm and decided midflight snacks was a good idea. On some of their longer flights, United recently made the midflight snacks into more of a tapas [music] concept. And so, I ordered some herb ricotta, black bean and corn empanadas, and some chicken. The turbulence clearly made me hungry because all three of these were excellent. Then, 1 hour before landing, another hot towel arrived followed by breakfast, which I kept light with a cheese plate. Very restrained of me. One thing is for certain in all of this, you will not go hungry. And if you ever give yourself the chance, you can get a great sleep in as well. So, would you fly Polaris if you had the chance? Let me know in the comments. I'd love to hear your thoughts.

started on making up the bed. We were actually   given a choice between a soft mattress topper 
or a firm mattress topper, and I chose the   firm one. Here's a more detailed look at what 
the mattress topper looked like. It's actually   quite plush and thick, and I found it to be very 
comfortable. As for the bedding, you get a fluffy   standard size pillow, a second larger but 
thinner pillow that is good for your lower back   while sitting, a thinner day blanket 
as well, as a thicker size comforter for sleeping. We also get a set of pajamas and 
in first class they actually let   you keep them. In business class, Japan 
Airlines makes you return the pajamas. And here's what the pajamas 
look like when they're on,   in case anyone was wondering. And I 
did find them to be very comfortable. When the bed is in fully lie flat mode, it's 
around 203 cm or approximately  80 inches. And   with no foot well blocking your feet and a huge 
width, I don't see anyone having trouble fitting   into this bed. Unless of course you're taller than 
80 inches, in which case all I got to say is damn. All right, now let's talk about the inflight 
entertainment. The screen is 4K and at present   time it is the largest in the industry at 43 inches 
or 109 cm. There is a remote and this is what   it looks like. I normally never use remotes on 
airplanes, but with a massive 83 inch or 210 cm row   pitch, there is no way I could reach that screen 
while sitting. In terms of entertainment, I found   the option to be very balanced. Good amounts of 
both international and western options. They even   had shows and movies from Hulu and Disney Plus. 
But the best form of entertainment for   any aviation lover, of course, are these onboard 
cameras [music] for the ultimate views in the sky.   And for those of you wondering about 
Wi-Fi, it is complimentary. Although I   was never able to get the wifi to
work during this particular flight,   so unfortunately I can't comment 
as to how fast or not fast it was. Okay, now let's talk about audio because you 
have three options to choose from. First   is these bang and  olufsen headphones they provide. 
They are noise cancelling and  the quality   was really good. The second option is you 
can connect your own headphones using   Bluetooth. And finally, you can use the speakers 
that are built directly into the headrest.   You're supposed to fold the speakers over your 
ears while the sound plays. They do have these   in business class as well. And like I mentioned in 
my video about their business class, while   I do think this is a unique idea, the execution 
falls flat for me. In my opinion, I felt like the   sound quality is much better if you just 
use the provided headphones or you used your own. Okay, so now is the point in the video 
where we have to talk about cost. All right, so as always, let's talk about cost as 
well as what I paid. So, first what I paid I did   use points for this and I used British Airways 
Avios and one way between LAX and Tokyo Haneda   was 103,000 British Airways Avios plus around 
$273 Canadian in taxes and fees. But at the   time that I booked this, there was a 30% transfer 
bonus between British Airways Avios and AMEX. So,   it's basically like I really paid 72,100 British 
Airways Avios, which I personally feel like was   well worth it for this amazing first class 
experience. And now, let's talk about cash   cost. So, as always, I got to put up my little 
disclaimer first before I show you  the   cash cost that the prices you are about to see 
are just for this very specific route on this   specific day. If you are looking at cash costs, 
you might see a cash cost that is higher or lower   just because that is the dynamic nature of flight 
pricing. All right, now that that is out   of the way, let's talk about it. So, the cash 
cost roundtrip between LAX and Tokyo Haneda in   Japan Airlines first class on their A350. Here 
it is. The roundtrip cost in USD was $17,516. Let me know what you think about that price and 
then let's check out the pre-arrival meal. So,   there's not actually a preset pre-arrival 
meal, but you can order anything off the   à la carte  menu and essentially create your 
own meal. You can even place your order   through the inflight entertainment and the 
crew brings it to you when it's ready. I   ordered the caviar and the JAL noodle, which 
is a tonkatsu flavored miso ramen noodle. Both   were absolutely delicious and let me just say 
that ramen and caviar make a great pairing. After the caviar and the noodles, we're 
of course given another hot towel for our   hands. And soon enough, we start to 
make our descent into Tokyo Haneda. And as we get ready to land and deboard, let's 
talk about Japan Airlines first class on the   A350 for a little bit. Overall, everything is what 
I've come to expect from Japan Airlines.   There's no denying that the seat is gorgeous 
and in true Japanese style, thoughtfully   designed. Service, again, as usual for Japan 
Airlines, was attentive and excellent. And   the food and overall soft product was great as 
well, especially that  mattress topper. And while the overall experience was great 
and I'd happily take it over and over again   if I found a good award pricing or if I won the 
lottery of course it doesn't quite have the wow   factor that a shower in the sky or a double bed 
might have. But are those things that you really   need or is it just enough to know that you're 
going to be taken care of at some of the highest   levels? Let me know what you think about Japan 
Airlines first class on the A350. And if you've   enjoyed the video, please do like and subscribe 
so that we can fly together again soon.

reviews.transcript_full: This A350 isn't what it looks like at all. This is Singapore Airlines medium-haul Airbus A350 and it uses a different business class product compared to the airline's long-haul configuration on the same aircraft type. Starting at Melbourne Airport, Singapore Airlines operates a dedicated lounge here and overall it's a fairly efficient space rather than a flagship style lounge. The first thing you notice is how controlled the environment feels. It's quiet with no real crowding and seating is properly spaced. There's a mix of dining tables, standard lounge chairs, and a few quieter areas if you want some privacy before boarding. The layout is practical rather than decorative. Food selection is moderate. There are a couple of hot dishes, some lighter options, and everything is kept clean and regularly refreshed. Nothing looks overused or left sitting too long. It's not an extensive buffet, but it's reliable. Drinks are self-serve including a coffee machine, juices, and soft drinks. Overall, the lounge does its job well. It's not a destination in itself, but it's a comfortable and functional pre-flight space. Boarding begins on time. The aircraft is an Airbus A350 in the medium-haul configuration. Externally, there's no difference compared to the long-haul version. Same fuselage, same wing design, >> [music] >> and the same Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines. Once on board, the cabin layout is where things change. Business class is arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. Every seat has direct aisle access, which is standard for this aircraft type. The cabin itself is clean and quite minimal with neutral tones and soft lighting. It feels modern but not overly styled. The seat is Singapore Airlines regional business class product. It's a wide seat with a fixed shell design. So instead of reclining backwards into the space behind you, the seat moves within its own footprint. That changes how the seat feels compared to more traditional designs. On the side, you have a large console area. >> [music] >> There are multiple storage compartments which are deep enough for personal items like a phone, passport, and headphones. The table is solid and stable, suitable for both dining and [music] working. In front of you, there's a large screen positioned at eye level. Controls are simple and responsive without unnecessary complexity. From a usability perspective, the layout is very logical. In terms of comfort, the seat is noticeably firm. You don't sink into it. You sit more on top of it, which gives good support but less softness. Back support is strong, especially in the upright position. This makes it suitable for working or eating but less relaxed for lounging. Leg room is generous overall. However, the footwell is slightly angled. Depending on your seat position, your body sits at a slight diagonal. Window seats angle outward while center seats angle inward. It's not a major issue, but it becomes more noticeable over time. >> [music] >> Now, moving to the bed function. This seat converts into a fully flat bed using a single control. You press one button and the seat smoothly reclines forward into position. Everything happens within the fixed shell. The transition [music] is controlled and consistent. Once fully flat, the bed length is sufficient for most passengers. You can stretch out fully without restriction. Width is adequate, although not particularly wide compared to newer designs. The main characteristic here is firmness. The sleeping surface is quite firm with limited cushioning. It feels more supportive than soft. So, while it's fully usable for sleeping, it's not the most comfortable bed in this category. Back in the seated position, the product works very well. For dining, working, or watching content, the seat is practical and well designed. Everything is within reach and the layout supports usability. Pushback is on time. Takeoff from Melbourne is smooth and as expected, the Airbus A350 is very quiet during climb. Cabin noise remains low throughout the flight. After takeoff, meal service begins. Presentation is clean and consistent. Portions are balanced and the service flow is efficient. It's not overly elaborate, but it's reliable, which is typical for Singapore Airlines. Mid-flight, the cabin remains calm. Lighting is kept low and there's minimal disturbance. A quick walk through the cabin shows consistent layout and design across all seats. The lavatory is compact but clean and well maintained. No issues from a functional standpoint. Later in the flight, a second meal is served. Again, consistent in both quality and presentation. No major variation, but no noticeable weaknesses, either. [music] >> Can I get some water, ice, please? >> Yeah. >> Thank you very much. >> You're most welcome. >> As the flight progresses, the overall concept becomes clear. This is not a business class product designed to impress immediately. It's designed to function efficiently over a medium-haul duration. Cabin preparation for arrival is smooth. Taxi to the gate is straightforward. Overall, this product sits in the middle of the business class range. It offers a solid layout with direct aisle access and a very quiet aircraft platform. The seat performs well in upright mode and supports productivity and dining effectively. However, comfort is not its strongest point. The seat and bed are both firm, and the angled layout may not suit all passengers. Compared to newer long-haul business class products, this one feels slightly dated in terms of comfort, even though functionality remains strong. >> [music] >> At the same time, it's clearly ahead of older generation seats that lack direct aisle access or full flat capability. So, it occupies a middle position. Final assessment. This is a practical and well-engineered business class product. It prioritizes consistency, usability, and efficiency over softness and luxury feel. Best suited for medium-haul flights where space and function matter more than maximum comfort. If your priority is a softer, more relaxed seat, this may not be ideal. But if you want a predictable and well-structured experience, it delivers. That's ultimately what defines this Airbus A350 configuration.

reviews.transcript_full:
Today I'm flying with a giant which is 
literally unknown in the Western world.   It operates more than 800 aircraft and carries 
three times as many passengers as British Airways.   Yet it's much less known than many 
smaller airlines. This is China Eastern,   one of the China's "Big 3" airlines. But all 
that massive scale is still mostly busy serving   domestic routes. That's why internationally it 
flies rather low on the radar screen of many.   Exploring Chinese airlines and being a bit 
suspicious, I first went private. For starters,   I was really impressed by Hainan Airlines, smaller 
private carrier, of course, by Chinese standards   and arguably the best in China. Then I raised 
the stakes and flew First Class with Xiamen Air.   That was a really bizarre experience. As I gained 
more confidence, I moved to state-owned airlines,   starting with Air China. They passed, which 
is another way to tell I wasn't impressed.   But it was clear that efficiency was more 
important than experience. And today,   I'm very curious to test China Eastern. Let's see 
where I will land on my China aviation adventure.   One thing I can tell, it was quite an 
experience. Which one? You will find out soon.   Today's flight is Istanbul to Shanghai on China 
Eastern Airbus A330. It's 4,300 miles and almost   10 hours. And I'm flying from Istanbul Airport 
where it somehow feels I know every corner.   But I got myself thinking it's the first time 
I'm flying from here, not with Turkish Airlines.   That's definitely a hurdle for China Eastern to 
meet as the comparison bar for sure will be high.   Istanbul airport meets me with a familiar buzz, 
but I feel lost. I could navigate to fancy Turkish   business checkin zone with closed eyes. But where 
do I go with China Eastern? There are check-in   desks turned out to be actually at the very end 
of the terminal and very modest. But it worked.   There is life beyond Turkish indeed. Trying my 
luck with fast track, but not this time. Unlike   few other Sky Team airlines, China Eastern doesn't 
have a deal with airport operated IGA Fast Track.   So today we'll have to queue for immigration and 
security, which in Istanbul can take time. Well,   it's not uncommon for an airline to be squeezed 
in an airport dominated by another airline.   So no conclusions yet. Hope China Eastern will 
surprise me on board, which ultimately matters   more. Istanbul airport firmly sits on my list 
of the world's best airports. It feels more   like a giant luxury shopping mall than an actual 
airport. Now I'm to explore a different side of   it. The one that's not about Turkish Airlines. 
My aim is IGA lounge which serves Sky Team.   It's not hard to find, but once I come near, I 
start getting a vibe of a bus station. A bit of a   crowd, a bit of a chaos. All possible airlines are 
crammed in here with all the confusion it brings.   Inside you have more of the same. There are 
apparently different zones - dining, relax,   entertainment. But because of the crowds, 
everything feels pretty much the same:   busy, noisy, and chaotic. I'm circling around 
the lounge, looking for a quieter spot, like an   eagle looking for a prey. But ultimately decide 
to fly away as I concluded that having a beer   outside is still a better choice. So much for the 
lounge experience. Well, with another ground miss   the stakes are getting higher for China Eastern. 
They better get the flight right! Departing from   Istanbul is really two journeys in one. A flight 
itself and a walk to the gate which can take up   to 20 minutes. The airport is huge and there is no 
internal transportation, only your pair of legs.   I walk to the very end of the terminal and here 
I get the first surprise at the edge of nervous   tick. I see a China Southern plane. What??? 
But then I realized that the two flights are   boarding next to each other. That was a scare. 
The boarding is smooth, a pleasant contrast to   check-in and lounge hiccups, and I'm on my way 
to my today's ride, an Airbus A330. China Eastern   operates more than 50 of them. But this one 
is special. It has a modern 1-2-1 staggered   layout with 32 seats in business rather than usual 
outdated 2-2-2 layout they had since early 2000s   and still keep in a majority of their A330 fleet. 
There are only few of those new retrofitted planes   and I'm very eager to try it out. Well, 
China Eastern really made an effort here.   This might not be the state of the art business 
cabin, but it's a huge step forward from what   they used to have on their A330s before. This is 
a new generation cabin with fully lie-flat seats,   direct aisle access for all passengers and a fair 
level of privacy. But unlike some newer business   class products, it doesn't create that cocoon-like 
feeling - you still feel quite exposed. China   Eastern is using a well-known Thompson Vantage XL 
seat here. One of the early next generation seat   models that evolved business flying around 2010s. 
A very solid product which is also used by Delta,   SAS, and Quantas. But here China Eastern 
clearly got the off the rack basic model   with little or no customizations. The materials 
and finishes seem to be on the simpler side.   I'm somehow torn in making my mind about this 
cabin. For what China Eastern A330 used to be,   this is a major step forward, a modern, solid 
product. Can I call it best-in-class? Well,   not yet. It's a bit like when you come to Germany 
and you see that many taxes are E-class Mercedes.   Feels WOW at first. Then you get inside and you 
realize this is the bare bones model where you   don't have all the usual bells and whistles that 
give it a special experience. The form could be   excellent, but the content matters too. More here 
to explore, but now I'm switching to the service.   The usual rituals are followed properly. A 
wet towel and a pre-flight drink are here.   A good sign. A flight attendant brings a menu, 
which is not always the case on Chinese carriers.   On Air China and Xiamen, the menu was explained by 
the crew and details didn't go much further than   Western or Chinese. But China Eastern prepared its 
own challenge. It's a menu for a full year with   four different meal sets which are linked through 
color coding to four groups of non-consecutive   months. This is really not for an average 
mind! And I start feeling like a code breaker   deciphering Enigma. Finally, code is broken and 
I find the right section. For lunch, I will have   two choices of soups, four choices for main with 
a good mix of European, Chinese, Turkish, which   is actually thoughtful. And of course desserts. 
Then we should have something before the arrival.   But I can't figure out if this would be "Late 
Meal" or "Breakfast". I will handle this dilemma   when the time comes. On a single foldout of 
beverage menu, China Eastern manages to put   what takes 10 pages for others. Efficiency over 
fanciness. Interestingly, some wines are marked   First Class only. I was just feeling so proud of 
being a business class passenger and suddenly I'm   reminded that I'm still second tier, even if there 
is no first class on this plane at all. Finally,   I cannot hold a smile seeing very brief: whiskey, 
vodka, rum. Simple and to the point. You get it   for free. So why ask silly questions what brand it 
is? Enjoy the surprise. Overall, the menu sounds   right, but something tells me that reality might 
be slightly different with China Eastern. Well,   the new cabin showed me where a China Eastern 
is heading, while the menu well reminded where   they came from. Let's see how far they managed to 
get on this journey. We depart right on time. A   score for China Eastern. I have another glance at 
China Southern which almost gave me a heart attack   and also notice another Chinese carrier 
right next to it - Sichuan Airlines.   Might be a good idea for the next trip and 
a chance to try their atomic spicy cuisine.   Istanbul is a kingdom of Turkish Airlines and 
there are red and white tails are everywhere.   Turkish went a long way from being literally 
unknown to the larger world till early 2000s   to becoming a major player with massive 
network and award-winning service.   It's interesting what would be a journey 
of China Eastern. Despite its massive size,   to the rest of the world it's in a very similar 
position today what Turkish used to be in the   late '90s. For China Eastern, it all started in 
late 80s when China decided to break its state   aviation monopoly. And China's Big 3 was born. 
Air China in Beijing, China Southern in Guangzhou,   and China Eastern in Shanghai. All still 
government owned, but all went in their own ways.   Air China became flag carrier and a status symbol. 
China Southern focused heavily on domestic routes,   and China Eastern became an airline for Shanghai. 
It tried to balance focus on domestic markets   with international network and focus on business 
passengers. Later it acquired several regional   players and now has multiple hubs across China 
-- but it still remains a quintessential Shanghai   airline. Historically, China Eastern had what 
analysts call "inconsistent brand image",   while I would rather say they were blunt. 
Decent planes, but average cabins and comfort,   average service, and no any kind of distinctive 
positioning. In the last decades, they have been   investing heavily in planes while also trying to 
bring their service in line with their ambitions.   I can see that on a hardware side they did make 
a progress but I still need to be convinced   about the soft product and the upcoming 
lunch would be the best place to start.   I am fixing a tray table right away as if doing so 
can bring the food faster. It's adjustable which   is a plus but shaky and I struggle to understand 
the idea behind that strange curvy shape.   The usual continuation would be "a white cloth 
is served", but in our case, it's not a cloth,   but a paper towel. Which immediately brings the 
vibe of a cheap diner rather than an upscale   business class service. Attention to detail 
doesn't seem to be a virtue of China Eastern,   and this is something that they will 
keep reminding me for the next 8 hours.   Drinks come. I got a glass of Chilean Savignon 
from Frontera. A perfectly drinkable but clearly   no frills wine. Comes with mixed fruits and nuts 
in a very Chinese plastic pouch. Enjoy the nuts,   but could do without all the plastic. The 
meal itself starts with an appetizer and soup.   You can make your own judgment, but this is not 
something that impresses you just by its looks.   I wanted to give China Eastern their best 
chance by leaning towards Chinese cuisine,   which they should be most competent with, but it 
looks like they didn't appreciate my generosity.   I got a creamy fish soup, lukewarm and with fairly 
little flavor. The appetizer, according to menu,   was supposed to be grilled shrimp with smoked 
swordfish, but it looked like shrimps took a day   off and were swapped with salmon. The taste 
was okay, but clearly no time was wasted on   trying to present it better. Interestingly, China 
Eastern provides both western cutlery and Chinese   chopsticks, which is thoughtful. It's interesting 
how rays of customer focus come in some places,   but are totally blocked by clouds of practicality 
in the others. For the main course, I got chicken   Kung Pao with vegetables and steamed rice. By 
now, I don't expect too much from the looks.   The less expectations, the less disappointments. 
But what I got somehow went beyond. Either China   Eastern totally managed to re-imagine chicken 
Kung Pao the way no one could think before   or again the menu had some gaps with reality. 
Well, it was chicken in some kind of sweet sauce   and it was eatable. But I had Kung Pao in a 
food court few weeks ago and I have to tell   it was much better. What else? China Eastern is 
trying to serve a multicourse meal. So, we still   get fruits and mini cheeseplate. It's difficult 
to spoil those, but they still follow the model   China Eastern established earlier. They give the 
minimum possible option that would qualify for the   "We did it". The nice surprise though is an 
ice cream. We get a perfect Movenpick box   and this gets me in a better mood. Once the 
desserts come, I cannot hold my smile again.   It's not a Sacher Torte or some fancy pastry. It's 
a KitKat bar. Well, actually two of them. I love   KitKat, but this is yet another piece in China 
Eastern puzzle. It's all about doing the least   effort while still ticking the box. I don't know 
if this is the intent or just how things work out,   but this is how my experience with them is shaping 
out. I am done with the meal. It might not be   award winning, but it was quite big after all. 
Full stomach makes me more relaxed and hopefully   less picky. So, let's explore further the seat, 
amenities, and of course, entertainment. What you   immediately see is that seat is quite spacious. 
You also get a lot of space for your belongings.   There is a big console by the window where you 
can place your stuff as well as a decent storage   compartment. Power outlets are right by your 
hand: Universal and USB type A, no type-C though,   which hints that this is a little older generation 
of seats. The remote has a built-in screen,   which I always like as it allows you to track the 
route while watching something on the main screen.   The controls are usual, so nothing to decipher. 
What's good is that they are mirrored on a lower   panel, which you can reach when the seat is in lie 
flat position. You can argue about materials and   finishes, but from the practicality perspective, 
the seat definitely gets the job done.   But what about in-flight entertainment? The seats 
are equipped with an 18" HD touchscreen monitors.   Very similar to what Delta and Quantas are using. 
Not award winning these days, but definitely   competitive hardware. But let's see what's 
inside it. And here I'm up to a surprise. The   media content is extremely basic. There are barely 
some 20 international movie titles, mostly old and   somehow heavily skewed to cartoons and superhero 
movies. It is even worse with the series.   There are just few in English and none that I 
even remotely heard about. Here I start feeling   annoyed. I could put up with the food, but this is 
10 hours dayflight. You're in business and there   is nothing to watch. I'm sorry, China Eastern, 
but this is not how it works in 2026. Checking   the headphones largely loses its meaning by now as 
there is not much use for them. On other airlines,   I could brag why don't they have a branded pair or 
if Bose is better than Harmon Kardon, but here we   are in a class of its own. This is the most basic 
headphone set I have seen so far in business.   It's generally what others give you in economy 
on long haul. But strangely here it makes sense.   Since there is not much to watch, why splurge for 
expensive headphones? I'm annoyed, but I cannot   argue with the logic. My last chance to entertain 
myself on this flight is to figure out Wi-Fi.   It's a bit complicated and there are many 
clicks to make, but ultimately I get there.   Wi-Fi connected. This is much further than I got 
in last couple of flights with Chinese carriers.   It's really surprising that country which 
literally lives online on the ground is still   struggling to figure out internet in the sky. But 
there is a surprise here too. We have Wi-Fi. But   it doesn't mean we have internet. The connection 
is so slow that after 15 minutes I totally give   up. The only thing it was actually good for was to 
fill in the lending card for Chinese immigration.   As if trying to compensate for the lack 
of proper entertainment, China Eastern is   providing newspapers. A nice touch, but probably 
too late for me to learn Chinese, at least for   this flight. So, it looks like that for a change, 
I will have a flight where my mind is not going   to be bothered by movies, surfing web, or doing 
emails. Well, peace of mind is a luxury, too.   And here at China Eastern delivered in full, even 
if not asked for. Meanwhile, I noticed something   interesting. There is a small round module below 
the screen which looks suspiciously like a camera.   Is this a hello from a Big Brother or is crew 
keeping an eye on annoying airline reviewers?   I doubt it is a surveillance camera, but honestly, 
I have no idea what else it could be. So,   if anyone knows, please let me know. And finally, 
amenities. Pillow and blanket were already on the   seat from the start. They are big and functional, 
but there is no way to mistake them for Armani   Caza bedding on Etihad . This is more of a summer 
camp vibe. There is also a pouch with slippers.   Check. Amenities come in a small fabric pouch 
which does look quite authentic. Unfortunately,   the contents tell a different story. It is the 
purest form of business class basics. An eye mask,   comb, toothbrush, and ear plugs. Everything is 
double and triple wrapped and boxed in plastic.   Many airlines now turn a mini kits into 
collaborations with artists and fashion houses.   Here it almost looks like China Eastern cooperated 
with an Association of Plastic Producers.   I'm done with almost everything and at 
the absence of any decent entertainment,   my best option is to get some sleep. This is 
a red-eye flight. Still a daytime for me, but   will arrive early in the morning. So catching some 
sleep is not the worst idea. I'm checking if there   are any mini mattresses, but no luck. Well, not 
having entertainment and internet might have been   a blessing in disguise. I managed to get a decent 
sleep instead. And now ready to check out the   second meal service. Time-wise, breakfast would 
probably make much more sense, but we get what   China Eastern calls "Light meal". By now, I know 
that menu is more of a guideline than a guarantee.   Tuna salad somehow turned into grilled salmon, 
but I did get sauteed shrimps with veggie and   steamed rice. Salmon tasted like it was cooked a 
week ago, but shrimps were actually pretty good.   And somehow this light meal turned out to be 
better than the main meal earlier on. Wonder   if China Eastern kept the best till the landing 
as it's often the last impression that stays with   you. Now it's the time to conclude and to make a 
verdict. I came with low expectations and with all   the baggage of stereotypes about China state-owned
