reviews.transcript_full: Today I'm trying out Etihad Airways' Airbus A380 First Class. A 10-hour flight from Abu Dhabi to Tokyo. Delicious meals. Onboard shower experience. Amenities and pajamas. Fully flat bed. Onboard lounge. New services. Please enjoy! I'm currently in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Etihad offers a free chauffeur service within the UAE. I will be taking the Etihad Chauffeur car. Mineral water and an in-flight magazine are provided in the car. The interior is luxurious and comfortable. Free Wi-Fi service is also available. Passengers can adjust the air conditioning in the car. I'm now heading to Zayed International Airport in Abu Dhabi. The free chauffeur service is available within the UAE, so transfers from Dubai to Zayed International Airport are also possible. We can see the futuristic airport building. By the way, the chauffeur service can be booked through the Etihad website. Arrived at the airport. The car has the words "Etihad Chauffeur" on it. This is the airport departure lobby. The check-in areas for First and Business Class are separate. This is the business class check-in area. Further inside is the first class check-in area. It says "The Residence & First". The Residence is a class beyond first class. Check-in is here. Drinks (water and Arabic coffee) and dates are served. A boarding pass case. This wasn't there before, so is it a new service? First class boarding pass. I went through a dedicated security checkpoint and entered the restricted area. Terminal A, where we are currently located, officially opened in November 2023. Approximately 3 billion US dollars were invested in the construction of the terminal. There are 163 shops and restaurants inside. Let's go to the Etihad lounge. There is a souk on the way. The entrance to the lounge is near gate C29. We are currently on the 3rd floor, so we will take the elevator to the 6th floor. The lounge is a three-story building, with floors 3, 5, and 6. The first class lounge is on the 6th floor. There are arabic coffee and dates. The coffee cups are made in the UAE. There are not many people in the first class lounge. We can see the parked airplanes from the panoramic windows. We're looking at the dining area. The buffet has a variety of dates, croissants, baklava, fruit, macarons, sweets, and light meals. Looks delicious. The drinks corner. Lemon iced tea and infused water. Dilmah tea from Sri Lanka. Earl Grey and other varieties. Coffee machine. Soft drinks such as cola. There is also an à la carte menu. We can enjoy gourmet dishes with wine. Three appetizers. Three soups. Seven main courses (more than on the plane). Six desserts. Soft drinks, coffee, and tea. The wine list. The champagne is a high-end one befitting first class. The wine menu is similar to the one on the plane. The champagne is Veuve Clicquot Ponsardin La Grande Dame Brut 2018. This champagne sells for about 215 USD outside of the airport. I ordered Robian Tahta. This is shrimp rice, an authentic Emirati dish from the UAE. The taste is not as strong as it looks. I’ll have the Robian Tahta topped with Dakous (spicy tomato sauce). I ordered only one item at the lounge, as I wanted to enjoy the meal on board. The lounge is a tranquil space with a luxurious atmosphere. At the very back is the relaxation area. You can rest in a quiet area with partitions. Daybeds and recliners are provided. There are three shower rooms in the First Class Lounge. Amenities such as toothbrushes are available upon request. Hair dryers are provided.  There is a toilet and a separate shower booth.  There is a hand shower and a rain shower. Shower gel, conditioner, and shampoo are provided. Head to the Be Relax spa, located on the 3rd floor of the lounge. First-class passengers can receive a complimentary 15-minute massage. I can choose the areas to be massaged, such as my back, head, or legs. I had a 15-minute massage here. After the massage, I was given water. It’s amazing that the 15-minute massage is included for free. Another massage room. Men's grooming salon. Skincare products and beauty products. Ladies' beauty salon. Single treatment room. Couple's treatment room. It was a well-equipped spa. Let's take a look at the business class lounge. In fact, the business class lounge occupies most of the lounge. On the 3rd floor there is a buffet-style dining area. Various international dishes, salads, desserts, etc. To the 5th floor. By the way, there is no 4th floor. There is a game room, a family room, and boarding gates (D43 and C27). This is the game room. To the 6th floor. On the 6th floor there is a roof lounge, a smoking room, and prayer rooms. That is the roof lounge. There is also a dining area. The buffet in the business class lounge is also excellent. Returning to the first class lounge. Today's flight departs Abu Dhabi at 9:25 PM for Tokyo/Narita. The first-class fare is 22,955 AED (6,250 USD). Since there is still time before boarding begins, I will go and check out the boarding gate. The boarding gate for today's flight is D43. The airport is bustling and seems to be operating almost as usual. Today's aircraft is the double-decker Airbus A380. The Airbus A380 has been in service on the Tokyo/Narita-Abu Dhabi route since June 18, 2026. The main deck of the Airbus A380 has 405 economy class seats, and this is the boarding gate for economy class. Business, First, and The Residence passengers board from the lounge. We can also get to gate D43 from the 5th floor in the lounge. Boarding begins around 8:40 PM, 45 minutes before departure. Unfortunately, I cannot see very well the Airbus A380 I'm going to board today... The upper deck of the A380 has 70 business class seats, 9 first class seats, and 2 The Residence seats. It's finally time to board. We are boarding from the upper deck. After boarding, a flight attendant escorted me to my seat. The seating arrangement in first class is 1-1. There are a total of 9 seats (apartments). The seats in row 5 (5C and 5H) are rear-facing aisle seats. These seats are close to the galley and are less popular. The seats in row 4 (4A & 4K) are forward-facing window seats. These are popular seats. The seats in row 3 (3A & 3K) are rear-facing window seats. The seats are arranged in alternating colors, either cream or dark brown. The Residence (accommodates 2 people) is located at front left of the cabin. It is a three-room private suite with a living room, bathroom,  and bedroom. There is a staircase in the center of the cabin's front, and two lavatories (one with a shower) to the front right. Seat 1H is a rear-facing aisle seat. Seat 2H is a forward-facing aisle seat. My seat (apartment) is 4A.  It is a Poltrona Frau leather armchair. It has a plush headrest. The seat width is 30.3 inches (77 cm). Let's sit down. It's a very spacious seat. As the name "Apartment" suggests, it's more like a room than just a seat. I ordered champagne as a welcome drink. The champagne is Perrier-Jouët Belle Epoque Brut 2016 (Approximately 220 USD). Dates and a wet towel are also provided. Each apartment has a private wardrobe. Inside are a hanger and a pair of slippers. The wardrobe is not spacious enough for large luggage. The in-flight slippers are by Giorgio Armani. The shoes can be stored under the bench seat. The slippers are comfortable. Here is the dining table. Arabian-style lighting. Adjustment switches for the seat and window shades. Seat controller and small item storage space. Two USB-A ports, an HDMI port, a headphone jack, and a universal power outlet. 24-inch (61cm) touchscreen. An Arabic-style cushion. A refreshing cream-colored blanket. In the magazine storage space... Airbus A380-800 Safety Card Waste bag. Etihad's in-flight magazine. Bed linens are placed under the bench seat. The Arabian-style lighting is cool. Premium noise-canceling headphones. Apparently, they are Sennheiser PXC 480 headphones from the German brand. Stylish reading light. Headphone storage space. Screen remote control. A vanity with lighting and mirrors. It's practically home. Cocktail tray. Storage space. The minibar contains mineral water, sparkling water, two cans of Sprite, Diet Coca-Cola, and Coca-Cola. Bed linens are also placed here. It's a wonderfully equipped apartment. Relaxing with champagne. Further service of Arabic coffee. I received a postcard from the destination. It has a welcome message . Let's take a look at the screen. The languages ​​are English and Arabic only. After the screen starts up, an advertisement plays. About the in-flight Wi-Fi. The screen has an easy-to-read layout. Let's start the flight map. It's an easy-to-read flight map. We can see three external live camera feeds. Live camera feeds of the tail, forward, and downward. Before departure, amenity pouches containing pajamas were distributed.  The captain's pre-departure speech began. The flight number is EY800, and the flight is scheduled to last 10 hours and 20 minutes. The seatbelt sign is over there. There are no individually adjustable air nozzles on the ceiling. The Arabian-style lighting on the ceiling is nice. By the way, first class and the residence are full on this day. The Tokyo/Narita to Abu Dhabi route seems to be in high demand, and the A380 was introduced on this route on June 18, 2026. It seems there are many passengers from Europe or the Middle East. My apartment has three windows. In-flight announcements are primarily made in Arabic and English, while Japanese announcements are also provided on the Tokyo (Narita)–Abu Dhabi route. Before departure, I was asked about the meal after takeoff and the time for my shower. I booked a shower 2 hours and 30 minutes before landing. The in-flight safety video began. This was filmed at the Louvre Abu Dhabi and released in March 2021. Etihad cabin crew members primarily give safety instructions, while employees from other airlines act as passengers.  The safety video is tailored to the A380. It is a likable safety video, free of unnecessary theatrics. An A380 safety card appears. After the English safety video ends, an Arabic safety video is broadcast. Once the safety video is over, it's time to depart. From the window of seat 4A, we can see the two engines. If you want to enjoy the view, a window seat is recommended. Even from an aisle seat, you can see the outside view via the live camera outside the aircraft. The flight is delayed by about 20 minutes. The plane enters the runway. The control tower has a unique shape. It is equipped with four GP7200 engines manufactured by Engine Alliance, which power the large 486-seat aircraft powerfully and quietly. During takeoff, we could see the futuristic airport building. A beautiful night view of Abu Dhabi. We couldn't see Ferrari World, etc. 9 hours and 48 minutes remaining until arrival in Tokyo/Narita. I'm looking forward to relaxing on board. The distance from Abu Dhabi to Tokyo/Narita is approximately 5,667 miles (9,120 km). The direction and distance to Mecca, a holy city in Islam, are displayed. I haven't had a good look at the outside of the plane yet, so I'll take a good look after arriving in Tokyo/Narita. We've reached cruising altitude and the seatbelt sign has been turned off. The cabin lighting sets the mood. It's an orange color, like a sunset sky. After takeoff, the cabin crew closes the doors. I'll try connecting to the in-flight Wi-Fi (ETIHAD WI-FLY). We can use the Wi-Fi now. Let's look at the general Wi-Fi usage fees. Chat is 3.99 USD. Surf is 24.99 USD. Stream is 29.99 USD. First class passengers can use Wi-Fi (Surf) for free. If you're an Etihad Guest member, you can use the chat for free. After takeoff, the door was closed, creating a semi-private space. We were also given snacks, a service that wasn't offered before.  There are energy bars, chocolate, a mint tablet, popcorn, potato chips, jelly beans and sweet chili mix, and a ginger shot. It's a service similar to that of Emirates, the UAE's national airline. There is a galley and a lounge behind the First Cabin. This is the lounge, named The Lobby. It is available to Business, First, and The Residence passengers. There is a circular leather sofa that can seat up to six people, and its design is modeled after a traditional Arab "majlis". Cocktails and wine are available in the lounge. The champagne is business class quality, cheaper than first class. The Arabian design here is also nice. There is one shared screen. There is a wine cellar. A variety of alcoholic drinks. Wine glasses are neatly arranged. Let's take a look at the first class wine list. The champagne and rosé champagne are befitting of first class. Four types of white wine. Four types of red wine. The dessert wine is 2012 Chateau Rieussec 'Les Carmes de Rieussec' (approximately 40 USD). The fortified wine is W & J Graham's 20 Year Old Tawny Port (approximately 70 USD). Sake is also available. Cocktails, spirits, beer, soft drinks, mocktails, coffee, and tea. I ordered a mango mojito. Kalamata olives, almonds, cashews, peanuts, and cherry tomatoes and cheese. All three are just the right amount. The mixed nuts are delicious. The olives too. Let's close the window shade. We can operate the shade with just the press of a switch. We are currently over India. The dining table is wood-grained and a good size. Let's look at the menu. Meals are à la carte. The menu is written in English and Arabic. There was no Japanese menu available. There are two kinds of bread, and they are nicely warmed. Butter, olive oil, salt and pepper. A signature dish of first class is caviar. 20g of Osetra caviar from the UAE brand Numero Uno. It looks delicious. Lemon, blinis, sour cream, onion, and a boiled egg (white and yolk). A shell spoon specifically for caviar. Cutlery from the British brand Studio William. The tableware is from the Japanese brand Nikko. I will have the UAE's Numero Uno caviar. Apparently, it is a brand that has the patronage of the UAE royal family and  has a processing and distribution facility in Abu Dhabi. The table can be moved back and forth, so we can go out into the aisle even while eating. Perhaps because first class is full, we are taking a while to get our food. For the appetizer, I chose Harira soup. It is a traditional Moroccan soup, made with a tomato base and lentils and chickpeas. It was a rich and flavorful soup. Two hours had passed since departure when I finished the appetizer. Before the main course, we were served a palate cleanser of lemon sorbet. It was a refreshing lemon-flavored sorbet. Of the five main course options, I chose the Stir-Fried Udon Noodles. In addition to udon noodles, it contains teriyaki tofu, broccoli, and green onions. Since a plain udon dish is too high in carbohydrates, tofu and broccoli were likely added. The udon had a rich flavor. However, udon is inexpensive to make, so I wondered if I should have chosen meat or fish instead. Since I was there, I ordered red wine. Red wine 2017 Symington Quinta do Ataide 'Vinha do Arco' Touriga Nacional (approximately $25 USD). For dessert, I ordered banana chocolate pudding. It was served warm. Rich chocolate sauce. It was a soft and delicious banana chocolate pudding. Served with dark chocolate ice cream. I ordered jasmine green tea. I finished dinner about three hours after takeoff. There are 6 hours and 50 minutes left until arrival in Tokyo/Narita. I think we only get about four to five hours of sleep at most. Let's take a look at the lavatory. This is a lavatory without a shower. I'm glad it's a spacious lavatory. Diaper changing table. Changing table? The lavatory has a chic interior. This Arabian-style pattern is actually made from this. The toilet is clean. There is a full-length mirror at the entrance. A makeup mirror. Skincare products from the British brand ESPA. Hand and body lotion, aroma mist, and body wash. Tissues, towels, and paper cups. Attendant call button and power outlet. A unique washbasin. The water temperature can be adjusted. There are no amenities such as toothbrushes in the lavatory. Toothbrushes are provided on the vanity in the apartment. A large amenity pouch. Designed by Giorgio Armani. It's more of a clutch bag than an amenity pouch. Giorgio Armani in-flight pajamas. There are two sizes: S/M and M/L. It says Made in China. Comfortable in-flight pajamas. The pants have pockets. When I returned to the apartment... the bed had been made. The bed is 80.5 inches (204.5 cm) long. A blanket. A down comforter. A mattress pad. Some say it's a little thin... By the pillow... A "Sweet dreams" tag. Two pillows. The pillows are slightly springy and of average firmness. In some apartments, you can connect two adjacent apartments by lowering a partition. There are three pairs (3A & 4A, 3K & 4K, and 1H & 2H). This allows you to spend time with your partner or children. Let's look at the amenities. Face mist and pulse point oil were provided. A list of basic amenities. A list of amenities that can be requested. Basic amenities are stored in a vanity equipped with lighting and mirrors. The pouch is by Giorgio Armani, and the skincare products are by ESPA. As mentioned earlier, ESPA is a London, England brand. Hand and body lotion, night cream for face, tissues, lip balm, mouthwash, small pouch, sheet mask, toothbrush and toothpaste, cotton set, dental floss, earplugs, and eye mask. There is also a trash can and a storage box for amenities. The amenities were excellent. The bed has a seatbelt. The bed is 26 inches (66 cm) wide. The narrow width of the bed might be a slight drawback. There's also a headphone jack here. Switches for the window shade and lights. We can also adjust the angle of the screen. We can enjoy in-flight entertainment while lying in bed. There is another remote control for the screen. I'll turn off the screen.  I'll turn off the lights too. It's a comfortable bed, although it's a little narrow. The cabin is quiet, and with earplugs, the noise is barely noticeable. There's only one power outlet, and it feels a bit far away. I'll turn off the light on my phone. It's so dark that I think I could sleep without an eye mask. It was a bumpy flight at times.  There were times when the shaking was so bad I felt my life was in danger... I heard something fall... I slept for about 4 hours. 2 hours and 42 minutes left until arrival in Tokyo. The person in the seat in front of me opened the window, and the cabin is brighter. The seatbelt sign stayed on for a long time, so I couldn't get to the shower for quite a while. I was able to take a shower two hours before landing. This is a lavatory with a shower. A bath towel and bath mat are provided. There's also a shower cap. We can use the shower room for 30 minutes. There's a fixed showerhead on the ceiling. The shower runs for 5 minutes.  There's a switch for the shower. We can adjust the water temperature. There's an attendant call button. ESPA body wash, shampoo, and conditioner. We can use the whole tube. Let's try using the shower. Wow...the water pressure is stronger than I expected. We can stop the shower by pressing the switch. The shower only runs for 5 minutes, so we need to stop it frequently. I took a shower and felt refreshed. A Swiss-made hairdryer is provided. There was plenty of time to dry my hair. Taking a shower on a plane is a great experience. It's already light outside. I'll order my breakfast. Let's look at the breakfast menu. Cereals, detox drink, cheese omelet, and fruit. Lounge snacks. Lounge and Grill. They have takoyaki on the menu. Breakfast has arrived. Morning Detox. Cheese omelet. Croissant and chocolate muffin. Fresh fruit. Strawberry jam. The cheese omelet was fluffy and delicious.  It was of high quality for an omelet served on a plane. It also came with potato rösti, cherry tomatoes, spinach, and sausage. Since I was there, I ordered takoyaki.  It was topped with a generous amount of bonito flakes. The surface of the takoyaki wasn't particularly crispy. It was thoroughly cooked through. Some of the takoyaki had large pieces of octopus in them. It was tasty, but it can't compare to freshly made takoyaki from a street stall. Let's try the seat controller. There is an item for cushion firmness. We can adjust the seat firmness in 5 levels. I prefer it softer, so I'll set it to 1. There's a sound from the seat... the seat has become a little softer. There are other functions as well. It has lumbar support adjustment and a massage function. With the flick of a switch, we can convert it to a bed position. Let's try converting it to a bed position. The bench seat in front moves, allowing me to stretch my legs. Let's check out the in-flight entertainment E-BOX. According to their website, they offer over 1,000 hours of on-demand entertainment. Let's start by looking at the movie section. There are new releases and movies from various genres. Let's look at new movies.  Surprisingly, there's a Michael Jackson movie. At the time of boarding, it was a movie that had just been released a few months prior... the audio languages ​​are diverse. The exact number of movies is not publicly announced, but  there are at least 200 available. I think there's a decent selection of movies. On live TV, we were able to watch the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Let's take a look at the TV shows. There's a section called Etihad Wellbeing. It introduces stretches and other things to do on board. There's also a section called Abu Dhabi. It introduces Abu Dhabi's culture and tourist information. Let's look at the audio. You can listen to the Quran, the holy book of Islam. Let's look at the Games. There are 15 different games available. About Etihad. Etihad is the national airline of the UAE, established in 2003.  It is based in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE. It has received numerous awards. Its slogan is Connecting the world through Abu Dhabi. The number of destinations it serves is increasing every year. About the lounge at Zayed International Airport. About the state-of-the-art Boeing 787 aircraft. About Etihad's The Residence. It is the ultimate three-room suite. First class is offered on the Boeing 787, Airbus A380, and Airbus A321LR. I think the A380 apartment is the best. About the Etihad Guest mileage program. I received a Japanese customs declaration form and a ballpoint pen. It's an Etihad ballpoint pen. This is the first time I've received this ballpoint pen. I also received a coffee cup. I didn't receive one before, so I think it's a new service. A wet towel service is provided before landing. And even chocolate service. UAE-made chocolate. Two chocolates. Captain's speech before landing. We are already over Japan. The plane will begin its descent shortly. There are 44 minutes left until we arrive in Tokyo/Narita, but it's really going by so fast. This apartment is so comfortable, I wish I could stay on longer. I didn't get enough sleep, so I wish the flight was another 3 hours or so. I spotted Poltrona Frau written on my seat. It's a luxury furniture brand founded in Italy in 1912. Let's check out the in-flight magazine. It lists Abu Dhabi's tourist attractions. The Louvre Abu Dhabi, where the safety video was filmed. The success story of the Airbus A320 family. Etihad's fleet list. The Boeing 787 family has the most with 47 aircraft. The next-generation Airbus A350 has increased to 12 aircraft. There are currently 7 Airbus A380s in operation (originally 10). The Airbus A320 family has 32 aircraft. There are fewer Boeing 777-300ERs, with 7 aircraft. They serve more than 40 countries and more than 100 destinations. An early satisfaction survey for today's flight. Footage from the tail fin live camera. Chiba Prefecture? The Japanese landscape is already visible. The greenery is beautiful. The plane is now in its final approach for landing. We need to return the seats to their original position. We can see a long river.  It's getting cloudy. The industrial area of ​​Chiba Prefecture? The plane is descending. The airplane is plunging into the clouds. The plane shook a little. We can see the runway at Narita Airport. We'll be landing soon. It was quite bumpy during landing. We landed safely. Let's look back on the flight until we reach the gate. Overall, it was a very satisfying flight. The food, amenities, seats, and service were all excellent. Personally, I had almost no complaints, but online, the following points have been mentioned as drawbacks: slow Wi-Fi speed, poor response of the screen remote and touch controls, small storage space under the seat, far from the window if you're in an aisle seat, inability to adjust the air conditioning, and hard beds. Personally, I like the experience of taking a shower on a plane, so Etihad's A380 First Apartment is a product I really like. There's a lot of discussion online about what constitutes the world's best first class, but I think it really comes down to personal preference. We'll soon be arriving at the gate. Terminal 1 has a distinctive circular satellite. As we arrive at the gate, the disembarkation music starts playing. I like this disembarkation music. During takeoff, landing, and the flight, I mainly kept my backpack on the bench seat. When the bench seat was converted into a bed, I placed my backpack on the armchair. During takeoff and landing, they didn't seem to be too strict about luggage around the seats. Passengers from The Residence and First Class disembarked first. After disembarking, I could see the Airbus A380 from the window. The words "Airbus A380-800" are on the front of the aircraft. It has two engines on each side, for a total of four engines. The UAE flag is painted on it. The word "Etihad" is written in Arabic and English. The aircraft registration is A6-APE, and it was delivered to Etihad in October 2015. It operates not only to Tokyo (Narita) but also to Paris, London, and Toronto. I'd like to try flying in business class on an Etihad A380 in the future. Entering Japan. Thank you for watching.

reviews.transcript_full: Welcome aboard Austrian Airlines' Boeing 777 Business Class Enjoy the full Austrian Airlines Business Class experience The video shows the Business Class seat, amenities, and food Expect some turbulence during the 9 hour flight ... And some spectacular views of the Maldives during landing Welcome to Vienna International Airport in Austria Austrian provides dedicated check-in for premium passengers Vienna Airport handled over 30 million passengers in 2025 Several Austrian Airlines lounges are located at Vienna Airport. This lounge is located in the non-Schengen departures area Most seating areas are arranged around coffee tables Red and green accents reflect Austrian Airlines’ colors A self-service buffet is located in the center of the lounge It's a short stroll from the lounge to the gate  This is the Boeing 777-200ER that will fly us to the Maldives Built in 2007, the plane has registration code OE-LPD Boarding begins on schedule Austrian Airlines' B777 Business Class cabin features 32 seats The lie-flat seats arranged in a staggered configuration The center seats are arranged in pairs, perfect for couples Window seats alternate between one and two per row 2K is my window seat for the 9 hour flight to the Maldives The best seats in the Business Class cabin are the throne seats These solo seats have two side tables and feel more private We have a full flight tonight to the Maldives The captain welcomes everyone onboard A welcome drink is offered (water, orange juice or Champagne) The welcome drink is served with some mixed nuts  Austrian's famous Flying Chef joins this flight The chef plates, garnishes and adds final touches to every meal The chef visits every Business Class seat to present the menu Austrian Airlines' safety video is shown prior to departure We're leaving the gate at 7 pm local time (on time departure) The cabin lights are dimmed prior to takeoff Austrian Airlines' Boeing 777 is powered by two GE90 engines Each GE90 engine produces over 90,000 pounds of thrust The GE90 is one of the world's most powerful jet engines Have you ever flown with Austrian Airlines?  Let's have a look at Austrian Airlines' Business Class seat A reading light and universal power outlets are built into the seat  A wired handset is located below a flap in the armrest A panel with the seat controls is easy to reach Storage space around the seat is rather limited In front of each seat is a HD entertainment screen  The seat's footwell is located beneath the screen The fold-out tray table is released at the push of a button A hot towel is distributed shortly after takeoff Austrian’s amenity kit is created by Vienna’s MAK Museum The bag & eyeshade features a Wiener Werkstätte design A warm, high-quality blanket and fluffy pillow are provided Noise-cancelling headphones are offered Let's have a look at the menu on tonight's flight Austrian Airlines collaborates with DO & CO for its catering Dinner service is delayed because of turbulence Are you afraid of flying through turbulence? Leave a comment Dinner service resumes shortly after the turbulence subsides The crew rolls a selection of starters through the cabin Starters: salad, roast beef, coleslaw & baked Emmental cheese Soup: clear beef broth with Tyrolian cheese dumplings Main course: braised beef with potato salad & tartar sauce  A selection of cheeses and desserts is offered Desserts: Demel's Esterhazy cake, vanilla crème fraîche & fruits There are three lavatories for the 32 Business Class passengers The seat reclines in a bed with a length of 2 m (6.5 ft) Unfortunately, the flat bed's foot compartment is quite narrow Each Business Class seat has its own 15-inch HD touchscreen The entertainment selection is decent, with many films & series Content is available in 20 languages and updated monthly Unfortunately, Austrian's B777s are not equipped with WiFi A few hours later: we're waking up above the Indian Ocean Breakfast service is postponed due to some more turbulence Look at the movement of the wing and engine A hot towel is provided before breakfast to freshen up Breakfast starts with an energy shot (apple, carrot, ginger, lime)  Main course: freshly prepared eggs sunny side up with toast The breakfast is served with muesli and strawberry yoghurt The First Officer is announcing our approach to Male We get some stunning views of the Maldives on approach Austrian Airlines was founded in 1957 Vienna has been the airline's home hub since the beginning Austrian Airlines joined the Lufthansa Group in 2009 Austrian operates a mixed Airbus and Boeing fleet Its long-haul fleet consists of Boeing 777s and 787 Dreamliners The Boeing 787 is gradually replacing the older 777 aircraft The airline also operates Airbus A320-family aircraft These modern jets serve shorter European routes The airline is famous for serving Viennese coffee onboard Austrian Airlines has been a Star Alliance member since 2000 Thx for watching my Austrian Airlines 777 Business Class video

reviews.transcript_full: This is the best way to fly business class within Europe, but only if you pick the right flight. That's because Turkish Airlines offers a business class seat that nobody else in Europe has. We're flying Turkish Airlines business class at its best today on Marcus Travels. My route today is from Milan Malpenza in Italy to Dubai in the United Arab Emirates via Istanbul in Turkey. The first leg is 3 hours and the second leg is around 4 and 1/2 hours. The flight from Milan to Istanul is operated by a widebody Airbus A330 today and that's going to make all the difference. The second leg to Dubai was supposed to be a Boeing 77, but Turkish Airlines swapped the aircraft to an older A330. This will be a full review of the newer model, plus I will highlight relevant differences to the older model as well. For this morning flight from Milan, I spent the night before at one of the airport hotels. This is the Tribe Milano Malpenza. It's a modern airport hotel with a badly designed shuttle bus service. Welcome to the Milano Malpenza airport. I checked in for Turkish Airlines at the business class desk. The process was very efficient. The lady was very friendly. Good first impression. One thing that makes me feel very special is that I got two priority tags on my bag. One Star Alliance and one Turkish Airlines. This is my first time here at MXP and uh the first impression of the airport as a whole is not excellent. There's just renovations going on everywhere. the hotel shuttles were not in the signposted places due to that renovation. I think once they get that sorted out, I'm sure it'll look nice. At the moment, this just looks like a very generic airport from the '7s. It is not very charming. I paid for this trip myself so that you get a non-sponsored and authentic travel review. Welcome to my channel, Marcus Travels. We'll talk more about the price and the value for money at the end of the video. I don't know if it's fair to complain about the miserable state of this airport since they are renovating it. Maybe I would hold a judgment until I see what comes of it. Though, one thing that I do like is that even here in the check-in halls, they have big windows so you can see the gates and the action on the ramp. That gives a great first impression as you first arrive here. Now, let's make our way to the lounge and find out if they also have beautiful ramp views from there. At check-in, I received my two printed boarding passes, plus a lounge invitation. Welcome to the premium lounge here at Malpenza airport. This is a kind of a contract lounge that a bunch of different airlines are using, and I think for a contract lounge, this is pretty solid. In terms of the interior design, it may not be the most beautiful, but in terms of the catering, what they have on offer, there's a good selection of different hot and cold foods. And uh that selection of pastries under the dome there, for example, that's uh pretty extensive. Another thing that I find unusual is that they have Red Bull Zero in the fridge. I don't think I've ever seen Red Bull available in an airport lounge before. In addition to the catering, I think one of the other things that a good lounge provides is peace and quiet. And here, this lounge really overdelivers. When I entered, there were only three passengers in the entire lounge. There was almost more staff than there were passengers. So, the atmosphere here is really, really quiet. Now, maybe there's no more than 10 passengers, and it's very, very quiet throughout. I have this whole back section of leather armchairs to myself where so few passengers, there's so much space. We're almost in a situation where each passenger could get their own block of the lounge just for them. Another thing that the lounge delivers is a nice view of the ramp. There's a number of Air China aircraft outside the window and I think I saw a Singapore Airlines aircraft there as well. With that, it's time to leave the lounge. Let's head over to the gate and board this Turkish Airlines A330 over to Istanul. There is now one challenge that comes into play. Turkish Airlines has on a few occasions asked me to not film on board a specific flight. So, on the assumption that they don't like me doing that, I think I'm going to try to be a little bit more sneaky and film with my phone instead of with my big camera. I think once we're on board, you might see a difference in the video quality. It's not necessarily going to get worse because my phone actually has better image stabilization than my camera does. At this point, just wish me luck that I'm actually allowed to film on board. Welcome aboard the Turkish Airlines A330. I'm in the last row of the business class cabin. This is row number five. The cabin is laid out in a 2 + 2 + 2 configuration. That may not sound so impressive, but remember this is an intrauropean short hall flight. These seats go flat and I don't know any other European carrier that offers this on regular flights within Europe. There is a privacy divider between the seats. There is storage in the foot stools and there's a light. The headrest on this seat is not adjustable. There was no amenity kit on this daytime flight, but there was one on the following flight to Dubai. What they don't have here are coat hooks, so I put my jacket in the storage box. On my right, I have the seat controls for turning the seat into a bed. There is no preset for any kind of relax mode halfway between upright and bed. Under the armrest, there's plenty of storage for personal items. I kept my phone in here, for example. Welcome aboard this Turkish Airlines A330300 which is going to take us from the Milano Menza over to Istanbul. I made myself very comfortable here in seat number five alpha. The leg room in this seat is pretty much unlimited, but that comes with one major limitation. We'll talk about that in just a moment. After I get seated, one of the crew members offers me a pre-eparture drink and wishes me welcome again. The expression welcome again is one that I don't often hear. Crews on Turkish airlines are generally not fluent in English. I have flown with them so many times over the years. I can say that with some confidence. And for reference, English is also not my first language. It is my third language. The pre-eparture drink I chose was the lemon mint. This is a non-alcoholic classic with many Middle Eastern airlines. On my right, I have the remote. We'll look at that in just a moment. Plus, there's a light button that does nothing. The level of privacy here is pretty good. The divider does a lot of work. I was able to see only one other passenger from my seat, but that of course was helped a lot by the fact that there was nobody sitting in the seat next to me. The armrest on the right cannot be moved and neither can the one on the left. Overall, this is a comfortable seat, especially taking into account that most other European airlines when they sell a business class product, they would only give you an economy seat with a middle seat blocked. the so-called Euro business. Before departure, the crew hands out printed menus. Do note that the glass from the pre-eparture drink is still on the table. They left it there for around 30 minutes. They could have picked it up when they brought me the menu or when they brought me the headphones, but it stayed there. I think they only paid attention when they noticed that I was filming the headphone bag. As the safety video plays, we are getting ready for takeoff. As we taxi out, let me say something about the background of this flight and the booking process. The reason I was in Milan was that I had booked the inaugural flight on the WhizAir Airbus A321 XLR. The flight was scheduled from Milan to Abu Dhabi. WhizAir was supposed to be one of the first operators of that brand new extra long range aircraft and the very first flight was supposed to take place on this day on June 2nd. Whizzer canled that flight about a month before departure. They offered no alternative flights because they don't have any other routes to the United Arab Emirates. They refunded me the ticket and I spent twice as much booking Turkish Airlines economy instead. Then I upgraded to business class with miles. I had no other business in Milan. Though I did take the opportunity to ride the best high-speed train in the world. Hit the subscribe button to be notified when that video goes live. Some people complain about the Turkish Airlines booking process. I've never had a problem, be it on their website or on their app. During this trip, another airline cancelled my flight that was beyond who I was supposed to fly back from Dubai. So, to get back, I booked with Turkish Airlines again, this time on the app. So, I'm actually thankful to Turkish Airlines for saving my whole Dubai trip, and I was pretty happy to fly with them both there and back in the end. For storage, we have small overhead bins, plus the bins on the floor. These boxes have a lid that opens. On the older A330 from the second flight, the lid does not open. It's just an open box and you can put your things inside from the front, but this is not obvious. It was clear that a lot of people had tried to lift the lid. It is partially attached with Velcro. Food and drink are included in the fair with and without alcohol. The tray table comes out of the armrest. This one time when I opened it for the first time, I managed to get it out correctly. Every other time the table got stuck. You can angle the table so that in theory you can exit the seat even when the table is deployed, but I did not try that. The crew member greeted me by name and took my drink order. That feels premium. The breakfast tray comes with a default starter and side dishes. From top left to right, we have a chia bowl with pineapple, a couple of marinated olives, jam and butter for the bread, a fruit salad, and a selection of cheeses and smoked ham. The menu says specifically that the jam is homemade strawberry jam from Bodum, plus countryside butter from Trabzon. It's clear that Turkish Airlines takes a lot of pride in their food and its local origins. I somehow doubt that someone made this jam at home, but uh what do I know? We also get these cute salt and pepper shakers. For my drinks, I chose black tea and water. The teacup would have been better with a real handle instead of this paper sleeve. There were three choices for the main breakfast item. an omelette, a porridge, and then the one that I chose, gleame. This is a traditional grilled flat filow pastry filled with spinach and white cheese. This was a fantastic breakfast. Turkish Airlines has consistently great food on board, even in economy, by the way, and today was no exception. I finished off the meal with a Turkish coffee which came with a cookie and most importantly a Turkish delight. The in-flight entertainment is good and it's a modern system. The touchscreen remote worked really well. On the older A330 from the second flight, the remote was more old-fashioned. It had physical buttons and they were not very responsive. One problem on both versions of the aircraft is that the monitor, which also is not the biggest in the world, is too far away. It's a result of the seat design with all this leg room. The selection of titles on the if is pretty broad. However, it varies between aircraft. I started watching an episode of Dune Prophecy on one flight on the assumption that I could continue on the next flight back home. That last flight was on a narrowbody aircraft and it had fewer episodes. The episode I had started was not on that system. Turkish Airlines sensors the content on the if heavily. Certain themes result in muted audio and the blurring of a portion of the screen. I even saw this on the fairly mild HBO series Silicon Valley as well as the Kendrick Lamar album GNX. This censorship is ridiculous nonsense. Turkish Airlines, if you don't like a specific piece of media, then just don't load it onto the in-flight entertainment system. Censorship is not the answer. On the fairly unique content on the Turkish Airlines system, you can find the Quran as well as some educational content about Islamic life. The older A330 had some super retro ports around the inflight entertainment screen. If you know what these are for, please let me know in the comments. The headphones that Turkish Airlines provides are made by Audio Technica. That's a Japanese brand that makes professional audio gear. The headphones were pretty good. They have no active noise cancellation, but the passive noise cancellation just by virtue of being well padded did a lot of work. There is Wi-Fi on board. Theoretically, I should be able to log in to the Wi-Fi with the Turkish Airlines app on my phone. This is theoretically a good solution because I'm already logged in to my account on the app, but this did not work. There is both a USBA port and a universal power outlet at my seat. The universal outlet was impossible to access when I was seated. That's because it's located kind of behind me. I literally had to get on my knees in front of my seat to insert my charger. As for the lavatory, the most distinguishing feature is that there are some premium amenities in here. There is a liquid soap, a hand lotion, some scented diffuser thing that I don't know how it's called, and a perfume. My only complaint is that the tray was placed too near the wall so that there's no space for your hand above the soap pump. Luckily, the tray can be moved easily. These kinds of premium amenities are also in the economy class lavatory. By the way, the bed on the A330 may not be completely horizontal, but it does go flat. The main limitation is that if you have a person next to you, you will have to step over them if they're sleeping. On my flight, the seat next to me remained empty, so I had no issues. There's a pillow and they have blankets, but I didn't actually use the bed because this was a daytime flight. I had basically just woken up from the hotel. After the meal service, the crew handed out hazelnuts. I've seen this before. They really highlight the fact that hazelnuts are from Turkey. Overall, the service was friendly. When I boarded, the flight attendant personally walked me to the seat, and that feels premium. There are certainly airlines out there that have a more rigorous training program for the cabin crew. I would rather have good food and mediocre service than the other way around. And what Turkish Airlines does is perfectly acceptable. As we begin our descent into Istanbul airport, we're going to talk about the price in just a moment. If you've gotten value from my video, consider booking me for one of your corporate events. I've been performing stand-up comedy for almost a decade and I have a keynote called Leadership Lessons from the Comedy Club where I teach you some communication skills that they don't cover in your traditional presentation skills workshop. Learn more at marcuspresents.com. So now for the price. I booked this trip as a one-way ticket from Milano Malpenza to Dubai via Istanbul. I paid €434 for the base economy ticket. That's around $500 US. Then I upgraded both segments with my Turkish Airlines miles. The upgrade cost was $53,000. Those miles were going to expire by year end anyway, so it's hard to put a value to them. So when it comes to the value for money, I look at it from a different perspective instead. Turkish Airlines is the only airline I've tried that offers a lie flat bed on a widebody aircraft on an intra European flight. That's cool. That's unusual. I like it. Sure, the seat is not competitive with the state-of-the-art of business class today, but for a 3-hour flight, it doesn't have to be. Turkish Airlines also flies these routes with narrow bodies sometimes and then you just get a big recliner in business class. But even that is better than the Euro business with just an economy seat with a middle seat blocked. There's other aspects too like the huge modern airport at Istanbul. I'll talk more about that in the next video I will link to in just a moment. The food is consistently great on Turkish Airlines. And then there's the schedule. That's a real asset of Turkish Airlines. When both Whiz Air and Beyond cancelled my flights by offering a lot of connections between the Middle East and Europe, Turkish Airlines really saved the day. They had so many different connections available. First from Milan to Dubai and then back home, Dubai to Basil, Switzerland. It was easy to find good and convenient options, and the prices were reasonable even when I booked the return ticket just 4 days before departure. So, Turkish Airlines really delivered exactly what I needed on this trip. For Turkish Airlines in economy class, click or tap the screen right here. That's another Middle East trip, this time to Qatar. In that video, I list five reasons why Turkish Airlines offers a very competitive economycl class product. So check out that video now.

reviews.transcript_full: Some of the world's best airlines are based in Asia. But when you actually look closely, they're not all excellent for the same reason. Some airlines win through crew service and hospitality. Some win through seat comfort [music] and cabin design. Some win through the sheer size of their network. And some win simply because they operate the newest, most consistent aircraft in the sky. This ranking looks at what passengers actually experience in 2026, [music] from the seats and service to fleet consistency, network strength, and overall value. One note before we start. Airlines like Qatar Airways, Emirates, [music] and Etihad are not included here. They operate on a different model entirely and deserve their own separate ranking. This is about Asia's full-service carriers, from Tokyo to Singapore, from Seoul to Taipei. Let's begin with number 10. Number 10, Thai Airways. At number 10 is Thai Airways, a carrier that has spent the last few years rebuilding itself >> [music] >> into something more focused. Flying out of Bangkok, it still carries one of the most recognizable senses of [music] hospitality in the region. Unhurried service and food that routinely ranks among the best in Asian aviation, with curries and regional dishes that feel like part of the identity rather than an afterthought. Since its restructuring, the fleet is tighter [music] and operations have visibly improved compared to a decade ago. But Thai Airways still trails the airlines above it in one key area, consistency. Aircraft swaps remain common enough that passengers can book one cabin experience and receive another. And the airline does not currently offer a true standalone premium economy product comparable to the dedicated cabins offered by the airlines higher on this list. It's an airline built on charm and cuisine, recovering steadily, but not yet operating with the precision of the carriers ranked above it. Number nine, Malaysia Airlines. Number nine is Malaysia Airlines, a full-service carrier in the middle of real modernization. Operating from Kuala Lumpur and holding One World membership, Malaysia Airlines offers genuine hospitality in the cabin, something reviewers repeatedly point to, along with a signature satay service that has become something of a calling card. That push includes new A330 neo aircraft with updated cabins and suites, a meaningful step forward. The issue is what it's replacing. Older A330 business class seating that varies significantly in layout and comfort from flight to flight, meaning your experience can depend heavily on which aircraft shows up at the gate. And like Thai Airways, Malaysia Airlines does not currently offer a true stand-alone premium economy product. The space between economy and business remains thin. What you get is a carrier with real hospitality and a modernization plan in motion, but one that hasn't yet closed the gap with Asia's most consistent operators. Number eight, Vietnam Airlines. At number eight, Vietnam Airlines might be the most underrated long-haul carrier in this entire ranking. Operating out of Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, its long-haul operation is built primarily around the Airbus A350 and Boeing 787, with very few older wide-bodies affecting the overall fleet. That matters because it means passengers get contemporary cabins nearly every time they fly long-haul. Vietnam Airlines also offers a true premium economy product on its 787, [music] nine, and A350 aircraft, a dedicated cabin rather than a repackaged economy seat. And it prices its long-haul routes to Europe and Australia competitively enough that it reliably over-delivers on value. Where it falls of the airlines above it is in the ground and in the finer points of service [music] consistency. Check-in lines in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City can be chaotic. And the polish that defines carriers like Japan Airlines or Singapore Airlines isn't quite there yet. But as a long-haul value proposition with modern hardware, Vietnam Airlines earns its place here. Number seven. Starlux Airlines. Number seven belongs to Starlux, the most exciting new airline in Asia and arguably the hardest one to rank. Based in Taipei, Starlux operates an extraordinarily young fleet, among the newest anywhere in the world, built around the Airbus A350. And it shows in every part of the cabin. The in-flight entertainment is sharp. The seat design is considered down to the material choices. And the overall aesthetic feels closer to a design studio than a traditional airline. Passenger reviews have been overwhelmingly positive since [music] launch, and it's easy to see why. Everything about the experience feels deliberate. So why isn't it higher? Scale and time. Starlux still operates a limited route network. It isn't part of a major global alliance, and its small fleet means that any single aircraft issue can ripple through the schedule in a way it wouldn't for a larger carrier. It also simply hasn't been flying long enough to build the kind of track record the airlines above it have spent decades earning. It's an airline built on where aviation is heading rather than where it's been. But it needs more time and more aircraft before it can compete with the network strength of the carriers ranked above it. Six, EVA Air. Starlux may be Taipei's newest carrier, but the city's other major airline has been quietly excellent for years. At number six, EVA Air rarely dominates headlines, but it outperforms expectations almost every time. EVA is known for cabins that feel clean in the literal sense. Spotless, well-maintained, unfussy. Its Royal Laurel business class is one of the most respected products in the region. And its true premium economy cabin, found mainly on the 777-300ER and select 787-9 aircraft, has long been considered a benchmark for the category. EVA's standing across the Pacific is particularly strong, built over years of dependable service on routes connecting Taiwan [music] to North America. What keeps it from climbing higher is size and a certain restraint. Its overall network is smaller than Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, ANA, or Japan Airlines, even though it maintains strong service across North America and key European gateways. EVA also tends to improve quietly rather than boldly. Cabins get upgraded steadily, but it's rarely the airline setting the trend. EVA Air isn't trying to be everywhere. It's trying to be reliable everywhere it flies, and on that measure, it rarely disappoints. Number five. Korean Air. Number five is Korean Air. A carrier whose real strength lies in scale. Korean Air calls Incheon home. And from there, it runs one of the most extensive trans-Pacific and Asian networks of any airline on this list, connecting Seoul to an enormous range of destinations across North America and beyond. Economy class is often praised for generous space, and the food, bibimbap in particular, has become something of [music] a signature. In business class, Korean Air's newer prestige suites represent a significant step forward in privacy and cabin [music] design, while the airline continues modernizing its long-haul fleet. Where Korean Air still trails the airlines above it is cabin consistency. Its new premium economy product is now rolling out across retrofitted Boeing 777-300ERs, finally addressing one of the airline's biggest historical weaknesses. But because that rollout is still underway, passengers can encounter very different cabin standards depending on the aircraft assigned. It's a network powerhouse first and a refined product [music] second, but that combination still places it solidly in the upper half of this list. Four, Japan Airlines. Korean Air wins on reach. Japan Airlines, at number four, wins on the seat itself, and may offer the single best economy and premium economy experience anywhere in Asia. Its Boeing 787s use a 2-4-2 economy layout instead of the [music] tighter 3-3-3 configuration most airlines have adopted, which quietly makes a huge difference in seat width and the number of middle seats you're likely to be assigned. That seat, branded Sky Wider, has become something of a favorite among frequent flyers. Its premium economy cabin builds on that same philosophy and is widely regarded as one of the best in the industry. [music] On the newest A350-1000 aircraft, JAL's flagship cabins bring that same attention to detail to business and first class, paired with food and service that regularly draws praise. So, why isn't Japan Airlines higher? Its global scale is slightly smaller than the very top carriers, and because its fleet spans several generations of aircraft, some passengers [music] still encounter older cabin variants that haven't been updated to the newest standard. JAL is exceptional at the seat level. >> [music] >> The gap is in scale and total consistency. Number three, ANA. Japan Airlines wins the seat. Its domestic rival, ANA, at number three, wins the operation, arguably the most polished in Japan. Punctuality and cleanliness are where ANA separates itself. The airline routinely ranks among the most reliable in Asia Pacific for on-time performance, and its cabins reflect the same discipline. Service follows the same pattern, attentive, precise, distinctly Japanese in its restraint. ANA's premium economy cabin includes something rare in the category, lounge access, which elevates the experience well beyond the seat itself. And when ANA's flagship business class product, The Room, is available, it's frequently discussed as being closer to first class than typical business class, with sliding privacy panels and a genuinely spacious footprint. The catch is that word, when. The Room isn't fleet-wide, and passengers booking business class on an older 787 will find a noticeably different, less private product. That inconsistency across aircraft is the one thing keeping ANA from climbing into the top two. Everything else about the airline is close to flawless. Number two, Cathay Pacific. At number [music] two, Cathay Pacific is the strongest comeback story among Asia's elite carriers. Hong Kong remains Cathay's [music] base, and the airline has spent the past few years rebuilding both its network and its reputation. And by most measures, it succeeded. Its economy class experience is frequently singled out as best in class. And on the ground, The Pier and The Wing lounges remain among the finest business class lounges anywhere in the world, spacious, calm, genuinely designed for long layovers, rather than just brief stops. In the air, Cathay's new Aria Suite is rolling out across its long-haul [music] fleet, joining an already strong product on the A350 and 777. And the airline's recognition through 2025 and 2026 reflects real momentum. What keeps it just short of first place is something harder to quantify, warmth. Service on Cathay is polished and professional, but passengers and reviewers alike note that it doesn't carry quite the same emotional warmth as Japan Airlines, ANA, or Singapore Airlines. It's an airline doing almost everything right, just not with the same human touch as the very best. Number one, Singapore Airlines. And that brings us to number one, Singapore Airlines. It isn't always the cheapest option, and it's rarely the airline you choose to [music] save money. But cabin for cabin, route for route, it's the most complete airline in Asia. Based at Changi, Singapore Airlines delivers a version of consistency [music] that few competitors can match. Economy class is comfortable and well executed across the fleet. Premium economy holds up as one of the strongest in the region. And business class, along with first class and suites where available, has defined the upper end of air travel for years. Its KrisWorld entertainment system remains one of the most extensive in the industry. And KrisFlyer members, membership is free to join, can access complimentary Wi-Fi, a small detail that adds up over a long flight. The trade-off is price. Singapore Airlines rarely competes on cost, and that premium is real. But what earns it the top spot [music] isn't any single seat or cabin. It's that the experience holds together across aircraft, across routes, across cabins, in a way no other airline on this list quite matches. No airline here is truly perfect. Singapore Airlines simply carries fewer compromises than anyone else. A list like this is never the final word. The right airline for you depends on the route you're flying, the aircraft assigned that day, the cabin you can afford, and what you actually value most in the air. Asia's best carriers all win in different ways. That's what makes this region so interesting to watch. So, we want to know, which airline would you move up this list, and which one would you move down? reviews.transcript_full: Welcome to the X-Pro Stay Channel.  Today, we are taking you along on Turkish Airlines flight 1888 Taka's from Vienna to Istanbul,  flying on the spacious Airbus A330.  If you're curious about the airport lounge experience in Vienna before we take off,  make sure to check out the dedicated lounge video right here on our channel.  Honestly, the flight was absolutely fantastic from start to finish.  Right after boarding, it was great to see that we received comfortable pillows, blankets,  and our own complimentary headphones for the flight.  As we cruised, I explored the Inflite Entertainment System.  The movie selection is massive, featuring everything from the latest blockbusters and  popular animations to a great mix of music and TV shows.  There is easily enough content to keep you entertained for hours.  Another huge highlight was the onboard catering.  For such a short flight, we actually had a choice between two different hot meals.  Turkish Airlines is truly amazing for this, because getting a proper, delicious meal in  economy class is a rare luxury these days. During the flight, I also visited the  lavatory and was really pleased to see how nicely clean and well maintained it was,  complete with good quality hand soap and lotion. It's always a big plus when an airline keeps  up with cleanliness mid-flight.  The only minor detail that didn't work was the connecting gate info screen,  which was supposed to display our transfer gates for Istanbul Airport.  Luckily, navigating the beautiful Istanbul terminal upon arrival was still very smooth.  To wrap things up, this Turkish Airlines flight from Vienna to Istanbul on the Airbus A330  was an absolute pleasure. From the great comfort pillows and headphones provided at the start,  to the spotless lavatory and the massive movie selection, they really know how to take care  of their passengers. Plus, getting a choice of two delicious hot meals on such a short economy flight  is something you rarely see these days. Despite the minor glitch with the connecting gate screen,  I highly recommend flying with them. Thank you for watching, and don't forget to subscribe to  XproStay for more travel reviews.

reviews.transcript_full: Welcome to Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, in early February 2025! Heading toward Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport Terminal 2, which opened in 2018. Today, we're flying on China Southern Airlines flight CZ 381 from Guangzhou to Brisbane, Australia. China Southern, Asia's largest airline, operates a massive fleet of 700 aircraft—with Guangzhou as its main hub. Checking out the China Southern Lounge in the international departures area. It scores a 6 out of 10 — a bit small and cramped. China Southern operates a fleet of 20 Airbus A350-900 aircraft on long-haul routes to Europe and Australia. Our aircraft for tonight's flight to Brisbane: an Airbus A350-900 (registration: B-32AV), delivered in October 2022. Boarding for flight CZ 381 begins at 20:07 at gate A147, 48 minutes ahead of our scheduled departure. Stepping into China Southern's Airbus A350-900 Business Class cabin, featuring a 1-2-1 zigzag seating configuration. The cabin offers a total of 28 lie-flat beds, giving everyone direct aisle access. Settling into seat 9A. It's a window seat featuring a great privacy divider between the galley and the lie-flat bed. Aircraft doors close right on time at 20:42 as the safety video begins to play. An in-flight security officer — known as a "Fangbao" — is seated right behind me, equipped with a bodycam. Fangbaos stay with the plane at outstations like Brisbane and fly right back to China, which is why they are seated in Business Class. Pushback begins at 20:49, 6 minutes ahead of our scheduled 20:55 departure. Taxiing out to Guangzhou's Runway 01R, which stretches 3,600 meters (11,811 feet). Taking off from Guangzhou at 21:12 China Standard Time. It's a surprisingly chilly night for the tropics, sitting at just 10°C. At 7,300 km, this is a short route for the A350 (15,750 km max range) — making for a very light, easy takeoff roll. Goodbye Guangzhou and Mainland China! Listen to the magnificent roar of the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines, each capable of producing 84,000 lbf of max thrust. China Southern selected the Recaro CL6710 model for its Business Class cabin. The seat extends into a fully lie-flat bed reaching up to 208 cm (approx. 6'10") in length. The great-circle distance between Guangzhou and Brisbane is 7,062 km, with a scheduled gate-to-gate block time of 9 hours and 20 minutes. Dinner service begins 40 minutes after takeoff at 21:52, starting with an amuse-bouche. The appetizer cart arrives at 22:10, offering pork pâté with mango salad or a prawn and chicken salad alternative. Cruising smoothly directly over Manila, Philippines. The main course — a Western option of beef with potatoes — is served at 22:16. The dessert cart comes around at 22:41 with a choice of fresh fruit, cheese, or ice cream. The entire four-course dinner concludes by 22:52 — just 1 hour and 40 minutes after takeoff. That is remarkably swift service. Economy Class features 307 seats in a standard 3-3-3 layout. Note that Premium Economy is not available on this configuration. Checking out the IFE. There is a decent selection of Western movies, but it doesn't quite match Emirates or Singapore Airlines. At 00:57 — 4 hours and 45 minutes into the flight — we are just about to cross the equator over the Maluku Islands in the Halmahera Sea. Watch the latitude value in the lower right corner of the flight tracking app flip from positive to negative! With La Niña in full swing in early 2025, this equatorial region around Indonesia is packed with remarkably powerful thunderstorms. Cruising through a turbulent Intertropical Convergence Zone tonight over the Arafura Sea, right between Western New Guinea and Australia. The pilots are constantly navigating around severe thunderstorm cells over the Gulf of Carpentaria. Anyone getting Air France flight AF447 vibes? First signs of daylight approaching at 03:30 China Standard Time. Flying over Northern Queensland, Australia. Time to set our clocks 2 hours forward, transitioning from China Standard Time to Australian Eastern Standard Time. The cabin crew begins serving breakfast at 05:50 — a full 1 hour and 45 minutes before landing. That feels a bit too early. Once again, opting for the hot Western option featuring an omelette, sausages, and baked beans. Total sleep time is just 5 hours between the end of dinner and the start of breakfast—a bit too short for a proper rest. The seatbelt signs switch back on at 07:00, 35 minutes before arrival. Chinese regulations mandate that all seats must be fully upright at the top of descent, significantly cutting down on flatbed relaxation time. That said, the 5-minute mood lighting show to wake up the cabin is a really nice feature by China Southern. Cloudy skies outside. February brings the rainy season here during the Southern Hemisphere's summer. Flying over Bribie Island with a view looking out toward the Sunshine Coast. Moreton Island stands in the background as the aircraft makes a turn over Moreton Bay. Lining up for Brisbane's Runway 19R, which is 3,300 meters (10,827 feet) long. Welcome to Brisbane Airport, Queensland, Australia! It's now 07:35 Australian Eastern Standard Time, marking a total flight time of 8 hours and 23 minutes. Taxiing toward Brisbane Airport's International Terminal. Despite the early wake-up call, this was definitely a dream flight in a modern, luxurious Business Class product between two amazing destinations. With ongoing terminal modernizations, the immigration, customs, and biosecurity checkpoints were a bit of an unpleasant zoo. Stepping out into the warm, tropical Australian air here at the Brisbane Airport station. Catching the Gold Coast Line train from the airport down to Helensvale, which takes around 90 minutes. Queensland Rail trains operate on a distinct narrow-gauge system (1,067 mm). Transferring at Helensvale to the G:link tram to reach our final destination: Surfers Paradise. Enjoy some beach impressions from the Gold Coast, stretching from Surfers Paradise down to Tweed Heads! What do you think about China Southern Airlines, especially their long-haul premium product? Let me know in the comments below. Thanks for watching! Please subscribe to my channel, doc7austin's DreamlinerCentral.

reviews.transcript_full: Greetings everyone from Kuala lumpur international airport. Thank you for joining us! Today we're experiencing Singapore Airlines business class on their shortest route, from Kuala Lumpur to Singapore. Singapore Airline deliver outstanding service—whether it's the cabin setup, the meals, or the overall service. So, can they still keep up the great service? Let's check it out together. This is the T1 Satellite Building. It's got this round design, and the gates are spread out in four different directions. There's no Singapore Airlines-operated lounge at Kuala Lumpur airport. Singapore Airlines runs at least 8 daily services,they are always full. Crazy busy! This 5.3‑year‑old Airbus A350‑900 will be taking me to Singapore. The crew's smiles gave me an instant sense of warmth as I boarded. This seat is pretty much the standard now for Singapore Airlines business class. You'll see it on most of their A350s and 787s. There are 40 seats in business class, from row 11 to row 21, with 4 seats per row. Only 40 minutes in the air, but they've still got a pillow and blanket set out for you, nice touch. Small sliding storage with USB and power， ideal for phone, earphones,or other little items. Touchscreen panel for all the controls. Lights, seat adjustment, IFE switch – everything's there. And the icons are so clear, you can't really mess it up." I've got to say, legroom is limited. When I lie flat and bend my knees, always touch the sides. For just rest, fine. But for a longer fligt, that would get uncomfortabl a little. Clever and thoughtful, love this design. Adjustable reading light. The headrest is soft and resilient. The pillow is so fluffy. The tray table is placed right below the screen, so it's really easy to use. And it fits in perfectly with the overall design of the seat. But the only downside is that it takes up a bit of legroom. Welcome drinks included orange juice, apple juice, and water. But since it was breakfast time, no champagne was offered. The crew brought another hot towel. Honestly, that woke me right up. Ambient lighting and reading light on and off. When you're sleeping or just don't want to be disturbed, you can press this button. The flight was so short that the seatbelt sign actually went off just five minutes after takeoff. Honestly, I thought it'd just be a bottle of water and a sandwich – but nope, they brought out a proper light meal and drinks too.  Option one is Japanese-style soba, a light noodle dish. Loved the texture of the noodles - nice and springy. So flavorful.  Option two is a Malaysian-style salad. Fresh ingredients, looks so healthy! Cheers, everyone! Now, let's see how this seat transforms into a bed. Fully flat, great privacy around the head. The only downside is the limited legroom. Full cabin view with Business class. So, do you think this 40‑minute business class flight is worth it? How would you rate the overall experience? Feel free to leave your comments! Looking forward to our next journey together, see you next time !
