reviews.transcript_full: The A380 on Singapore Airlines known to most for the streets on the upper deck, arguably  the most luxurious commercial aviation products have been built.  But today, I'm in economy, hosting 18.5 inches of seat width, one of the widest economy  seats owing to the sheer size of this aircraft.  Today's route is Singapore to Sydney on SQ-231, a red-eyed parting Singapore just passed  midnight with a total flight time of 7.5 hours.  Let's see what the A380 on Singapore Airlines actually feels like in the back of the bus.  Singapore Airlines operates out of Terminal 3 at Changi Airport.  In the world's best airport, 14 times by Skytrikes.  Checking counters are at Rho 3 and 4, with plenty of self-service kiosk if you want them.  I went to the desk as I wanted an actual boarding pass, not a floppy piece of paper from a  kiosk.  The entire process took about 10 minutes with the queue and if you're short on time,  the kiosk with automated backdrop make it even faster.  Not long after, I was ASI.  The transit area at Changi is its own thing entirely.  Food and beverage, luxury duty-free, liquor, versalaction is immense.  There are well-designed seating spaces everywhere you look from proper lounging areas to productivity  setups to dining.  It was passed 11pm and I wasn't feeling particularly hungry, so I found a quiet corner and said,  I love this airport.  It's the only one in the world where you genuinely don't feel like lounge access is necessary.  Today's departure gate is B7, roughly a 5-minute walk from the immigration area in Terminal  3.  If there's one thing that consistently gets brought up as a friction point at Changi,  it's the security screening that happens at the gate itself.  I got through security almost immediately only to be greeted by a packed seating area.  Fun fact, the aircraft taking me to Sydney tonight is on its first commercial flights of  the coming out of months of maintenance in Spain.  During an A380, an economy is a serious waiting game and the numbers explain why.  Business class alone is 78 passengers.  By the time you work through sweets, business, premium economy and however many economy zones  they have carved out, it makes you acutely aware of how far down the food chain you are.  The line moves slowly and I eventually made my way to 66h.  I selected this seat right before checking after spotting what looked like an empty row  on the seat map as it turns out the whole row was mine.  Having a whole row to yourself on a packed red-eye flight is like winning the lottery.  People call it the poor man's business class but I prefer the term make shift business  class.  After what seemed like a long-browling process I finally settled in and the first thing  waiting for me was the signature hot towel.  After 30 minutes of shuffling down an aisle with a couple hundred people, it's a huge  stress reliever.  The seat itself 32 inches of pitch and 18.5 inches of width.  Above average for economy and noticeably so at 178cm tall I had enough leg room.  The in-flight entertainment screen is 11 inches with an adjustable angle to touch response  is decent not laggy.  Load screen on the left you get a USB-A charging point, reading light controls, call button  and a two pin headphone jack.  On the subject of the provided headphones it's not the best.  If you can bring a blue-tooth transmitter that plugs into the two pin jack and pair it  straight to your airport.  The sound quality difference is significant and on a long flight it's worth it.  The new tray table has a vanity mirror built in, it's an odd placement but it's there  if you need it on the right there's a cup holder.  Useful between new service when you want somewhere to put a drink, standard blanket and  pillow provided, worth noting for window seat sleepers.  The A380 is so wide that the wall is too far to lean against.  Chris World is extremely well stocked.  Singapore Airlines updates their library regularly with the latest blockbusters.  You'd be hard pressed to fault it.  We push back slightly late.  The flight was intentionally delayed to allow some connecting passengers to make it.  Our estimate economy was around 85% full and we taxied out to it, run way zero to center  and took off into the moonlit skies.  Shortly after takeoff, refreshment service comments.  Two options were offered, mozzarella, mushroom pizza bar and margarita pizza bar, along with  coffee or tea, beer, soft drinks, wine and cocktails were available too.  I went with the margarita pizza bar and it delivered cheesy, good umami and the bread texture  was decent.  It's a great late night snack, just don't expect the quality of a naveli pizza.  After the crew made their rounds to clear the rubbish, I got comfortable in my makeshift  business class seat.  It was amazing.  And I wholeheartedly endorsed gaming the system to snack a whole row for free on empty flights.  Keep checking up to when checking closes.  Singapore Airlines offers complimentary wifi to every economy passenger, but only if you  tag your ticket to your Chris Flyer account during checking.  Speeds are solid for general browsing but don't expect to stream 4k videos on your phone.  On this front, airlines like Carter with Scarling have an edge.  Singapore Airlines is planning to upgrade their fleet with Starlink from 2027.  So this is only going to get better.  After the best economy sleep I've had, breakfast came around.  I went with the scrambled eggs with cheese and chicken sausage, accompanied by a fruit  platter, strawberry yogurt and a bread roll with butter.  Full beverage service was available with hot and cold options.  There are usually three options for mains on flight to Australia.  Western, Indian and an East Asian or Singaporean option.  The metal cutlery is a nice touch and its genius marketing on their part.  Research shows that the tactile experience of handling heavier items triggers a higher  perceived value.  For an economy meal, it was solid.  If they had offered the Singaporean fried carrot cake, I would have gone for that.  As new service wrapped up, we were fast approaching Sydney.  The crew prepped the cabin for landing and soon we were on approach.  Follow me on Singapore Airlines is one of the best in the industry.  It's not easy to differentiate an economy class, but there are some standout features  such as the hot towel service and above all, the crew.  I've flown an economy class on other five star carriers and while the hard product  is often comparable, the crew experience ends to fall short.  On Singapore Airlines, the crew is the difference maker.  It's what the brand has been built on and it's what keeps me coming back.  As I've mentioned in previous videos, the crew have the ability to straddle both eastern  formality and western casualness in a way that's unique to places like Singapore.  Beyond the product itself, what Singapore Airlines is really selling is trust.  You're buying the confidence that you'll be taken care of.  That if something goes wrong, it gets resolved quickly and competently.  That's why I would gladly pay a premium for Singapore Airlines economy.  If you would like to check out my return flight to Singapore in business class, that video  is up right now.  Drop a like and subscribe if this was off-value to you and I'll see you in the next one.

reviews.transcript_full:
Hello everyone. Welcome back to another video. I 
apologize, it's been a while since I last posted,   but today I'm so excited to fly Etihad's business 
class on their A380 from Toronto to Abu Dhabi.   If you've looked at my other videos, you'd 
know that I rarely fly business class. So,   while I am stoked to fly today, I still want 
to make it a fair review. As always, I'm so   grateful for the opportunity to do things like 
this. So, don't mistake any criticism for a lack   of gratitude. Etihad departs from Terminal 1 at 
Toronto with business and first class passengers   using the Plaza Premium Lounge in the domestic 
area of Terminal 1. We arrived a little late,   so we didn't go inside. The lounge is sufficient, 
but it can get crowded during peak times. Now, for the seat map. On the Etihad A380, the 
entire main deck is filled with 405 economy seats   in a 3-4-3 layout. The best economy seat here is 
69D because there's a missing seat in front of it.   Similarly, both 76A and 76K have almost 
infinite legroom. Moving to the upper deck,   there are 70 business class seats in a staggered 
1-2-1 layout. Half of the seats are closer to the   aisles and face backward, while the arguably 
better other half are closer to the windows   and face forward, offering more privacy. In the 
center are the honeymoon seats, which are close   together in private for people traveling 
together. First class, on the other hand,   has nine seats in a staggered 1-1 layout with 
some seats being closer to the aisle or window   and some facing forwards and backward. And of 
course, seats 1A and 1C are the Residence. My   seat on today's flight is the more exposed 13C, 
but regardless, it's still a great product. At each seat, there is a plush blanket...
...a really nice mattress topper... ...and a large pillow... The noise cancelling headphones 
provided are very good. ...with the nicest slippers I've ever seen. The amenity kits are from Armani 
Kasa and have various Espa products. Now for a seat tour. In front there's an 18.5   bright touchscreen IFE. Below that is 
the footwell with storage beneath it. To the right is the standard 
Panasonic remote for the IFE   that extends. You can view the flight map 
on it independently from the main screen. Below are some seat controls. And next to the   seat is a storage cubby with 
headphones and a water bottle. Just above is a modern mood 
light and a reading light. Next to the if there's a large table. 
It can be pushed forward so that you   can leave the seat while eating with a 
table light above. Next to the remote,   there's a control panel 
for various seat functions. The seat has lumbar support, 
which while it sounds cool,   it basically feels like sitting on 
a balloon. If it fails and deflates,   it's basically like sitting on a metal 
bench. There is also a privacy partition   at all aisle seats. As this is an A380, there 
are large storage cubbies at every seat on the   upper deck as well. There aren't individual 
air vents, but the flight was cold enough. Now for the if It's called E-Box with the 
home screen laid out in a series of, well,   boxes. The touch screen isn't the most responsive, 
but that's why there's a remote. There's plenty of   movies and TV shows with a search menu 
at the bottom to easily find content. There's also live TV... ...a kids menu... ...seat to seat... ...chat and call... ...and outboard cameras and a movie map. Dinner service started with a bowl of 
warm nuts and a drink of your choice. I got the Arabic Mezze to start, the beef short 
rib as a main, and the cheese plate and ice cream   for dessert. The meal overall was very high 
quality and delicious, with no complaints. After that, I got a hot chocolate which came 
with...more chocolate. (It was really good,   though). The bar on board, referred 
to as the lobby, is a nice place to   hang out with the self-service bar, too. 
While it is dark and possibly uninviting,   it is a really cozy place to be in after 
sitting for hours in the same place. All the toilets on board are spacious and 
kept very clean throughout the flight. It   has more amenities from Espa and overall 
they just look super cool and modern. There is Wi-Fi on board, with Etihad guests 
receiving free messaging. I didn't purchase   Wi-Fi, but it's roughly $20 for the entire 12-hour 
flight. I made the most of the flight by trying as   many things as possible off the all-day menu, like 
these blueberry soufflé pancakes and the granola   yogurt bowl, which, for some reason, came with a 
cheese plate and cookies. Maybe I'm just easily   impressed because I don't fly business class 
often, but they both tasted really, really good. Listen, it's not often I'm able to fly business 
class like this. So, yes, I was easily impressed.   However, I want to evaluate the aspects of the 
product by talking about two distinct things:   the hard product and the soft product. The 
hard product is the seat itself and the cabin,   while the soft product is a service, food, and 
amenities. Let's start with the hard product.   The seat came out roughly 10 years ago, 
and while it looks modern and good, there's   definitely some wear and tear with some of the 
things like the windows wouldn't work properly. Also, backwards facing seats have slightly less 
pitch by a few inches, so if you're tall like me,   it may be a bit tight in the footwell. Besides 
that, the food was really good and high quality.   The amenity kit had sufficient amenities, and 
while the crew from Middle Eastern Airlines   can be hit or miss, the crew here were pretty 
friendly. I especially like the mood lighting   in the cabin with many elements featuring the 
Lights of Abu Dhabi theme with a lamp that   mimics sunlight under a palm tree, and triangles 
basically everywhere. A lot of thought and work   went into making this product and cabin, and it 
definitely still feels like this 10 years later.   I really enjoyed my time on Etihad today. And 
while I don't fly business class too often,   hopefully this gives you an insight into the 
experience on board. Now, time for landing. Thank you.

yt_comments.text: Not bad for a startup, but of course there are flaws: 1. No personal airvents 2. No universal power outlets in economy, I think only included in business class, which is a shame. 3. Weak Wi-Fi for a premium full service carrier that is digitally native (should have just stuck with StarLink) 4. Average lavatory, very ordinary, nothing special like Emirates Or Qatar Airways. 5. No onboard external cameras (forwards and downwards) QR and EK offer them on almost every aircraft and dreamliners are supposed to have them. 6. Safety Video seems to have used lots of AI and CGI (not necessarily a complaint but apparently some were bothered by it.) 7. Tray table cannot be extended, if seat in front reclines, can be difficult for the passenger. Some of the positives: 1. Very aesthetic mood lighting 2. Premium cabin with generous recline 3. Comfortable seats 4. Generous meal portions even for a short haul domestic flight 5. Massive screen (13.3inch for economy) with Wi-Fi (regardless of speed as some airlines don’t even offer it) and responsive. 6. Experienced staff, lots of former cabin crews from EK, QR, EY etc. 7. Metal cutlery provided, lavender scented hot towels, branded soaps and other little touches that make the experience much better 8. In-built headphones inside the headrests for passengers in premium economy and business class 9. Business elite is said to be even better than some airlines first class suites 10. Bluetooth pairing with personal headphones 11. One of the best in-flight map, interactive experience with the IfE, good content for a start-up, with games, music and much more. 12. reviews.transcript_full: Hello everyone and welcome back to my Disneyland series. Today we are talking all about our experience flying Southwest Airlines. I've actually only ever flown Southwest my entire life. So when they announced they were getting rid of open seating and switching to assigned seats, I was really curious to see what the experience would be like. This trip was also our first time flying with four kids and traveling carry-on only, which honestly made me nervous. Especially because my son Asher is autistic. We were originally assigned one of the last boarding groups and Southwest no longer offers family boarding the way they used to. Thankfully things ended up going much smoother than I expected and I was really impressed with our experience. So if you're flying Southwest, traveling with kids, traveling with an autistic child, or just curious about their new boarding process, here's how everything went for us from check-in all the way through landing in California. One thing I really appreciate about Southwest Airlines is that families can check strollers and car seats for free. You can do this at the ticket counter before security or at the gate if you'd rather use the stroller throughout the airport. We gate checked ours so it would be waiting for us on the jet bridge as soon as we landed. Okay, now you've checked in, printed your boarding pass, made it through security and found your gate. It is now time to board your plane. As I mentioned earlier, our family had been assigned the last boarding group, group eight. Normally that wouldn't be a big deal at all, but for our family it was a little more complicated. I know some families actually prefer to board last with their young children and that just works better for them. For us, with Asher being autistic, we absolutely need that extra time to get him on board, familiarize with his seat, comfortable with the seatbelt, and to just adjust before there are too many people on board. Southwest no longer offers family boarding the way they used to. Instead they offer pre-boarding for customers with disabilities or anyone who needs additional boarding assistance. Even though Southwest states only one person will be able to accompany the disabled passenger, I just explained my 5-year-old is autistic and asked if we could pre-board. The gate agent immediately said yes. I then asked if our entire family would be able to board together since it was just me, my husband, and our four young children. I am so grateful they also said yes to that without hesitation. We had a backup plan just in case, but I'm so thankful they were able to accommodate all six of us this time. It changed the whole entire flight for us. I can't guarantee every family's experience will be the same as ours, but it never hurts to politely ask. Once boarding began, it was surprisingly quick. I had heard stories that assigned seating actually slowed down Southwest's boarding process, but that wasn't our experience at all, and both of our flights were completely full. The boarding process was very efficient, and I feel it was faster than when we would board with open seating. I think people choosing and changing their mind while on board made it take longer. Okay, now we are officially on the plane and ready to take off. Southwest is in the process of upgrading all of their planes. These upgrades will include extra legroom seats, USB ports in the seatback, adjustable headrests, and device holders above your tray table. I did not expect us to have an upgraded plane from Austin International Airport to LAX, but we got so lucky. And wow. These upgrades are amazing, okay? Like just outstanding. The standard seats felt like I had more legroom than in the past. The device holder was awesome. It held our Kindles, iPads, phones, and they were more eye-level versus having them much lower on your lap or on your tray table. And the adjustable headrests, oh my goodness. I slept so good with the headrests, and it was the first time ever on a plane that I did not need a neck pillow to sleep because they just supported my neck and head so well and were oh so comfortable. On flights 250 miles or more, you will be served complimentary graham crackers, pretzels, and drinks. Here's what you can get for free during your flight and here's what you can pay extra for if you would like an alcoholic beverage. Unfortunately, and this is like the only thing I wish Southwest would change, is this is the only food offerings on board no matter how long your flight is. I do wish they were heavier options available for purchase, maybe like a snack pack, fruit and cheese tray, or sandwich, or something like that. Southwest Airlines doesn't have screens in the back of their seats. They do offer tons of free movies, TV shows, and even live TV for their in-flight entertainment. They offer a great range of movies from classics to new releases like The Housemate, Wicked for Good, and Zootopia 2. To access the in-flight entertainment, just turn on airplane mode on your device, connect to Southwest Wi-Fi, and then open up your Southwest app and click on flight entertainment and it will guide you right through. Southwest also has just introduced free Wi-Fi for Rapid Rewards members. You can sign up for the Rapid Rewards for free on the Southwest website. You can then connect to the free Wi-Fi the same way as accessing the in-flight entertainment. Just sign in with your Rapid Rewards info and password when prompted, watch one quick ad, and then free Wi-Fi for the rest of your flight. Now, on the flight to California, the Wi-Fi was extremely slow and eventually stopped working altogether. So, I switched to their free movies and ended up watching Jurassic Park 2 until I fell asleep. The Wi-Fi seemed to work for simple things like if I needed to look something up on Google, but then trying to stream Hulu on it just did not work at all. It buffered a ton until it just cut out altogether. On the flight back from LA, the Wi-Fi just would not work at all even for simple web browsing. They also offer the option to buy Wi-Fi for $8 per device. We used this once on one of our previous flights years ago and I didn't notice any trouble at all with the paid Wi-Fi. It worked perfectly. Our flight attendants were great as they always are. They were friendly, very conversational with us and they gave us a lid and straw for the kids drinks that they ordered, which was a small gesture that made a big difference. So yeah, that was our experience flying Southwest Airlines to Disneyland. Overall, Southwest Airlines made what could have been a very stressful travel day feel smooth and effortless, especially traveling with four kids. The employees were incredibly kind and helpful and thankfully we had no major issues at all. So if you're thinking about flying Southwest, hopefully this gave you a little idea of what the experience is like. Thank you so much for watching. Next week we're finally getting into the actual Disneyland portion of this trip and I cannot wait to share that with you because this trip was absolutely incredible. Make sure you're subscribed if you'd like to follow along and I'll see you in the next one. Bye everyone. That was our journey as our first time traveling with four children on Southwest Airlines. If you made it this far, thanks so much for watching and subscribe to see our travel day and actual days at Disneyland next week.

And by 1997, just a few years into this gold rush, four out of six of the major newcomers were already dead. I guess, speaking of being killed, East-West Airlines, one of the biggest of the new carriers, [music] in 1975, its founder, a Mumbai travel agent named Thakiyuddin Wahid, was literally assassinated on the street outside his office. Police suspected gang involvement from day one. There were all sorts of shady accusations thrown around, but either way, I guess that's just kind of the market that this was back then. East-West itself was shut down under a year later. So, that's our first wave. Mostly underfunded startup airlines in what I guess we can call a hard-to-navigate system. Of course, all of these deaths, literally an actual death, didn't stop people from trying. The prize was simply too big. So, in the early 2000s, there's a second wave, but this time things were a bit different. This time around, there were billionaires, conglomerates, and proven airline operators entering the fray, [music] and well, also low-cost carriers this time. All arriving at a time when the Indian economy was taking off. Surely, they would all be fine this time around, right? But, before we get to the rest of the story, let's first get on this Indigo flight. And we also have a message from this week's video sponsor, Soundcore. This is, of course, the audio sub-brand of Anker. Now, I've been using these Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro and the Liberty 5 Pro Max for the last few weeks, including on a trip to India and the Maldives. I of course had to test that out on one of my flights. >> This is uh no headphones at all, just using the iPhone microphone. Flying from Kuala Lumpur to Adelaide. And this is the another very popular brand of headphones. I'm flying from Kuala Lumpur to Adelaide. Okay, quick test of the audio on these. Um added sound. I'm currently flying from Kuala Lumpur to Adelaide. >> Yeah, they are ridiculously good at cutting out background sounds. You basically can't tell that I was on a plane there. And look, as the sophisticated businessman that I am, this is important. If I'm in an airport, at a train station, on a busy city street and I need to take a call, I don't want to always have to be apologizing for the noise around me. I just want to be heard loud and clear. Now, you might be thinking, what's the difference between the Liberty 5 Pro and the Liberty 5 Pro Max? Well, it all comes down to the case. The Max has a 1.78-in AMOLED touchscreen that lets you control your music and your noise cancellation levels all without having to pull out your phone. And it also has this AI note-taking feature. You can just double tap the case to start recording and once you're done, this automatically gets uploaded to the Soundcore app and it auto-generates a transcript with speaker and a summary and it even produces a to-do list from that recording. For me, this is particularly useful for quickly remembering those random video ideas that I want to get back to later. Now, let's get back to our regularly scheduled programming. >> Welcome to Indigo. We would love to to off with you at the earliest. >> So, it's the early 2000s. The Indian economy is booming, the middle class is exploding, and well, the aviation landscape is still very full service. We've got Air India, Indian Airlines, and the two survivors of that first wave, Jet Airways and Air Sahara. Flying is still something only really rich Indians can do, but the opportunity for a low-cost alternative is obviously enormous. And this is where Indigo finally enters our story, though not in the way that you'd expect. Indigo doesn't start with a flashy launch event or aircraft order. No, it starts with Rahul Bhatia being asked to resurrect a dead airline from that first wave called Modiluft. Modiluft was launched in 1993 as a partnership between an Indian businessman, S.K. Modi, and if you can't guess from the name, Lufthansa. But after just 3 years of operations, the partnership exploded and the airline stopped flying. Now, that should have been the end of the story, but the remaining corporate corpse still held something extremely valuable, an airline operating license. And in a country where getting a new license means running the government gauntlet, a pre-existing license is worth real money. So, in 2000, a London-based Indian investor named Bhupendra Kansagra picks up that corpse and starts planning a low-cost relaunch. Now, he doesn't just do this alone. He also approaches a Delhi businessman to help him pull it off, Rahul Bhatia. But why Bhatia? Well, Bhatia wasn't an airline operator, but he had spent years inside [music] of the Indian travel trade. His family's company, InterGlobe, had spent years operating as a GSA. I guess we need a bit of a quick explainer here. Back in the day, if you were a foreign airline flying into India, unless you were huge, you generally didn't build your own sales operation in the country. You appointed a general sales agent, a GSA, instead. This was the one local company that would essentially be your entire commercial presence in the country. This was of course the pre-internet era, so virtually every plane ticket was being sold through a travel agent. Being a GSA was a pretty powerful role, and well, InterGlobe was the GSA for the who's who of foreign airlines, United, Delta, Virgin Atlantic, that sort of thing. So, if you're trying to resurrect an airline in India, Rahul Bhatia is a pretty useful guy to have on your side. And as the project progressed, he even coined the name for this reborn carrier, IndiGo, as in India on the go. >> But hold up. Wait a minute. Something ain't right. >> If you're paying attention earlier, then you might be asking, "Where is Rakesh Gangwal in all of this?" The other co-founder of IndiGo. Well, this airline, the revived ModiLuft, is not IndiGo. The relationship between Bhatia and Consagra never worked out, and Bhatia ended up walking away entirely. The airline would actually end up being SpiceJet, which still operates today. But when Bhatia walked away from that failed revival, he left with two things. The first was a decision. He still wanted an airline, but the next one would be his own, built from scratch his way. And the second thing was, well, that IndiGo name, [music] the one that he coined himself. It was, however, still legally inside the company that would become SpiceJet. So, Bhatia had to buy it back, by his own accounts for 25,000 rupees, only a few hundred US dollars at the time. Not a bad deal, really, in hindsight. So, it's around 2004, and Bhatia has a name and the decision. What he doesn't have is someone who can actually run an airline. He needed a world-class operator. He earned his way into IIT, India's famously brutal elite engineering school, and like a lot of ambitious Indian engineers of his generation, he then made the jump to America, where he eventually became a consultant. >> They're not good. >> No, they're not all airline-destroying demons. He would go on to rise up through the ranks. There was a short stint at Air France, and then in 1998, he became the president and CEO of US Airways. Quick aside, as far as I can tell, this made him the first Indian-born boss of a major American airline, and quite possibly of any major airline outside of India. Anyway, his time at the top was, well, educational. He ran US [music] Airways for a genuine turnaround attempt, and then resigned in 2001, right as the post-9/11 collapse was engulfing the entire American aviation industry. US Airways went bankrupt the following year, though, honestly, I think that one was more about 9/11 than it was about Gangwal. Either way, this was a guy who had seen how big airlines work, and he's seen how they die. And as luck would have it, Gangwal just happened to be an old friend of Bhatia's. The story goes that the two had crossed paths at United's headquarters in Chicago back in the mid-80s, and they'd stayed in touch ever since. Now, Gangwal took some convincing, and I guess can you blame him? He'd spent decades watching airlines lose money in the best aviation markets on Earth, and Bhatia [music] was pitching him an airline in one of the worst. There's actually a little legend about the moment that he finally agreed. The deal, supposedly, was that when the two of them eventually lost all their money on this venture, they would shake hands and stay friends. I guess that tells you something about their expectations going in. Either way, by the end of 2004, Gangwal was in. The company was quietly incorporated as InterGlobe Aviation, and then there was absolutely nothing. No press, no parties, no announcements, not until June of 2005, when they stepped onto the world stage in just about the loudest way possible. At the Paris Air Show that year, this airline that nobody had heard of, that had never flown a single passenger, and that didn't even have all its own permits yet, announces with Airbus that it was ordering 100 A320s. [music] At the time, it was one of the biggest single orders Airbus had ever received. At list prices, it was worth around 6 billion US dollars. But, of course, it reportedly came with enormous discounts. Anyway, IndiGo launched its first flight on the 4th of August 2006 from Delhi to Imphal via Guwahati. Year after year, plane after plane, almost exactly to plan. Until it was the biggest airline in India. Well, part of that, as we'll see, is some genuine secret sauce in how this airline is run. But, I guess the simpler part is that one by one, almost every other airline in India fell over. So, before we get to the secret sauce, we need to get to this bigger question. Why does the country keep killing its airlines? >> [music] >> Well, by the mid-2000s, the battlefield looked something like this. On one side, there's the established full-service carriers: Jet Airways, a polished market leader, Air Sahara, its smaller rival, and the two old [music] state carriers. And on the other side, we've got the new low-cost wave. There's Air Deccan, SpiceJet, GoAir, and IndiGo. And well, there's also one more, Kingfisher. Founded by the liquor and beer billionaire Vijay Mallya, this one was not low-cost. It was premium, or well, not even premium, more like ultra-premium. [music] So, we've got, say, nine airlines, half of them brand new, all piling into one market at exactly the same time. That kind of crowding does something very predictable. Fares dropped through the floor. And in that sort of environment, the airlines with the lowest costs are the only ones that can really survive. Now, you might assume India would be a cheap place to run an airline. Companies have been outsourcing work there for decades, and labor has been a real cost advantage in the country. But, funnily enough, India also has some of the most expensive jet fuel on the planet. We'll come back to exactly why in a little bit. But, rock-bottom fares and sky-high costs leads to a rather inevitable outcome, collapse. Now, I could give you five separate obituaries here, but this is really not necessary because almost every one of these airlines died of the same disease, >> [music] >> costs. The first big one to fall was Air Deccan. Air Deccan was founded by a former army captain named J.R. Gopinath, who, as the story goes, had this big epiphany on a Southwest Airlines flight in America. He was [music] sitting next to a working-class carpenter, and he wondered why a carpenter could fly in America but not in India. So, Air Deccan was built for the common man. Literally, it ran promotions selling tickets for one single rupee, and it grew like wildfire. [music] Within a few years, it was carrying around a fifth of India's domestic traffic. And as a revolution, Air Deccan absolutely [music] worked. It proved that ordinary Indians wanted to fly, and it brought millions of first-time flyers into the sky. But as a business, there was a problem. Deccan had the cheapest fares in India without having the cheapest costs. And a lot of those tickets were being sold for less than the cost of actually flying the passenger. But eventually, the losses piled up to the point where selling the airline became the only way out. [music] The buyer, of all people, was Vijay Mallya, which is a little strange, right? The king of ultra-premium suddenly buying the common man budget airline. Well, not really, because what Vijay Mallya wanted was not the Air Deccan brand. What he wanted was Air Deccan's age. See, India used to have this protectionist rule called the five and twenty rule. An Indian airline could not fly internationally until it had completed five years of domestic operations and built a fleet of at least twenty aircraft. This was very convenient for the established [music] players, who already qualified, but it was a hard lockout for every ambitious newcomer. >> [music] >> And Kingfisher, at this point, was two years old. Deccan was four. So, by buying Deccan, Mallya could inherit its clock and get to the prestigious international routes faster. So, that's exactly what he did. In India, it was not enough to be popular, premium, connected, state-backed, or even cheap. If your costs were wrong, the market would eventually catch up to you. You can have all the money, aircraft, staff, and demand in the world, but if you can't get a workable slot at the airport people actually want to use, you can't grow where the market is. I mean, they also only employ female flight attendants because it's on average they're lighter. [music] And then I guess after the six odd years, just as these planes are starting to get old enough to need [music] expensive heavy maintenance, and just as their fuel burn starts falling behind the latest models, they hand them back to the leasing [music] company and replace them with brand new jets straight off the production line. So, we've got a system where taxes are stacked [music] on top of taxes. And I guess for the accountants in the crowd, these all sit outside of the GST VAT system. So they're burning extra fuel to carry fuel to dodge fuel tax. This is the system every Indian airline operates in. Nobody can negotiate with it and nobody has managed to lobby it away completely. [music] And this is precisely why the young fleet matters so much for IndiGo. New planes burn less fuel than old ones. This is [music] actually a thing. But more importantly, the latest generation of jets like the A320 neo burn significantly less fuel, around 15% less. So IndiGo's eternally young fleet isn't just vanity, it's not just about maintenance. It's pretty much their most powerful cost weapon in Indian aviation. And that pretty much is the IndiGo model. You take the traditional low-cost airline system, run it with total discipline, but then add in one crucial modification for India specifically. You never fly old planes. And for 20 years, that kind of simplicity was the whole IndiGo story. And it's what made them the most dominant airline in India. But now that they've sort of won the domestic market, it's time for the next steps. And well, the future, that's not looking quite as simple. Yeah, that was a really modern aircraft, wasn't it? One of the A321 neos. They've got, I think, over 100 of them. The IndiGo planes are everywhere. They're massive. Yeah, anyway, it wasn't particularly good in any way. It was just clean and modern. There wasn't any charging, which is a little annoying. All my cameras are now well and truly dead, but that's fine. We're done. No more filming today. reviews.transcript_full: Three of the largest airlines in the Americas filed for bankruptcy within 7 weeks of each other. A fourth airline, far smaller than any of them, stopped flying entirely in the same crisis. Not most of its flights, but every single one. Its fleet sat parked for five straight months, and yet it never filed for anything. That same airline now posts operating margins that beat carriers many times its size, year after year, with one of the strongest balance sheets in the industry. And the strangest part of the story is that the decision that saved it was made 40 years before the pandemic ever existed [music] by people who had no idea a pandemic was coming. This is the story of Copa Airlines, the flag carrier of Panama, a country of around 4 and 1/2 million people. So, how exactly did the smallest player turn into the strongest? To answer that, we have to go back to 1944, to a small office in Panama City, where the whole story begins with an American partner that would eventually walk away. On June 21st of 1944, a group of Panamanian investors sat down with executives from Pan American World Airways and signed the documents to create a new company, Compania Panamena de Aviacion, Copa, for short. Pan Am took a 32% stake and brought the technical knowledge. The Panamanians brought the capital and the country. It took three more years before the airline actually flew. On August 15th of 1947, Copa lifted off for the first time, >> [music] >> operating three Douglas C-47 aircraft on domestic routes inside Panama. Three planes, three cities, a flag carrier in name only, working a route map that would fit on a postcard. For almost two decades, that is all that Copa was, a small domestic airline in a small country propped up by an American partner. The first international flight did not happen [music] until the 1960s, when Copa added three weekly services to San Jose in Costa Rica using a tiny mix of Avro 748s and Lockheed Electra 188s. Kingston in Jamaica followed. Then Cartagena and Barranquilla in Colombia. By the end of that decade, Copa had finally crossed the border, but only just. Its world still ended a couple of hours from home. The first turning point came in 1971. [music] Pan Am, dealing with its own problems and pulling capital out of regional partners across Latin America, sold its stake in Copa to a group of Panamanian investors. For the first time, the airline was wholly Panamanian [music] owned. No foreign safety net. No big brother in New York covering the gaps. If Copa was going to survive, the people in Panama City would have to figure it out themselves. And almost immediately, they ran into trouble. By the end of the 1970s, a domestic rival called Air Panama was eating into the routes [music] Copa had spent 30 years building. The math at home was getting worse >> [music] >> every year. Panama is a small country. S2 domestic airlines fighting over the same handful of cities is a slow death for both of them. Copa's leadership sat down to make a choice, shrink and die quietly or do something almost nobody in aviation would advise. [music] They went for the second option. In 1980, Copa walked away from the domestic market entirely. Not reduced, not restructured, gone. The airline that had been founded to fly Panamanians around Panama announced [music] it would no longer fly Panamanians around Panama. Every aircraft, every crew, every dollar of capital would now be aimed outward. The same year, Copa took delivery of its first jet aircraft, a Boeing 737-100. The propeller era ended, the international era began, and the country itself, not the passengers, became the product. At first glance, everybody thought that idea was ridiculous. Panama's population was smaller than many American cities. Nobody looked at a map and thought, "This is where one of the most profitable airlines on Earth should be born." But, Copa's leadership had noticed something the rest of the region [music] had not. Panama sits at one of the most useful pieces of geography anywhere on the planet. North America above, South America below, the Caribbean beside it. A narrow strip of land that connects everything. From Panama City, a single Boeing 737 could reach almost [music] every major city in North, Central, and South America without ever needing a wide-body. That unlocked a kind of math nobody else in the region could do. Two mid-size cities on opposite ends of the Americas might never have enough demand to fill [music] a direct flight between them. Run them both through Panama City, and the passengers from a dozen of those thin routes [music] meet in one place, get sorted, and continue on. A traveler from Guatemala connects to Buenos Aires. A traveler from Quito connects to Orlando. A traveler from San Jose connects to Santiago. All through one airport. But, there was a problem. In 1980, the airport was not [music] ready. Panama City's main field had limited capacity and limited reputation. So, through the '80s, Copa expanded slowly. Flights to Miami, to San Juan, and to Santo Domingo. Building experience, building credibility, building a route book. The real Copa Airlines, the airline that exists today, was born in 1992. That year, the airline moved its operations to Tocumen International Airport on [music] the edge of Panama City. And shortly afterward, branded the entire concept as the Hub of the Americas. >> [music] >> And then the expansion began for real. Between 1992 and 1997, Copa launched flights to Caracas, Mexico City, Santiago, Cali, Bogota, Quito, >> [music] >> Guayaquil, Lima, Buenos Aires, and Havana. 10 major Latin American capitals in 5 years. The route map [music] went from regional to continental. But it was still a small airline operating an aging fleet. And to get to the next level, it needed help. Help arrived in 1998 when Continental Airlines of Houston [music] took a major equity stake in Copa, eventually rising to 49%. The deal changed everything. Copa got access to Continental's operational systems, its scheduling discipline, its training programs, its purchasing power. >> [music] >> The livery was redesigned to look almost identical to Continental's. The fleet was modernized aggressively with new Boeing 737 Next Generation aircraft replacing the old jets. For the first time, the airline start to look and feel like a major international carrier. And here is something that [music] does not get talked about enough, well, at least in my personal humble opinion. The years under Continental's wing were a kind of management apprenticeship. Pedro Heilbron, who had taken over as chief executive in 1988 at the age of just 30, spent [music] the late '90s and early 2000s quietly absorbing how a serious airline runs itself. The discipline that would later astonish the industry was learned in [music] this period. The obsession with on-time performance, the fleet commonality, the refusal to expand without economic logic. None of it was invented by Copa. Most of it was learned from Houston. By 2005, Copa was ready to step out on its own. In April of that year, the airline acquired 99.8% of Aero Republica, a Colombian carrier with a fleet of MD-80s and DC-9s and a domestic network across 12 cities for roughly $23.4 million. It was $23.4 million. It was Copa's first acquisition. The Colombian operation would later be rebranded Copa Airlines Colombia. Eight months later, in December of 2005, Copa Holdings launched its initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange. The ticker was, and still is, CPA. A small airline from a small country was now a publicly traded company answering to American investors. The discipline that had been learned under Continental was now demanded by the market. The years that followed were a steady climb. New routes, new aircraft. The first Embraer 190 joined the fleet, making Copa the first Latin American operator of the type. The frequent flyer program was rebuilt, and in June 2012, Copa formally joined Star Alliance, the largest global airline alliance alongside United. New service to Las Vegas, Curacao, Recife, and Iquitos followed. The airline had gone from being a regional flag carrier to a fully integrated member of the global aviation network in roughly 30 years. And then in April of 2015, Copa placed [music] a single order that would define the rest of its story. 61 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft plus 10 options that were later exercised. A deal worth more than 6 and 1/2 billion dollars at list [music] prices. The airline was betting its entire future on one airframe family from one manufacturer. No Airbus, no wide bodies, nothing else. The same aircraft type Copa had been flying since 1980 would carry the airline into the next generation. That bet looked ordinary in 2015, but by 2020, it looked like genius. Because in the spring of 2020, Pedro Heilbron found himself sitting in one of the worst positions in aviation. Panama moved fast against the pandemic, very fast. >> [music] >> On March 23rd of 2020, international travel slammed into a wall. And within days, every Copa aircraft was parked on the ramp at Tocumen. The airport went quiet, the schedules disappeared, the passengers vanished. For nearly 5 months, Copa's entire network was effectively frozen. And that should have terrified anyone holding the stock. Because unlike most airlines on Earth, Copa had no safety net. Delta had a huge domestic market fall back on. American had one, United had one. Even most carriers in Latin America could keep a few wheels turning on domestic routes. Copa had no domestic operation at all. It had not had one since 1980. The single decision that built the airline was now the decision that exposed it. Now, look at what was happening around them. On May 10th of 2020, Avianca, one of the oldest airlines in the world, filed for bankruptcy protection in a New York court. 16 days later, LATAM, the biggest airline in South America, did the same thing. Before the end of June, Mexico's flag carrier, Aeroméxico, had joined them. Three of the largest airlines in the Americas went into Chapter 11 within 7 [music] weeks. And the airline that looked the most exposed of all simply stayed out of court. No bankruptcy, no restructuring, no emergency rescue. Heilbron waited. He lived off the cash on his own balance sheet. The cushion Copa had spent years >> [music] >> stacking up. When Panama finally cracked the door open in August of 2020, the airline restarted one route at [music] a time, 11 destinations, then more. By the end of the following year, it had won back [music] roughly 80% of its traffic. So, what did Heilbron know that the chief executives of three giant airlines did not? Simple answer, he knew exactly what was sitting in his own hangar. Walk through a Copa operation and the answer hits you immediately. Almost every aircraft looks the same. The airline built itself around the Boeing 737 [music] family and almost nothing else. The Embraer 190 fleet, the only exception in modern times, was sold off to Australia's Alliance Airlines >> [music] >> starting in 2020. Back to one type, one pilot pipeline, one maintenance system, one spare parts inventory, one set of procedures. That sounds boring, but at the same time it is also incredibly powerful because complexity is expensive [music] in this industry. Every new aircraft type creates additional training requirements, additional maintenance overhead, additional scheduling problems, [music] additional risk. Most airlines accumulate those complications over decades. Copa keeps stripping them out. >> [music] >> The result is that Copa runs some of the lowest unit costs of any full-service airline on the planet. [music] Operating cost for every seat it flies a mile sits at around 8.6 cents. Strip out fuel and that figure drops to roughly 5.8. Those are numbers a budget carrier would brag about with the only major difference being Copa is not a budget carrier. It sells business class. It is a full member of Star Alliance. And it still operates with low-cost economics underneath. Efficiency does something even more valuable than save money though. It creates resilience. Years before the pandemic, Copa was already building one of the strongest balance sheets in aviation. It resisted the trap that catches so many airlines. Cheap debt, expansion for the sake of expansion, growth without discipline. Instead, [music] it piled up cash, lots of it. Set Copa next to the airlines that filed and the picture becomes almost embarrassing. [music] LATAM, Avianca, and Aeromexico all spent years rebuilding themselves inside Chapter 11, shedding debt, shrinking fleets, reorganizing under court [music] supervision. They came out smaller, they came out wounded. In 2025, the supposedly fragile carrier in Panama posted a net profit [music] of $671.6 million on revenue of roughly 3 and 1/2 billion. Its full-year operating margin landed at 22.6%. Its net margin came in at 18.6. Earnings per share climbed almost 12% year-over-year to $16.28. Pause on those numbers for a moment. A strong airline in a great year fights to clear a single-digit operating margin. Many of the most famous brands in the sky would be thrilled with 5 or 6%. Copa earns more than 20 cents of operating profit [music] on every single dollar of revenue, and it has done that year after year for most of the last decade. The proof points stack up behind the headline figures. 11 times now, the aviation data firm Cirium has named Copa the most on-time airline in Latin America. Including in 2025, on-time performance in the fourth quarter ran at 89%. Flight completion came in at 99.8. [music] The board approved a quarterly dividend of $1.71 per share, paid four times a year through 2026. [music] And then came April 28th of 2026. On a stage in Panama City, Heilbron stood next to the president of Panama and the chief executive of Boeing Commercial Airplanes >> [music] >> and signed for 40 new 737 Max aircraft with options for 20 more. The deal is worth roughly 13 and 1/2 billion dollars at list prices. With the existing order book, Copa [music] is on track to operate more than 100 737 Max jets in the years ahead [music] and a fleet of more than 200 aircraft by 2034. Passenger traffic is projected to climb from around 20.9 million in 2026 >> [music] >> to more than 27 million by the end of the decade. A tiny carrier from a country of 4 and 1/2 million people is buying enough new aircraft to keep Airbus uncomfortable. The skeptic would still argue that all of this comes back to geography, that Panama just sits in the perfect spot. But geography alone does not explain decades of performance like this. Bogota sits between North and South America, but so does San Jose in Costa Rica, and so does Mexico City. None of them runs a hub anything like Tocumen. Plenty of airlines operate from favorable maps. Almost none achieve Copa's consistency. The difference is discipline. The willingness to keep saying no. No to complexity. No to unnecessary fleet diversity. No to growth that does not make economic sense. No to the temptation of becoming everything to everyone. That said, no strategy is invincible. In fact, the greatest strengths in Copa's story are also its biggest exposures. Start with the obvious one. Boeing. Copa is one of the most committed Boeing customers anywhere on the [music] planet. Every passenger jet it operates is a 737. And its entire forward order book is locked into the 737 MAX family. If Boeing has another deep production crisis, or another safety event that grounds the MAX again, Copa has no [music] plan B. There is no Airbus side of the house to lean on. No wide-body fleet to redeploy. The bet on a single airframe is total. Then there is Tocumen itself. The Hub of the Americas only works as long as the airport has the runway, the gates, and the terminal capacity to keep growing. Copa's plans assume an airport that can handle well over 100 MAX jets banking through [music] it in waves. If that infrastructure falls behind, every other piece of the strategy slows down with it. The wider region [music] is a constant variable. Latin America has been a graveyard for airlines for a reason. Currencies swing hard. The Brazilian real moved enough in 2025 to push a $6 million foreign currency loss into Copa's fourth quarter accounts. Avianca and Aeromexico are out of bankruptcy and rebuilding. LATAM is bigger than ever, plugging back into long-haul. Low-cost carriers like Volaris and Viva keep pressing on price. The competitive set is heating up. And politics is never far away. Copa is the flag carrier of a country whose hub status depends on staying neutral, open, and friendly >> [music] >> to every other government in the Americas. The day that gets harder, the model gets harder with it. The bet though is still pointing the same way. 40 more MAX jets ordered in 2026, options for 20 more on top, a plan for more than 100 MAX aircraft, a balance sheet built for shocks, the same disciplined playbook run by the same small group of people in the same small country for the next decade. For decades, aviation has operated on a simple assumption. Bigger is safer. More routes, more countries, more aircraft [music] types, more markets, more everything. Copa built one of the most successful airlines on the planet by believing the exact opposite. Fewer moving parts, fewer complications, more focus, >> [music] >> more discipline. And year after year, that approach keeps outperforming carriers that are far larger and far more famous. So, here is the question worth chewing on. Is Copa proof that the rest of the airline industry has spent decades confusing size with strength? Or is it a one-off success story that only works because Panama happens to sit in exactly the right spot on the map, and nobody else can copy it? Drop your answer in the comments. I want to read what you think. And if you enjoyed this video, do me a quick favor and hit the like button and subscribe to explain if you have not already. It is the single biggest thing that helps me and my channel grow, and it is completely free. Thank you for watching this video, and I will see you in the next one. >> [music]

reviews.transcript_full: For many travelers, Emirates and Dubai long seemed like a sure bit.  A global hub, a vast route network and the A380 have the symbol of comfortable flying.  However, recent regional tensions have led to a more critical view of things.  From what is currently apparent, what I saw and based on feedback from my community,  the onboard product has not been downgraded.  The greater risk lies in schedule changes, longer flight times, delays or aircraft swaps.  This report is therefore not a volatile crisis analysis.  Instead we ask a different long term question, what does Emirates actually offer on the A380  in business class right now?  Hello everybody from the upper deck of the Emirates Airbus A380.  Those of you who have been following my channel know that this is not about praising  airlines.  I am telling you when something is straight.  I am also telling you when something is not great at all.  The best example is probably in my flight report about the Airbus A350 of Emirates on one  of its first flights about a year ago to Edinburgh and that turned out to be a not very positive  report because I turned out to be one of the very few channels in the world who re-talked  about a significant flaw on that aircraft.  Anyway, airlines change over time, they get worse, they get better in service and also  interior design, etc.  So, this is reason enough for a new episode of my long series about Emirates and Dubai.  Here we go in 6.5 hours on Emirates business class on the Airbus A380 from Dubai to Frankfurt.  Welcome to the plane insider, I am Chris from TravelSing Fly.  Here you will explore the world's airlines up close from economy to business and first  class filmed live on board, authentic and full of detail.  We will also discover stunning destinations across all continents and learn how to make  premium travel possible through miles, points and insider know-how, built over 25 years  of experience.  Honest, inspiring and entertaining, it's your interview into aviation and travel.  This is the plane insider by TravelSing Fly, subscribe now and let's fly.  Before boarding I went to the lounge and here in Dubai, when it comes to Emirates it's  a really special experience because you don't have just a lounge but you have a couple  of lounges among them, there's the eight concourse lounge, the biggest one in the world with  more than 850 meters length, 3D big.  Then there's the famous Moishon Dome champagne lounge in concourse B with baguette or  kinds of different kinds of Moishon Dome champagne and overall it's a very good experience.  There's already a few reports about the business lounges and also the first class lounges  here on the channel, it's really worthwhile checking them out.  Now I'm showing you a few pictures of the lounge and then we go on.  Emirates operates several lounges in Dubai, for me the finest one is the one in concourse  B.  While not the largest, it's still huge and it features a health hub offering fresh, healthy  dishes at the cold buffet, alongside numerous hot buffet stations.  It also offers plenty of open seating and space, at least during the day, since peak  times at the Dubai transit hub outside of crisis periods tend to be around midnight and  in the early mornings.  In contrast, the much smaller lounges in the distant concoursee are often very crowded.  The food in beverage selection is identical across all Emirates lounges.  The B lounge now features a brand new section with numerous semi-private individual rest  areas, but the only downside is the lack of ceilings or wall barriers separating it from  the rest of the terminal allowing noise to drift unfiltered into the lounge.  The highlight here of course is the Moe is Shondor Shem Pain Down.  The incredibly long lounge in concourse A is also worth a visit.  Free sleep masks used to be available everywhere, but those days are gone now.  On the plus side, there's now wireless charging at the seats.  Regarding baggage rules, you have to be careful when flying Emirates as they allow only 40  kilograms in business class.  If you're not aware of this, you could easily end up paying hefty excess baggage fees. reviews.transcript_full: Hi, and welcome to our Air India A350-900 economy flight from London Heathrow to Delhi, India. Air India operates its daily London Heathrow to Delhi, India flights from Heathrow Terminal 2. Air India's baggage drop can be found in section B, where they use a heavily automated self-service check-in system. But, don't worry, there are plenty of staff on hand if you have any issues with the system. This is also the last chance that you will have to change your seat. Air India now uses a full check-in system online, which can be done either through the website or the app. Unlike other airlines, Air India does not have a bidding system for going for premium economy and business class. However, they do have last minute deals for business class and premium economy if there are seats left on the flight at a fixed fee. So, before going to our gate, we're just going to quickly go into Heathrow Terminal 2 Number 1 Lounge. I got this on an offer using the Barclay card DragonPass. So, I only had to pay 20 pounds for entry per person instead of up to 50 pounds per person. I will have the full review of the Number 1 Lounge for Heathrow Terminal 2 on my channel, if you so wish to watch it. It is the one before this video. This was my first time using this lounge, and it is very disappointing. I cannot say just how much a waste of money this lounge is. If you have the option to go to another lounge, use a different lounge in Terminal 2. Anyway, back on it with our journey, let's get to the gate. So, Air India opened up the gate at Heathrow incredibly early, as much as over 2 hours before the scheduled takeoff. Now, in fairness, where they were, it was a long walk from that main area where all the restaurants are. So, do be prepared to walk a good 10 to 15 minutes to get to the gate. And with the gate being opened up so early, amazingly, and no one here. People have got onto the plane, and as you can see, no queue at all. Now, obviously, I don't know if Air India is like this every day out of London Heathrow, but if it is, this is fantastic. No queues, no waiting, uh straight onto the airplane. All of the cabin crew came across as very pleasant, and we made our way to the very back of the plane, where we had the last row for our seats. So, immediate impressions, I'm looking at this, and I'm thinking, "Oh my god, this seat is small. I'm 6'3, I'm going to be squished into this." We then discovered that the overhead holdall is not for us, and it's only for the cabin crew. Once the luggage was away, the cabin crew do come around and give out water. Immediately sitting down, I did notice just how little room there was for my legs. The pitch on this is apparently 30 in, so for me, there was just no room at whatsoever. My knees were digging into the person's in front of me chair. One of my first observations then was the Wi-Fi. Now, it did say that there was free Wi-Fi available, however, it was not available at all on this flight. On the return journey back, it was working, however, and it was getting a mere 10 megabytes at best. So, the usual things that you'll find, the catalog for Air India, and the safety instructions in the pocket in front of you. The in-flight entertainment system did appear to be quite responsive, and did have a wide selection available from Western and Indian TV and film. And a nice little feature that they brought over from the A380, the cameras in both the tail and the landing gear. The navigational system did have a child's mode as well, and if you wanted to find out where dinosaurs were, this was your opportunity. Apparently, there's dinosaurs in Russia. The screen itself, it is a tiltable screen, coming with two auxiliary ports, a USB-A, and a USB-C port for charging. Being a relatively new aircraft, both of these are actually working, which was a relief and it would charge up the phone quite quick. Being a relatively new aircraft, the seat itself wasn't too comfortable and the headrest felt like it had been worn quite a bit already. Although to my surprise, the seatbelt had a lot of excess on it. Usually these don't have a lot of excess on these days. So to have one with that much excess was quite a surprise. So it was becoming quite apparent that this aircraft was going to be flying out quite empty. Now, from what you can see here, we're looking no more than 50 to 60% capacity on board. Okay, so let's have a look at the items we get then. So the earbuds, they are cheap but they work. So not to complain. The blanket, yeah, fine. Pillow, could do with a bit more stuffing in it. There appears to be a jacket hook holder thing on the seat in front. You can pull it out, however, I don't think anyone actually uses these. Somehow the table tray seems to have been set really low. Now, I don't know if this is just a Air India thing or if this is a common thing across A350s. However, I could not get this flat on my legs. It was really nice to see Air India's unique video that they have done for their safety video. This is available in English as well as other languages. So pushback was right on time, if anything a little early, so that we could go and join the Heathrow queue to take off. From pushback to actually taking off it took all of 15 minutes and for Heathrow, 15 minutes is exceptionally good. Unfortunately, being in the middle of row, I was limited to the onboard cameras and unable to see out the window. However, it was an opportunity to see the internet that they have on board and it is not a Starlink. Right then, off to Delhi, all of 9 hours 22 to go. This flight is taking a little bit longer than normal. It is currently having to fly over Saudi Arabia and Oman to get to India. Currently, it is unable to fly through Pakistan airspace. I'm unsure how often the cabin crew gets stuck in these toilets uh when they have the trolleys placed in front of the toilets. Fortunately, someone did come to their rescue and open up the door for them. So, getting into the flight now then, able to put the seat back into recline. It had a fair recline. So, as you can see, that does go some way back and the chair arm it were able to raise this up and actually create a little bit of room. This does seem to be the standard now where there is absolutely no leg room, but they give you the opportunity to lean back. So, getting up for a walk and stretch our legs, go for a walk down the cabin. It does appear that a lot of the seats are empty on this and again, 50-60% capacity at best. So, the toilets then. It is a relatively new aircraft and it is still looking in good condition. Uh nice to see that they've actually put lights into the mirror. So, this is something that I've not seen before. But, as usual, the toilet space they give you minimal toilet space. It is very cramped, very tight. Right then, back to the seat then for our first meal of the flight. Now, I'm not sure how I was meant to get this onto my legs and it be flat without losing some of my legs. So, with the flight being in the morning, obviously, this was going to be our first breakfast meal. The breakfast itself was a mixture of continental and a little bit of a fry-up. However, with this being a Air India flight, there was no beef or pork options available. So, it was either chicken or vegetable options. Although, it was nice to see that no expense was spared on the Lurpak for the croissant. After breakfast then, the first round drinks that came around and there was plenty of opportunity here to have multiple different beers, wines, spirits, soft drinks and the snack of choice for airlines now, crunchy corn. So, taking the opportunity to get a movie in. Pleasantly surprised to see that they had F1 the movie on here. And this kept me entertained pretty much all the way to Saudi Arabia. So, with the time zones kicking in and wanting to get some rest, the cabin crew actually did ask us if we wanted to move to the front and take the opportunity to have the seats with a lot of legroom. So, these seats are usually reserved for families with small children, babies. However, we took the opportunity here to make the most of it. So, we were just able to spread out here, utilize the middle chair, and have a lot more room. So, the dinner meal. This was something I was looking forward to, hoping for a really nice Indian curry. Unfortunately, this wasn't really the case. As you'd expect, airplane food, it has its way with food, and just in general, it was not that appetizing. So, a second trip to the bathroom, and throughout the flight, this has been cleaned, it is being maintained fairly well. The bin does look like it needs to be emptied, a little bit few things picked up. However, overall cleanliness for the flight of this duration is pretty good. So, overall then, with 30 minutes left to go on the flight, it was quite a pleasant flight. I don't know whether this was purely because it was quite empty, a night flight, it was quiet, we had the room to move around. It wasn't that bad. So, for an economy flight to India, this was quite cheap, and I'd fully recommend going using Air India to fly to Delhi to anyone.
