reviews.transcript_full:
Welcome back to Travel Expertos. Today we’ll be flying with Emirates in Business Class onboard the Boeing 777-300ER from Tokyo Haneda to Dubai on flight EK313. This flight is scheduled for just over 10 hours and will give us the chance to fully experience Emirates’ newer Boeing 777 Business Class product featuring direct aisle access, fully flat beds, premium dining, pajamas, lounge access, and one of the best entertainment systems in commercial aviation. In this full review, we’ll cover the entire experience from the chauffeur transfer through Tokyo, Haneda Airport Terminal 3, check-in, the Japan Airlines Sakura Lounge, boarding, seat 10A, dinner service, bed comfort, sleep quality, breakfast before arrival, and finally our arrival into Dubai before continuing our trip to Frankfurt onboard Emirates First Class. Let’s see how Emirates Business Class performs on this overnight flight from Japan to the Middle East. Our journey begins in central Tokyo with Emirates’ complimentary chauffeur drive service. One of the major advantages of flying Emirates Business Class is that the premium experience starts before you even reach the airport. Instead of navigating Tokyo’s busy evening transport system with luggage, Emirates provides a direct private transfer to Haneda Airport Terminal 3. Tokyo at night feels incredible from the back seat of the car. Soon enough we've reached Tokyo Haneda international airport. The drive to Haneda was smooth, comfortable, and surprisingly fast considering Tokyo traffic. We have now arrived at Tokyo Haneda Airport Terminal 3. Haneda is widely considered one of the best airports in the world thanks to its cleanliness, efficiency, modern design, and proximity to central Tokyo. Compared to Narita, Haneda is significantly more convenient, especially for premium passengers connecting quickly into the city. Tonight the terminal feels calm, modern, and extremely organized. Even during busy hours, the airport maintains a very quiet and premium atmosphere. Haneda was open in late of October 2010. We now head toward the Emirates check-in area for EK313 to Dubai.  Checkin counters were organized and split into First,Business,Premium Economy and Economy class The whole checkin process was well organized efficient and fast. After check-in, we continued through security and immigration. Haneda’s security process is extremely efficient compared to many major international airports. Even during evening departure waves, the airport moves passengers quickly without feeling chaotic. Once airside, we headed through the terminal toward the lounge area. Emirates Business Class passengers departing Haneda have access to the Japan Airlines Sakura Lounge, which is one of the more interesting partnerships in the Emirates network. As we walk through the airport you may notice how clean and spotless the terminal and airport actually is. Soon enough we reach Jal's Business Class lounge at Haneda. Japan Airlines Sakura lounge is located on the 4th floor (1floor above the terminal.) We are now inside the Japan Airlines Sakura Lounge. Food options included Japanese dishes, light snacks, bakery items, drinks, and self-service beverage stations. The lounge provides showers, changing rooms, and spotless bathrooms. The lounge has a very different atmosphere compared to Emirates’ own lounges in Dubai. Instead of flashy luxury, the focus here is calm design, efficiency, privacy, and Japanese hospitality. Large seating areas overlook the apron, offering excellent nighttime views of aircraft movements around Haneda. The lounge atmosphere is extremely quiet, making it a very good place to relax before an overnight departure. Compared to some overcrowded international lounges, this feels far more peaceful and refined. After spending some time here relaxing before the flight, it is now almost time to head toward Gate 144 for boarding. We are now leaving the lounge and heading toward Gate 144. Haneda’s terminal design is simple to navigate, and even the longer walks remain pleasant thanks to the modern architecture and clean layout. Waiting area is divided into Business and First class cabin together and Premium and Economy class together. Our flight is delayed due to bad weather on way to Tokyo, the plane has not even landed yet. Soon enough our plane arrived to our gate. Delay was unfortunately accumulating due to the late arrival of our aircraft. Our aircraft for today is a 6year old B777-300ER registration A6-EQO Soon enough the boarding started with First and Business class passengers boarding first. And its time to board the bird. First and Business class passengers board via the first jet-bridge and Economy and Premium economy passengers via the second one. Have you already flown Emirates? If yes what was your experience? Leave a comment about it please. First class cabin features 6seats in 1-1-1 layout, with middle seats featuring artificial windows via outdoor cameras. The cabin now features direct aisle access for every passenger in a 1-2-1 layout 10A is our seat for the next 10hours to Dubai.  This flight is configured withe the new 4cabin layout featuring new seats in all cabins.AND THEY ARE STUNNING! All business class feature a huge IFE screen, private minibar and much more. My window seat features two windows. As the boarding continues let's have a short peek of this beautiful seat. Located under your IFE screen there is a small pocket storage for travel documents and other necesities. The seat headrest is the most comfortable one I have ever experienced. A comfy pillow is stored at every seat as well. At your seat headphones together with eye mask and slippers are already waiting for you. The ceiling is full of starts again :) Every seat features an iPad, controls for windows, a mini bar, power sockets, air vent and much more. There is also an enclosed storage bin by your seat. Cabin crew walks by and hands out hot towels. And in no time we pushed back from our gate. We pushed back 40minutes behind schedule unfortunately. So far the seat feels incredible, with leather and comfortable seat and high privacy even though not featuring sliding doors as Qatars Qsuite. As preparation for take off Emirates safety video is played. As we roll towards our run way please enjoy taxi and later on stunning Take Off out of Haneda. Take off 1:07 AM Tokyo Time. And we are in the air. Bye bye Tokyo. Once in the air the cabin lights turn the cabin into a stunning place to relax. Soon after cabin crew hands out pre daparture drinks (as there was no time before the take Off. I went with orange juice this time. Let's have look at today's menu. Cabin Crew also hands out amenity kids to every passenger onboard - in my opinion those are the best ones out there.  The amenity kid is packed with accessories. (Emirates also features men and women kits) The kit includes essentials for overnight travel such as dental products, skincare items, earplugs,  and other comfort accessories designed to make the long flight more comfortable. Emirates also offers Pajamas for their Business class passengers. Alongside with an eye mask and slippers. Slippers are really comfortable and easy to wear. Emirates provides their business class passengers with noise cancelling headphones. Those headphones are really comfortable to use and block outer noise perfectly. You plug them next to other power outlets. Blanket is thick and very comfortable. Overall Emirates really went all out with amenities. Let me know if any other airline does it better in Business Class. Seat controls are located by your seat and have plenty of options and are easy to use. An armrest is located by your seat for more comfort when in lounge position. In front of you there is an huge IFE screen featuring the world's best entertainment system ICE. Overall this is one of the best business class seats out there in my opinion. I really like the way Emirates shifts and the colors of its interior in all four cabins. The seat windows are controlled electronically, you can control both of them at a same time from a separate button. Featuring two level of shades - half shade and completely black. Or you can directly control window by window, with the bottom underneath. This is featured in all cabins except Economy Class. It is really easy and simple to use and makes great visual impact of the cabin. There are 38 business class seats spread across two cabins from row 3 to row 12. As we get more and more comfortable in our seat let's have a peek of business class bathrooms onboard this flight.  The lavatory remains clean and well maintained, featuring premium hand products, towels, and additional amenities. And now it's time to start Emirates famous onboard dining. The late-night meal was served about 40minutes after take off, I decided to try the sushi selection together with a cheese plate. The whole meal presentation looked stunning together with an apple juice and sparkling water.  Emirates provided each passenger with a metal cutlery and also chop sticks. For an overnight Business Class flight, this feels more refined and lighter compared to a heavy full dinner service. Overall, the quality was excellent and presentation remained one of the strongest aspects of the Emirates premium experience. After dinner I made my way to the bathroom and it was time to change into Emirates Pajamas. Emirates provided a male and female option. They felt really comfortable not as a piece of low quality clothes. As I left to change into my pajamas the crew prepared the mattress topper for the seat. This is something only the top tier Arlines do. As we were approaching Shanghai the whole cabin was falling asleep slowly. In the meantime let's have a look what our tablet has to offer. The iPad allows you to control the entertainment system, moving map, lighting, and seat functions without needing to use the main screen. It feels modern, responsive, and genuinely useful during the flight only few airlines actually offer this feature even in First Class. Emirates really went all out with these new seats, and to be honest I find them even better than Qatar Airways Q-suite. It's time to put the tablet back in place and look at different features of this wonderful seat. Next to the seat is Emirates’ signature personal mini bar. Inside, there are 2  bottled water and one Sparkling water and a glass available throughout the flight. Together with some snacks. The snacks featured are, M&Ms, mixed nuts and jelly beans. There is also an additional storage above the bar for glass of drink, headphones to anything else you'd need. The reading light by side features 3stages of brightness.  You can also play with your personal seat light by your seat controller. Now let's have a look at world's best IFE ICE. The whole system is well organized providing countless of entertainment. Now it's time to turn our seat into bed. The provided mattress is big and thick All in all the seat is looks spectacular when in bed mode. The cabin lights make this cabin one of the most beautiful ones out there. In the meantime let's have a look where we are. Before going to bed let's head to the bathroom and brush our teeth. Emirates provides its passengers countless amenities in their clean onboard bathrooms. Now let's head to our seat and sleep. Lets take of our slippers and get comfortable in our bed. The seat converts into a 78.6" long flat bed. There is enough space even for back sleeping people and the footwell is wide and comfortable as well. Let's turn the lights down and use the sleeping mask for even greater comfort. We are somewhere over china at this time of our flight. Let's put the blinds down as well. As you may see the minibar is really helpful as you'll never ran out of water. The cabin lights and stars make it perfect place to sleep in. Good night everyone. Good Morning somewhere above India. Most of the cabin is still asleep but we are going to wake up now. Lets turn the seat lights one letting the crew now you are awake so they can come and offer you snack, drinks and more. This mattress was the reason I slept like a baby on this flight. Now let's head to the bathroom to freshen up. Back to our seat we have enough time to relax in the relax position and enjoy more of the ICE entertainment. Emirates uses Mercedes inspired S-lounge leather seats. The pathways between the seat and alley is not as narrow as it may seem. Let's watch some movies in the meantime. In the meantime outside the sun starts to rise. The service continues with a hot towel prior to breakfast. Emirates offers its IFE in countless of languages. Emirates also provides information for arrival gate baggage collection course and departure gates of other flights if connecting. As a proud airline Emirates has a section only about their history, fleet and much more. As the sun starts to rise we are approaching Dubai. Soon enough the tray table is set for our breakfast. This morning’s meal includes a cheese omelette with sausages and spinach, alongside fresh fruit, yogurt, croissant, butter, and preserves. Doesn't it just look fabulous? reviews.transcript_full: Hi there. My name is Earl and welcome back to Biyahe Jimenez. It's been more than 2 years since my last Cathay Pacific flight, so I'm really excited to fly with them again. Cathay Pacific was the first airline I flew with when I started this channel, making this return feel extra special. In this video, join me on this quick hop from Manila to Hong Kong aboard a Boeing 777 in economy class with Cathay Pacific. >> [music] [music] >> I arrived at the airport about 3 hours before my flight and the terminal was actually pretty peaceful. There have been a lot of changes since my last international flight through Terminal 3 back in 2024. The most notable would be the new food and retail areas that were opened by the airport's new operator late last year. Before we check in, let's take a quick tour of the new facilities. The old public area on the fourth level where all the fast food restaurants used to be has been downsized and now hosts only a handful of establishments. These include a Goldilocks branch and the newly opened Watson's store. The McDonald's branch on the opposite end is the only one that has remained in this area. Down at the arrivals area is the newly opened Tambayan Food Hall, an all-Filipino dining hub that can accommodate up to 2,000 guests and showcases a variety of homegrown and regional food concepts. Among them are Via Mare Select, the food court version of the well-loved Filipino restaurant. Aboitiz Cebuana Lechon from my hometown of Pasig City and the soon-to-open branch of Palm Grill, a Michelin Bib Gourmand recognized restaurant serving authentic cuisine from Southern Mindanao. The airport is now operated by San Miguel Corporation. So, the presence of a Ginebra San Miguel bar right in the middle of the food hall comes as no surprise. reviews.transcript_full:
Hi everyone.
This video is about my Cathay Pacific flight CX548  from Hong Kong to Tokyo in premium 
economy class First row window seat 30A.  This route is operated by the 
retrofitted Boeing 777-300ER aircrafts  equipped with the new premium economy 
class seats and the area suites.  Let's take a look at the retrofitted 
premium economy class cabin with me.  The scheduled departure time is 8:40am 
which makes it a popular connecting flight   for passengers arriving from Europe.
The cabin was quite empty this time.  Probably this reflects premium economy class is 
not quite attractive to short haul travelers.  The headset, the Cathay magazine and the safety 
instructions are in the storage space in front.  This space should also allow you 
to store a bottled water there.  The leg room in the bulkhead seat is 
generous which allows me to stretch my legs.  Although it may not be so 
important in this 3.5-hour flight.  The only weird part of this front row 
seat is the leg rest and the foot rest.  The leg rest does not rise high 
enough and thus the support is   not good even when I lowered the seat back.
I was so lucky that no one is sitting next   to me nor behind me so that I could show 
how the seat reclines to the full extent.  You can compare this to the leg rest in 
the seat in other rows as shown on Cathay's   promotional video.
Nevertheless,   I will still choose the extra personal space 
in bulkhead seats over the better leg rest.  Let's have a closer look at the headrest.
It can be adjusted in multiple ways to provide   a support that makes you feel most comfortable.
The leather-like material makes it looks more   elegant and highclass, and more 
importantly easier to clean.  Besides, the privacy wing provides added 
privacy when you are traveling on your own.  The reading light is also 
installed at the privacy wing.  Like the Airbus A350 premium economy class seat, 
there is a small storage space under the armrest.  The light is a very good improvement 
when the cabin lights were switched off.  In addition to the USB-C fast 
charging port under the armrest,   you can also find a USB-A charging 
port and universal power outlet.  The headset connector is also here 
under the cocktail mini table.  This is the headset provided 
in premium economy class.  Its noise cancelling effect is okay.
However, if you have big ears like me,   you may also find it is not quite 
comfortable to wear after a while.  It will be better if you bring your 
Bluetooth headset as it can now be   paired to the entertainment system.
The stunning 15.6-inch 4K screen   is fixed on the bulkhead.
As it is a bit far from   the seat for touch control, you can use 
the remote control to navigate the menu. Unlike the traditional remote control,   this one works like a trackpad, 
but it is quite intuitive to use.  The award-winning inflight entertainment 
system with new movies, TV series, podcasts,   and music added every month.
You will definitely find   something you're interested to watch.
Complimentary Wi-Fi is now offered to   cafe members in premium economy class.
However, if you entered other frequent   flyer membership at check-in, you 
cannot enjoy this offer like myself. Although you can find a cocktail 
mini table here, no welcome drink   was offered on this short haul flight.
There was also no hot towel service either.  Not a big deal. However, if Cathay wants 
to attract more revenue customers booking   premium economy class on short haul flights
These are actually some premium features   that customers would expect and 
it is not too costly to offer.  Here you can find your 
foldable table in the armrest.  As this flight departs before 
10:00 a.m., breakfast is served.  If it departs after 10:00 a.m. local time, 
nuts and drinks will be served before lunch.  There was no printed or onscreen menu, and the 
two breakfast choices are always dim sum set,   and egg and sausage.
As I had egg and   sausage on my flight from Manchester, 
I chose the dim sum set on this flight.  To be honest, breakfast in economy class 
and premium economy class are quite similar.  The only differences are croissant 
is served instead of white row   and food is served in stonewares.
Note that Prosecco is only   served in long haul flights.
Although the breakfast served on   this flight was nothing special, the late lunch or 
dinner served on my return flight was much better.  I had steak and mashed potato on 
the flight CX549 to Hong Kong.  If you have not tried dim sum before, these 
were actually quite tasty and worth a try.  The main dishes in premium economy 
class on Japan routes are similar   to that offered in business class.
Whereas on shorter routes like flights to   Shanghai, the same economy class menu was served.
On this route, try to pick a seat on   the left hand side.
If you're lucky that   the weather is fine, you will be able to see 
Mount Fuji when the flight approaches Tokyo.  This time I can barely spot 
it for a few seconds only.  Let me wrap up this short haul premium economy 
class experience with Cathay Pacific here.  First of all, the hardware, i.e. the seat 
is a big improvement. The big 4K TV and   the privacy wing are remarkably good.
I also love having the TV fixed on the   bulkhead instead of stowing under the armrest as 
I can still watch it during takeoff and landing.  This also makes it easier for passengers 
in the window seat to leave the seat.  About the service, to be honest, there was 
no notable difference from economy class   except the food was served in stonewares.
I was on this short haul premium economy class   only because I booked premium economy class 
return tickets from Manchester to Tokyo.  My honest opinion is that if I booked the short 
haul flight separately, I would definitely not   be paying the premium price for this slightly 
better seat for a duration of only 3.5 hours.  Last but not least, thank you very 
much for your time watching this video.  If you find it useful, please 
like and share this video.  Your subscription to my channel 
is also much appreciated.  Please enjoy the rest of the video for the 
approach to the Tokyo International Airport.

reviews.transcript_full: British Airways completed the overhaul of their Dash 8 Dreamliner fleet in early 2026, replacing the old Yin Yang Club World product with Collins Aerospace's Super Diamond Club World Suite. One-way business class seats on this route normally cost over $3,000, but the frequent sales often brings the one-way cost to under $2,000. We managed to book four round-trip award flights during peak season using BA's Avios. Here's how we did it. Check-in in Cincinnati was quick with little to no wait time due to this being the only British Airways flight of the day. The dedicated Club World check-in desk only had one person ahead of us in line for document verification and bag drop. It took about 15 minutes, including the time spent waiting in line, to complete the check-in process. Contrast this with Heathrow, where even with multiple Club World check-in desks, it took over 30 minutes to complete the check-in process. Security was one area where Heathrow and Cincinnati were pretty similar. The short time to clear security was due to fast-track security at Heathrow provided to Club World passengers in TSA pre-check in the States. Lounges, however, are where Heathrow takes the lead. Once a hub for Delta, CVG had European service to Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Rome, Manchester, and Zurich in addition to the current flights to Paris and London. That history left CVG with one large Sky Club and two common access lounges, The Club and The Escape Lounge. Since none of those lounges are One World member lounges, Club World passengers at CVG are given access to the Escape Lounge. The current Escape Lounge at CVG is small and lacks a bathroom, but it does offer decent enough hot food, cereals, and snacks. The lounge also has a full bar, though without any self-serve options, and generally has great staff. However, a few of the staff on this visit were far less than helpful. Overall, this is not a lounge I would go out of my way to visit. However, that is about to change. In part due to the demand of this British Airways flight, the new Escape Lounge is set to open in April 2026. The new lounge will be in a space once occupied by a Delta international lounge and be about four times the size of the current Escape Lounge at 6,700 square feet. Club World passengers will retain access to the newer larger lounge, which should help ease overcrowding when British Airways changes the Cincinnati route from a 787-8 with 31 Club World Suites to a 777-200ER with 48 Club World Suites. At Heathrow, overcrowding remains an issue despite Terminal 5 offering Club Lounges at Galleries North, South, and the B Gates. On this visit, the Galleries South Lounge had the lowest occupancy and open seating was plentiful. The lounge offered clean, family-friendly restrooms, a well-stocked buffet, and self-serve wine. If British Airways had announced our gate more than 30 minutes prior to boarding, we would have gone to the lounge in the B Gates as our departure was at a gate B36. Boarding was straightforward for both Cincinnati and Heathrow, and with priority boarding, we had plenty of time to get acquainted with the suite. The first difference I noticed between this Club World Suite design and the old Club World product, other than the door and direct aisle access, was the storage. The Club World Suite has storage near your shoulder where you'll find the amenity kit and water, a storage bin near your foot, storage under the footwell, and two side storage compartments, one of which houses the IFE remote. On either side of the remote, you'll find an electrical outlet and the headphone jack for the BA branded headphones. And for larger items, there is ample overhead storage. And the most obvious difference will be the privacy door. At this height, the door won't make the suite feel totally or partially enclosed, but when seated, the suite feels private without feeling cramped and feels on par with most other business class products. After takeoff, the FAs should enable the door to be closed, but if they forget, you can find the door release mechanisms on the wall just behind the door. One other notable difference is the IFE screen. Club World Suites comes equipped with an 18-in screen up from the 12-in screen of the old Club World product. The IFE provides a helpful seat guide and presents BA's High Life entertainment options. High Life has every major new release movie as well as some from popular British franchises. There's a fairly wide breadth of TV options as well, meaning almost anyone can find something to watch, even kids. One cool feature for kids was the dinosaur-themed flight map. And if you're unable to reach the touchscreen, the IFE can be controlled through the remote. Lastly, controls for the seat layout and the lighting can be found near the armrest. As we completed boarding, the FAs brought out menus and pre-departure beverages and started the safety video after pushback from the gate. >> Welcome, everyone. We will now demonstrate the safety features of this aircraft, and your attention is essential as this may be >> On both flights, after having reached cruising altitude, the crew came around to take meal service orders. On the flight out of Cincinnati, I started with the grilled citrus prawns and had the ribeye steak for my main. For dessert, I chose the festive options mousse cake. For drinks, I chose the Johnny Ginger to go with my starter and the Sura pair with the steak. However, the Sura was not loaded this evening, so I settled for the Pinot Noir. The prawns were served with warm bread and an artichoke and sun-dried tomato salad. The prawns served cold were great and the spice on the prawns was well balanced by the mango salad. After the strong start, I had high hopes for the steak. The steak, however, was disappointing. While well seasoned, the steak was overcooked, but I did get to see how well built the tray table was as I struggled to cut through the meat. My dinner service on this outbound route ended with the well-executed mousse cake. The breakfast service commenced roughly 2 hours outside of London. I opted for the chia pudding with seasonal fruit and muffin. The chia pudding, while listed as a strawberry pudding, was topped with coconut flakes and was much better than expected. However, British Airways could have saved money by not offering the muffin. And the best part of the breakfast was the fresh fruit. On the outbound dinner service from London, I started with the burrata and had the traditional Christmas dinner for my main course. And for dessert, I had the brioche bread and butter pudding. On this return flight, I only had cocktails, opting against the wines they had on offer. I paired the winter warmer with my starter and main course and at the behest of the FA, I had the Singleton Scotch with dessert. The winter warmer and the burrata with the tomato and basil pesto set this meal service off with a great start. The great service continued with the Christmas dinner. The FA tasked with preparing the meals managed to heat the turkey without drying out the meat and the cabbage was near perfect for a reheated airplane meal. Rounding out the meal service was the bread pudding. For the pre-landing service, I had the niçoise salad and a roasted ham sandwich. Catering on British Airways usually makes the headlines for the wrong reasons, but the catering and the flight crew on this return leg outperformed BA's usual reviews. The FAs were even great with the kids meals, helping us make modifications to best fit my children's preferences. Between the dinner and the breakfast service on the outbound flight, I tried out the bed in Club Suite. The bedding from The White Company comes with a small seat cover, duvet, and pillow. When converted into a bed, the seat is long enough to fit most heights and the footwell wide enough to be comfortable for most back sleepers. However, the lack of mattress topper places BA's business class behind some others like United and Qatar. Overall, Club Suite is a huge upgrade over the old Club World product. The main downside for both, however, is the lack of onboard Wi-Fi, though BA has begun to add Starlink to the 787 Dreamliners. While not the best value for a points redemption and the high taxes when traveling through Heathrow, if you have the points to burn and need to fly to London, BA still offers a better value over some other airlines like Delta. Booking 355 days out, we booked the four award seats that BA released for each leg of the trip. In total, we used 720,000 points and paid 3,000 in taxes and fees for a roughly $19,000 round trip ticket for four passengers. We didn't utilize any sign-up bonuses to earn the points for this trip. Rather, the points were earned using our normal spending that was driven primarily by our American Express trifecta and also our Capital One Venture X card. Both American Express and Capital One transfer to British Airways at a one-to-one conversion and the process to transfer the points is simple and fairly quick. Some other airlines may have better beds and higher cent per point redemptions, but the wide availability of British Airways' transfer partners and the upgraded Club World Suite make British Airways a worthwhile use of points. And most importantly, the FAs on both of the flights were great and made the trip feel special for my children. Until next time, thanks for watching.

reviews.transcript_full: In today's video, I'm flying business class from JFK to Lima with LATAM Airlines in one of their Boeing 767-300s. I'll be taking you through every part of my experience and towards the end, I'll share exactly how much I paid for this flight and whether I think this business class product is worth it. But before we get started, don't forget to give this video a thumbs-up. And if you enjoy content like this, consider subscribing to the channel and hitting that bell button so you get notified when I upload a brand new video. And with that out of the way, let's get started. This journey begins at JFK, where LATAM has a dedicated check-in line for business class passengers. The staff member checking me in was very polite and informative. She explained all the perks of flying in business class with LATAM, which includes access to the Delta One Lounge here in JFK and a dedicated security line. However, aside from that, there wasn't anything particularly special. No separate seating area or special pre-boarding zone. Still, the process was quick, friendly, and efficient. This is the private security entrance that leads directly into the Delta One Lounge, which means you can skip the regular lines altogether. >> Right off the bat, I have to say that the Delta One Lounge here at JFK is phenomenal. It's incredibly spacious and beautifully designed. Even during peak hours, it never felt crowded. There's a massive buffet offering a variety of options. I was able to enjoy breakfast and lunch here. And everything I tried was delicious. But what really sets this lounge apart is the ala carte dining area, where you can order gourmet dishes freshly prepared to your liking. Something that truly elevates the experience. There are multiple work pods, plenty of charging stations, and even spa-like amenities. The showers were outstanding, clean, modern, and stocked with high-end toiletries. The only minor issue was that the water temperature fluctuated a bit. But I'm honestly just nitpicking here. You've also got a full-service bar, multiple drink stations, spotless restrooms, and great views of the planes. In short, this lounge is as close to perfection as it gets. But before I knew it, it was boarding time. So, let's make our way over to the gate. The Boeing 767-300 I'll be flying in today has a staggered 1-2-1 configuration, which means that everyone in business class has direct aisle access, but the window seats alternate between being closer to the window and farther from the window. In this flight, I'll be in seat 3L. This seat has a clean, modern look with a subtle gray and red color scheme that I really like. Waiting for me at my seat was a full bedding set with a pillow, duvet, and mattress pad, all nicely packaged like a sleeping bag. There's also a menu, a bottle of water, a pair of slippers, and an amenity kit, which we'll check out later. And you get noise-canceling headphones, too. There's also a reading light and a universal power outlet along with a USB port. The IFE remote control can be found in its own little compartment here, close by to the seat controls. And there is some storage space, but I don't think it's enough. I do, however, like that there's a rail guard for the open storage space. It does a good job at keeping everything you place there from moving or falling off. However, there was no storage space under the footwell. And here's the tray table. The window seats that are closer to the window provide a good amount of privacy. You're not in a closed suite, but unless you lean forward, you can't really see your neighbors. And I appreciated the adjustable armrest, which adds a bit of shoulder space when you're lying flat. That said, this seat does feel a bit tight, and the footwell is extremely narrow, which makes moving around, especially when sleeping, pretty tricky. I also noticed some visible wear and tear on the surfaces. Still, it's functional and comfortable enough for a mid to long-haul flight like this. Soon after reaching cruising altitudes, service started with a warm towel, followed by a welcome drink and some nuts. The menu offered a great variety, plenty of drinks, multiple main courses, and options for various dietary preferences. >> I chose the ravioli, which was nicely presented and tasted good, though it wasn't particularly memorable. The main downside was that all the courses were served at once, which takes away from that refined multi-course dining feel. Also, the drink glasses were a bit dirty, which is a real letdown, especially in business class. Unfortunately, the restroom was easily the weakest part of this flight. It was incredibly cramped and the sink didn't drain properly. Furthermore, there were no special amenities, just soap. Definitely below what you'd expect in business class. Each passenger received an amenity kit designed by one of various South American artists that collaborate with LATAM. On this flight, I got one by Judy Kaufman. These amenity kits are reusable and collectible, which adds a fun touch to it. Inside, you'll find earplugs, an eye mask, lip balm, hand cream, socks, a bamboo toothbrush, and toothpaste. Most of them from Feito Brasil, a luxury Brazilian brand that specializes in artisanal, vegan, and sustainable cosmetic products. It's great to see that LATAM puts real thought into the design and eco-friendliness of these kits. Also, them coming in multiple designs is somewhat unique and makes you want to collect them all. The in-flight entertainment setup was actually quite nice. The screen was perfectly sized for the distance from the seat. It was responsive and had a solid mix of movies and TV shows, both new and classic titles. The noise-canceling headphones worked very well, and so did the remote control, although getting it out of its holder was a bit awkward. Unfortunately, there was no Wi-Fi on this flight, not even for purchase, which is a big miss in 2025. And the moving map wasn't available, either. Still, the system performed well overall and kept me entertained throughout the flight. When it came time to rest, I put the seat into bed mode. The pillow and duvet were super plush and comfortable, and the cabin was kept at a pleasant temperature throughout the flight. Unfortunately, the sleeping experience itself wasn't great. The seat felt narrow, and the foot well made it almost impossible to turn your body. The lowering right armrest does give you a bit more space, but overall, I wouldn't say this bed setup is very comfortable. About an hour and a half before landing, the pre-landing meal was served. There was a choice between a roast beef sandwich or a falafel burger, with dessert options of chocolate ganache or seasonal fruit. I chose the roast beef sandwich, which came with chips and the chocolate ganache. It was okay, edible but far from impressive, and presentation was pretty basic. The cash price for this business class flight with LATAM Airlines I took in late May of 2025 was around $2,000, but instead of paying cash, I redeemed 50,000 Virgin Atlantic points and paid $55.80 in taxes and fees. But thanks to a 30% transfer bonus from American Express, I only had to transfer around 39,000 MR points. With that bonus, my redemption value came out to be about 5 cents per point. A fantastic deal, especially for an 8-hour international business class flight that includes Delta One Lounge access. But now, let's see how I'd rate this business class experience with LATAM Airlines. The ground experience. The ground experience gets an 8 out of 10. The standout elements here were definitely the priority security line and access to the Delta One Lounge, both of which made the pre-flight experience feel truly premium and stress-free. However, aside from those highlights, the rest of the ground experience, including check-in, boarding, and arrival, felt pretty standard and didn't really offer anything above what you'd normally expect. The seat and cabin. The seat and cabin gets a 6 out of 10. The seat itself is decent and visually appealing, with a good level of privacy and a comfortable cabin environment overall, but in bed mode, the space feels tight and the narrow footwell makes it difficult to get comfortable. On top of that, the onboard restroom was a major weak point, cramped and lacking in amenities, definitely below business class expectations. The onboard dining. The onboard dining gets a 6 out of 10. There's a solid foundation here with a good variety of options and meals that are decent in both taste and presentation. However, a few execution issues really hold this back, things like the dining service style and the poor cleanliness of the glassware. The IFE and amenities. The IFE and amenities get a 7 out of 10. There are definitely some strong points here, especially with the amenity kit, which is both stylish and thoughtfully designed, and the overall entertainment system, which offers a good selection of content. But the biggest drawback is the lack of Wi-Fi, which is a major miss for a long-haul business class flight today. Limited storage space at the seat is another small downside. The onboard service. The onboard service gets a seven out of 10. The crew was friendly, professional, and did their job well throughout the flight. That said, the service felt more reactive than proactive, and there weren't many personalized touches that made the experience feel truly special or memorable. Averaging everything out gives this business class experience with LATAM Airlines an overall score of 6.8 out of 10. It isn't among the elite products, but it's a solid and mostly comfortable way to travel, especially when you factor in the amazing Delta One Lounge access and the great redemption value using points. The seat could use an update, and the food and restrooms definitely have room for improvement, but for an overnight 8-hour flight to South America, I'd say it's absolutely worth it and would fly in this business class product again, especially if booked with points. But ladies and gentlemen, that is just my opinion. What do you think of LATAM's business class product? Would you fly it, or would you fly to South America with another airline? Let me know in the comments section below. But for now, I just want to say thank you so much for watching, and I will see you in the next one. Take care.

And we again have exchanged stories of flying and all sorts of things. So, from about 35,000 ft in the sky as these bumps start to come as we descend into Hamad International Airport. A big thank you for watching. reviews.transcript_full:
Today I am adding a new airline to my 
list. My flight on All Nippon Airways   takes me from Sydney to Tokyo Haneda on 
their Boeing 787 Dreamliner. But with   JAL and Qantas also offering this exact 
route, where does ANA fit in? Stay till   the end because I'll show you how to fly this 
airline’s business class for less than 1000   AUD.
 
 
The check in line was completely empty   as I arrived just 90 minutes before my flight.
The baggage allowance in Economy is 2 checked   bags, each up to 23 kilograms — which is 
actually quite generous compared to most   carriers. Thanks to their partnership 
with VA, if you happen to have Velocity   Gold status or above, you get an 
extra 23kg of baggage allowance. After check in, it was through 
immigration and security,   and then a seriously long walk to Gate 53.
Unfortunately, the Velocity partnership with ANA,   doesn’t extend to lounge access - another 
casualty of the mis-mash of Velocity partnerships.  But by the time I got to the gate, 
it was already time to board anyway. The boarding process was impressively organised. 
In what I think is a first for Economy class,   ANA boards its window seat passengers 
board first. If you think about it,   this makes sense and should at least in theory 
reduce that awkward shuffle in the aisle.   ANA was the launch customer for the Boeing 
787. It has a fleet of 86 of these types   with many more on order. Today we are on 
the 787-9 specifically the international   configuration with 192 economy class seats. The 
seat configuration is the standard 3-3-3 layout. The disappointing part of this seat layout   is that they used to run a wider 2 4 2 
configuration, but this didn’t survive.   That leaves Japan Airlines the only one that 
has stuck with 8 across layout on the 787. At around 17 inches wide, today's 
seat is on the narrower side.  On the seat pitch front, at 33 to 34 
inches, it is among the best you'll   find in economy. The seat itself covers the 
basics well with a coat hook, USB C charging,   split seat pockets and AC power under the seat.   The footrest is a genuinely nice touch that 
you don't see on many economy products anymore. Amenities wise, you get a pillow and blanket 
— simple but appreciated on a 9 hour flight.  And after all those comments about seat width,   I lucked out today with two empty seats next to 
me, which made a very comfortable difference. We pushed back right on time as ANA treated 
us to their Pokémon themed safety video. One   of the most charming safety videos I've 
ever seen and very on brand for Japan. Shortly after takeoff, the crew came 
through with the pre meal service.  Wet wipes, a packet of rice crackers — which were 
actually really tasty — and some orange juice. The tissues on board are made 
from recycled green tea leaves.   It's a very Japanese touch and 
I thought that was really cool. Since this was my first flight with them,   I played it safe and went with a special 
option specifically the Hindu meal.  And right away, one thing 
stood out, the metal cutlery.  I don’t know about you, but for me, that's 
a mark of a premium airline even in economy. The tray itself was pretty substantial. 
Alongside the main there was a salad,   cheese and crackers, fruit and dessert. The 
main was a chicken curry with rice — fragrant,   well seasoned, decent portion. It actually 
reminded me of the meal I had on Malaysia   Airlines. Although thankfully I didn't spill 
this one. Overall, a solid meal service for   economy and better than I expected. Maybe I 
don’t need to order a special meal next time. After the meal service, the cabin windows were 
dimmed even though this was a daytime flight.  I took the cue and managed 
to get a few hours of sleep. Before that though I spent some time with 
the entertainment system. And this seems to   be a bit of a theme with Japanese airlines 
— the content library is well stocked, but   titles are displayed as lists rather than grids, 
which makes finding anything a bit of a chore.  On the plus side there was WiFi on board, and 
the messaging version was completely free.  On a day flight that was pretty valuable and 
it made the whole experience far more passable. In between the meal services, the galley was 
stocked with snacks and drinks that you could   help yourself to — water, juice, light snacks.
Here is a look at one of five lavatories in   Economy class. It was pretty clean 
as you would expect from a Japanese   airline. This one was fitted with a change 
table and of course, it came with a bidet. With around two hours to go, as we flew 
past Guam, the second meal service came   around — a snack box. Inside was a bread 
roll, some fresh fruit and dried fruit.   It was decent but honestly a bit light for 
a 9 hour flight. The second service could   have been more substantial — but this has become 
pretty standard across the industry these days. The rest of the flight was uneventful and we 
eventually began our descent into Tokyo-Haneda.  So where does ANA sit among the 
three airlines on this route?  Against Qantas, I think ANA wins pretty easily 
with a newer aircraft type offering a better   hard product and features like WIFI on board. 
Against JAL, it's a closer call. JAL still has   the edge in terms of seat comfort with their 
2 4 2 layout. The food and onboard services   were similarly good to each other while 
the IFE was equally bad in both cases.  Overall, ANA economy is a solid product 
and is a comfortable way to get to Japan.   But I probably won’t rate is as high as JAL. 
Let me know what you think in the comments. So, to that business class upgrade tip. ANA is 
a Star Alliance member and their flights can be   redeemed using other Star Alliance program 
including Avianca's LifeMiles program. I   paid 25,000 LifeMiles for this economy 
ticket flying out of Sydney. But here's   an interesting quirk — if you book from the 
Tokyo end, economy drops to just 20,000 miles   and business class exactly double that at 
40,000 miles. Buy those 40,000 miles during   a LifeMiles sale and you could be sitting in ANA 
business class for less than 1000 AUD. That is   the real sweet spot on this route. Just keep 
in mind that award availability is limited,   so always check this on the Aviance website before 
you buy — and never purchase miles speculatively.

It's population had been booming and it peaked [music] at just over 8 million people. But then the Great Famine of the 1840s struck. Basically, the potato crops across Europe were infected with blight, and while this did have effects across the whole European continent, it [music] struck Ireland particularly hard for a number of reasons that I won't dive too deeply into here, but [music] Ireland particularly depended on potatoes and British policy compounded the disaster. Long story short, over a million people died during the famine and in the years followed over a million more left. And the leaving never really stopped. Decade [music] after decade, generation after generation, if you were young and Irish for the next 150 years, the [music] default assumption was that you might just have to leave to find work. [music] So, when you're in Ireland and your people are scattered across the entire planet, flying isn't a luxury. It's [music] the kind of thing that holds it all together. I'm not going to sit here and pretend that a modern-day airline should be a major player in aircraft leasing. But, they did have a 45% stake in one of the early companies that started the whole thing. I guess we can kind of count this as our first what could have been situation. Now, this is a bit of a tangent, but I think it's quite interesting really that even after the GPA collapse, the whole aircraft leasing industry stuck around in Ireland. The big reason is that Ireland had quietly built up one of the most attractive tax environments in the world for exactly this kind of business. If you're running a leasing company, it was hard to justify being anywhere else. I kind of touched on this in the Shannon video here. Go check that one out if you haven't seen it. But the wreckage of GPA itself ended up splitting into two companies, both still in Ireland. One became [music] GECAS, a part of the GE group, and the other through a whole bunch of restructurings and acquisitions became [music] Aircap. And then, rather remarkably, in 2021, Aircap would buy GECAS for about $30 billion, essentially gluing the two halves of GPA back together under one roof in Dublin, [music] once again the largest aircraft lessor on the planet. Today, Ireland is home to over 50 aircraft leasing companies, including 14 of the top 15 globally. And the industry, depending on how you measure it, is worth roughly a quarter of a trillion euros. But [music] anyway, let's get back to Aer Lingus. Through the '60s, '70s, and '80s, it just kept growing. [music] There was more routes, more planes, more staff. And like a lot of government-owned airlines of this era, it started branching out into things that weren't really airline businesses. [music] There was hotels, a heavy maintenance subsidiary, a computer reservation system. It was becoming less of an airline and more of a sprawling national institution. And by the early 1990s, the weight of all of that was catching up. The airline was on the edge of collapse. In 1993, the government [music] had to bail them out. But before we get that though, I want to quickly touch on the people and well, we've got a quick word from today's video sponsor. Hi guys, I'm currently on a holiday in Seoul, South Korea. In July of 2004 he, along with his CFO Brian Dunn and his COO Seamus Kearney, went back to the government and this time asked for permission to approach private equity firms about a buyout. [music] The government killed it pretty much instantly. This led Walsh, along with his CFO and COO, to all resign in November of 2004. And they formally left their roles in late January of 2005. I guess we can sort of consider this the second oh what could have been moment for Aer Lingus. What could Willie Walsh have done with the airline if he had the freedom? [music] Either way, within three months of leaving Aer Lingus, Willie Walsh was announced as the next CEO [music] of British Airways. This was potentially one of the most consequential hirings in European aviation history and would go on to shape the future of, well, Aer Lingus. But before we get there, Ryanair does make a triumphant return to our story. >> Let's go. >> [music] >> With Walsh gone, the government did end up privatizing the airline anyway, just on their own terms. On October 2nd, 2006, Aer Lingus listed on [music] the Dublin and London Stock Exchanges. This was essentially what Walsh had first proposed, but structured so that the state retained around 28%, just over the blocking threshold [music] needed to veto any full takeover. The employees got a share scheme, too. So, politically it looked very different from Walsh's proposals, even if the [music] end result was very similar. Now, rather interestingly here, within 3 days of the IPO, Michael O'Leary, over at Ryanair, pounced. They had been quietly buying shares, and within 3 days they'd acquired a 16% [music] stake in the airline. And then, on October 5th, O'Leary went public with an offer to acquire the whole thing. His offer was for €2.80 a share, premium on the IPO price. Here's the thing that I find particularly interesting in all of this. O'Leary's formal proposal wasn't just Ryanair swallows Aer [music] Lingus. It was actually a two-brand strategy. Aer Lingus keeps its name, its management, its long-haul routes, and Ryanair's massive short-haul network would feed passengers onto Aer Lingus's transatlantic routes through Dublin. None of that really mattered, though. The Aer Lingus board rejected it the same day. The government also blocked it, using their 28% stake, and even the EU had their say in June of [music] 2007, formally blocking the merger between the two airlines. We'll get to that legal argument in a minute, but it was the first-ever prohibition of an airline merger under EU rules. But, O'Leary wasn't done, not at all. In December 2008, in the middle of the GFC, he came back with a second bid, €1.40 a share, [music] exactly half of what he'd offered the first time round. He pledged to double the short-haul fleet and create a thousand new jobs. The Aer Lingus chairman called it a rip-off, and the government slammed it as undervaluing the airline. Ryanair withdrew this bid. And then there was the third time, June of 2012, €1.30 a share this time, and by now Ryanair had built up a stake of nearly 30% of Aer Lingus. But, the EU blocked it once again. And after that third rejection, Ryanair's 30% stake was just [music] sitting there, too big to ignore, but too small to force a deal. And it was poisoning everything. It was blocking Aer Lingus from raising capital, deterring buyers from even approaching, and giving Ryanair an incentive to deliberately weaken a competitor. We'll get back to what happened with this stake in a minute, but while all of these takeover attempts were occurring, Willie Walsh was busy over in the UK. Willie Walsh had gone to BA and done his classic thing. He'd slashed costs, fought a vicious war with the Unite union that involved 22 days of cabin crew strikes, and drastically improved their profitability. But then, he did something even bigger. In 2011, he merged British Airways with Iberia to create a new group called International Airlines Group. Walsh was, of course, the new CEO of this whole group. And from there, [music] he moved fast. They've been blocking an Aer Lingus acquisition for years. [music] Well, the thing is, the government was always open to selling. They were just never open to selling to Ryanair. That was [music] the sticking point all along. And beyond that, Ireland had been through hell in the years prior. The 2008 financial crisis hit the country incredibly hard. They ended up in the EU IMF bailout program. There was years of austerity that followed, and part of the government's recovery strategy was selling off state assets to raise capital. But beyond the money, there was a genuine strategic argument, too. The European airline industry was consolidating fast. Air France had merged with KLM, Lufthansa had swallowed up Swiss, Austrian, and Brussels Airlines, and well, there was the IAG merger. reviews.transcript_full: First class, business class, premium economy, and economy. What's the difference in all four cabins on British Airways? And is it worth paying for those more premium cabins? I've personally flown all four multiple times, and today I'm breaking down what to expect in each class from the ground experience to the seats, to the onboard dining, drinks, and overall experience. So, let's start with the experience on the ground at check-in. In economy, or World Traveller as BA calls it, you'll use the standard check-in desks, and checked luggage allowance varies based on the exact fare type. Basic fares come with no checked luggage, where a standard fares get one 23 kilo bag. In premium economy, or World Traveller Plus, you'll get a dedicated check-in area at Heathrow, and at out-stations you'll be able to use priority check-in lines. Each passenger can check in two 23 kilo bags. Once checked in, both economy and premium economy will then head through the standard security lines. In business class, or Club World, you'll get dedicated check-in area, two 32 kilo check bags, and you can head through fast track security. This fast track security doesn't often make a huge difference at Heathrow, but at some airports and at some times a day, it can be a big time saver. First class passengers will get access to the first class wing, a closed-off check-in area that's recently been refurbished with a new burgundy design that feels very Qatar Airways. There's an area to sit and get refreshments, but generally check-in here will be very quick and much more friendly than I found at the other desks. Once checked in, you can then make your way through a separate security area and a very fast security channel that then deposits you directly into the first class lounge. It is worth noting, too, that status with BA and its Oneworld partners can allow you to access some of these perks regardless of travel class. For example, silver status will also get you business class check-in and fast track. Gold will allow you to use the first class wing, and both grant extra luggage. Once through security, economy and premium economy passengers who don't have status will be killing time in the terminal before boarding. Business class passengers, or those with silver status, will have access to BA's network of business class lounges. At Heathrow Terminal 5, which is BA's main hub, there are three business class lounges: the Galleries North Lounge, Galleries South, and the B Gates Lounge. The North Lounge is the most conveniently located near security, but as such it tends to be the most full. The South Lounge has the biggest capacity, but can also get very busy. The B Gates Lounge tends to be the least busy and a little more relaxing, but it has the inconvenience of being located over the B Gates, which can be a bit of a walk if you're departing from the A Gates. All of these business class lounges will feature a variety of seating options, a buffet of food with quite a bit of variety both in terms of choice and quality. I've had some pretty terrible and some very good food from here, but for the most part it's decent, nothing special. You'll also find bar areas with self-service beer, wine, sparkling wine, spirits, and some pre-mixed cocktails. If you're traveling outside of Heathrow or from Heathrow Terminal 3, then you may access some nicer versions of BA's own lounges, as well as access to lounges of their One World partners, such as Cathay Pacific, Qatar Airways, or Qantas. First class passengers, meanwhile, will arrive in the first class lounge straight after security. However, although this lounge is called the first class lounge, you'll find very few first class passengers in here. The lounge is mostly used by those with gold status and offers a slightly elevated offering compared to the business lounge, including some improved food options, free pour champagne, and a manned bar for cocktails. But for those actually traveling in first class, who want to exit the first class lounge and move over to the Concorde Room. This is exclusively for those who have first class ticket or the very difficult to acquire Gold Guest List status. In here you'll find a quieter space with Concorde memorabilia, including a Concorde nose cone out on the terrace, an elevated drinks offering including high-end spirits and champagne, plus the a la carte Concorde dining room. Plus, if you're here for a longer connection or just want a bit of privacy, you can book some time in one of the private cabanas. These are already set up for rest, work, and showers. And after a bite to eat and maybe a few cocktails, it's time to head over to your gate to board the flight. BA board their flights in boarding groups, and your group will be determined by the higher of your status level or ticket class. Gold guest list go first, then it'll be first class or gold status passengers, followed by business class or silver, then premium economy and front status, and then finally economy. And once on board, this is where we start to see the biggest difference in the experience. So, let's start with the seats. In economy, as you'd expect, the seat is pretty basic, but I've got to be honest, I do always pay for the extra legroom ones. Even though I'm only just turning 36 at the time this video comes out, my legs and knees can't really handle not being able to stretch out on a long flight. But in terms of the seat itself, it is pretty narrow and firm, but it does at least have an adjustable headrest. You get a small in-flight entertainment monitor, which on these exit row seats is stowed in between the seats, and you also have a small tray table stowed in here, too. Aside from that, not a lot to call out, and you won't find a huge amount of variation compared with other airlines' economy seats. In premium economy, you get a bigger, wider, and overall much more comfortable seat. Plus, even the standard seats here have plenty of legroom. The seat can recline quite a bit, which can be both a good and a bad thing. It certainly adds a lot more comfort, but when that passenger in front reclines, it really closes in that space a lot, and it can make it difficult to get out of your seat, especially if you have mobility issues. You also get a footrest that folds down, as well as a leg rest. However, I don't find the leg rest on these seats to be too effective, unfortunately. Between the seats, you have a small drinks table, and unlike in economy, you don't have to share your armrest with the passenger next to you. And the tray table also folds out from the side here. So, let's start with the older Club World seat. So, you do have less privacy in the club suites unless you are fortunate enough to get one of the ones that does have the door. A really great level of adjustability and easily one of the most comfortable seats I've ever sat in in a flight, even comparing it to other first class products. And something I love about some variations is that you can be joined by your travel partner to sit on the foot rest for buddy dining. Next up, before we get the flight underway, what is the difference in pre-departure service? So, before take off in economy, you get nothing apart from a safety video. Up in premium economy, you're welcomed with a glass of sparkling wine, and you'll also receive a menu for the main meal service. An amenity kit will be waiting in the seat for you. Up in business class, you'll get a welcome glass of champagne and a full food and drinks menu, and your amenity kit will be stored somewhere in the seat. If the crew are on the ball, they'll greet you individually and take your meal order before take off. Up in first class, however, you'll be escorted to your seat, where you receive a nicer and larger glass of champagne that will be topped up as you wait. You'll also get a selection of nibbles to accompany this and a hot towel. The crew will greet you personally, ask about what you'd like for your meal and when you'd like to be served it, and you'll be offered an amenity kit, pajamas, and slippers. So, what do you actually get in each of those amenity kits? In premium economy, you'll get a basic eye mask, socks, a lip balm, toothbrush, toothpaste, and a pen. In business class, amenity kits are provided by The White Company. These include a nice and soft eye mask and socks, earplugs, a dental kit, and three White Company products, a lip balm, a moisturizer, and a pulse point, but I've never quite understood what that one's for. If, however, you're flying from Gatwick, BA now have a completely different kit on these routes. These are brighter, colorful bags with different designs from different UK artists, and with products provided by Anatomē, including a moisturizer and a multi-balm alongside the standard items like eye mask, earplugs, dental kit, and socks. First class amenity kit is really excellent. In the men's kit, you'll get an even better eye mask and socks, several Elemis products, including facial exfoliator, shaving gel, lip balm, deodorant, moisturizer, and eye cream. The kit also includes a first class pen, earplugs, dental kit, and a comb. The women's kit is similar, but contains different versions of the products, and it also includes a facial mist instead of the shaving gel. Now, let's get up in the air and see how the onboard service compares. Once at altitude in economy, it shouldn't be too long before the crew start the drink service. Although, if you're sat further back in the cabin, it might take a while before they get to you. You'll be able to order beer, wine, basic spirits and mixers, and soft drinks. On my most recent economy flight with BA, I asked for a gin and tonic, and they automatically gave me two of them, which I did think was quite a good level of a service. Accompanying this was a small bag of pretzels, and that lasted me until the meal service arrived. Meals are all served on a single tray, and it's a decent volume of food. You can't expect anything too high quality here, and you don't get any proper cutlery or crockery, but I've never really had a terrible meal here, apart from if it's a breakfast service. You'll also be offered red or white wine with your meal. A small and often not particularly tasty snack will be served later in the flight, but it's rare for those to be very substantial or good quality, particularly on shorter routes. Up in premium economy, the options aren't too different from economy. Meals are typically higher quality up in premium economy, with the main course of the main meal being a little closer to what you might get in business class, and the presentation is generally better, too, with proper cutlery, crockery, and glassware. The second meal or snack, however, is the same as what's served in economy, so nothing to get too excited about there. It is worth noting as well that BA do often run out of meal options if you seat towards the back of the cabin, and you can't pre-order your meal with BA in any cabin. But, I do think the problem of running out of meal choice still seems to be a bit more prevalent in premium economy and business class. Additional snacks in premium economy can be found in the galley or occasionally brought around by the crew. In business class, the onboard service starts with a hot towel and then a drink service. The menu has a small selection of cocktails and spirits, plus beer, wine, champagne, and soft drinks. Not a bad range, but nothing insanely premium on offer here. Drinks are served in nice glasses, alongside a bag of nuts, which are very tasty. But, perhaps less of a premium touch than other airlines to serve in a bag rather than a separate dish. The meal will be served on a tray, but it will be delivered in separate courses, unless you've opted for a speedy meal service on a nighttime flight. You'll choose from light starters that are served alongside some bread and maybe a small side salad. Main courses then follow, and whilst presentation is rarely a strong point, food tends to be decent and a decent elevation as well from premium economy. Although, I have unfortunately found that the food quality can vary quite a bit. The desserts on offer are typically light, but nice quality, and there's also an option of a cheese course. Then later on in the flight in business class, you'll typically get a second meal that will all be served on one tray for a quicker service. But again, quality isn't consistent on BA, so some are really great, others not so much. I do find that breakfast is often a particular weak point, but that's true in all the cabins. Outside of meal times, you'll be able to find snacks and drinks to help yourself to in the galley in what BA refers to as the the kitchen. On quite a few recent business class flights, service has been very limited or non-existent between those meal services. Up in first class, you can generally expect a much elevated offering compared to business. After receiving a hot towel, you'll then get your initial drink service, and the drinks on here are a lot more premium than business class. I'm talking higher-end champagne and more premium spirits such as offering Johnny Walker Blue Label rather than the Black Label that they serve in business. You'll also find a more extensive menu, a good selection of cocktails, and the drink service is a lot more proactive in first with the crew seeming keen to offer top-ups. As for the meals, well, once again, it can be a little bit mixed in terms of quality. I've flown first class on BA twice, and the quality and presentation of food was night and day between those two flights. On that first one which departed from Heathrow, all the food from the amuse-bouche to the starter to the main and then the desserts were all excellent quality and beautifully presented, with that presentation including elevated crockery and cutlery compared to business with business class. I thoroughly enjoyed my meals here, and I also got to enjoy dining with my partner Kelly for that second meal service with the buddy dining seats. On my second first class flight, however, which departed from Jeddah, the drink service was still excellent, albeit slightly delayed due to the need to depart Saudi airspace before alcohol could be served, but the food offering was pretty weak. So, not sure if that was just a blip, but it seems like catering out of Heathrow is likely a more reliable option for a good meal. A quick word now on entertainment. So, in all classes, you get access to BA's Highlife entertainment system, which I do rate as one of the better ones out there in terms of films and TV shows available. I have definitely had premium economy screens that were better than some of the older business class screens for example. Earphones and headphones are provided in all classes. Wi-Fi is available in all classes with economy, premium, and business having to pay typically around £18 for a full flight whereas Wi-Fi is free in first class. Basic messaging is free for everyone in any class if you've got a BA Club account and BA have started the process of rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi for all passengers across the fleet, but it will take a bit of time before all that's fully rolled out. What about when it's time to sleep? Whilst both economy and premium economy might provide a pillow and blanket, if you're anything like me you're probably not getting much sleep on these. In the old seat there's no cubby making it a lot more spacious and comfortable for your legs. Plus if you're in a window seat with a privacy divider up, it's an incredibly private space. A few trade-offs with this one though. If you're in an aisle seat someone might need to step over your legs whilst you're sleeping to get out to the aisle which isn't great. It's really comfortable when set up. What about the different levels of service that you receive from the crew? Well, in first class, I've so far always found this to be absolutely fantastic. Attentive and friendly crew who check in regularly to see if there's anything you need and also to make conversation without it ever seeming overbearing or annoying. In all of the classes though, I've just found it to be incredibly inconsistent. At times, service can be fantastic. Other times, it's nonexistent or just plain bad. Majority of the time though, it's probably somewhere in the middle. Just okay, nothing that'll blow you away, but hopefully nothing that'll also leave you too disappointed either. Although, I've got to say more recently, my experiences have been a bit more in the disappointing side, particularly in business class and premium economy. But overall, which one to book will a lot of the time come down to cost or availability of reward seats if you're using Avios. It's difficult to say definitively if one is worth your money over the other without knowing both your personal financial circumstances and also which of the elements discussed you value the most. But most importantly, are the specific price differences on your route and dates. BA pricing is variable and demand-driven. So, there are times you'll see a premium economy fare extortionately higher than economy, whereas at other times, it might only be a tiny price difference. I've also seen plenty of times where the higher cabin was actually cheaper. For example, first class cheaper than business class or business class cheaper than premium economy. But hopefully, this video at least gives you a clearer understanding of the differences in each cabin to make a decision on which one you want to go for based on the pricing you're presented with. reviews.transcript_full: Tonight I'm flying China Airlines A350 business class between Sydney and Taipei, a quick overnight run, and honestly one of the most comfortable ways to cross this route. My flight was scheduled for 10:10 p.m. Sydney time, and it pushed back right on time. Before boarding, I stopped by the SkyTeam Lounge at Sydney Airport, but for some reason it was absolutely packed that night. [music] So, I didn't stay long, and I basically skipped food and drinks there. On board, China Airlines A350 business cabin is a 1-2-1 layout, so everyone gets direct aisle access. The cabin feels spacious, and even with the middle overhead bins removed, there was still plenty of overhead luggage space, >> [music] >> which is always a nice surprise on a full flight. Service from the cabin crew was top-tier throughout, >> [music] >> and I really appreciated the cabin temperature, comfortable, not too warm, and not freezing, [music] which makes sleeping so much easier on an overnight flight. The travel kits were excellent, >> [music] >> a pair of slippers and a Moschino vanity kit with genuinely good quality skin care items, plus a really cute Moschino luggage [music] tag, which I actually want to keep. I also loved the little table lamp. It's a small detail, but it makes the whole space feel more premium and cozy. Because it's an overnight flight, >> [music] >> I mainly slept. I didn't spend much time with the entertainment system, but I did notice one thing missing. There are no external cameras, so you can't watch the outside view from different angles like on some other airlines. That said, they do offer free Wi-Fi, and the speed [music] was good enough for messaging, including photos and using most of my usual iPhone apps without issues. After departure, dinner was served with an entrée, soup, and main course. I chose the seafood, and it was honestly delicious, especially since I hadn't eaten much before boarding. The drinks list was impressive, too, and I had a glass of Laurent Perrier Brut Millésime 2015, a vintage champagne you don't see every day. It was absolutely divine. I got about nearly 6 hours of sleep, then woke up for a Chinese-style breakfast, which I really enjoyed. We arrived in Taipei at around 3:45 a.m., about half an hour early, great for punctuality, but not ideal if you're actually going into the city. At that hour, hotels aren't ready for check-in, and public transport is limited, so it can be inconvenient unless you're transferring to an early morning flight. On the way back, departure was 10 to 12 at midnight, [music] and I used the China Airlines Lounge at Taoyuan Airport T2. Compared to the SkyTeam Lounge [music] in Sydney, the food and drink here were much better. It felt like a proper preflight meal. Because it's such a late departure, I prefer to eat before boarding and go straight to sleep. I asked the crew to move my main meal to the morning and cancel the original breakfast, and that plan worked perfectly. After takeoff, I slept really well, nearly 7 hours, which is exactly what I want on a flight like this. Finally, I need to talk about the seat. The seat itself is very comfortable for sitting, and the overall personal space is great. My only real critique shows up in bed mode. When you go fully flat, the seat base stays firm and flat, but then your body can feel the inward curve on the backrest section, which creates a small gap behind your lower back. It's uncomfortable to lie on an uneven bed, but not a deal-breaker. I believe a thin mattress pad would probably fix it completely. Overall, China Airlines A350 business class between Sydney and Taipei is a really solid product. Great service, a comfortable cabin, strong food and drinks, and reliable Wi-Fi, just with that one small bed mode gap that I hope they'll address with a mattress pad in the future. Thanks for watching.
