reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Melbourne. Over the next two nights, I will be travelling on a private steam-hauled sleeper train from Melbourne to Deniliquin, with a number of stops along the way. I will be sleeping in a wooden-body sleeper carriage built in the 1920s, cruising the Murray River on a paddle boat, and marvelling at the spectacular Moama Winter Lights Festival. So, without further ado, let the journey begin! This trip is organised by Slow Rail Journeys, also known as Seven-O-Seven Operations, a Melbourne-based, not-for-profit railway preservation group run by volunteers. They operate heritage trains across Victoria's broad-gauge network. Tonight, I'll be aboard the Riverlander, travelling to some of the finest attractions and events in the Riverina region. The train departs from Southern Cross Station, the hub of Victoria's regional rail services. My evening began at the Savoy Hotel, just across the road, where everyone was invited to a bon-voyage dinner. The buffet featured a variety of options, including salad and bread as starters, along with rice, pasta, chicken, boiled vegetables, cakes, and fruits. During the meal, Matt, the vice president of Slow Rail Journeys, gave a welcome presentation and safety briefing. I also received my cabin assignment for the next two nights. About three weeks before departure, I was emailed to select my preferred meal times, and this dining card confirmed my choice of a later sitting. When it was time to board, we were escorted to the platform as a large group. Given the incident I had just a month ago, this made me feel safe. The moment I entered the station, it felt like I had entered the elegance of a bygone era. This train is a moving museum of Victoria's railway history, featuring iconic carriages and locomotives from the 1920s, 50s, 60s and 80s. It consists of three locomotives and twelve carriages and will carry 91 passengers and an amazing crew of 12 volunteers. Carriage Goulburn is the oldest of them all, built in 1908 as a dining car, and is now used for private charters. Tonight, I'll be sleeping in the WANDO, it entered service in 1923. Travelling overnight in a 100-year-old carriage is sure to be an incredible experience! I'll show you my cabin later. Moving forward, I believe many of you would recognise these fully restored carriages from the 1960s, they were once part of the Southern Aurora train that ran between Melbourne and Sydney. These carriages were jointly purchased by NSW and Victorian Railways. They provide two types of cabins: the single cabin includes a lower bed at night that converts into a lounge seat during the day, a sink, a power outlet, heating, air conditioning, and a large window. Toilet and shower facilities are shared with other passengers. These cabins are similar to the Gold single cabins on the Indian Pacific, the Ghan, and the Sleeper on the Spirit of the Outback. The twin cabins include a three-seater lounge that converts into an upper and lower bed by night. It has a full en-suite shower and toilet, a power outlet, heating, air conditioning and a fold-down table. If comfort is your priority, this is the best cabin offered on the train. After passing the kitchen, dining and seating cars, the train's colour scheme suddenly shifted to red. Welcome to the old Overland! Club Car Number 1 was built in the 1970s as a first-class Club Car and is now the social hub of the train. These sleeping cars were built in the 1950s for services between Melbourne and Adelaide. The standard twin cabins are slightly older than those on the Southern Aurora;  they, too, have a three-seater lounge by day that converts into a bunk bed by night. Originally, the en-suite included a shower, sink, and toilet. Unfortunately, the toilet lacks a holding tank, so passengers need to use the toilet in other carriages. This is where the volunteers stay: a former Overland roomette sleeper carriage with a central corridor and ten sleeping compartments on either side. Each roomette has a sliding door and curtains for privacy. Three locomotives are used to power the train, each representing a different era of Victoria's railway history. At the back is a V/Line N class diesel-electric locomotive built in 1985. The N class is still the workhorse of V/Line's passenger services to Warrnambool and Swan Hill. Next, there's the A66, painted in V/Line's iconic orange and grey livery. Originally built in the 1950s as B class locomotive B66, this class represented Victorian Railways' first step towards dieselisation. And the star of the show is the R-class locomotive. After numerous delays caused by the Great Depression, World War II, manufacturing defects, and corrosion damage, the R class finally entered service in 1951. Features such as the smooth riding characteristics, large, comfortable cab and the mechanical stoker made them popular with crews.  Despite its success in express passenger service, they were almost immediately replaced by the more advanced B-class diesel-electric locomotives from 1952. As a result, the R class was very short-lived in Victoria's passenger services. Today, only two remain operational in the state: R761, owned by Steamrail Victoria, and R707, by 707 Operations. The train is about to depart, all aboard! This WANDO carriage was introduced in 1923 for services between Melbourne and Mildura. This was initially a two-berth smoking lounge that were charged at a lower rate than the other compartments when occupied. It has a Clerestory roof, and the decorations are simply beautiful. The rest of the carriage has nine enclosed cabins. I was allocated cabin 8.  I paid $1,000 for this trip, there was no single supplement, and it included meals and off-train excursions, in my opinion, it was an excellent deal. Compared to the single cabin on the Southern Aurora, my room feels quite spacious. Like other twin cabins onboard, the lower berth converts into a seat during the day, and at night, the upper berth can be pulled down. There's a reading light and a small storage shelf next to the pillow. The wooden sliding door can be locked, with the cabin's light switches above it. Opposite the bed, there's a mirror, more open shelves, and a wardrobe for each passenger. Next to the window is a wash basin. Two bottles of water, snacks and some toiletries were scattered around the cabin. What surprised me the most was having a power plug in this cabin, which kept my phone and cameras charged throughout the trip. The WANDO is the only sleeping carriage on this train with windows that can fully open, allowing me to enjoy the fresh air whenever I want. Neatly placed on the bed are towels, a hot water bottle, which I didn't realise at that time how much I'd appreciate having it later that night, and information about my carriage attendant, the train, the schedule and our off-train excursions. There are two modern toilets, one at each end of the carriage. The former conductor's room has been turned into a tea room, where you can wash your hands after using the toilet and make yourself a cup of tea. The WANDO has no shower facilities, but we were allowed to use the two shared showers in the adjacent carriage.  After passing through the three Southern Aurora carriages, I reached Lowanna, also known as South Australian Railways 783, built in 1942. The carriage was later converted into a Departmental Officers car, which involved fitting the vehicle with several sleeping compartments and a kitchen. The kitchen was still being used by the lovely volunteers to prepare gourmet meals for the passengers. This dining car was converted from a former V/Line carriage and will be used to serve us breakfast, lunch, and afternoon tea. Before I got to explore the rest of the train, the Rivelander arrived at its first stop, Gisborne, a charming regional town just a 45-minute drive from Melbourne CBD. We'll stop here for 35 minutes, and passengers are encouraged to step onto the platform and stretch their legs. Meanwhile, water is being pumped into the steam locomotive. Back onboard, Club Car No. 1 was built in 1970 for use as a first-class club car on 'The Overland'. Today, it is the social hub of the train. You can purchase a beer, a snack, soft drinks and other alcoholic beverages from the bar while striking up a conversation with fellow travellers. In addition to these couches, there's a seating car between the dining car and Club Car No. 1. This was a former V/Line carriage as well, now offering comfortable face-to-face reclining seats in a 2-2 configuration. After letting the 11:45 pm VLocity service to Bendigo pass us, the Riverlander is ready to continue its journey north. Overnight, the train will make a brief 14-minute stop in Bendigo before arriving in Echuca at 3:35 am. Returning to my cabin, it's time to get some rest. The quilt is thin, with only a light blanket inside. The single bed is very narrow, but the mattress is quite thick and incredibly comfortable. Since I booked the ticket, Slow Rail Journeys has repeatedly emphasised in their emails that this carriage does not have a heater, and for good reason. Travelling in the middle of winter with the clerestory roof windows wide open, it was freezing cold. I ended up sleeping with my puffer jacket on. Furthermore, as I anticipated, the ride in this century-old carriage is not smooth, and light from the corridor seeps through the glass on my sliding door. Many passengers I spoke to the next day mentioned that they couldn't sleep well.  So, this is certainly something to bear in mind when choosing to travel on an overnight train in Australia, as bumps and noise are common problems due to the country's outdated rail infrastructure. Personally, I slept quite well, as I'm used to and enjoy rail travel. When I woke up at 5:55 am, we were already in Echuca. The Riverlander had been here since 3:35 am. While everyone else was still asleep, I decided to take a shower. The amenity kit provides everything one might need. The nearest showers are in the adjacent Southern Aurora carriage. The space is much smaller than expected. There's only just enough room to hang my dry clothes and towel. Thankfully, the water pressure was strong, and the hot water came out instantly. Echuca is the terminus of V/Line's Echuca line services and the northernmost operating passenger railway station on the line to Deniliquin. Beyond this point, the tracks are used only by freight trains. Echuca is located on the southern banks of the Murray River, with Moama on the opposite side in NSW. Their relationship is similar to that of the twin cities of Albury and Wodonga. Welcome to NSW! It's currently only 5 degrees outside, the hot water bottle is such a life saver. Deniliquin is 71 km from Echuca by rail, it will take us about 2 hours to get there. As there are 91 passengers on board, and the dining car can only accommodate around 46 people at a time, we were split into two dining groups. This morning, those in Group 1 were invited to have breakfast at 7 am, while those in Group 2, including myself, were scheduled for 8:15 am. Breakfast was served buffet-style, with plenty of choices available. Deniliquin station once had three tracks and two platforms; however, the station building was demolished in 1984. Although the town is in NSW, there have been calls for the V/Line VLocity service to extend all the way here. I believe this would be a great idea, as the rail infrastructure is still in place, they would just need to rebuild the platform. After enjoying the substantial breakfast I plated for myself, it's time for our first off-train excursion: a visit to the town of Deniliquin. You might have noticed that the steam locomotive is missing. It was removed while we were in Echuca, and the two diesel locomotives are now attached at each end to power the train. This change was necessary because the yard at Deniliquin was demolished as well, leaving no space for the steam locomotive to move from one end of the train to the other. Deniliquin town centre is around 600 metres from the train. Slow Rail Journeys arranged hop-on, hop-off buses to take us to key attractions around the town. With buses departing every 15 minutes, it was very convenient. Deniliquin sits at a natural crossing point on the Edward River, marking the border between the Riverina and the Outback. The town gained the title of Ute Capital of the World in 1999 when ute owners gathered in Deniliquin to attempt a Guinness World Record for the "Largest Parade of Legally Registered Utes." They achieved the record with 2,839 utes in the parade. If you're a car enthusiast, be sure to visit The Depot. This 3,000-square-metre complex houses an impressive collection of vehicles, memorabilia, and interactive displays that transport visitors through time. Deniliquin was founded in the mid-19th century as a hub for the growing wool industry. Housed in the town's former public school, the centre pays tribute to the Peppin family, who pioneered the Merino sheep industry in the area. Built in 1926, the ram shed served as the main depot for inspecting and purchasing the top-quality rams. Today, with its distinctive thatched roof, this shed stands as one of the last of its kind in the Riverina. Napier Street and Cressy Street are two of the town's main streets. The town centre offers a charming blend of historic architecture and modern amenities. You can find a good selection of shops, cafés, and restaurants catering to a range of tastes. Across from the shops on Cressy Street is Waring Gardens, and today, being the fourth Saturday of the month, the Deniliquin Lions Club Market is taking place. The market is set beneath the shady Moreton Bay fig trees. The stalls are filled with old wares, seedlings, clothing, fresh fruit and vegetables, local produce, and more. I found a beautiful wine barrel for $15, and the $2.50 hot jam doughnuts were delicious. We were given 3.5 hours to explore the town at our own pace. Unlike The Ghan and the Indian Pacific, which only organise guided tours for everyone, I enjoyed the freedom to explore on my own. I even managed a quick stop at Coles for snacks and soft drinks before getting back on board. Deniliquin is the northernmost place we travelled to on this journey, we are now heading back to Echuca. Shortly after our departure, lunch was served in the dining car, and guests were once again divided into two groups. For drinks, We had the option of red or white wine, juice, and water. The main course was oven-roasted chicken breast with gravy, mashed potatoes, and green beans, and it was really tasty. At the buffet table, you could help yourself to some salads. Shortly after lunch, we arrived back in Echuca. We were given two options: Those wanting to attend the Echuca Winter Blues Festival could disembark here and take a shuttle bus from outside the station. Just as we approached the station, the rain started pouring down heavily, so I and most other passengers chose to stay on board. The train would continue to Rochester, from where we would catch a bus back to Echuca. This way, we could relax on the train and stay dry. While it might have seemed like a lot of back-and-forth travel and time-wasting, I wanted to enjoy as much train travel as possible and didn't mind taking a break from filming. Rochester is just 26 km from Echuca by rail. The Riverlander will stay here overnight, and guests were assigned to two buses based on the group number on their lanyards.  Next stop: Port Echuca. The Port of Echuca was once Australia's busiest inland port, it now offers several heritage experiences for tourists. For the next hour, we will board the PS Pevensey for a privately chartered cruise on the mighty Murray River. Built in 1911, this vessel may seem unremarkable at first glance, but it's essentially a floating museum. It was one of the largest cargo and towing paddle steamers on the river, with its original steam engine still intact, giving visitors a fascinating, close-up look at its mechanical operations. The Murray is Australia's longest river, stretching over 2,500 kilometres through NSW, Victoria, and South Australia. In the old days, the PS Pevensey hauled bales of wool from sheep stations to the Echuca Wharf, where they were loaded onto trains bound for Melbourne and shipped overseas. On the return trips, it brought goods and produce to stations along the river. Today, trucks carry cargo, and the Pevensey works as a tourist boat, capable of carrying up to 100 passengers per cruise. The upper deck cabins have been restored to recreate life aboard the steamer during its operational years. The one-hour cruise passed quickly, and on our return, the captain let me sound the boat's horn as we passed under the bridge. As the sky grew dark, we crossed the state border for the third time today to attend the magnificent Winter Lights Festival in Moama. Now in its fourth year, Moama Lights is an immersive 1 km-long sound and light trail that tells stories through state-of-the-art installations, projections, and cutting-edge moving light technology. This year's theme, Enchanted Nights: A Celebration of Light, honours the captivating beauty of Horseshoe Lagoon and the surrounding bushland. Highlights included illuminated ripples on the lagoon's surface, projections of children's art, glowing red gums, and remarkable indigenous works by First Nations artists. The light show certainly did not disappoint, together with the Murray River cruise, they definitely were the two highlights of my journey. After the incredible light show, we were taken back to Rochester by bus for dinner at the Shamrock Hotel. Situated in the heart of the town, this pub is over 112 years old. We were served an alternate drop menu, which included chicken parmigiana, fish and chips, and steak. I was lucky enough to get my favourite dish, steak. Given the challenge of catering for 100 people at once, the steak was a bit chewy and lacked sauce and seasoning, but the portion was super generous, and the food arrived quickly. Once I finished eating, I took a short stroll back to the train. The Riverlander is parked on a siding at Rochester Station, across from the V/Line platform. Back on board, it was almost 10 pm. It had been a long day, filled with history, cruising, and light viewing. Anticipating another cold night in my heritage cabin, I put on all the clothes I had packed. As the train was stationary, most passengers had a much better night's sleep. I was woken up by someone's alarm clock at 5 am. It was only 2 degrees outside, and even with a shirt, hoodie, and puffer jacket, it still felt freezing cold. Breakfast was the same as the day before, served buffet-style in the dining car. Afterwards, we had about 90 minutes to discover Rochester. Renowned artist Jimmy Dvate has transformed the town's silos into stunning depictions of local wildlife, paying tribute to the endangered species of the area. On the tall silo is a wrist-winged squirrel glider, and the shorter silo showcases the vibrant azure kingfisher, a small, dazzling bird commonly found near waterways. And at the back is a platypus. The Shamrock Hotel, where I had dinner last night, was once regarded as one of the most luxurious hotels in the state. Today, it continues to be a popular spot for both locals and visitors. Iddles Lane is home to a captivating mural dedicated to the life and career of legendary former Victorian homicide detective Ron Iddles. The mural traces Iddles' journey from his modest beginnings in Rochester to becoming one of Australia's most respected detectives. It also pays homage to Iddles' twin brother, Barry, and other family members who have contributed to the town's history. At 10:30, we boarded a coach for a half-hour drive to Colbinabbin to see some of Victoria's most spectacular silo art. The leftmost silo depicts the Colbinabbin Farmers' Picnic, which began in 1878. For sixty years, large crowds of up to two thousand people attended annually. Visitors from Rushworth and beyond would arrive by steam train and walk up the hill to the picnic. The next artwork highlights the significance of the railway to the Colbinabbin district. In August 1881, the Colbinabbin Railway League, made up of local farmers, pushed for a railway line to transport produce and livestock to Melbourne. The line was completed in 1913. These silo artworks affectionately tell visitors the proud history of Colbinabbin. Coincidentally, R761, the locomotive featured here is the exact steam engine that hauled our train from Melbourne.  After being detached early yesterday morning, the R761 rejoined us in Rochester and is now ready to take us back to Melbourne. The Riverlander's arrival has attracted much fanfare from the local community. Back in my cabin, I managed to stow the mattress, turning my room into a spacious and comfortable lounge. We departed Rochester at 12:30, and along the way, numerous rail fans took photos of our iconic train. An hour later, we reached Bendigo for a 75-minute pitstop. This was the train's last scheduled stop before Melbourne and my last chance to see it in daylight. During the stop, lunch was served in the dining car. There are salads and various dips on the buffet table. For the main course, I enjoyed roast lamb with gravy and vegetables. As we left Bendigo, the three locomotives picked up speed, averaging 90 km/h as we raced towards Melbourne. We did have to stop a few times at various sidings to let the VLocity trains pass us. At 4:30 pm, we enjoyed the final meal onboard. Notably, instead of loading all supplies from Melbourne, the Slow Rail Journeys team works closely with local Riverina and Central Murray businesses to provide catering and tours, benefiting the communities the train visits. The pastries, sourced from the award-winning Rochester Bakery, were absolutely delicious— what an excellent way to conclude an unforgettable weekend. Overall this whole journey was a travel back in time, as this single train features three of Victoria's most significant locomotives and two of Australia's most famous long-distance carriages: the Overland and the Southern Aurora. The heritage cabin I stayed in was especially memorable, it gave me a rare glimpse into what train travel was like in the 1920s. I loved being able to open the windows and take in the scenery from both sides. The mattress and the seats were both very soft. The only negative part was just the consistently freezing temperature in my cabin. All the volunteers onboard did an outstanding job looking after everyone, and I'm grateful for their efforts. The off-train excursions were well-organised and I appreciate the freedom of being able to roam at my own pace. As a not-for-profit organisation, Slow Rail Journeys provides a much more affordable experience. I would recommend it to anyone who loves rail travel in Australia and doesn't want to break the bank. Thank you so much for watching! It took me quite a while to edit this video. If you find it interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more train and flight reviews. See you all in my next video!

reviews.transcript_full: Aviation Geeks and Frequent Flyers Welcome to this new episode of our Flight Review  series, Brutely Honest.  This is the second part of our series on Iceland Air after covering their Transatlantic  Economy class product in a detailed review last month.  Today, we'll focus on Iceland Air's business class, if you can even call it that.  Instantly, you'll notice plenty of differences to other airlines' Transatlantic business  class products, so whether Iceland Air is worth choosing at all, we'll take a deep  dive in today's video.  I'm glad you've decided to join us, so let's get going!  Hello and good morning from Rainy Berlin.  Luckily, we get to escape this weather, heading to also Rainy, but warmer, Orlando, Florida,  flying aboard Iceland Air.  The airline has provided us with a ticket for today's journey at no cost, which is something  I want to be transparent with you about right from the top.  We've worked with plenty of airlines over the years, even with competitors of Iceland  Air, so we don't play favorites here at all.  And to ensure that, any airline providing us with a free ticket doesn't have to have  a say in what doesn't make it in the video, and also won't get to view it before it's  published.  They have no idea what I have to say about their business class product, so let's dive  right into it.  It's a quick train ride from Berlin City Center down to Brantenberg International Airport.  The construction of this airport was a national embarrassment for the country, ending up  more than twice as expensive as initially estimated, and opening more than 10 years later  than planned.  But my oh my, if it wasn't worth it, because this is one good looking airport.  Iceland Air operates three check-in counters for their Boeing 737 flight up to Keplavik,  one of them labeled Saga Premium.  You'll notice throughout the journey that Iceland Air is very careful to never actually  call their business class, business class.  It's always referred to as Saga class or Saga Premium.  In addition to the priority check-in counter, we get to use the priority security line and  get access to the airport's premium lounge.  All that can be checked on Iceland Air's incredibly detailed website, where for each airport  they fly to, they tell you if there is a fast track, which lounge is included, and even  when check-in opens, which I find very useful as somebody who always goes to the airport  very early.  Probably the lounge part is important, as Iceland Air does not have a contract lounge  at all of their destinations.  Lots of them are just small regional airports in Iceland and Greenland, which simply don't  have a lounge.  But at quite a few major airports, Iceland Air does not offer lounge access to Saga class  customers, including in Portland, Denver, Minneapolis, Chicago, Detroit, Pittsburgh, Newark,  Baltimore, Raleigh, Halifax, Paris and Nice.  Here in Berlin, they offer access to the Temporhoff lounge, which includes a hot buffet,  a variety of beverages including alcoholic ones, lots of snacks and a good apron and runway  view.  And there we can see our plane touchdown.  Today we're flying aboard Tango Foxchot India Charlie Oscar, a 2019 build Boeing 737-Max  8.  It's one of 21 Boeing 737-Max's in their fleet, 17 of which are the shorter Max 8 variant  and four of the longer Max 9.  They also still operate a handful of Boeing 757s and 767s with very similar cabins.  As Saga class passengers, we are allowed to board the plane first.  And after receiving an antibacterial wipe, we can get comfortable in the seat for our flight  up to Iceland, 3F.  Iceland Air uses the AVO interiors and dromedic seats in Saga class, similar to something  you'd encounter in domestic first-class on major North American carriers.  Waiting for us already is a pillow with a soft recuseable cover.  Being 180cm tall, the legroom is good and each seat comes with a footrest as well as  a standard seat back pocket and an adjustable entertainment screen with a USB-A port and  the audio port at the bottom as well as a coat hook on the side.  The headrests are adjustable vertically as well as on the sides.  The seats can be reclined and there is a tray table hidden inside the armrest.  There's another audio port at the bottom of the center console and on the other side  a universal power port.  In the ceiling above you will also find adjustable reading lights and personal air vents.  Before departure, we are also handed a half liter bottle of Icelandic water and a pair  of noise-canceling headphones.  As baggage loading is finishing up, look there's my suitcase.  We can sit back, relax and enjoy the engine view for takeoff.  The first leg of our journey is slightly under 4 hours with the onward flight to Orlando  clocking in at over 7 hours.  You'll notice a difference in the meal services offered on each flight and they are representative  of what you can expect between Europe and Iceland as well as between Iceland and North  America.  The Europe to Iceland service starts off with a round of beverages where I decided to  go with some non-alcoholic beer which was served alongside some savory cheese crackers.  Hot towels were handed out too and for the main course only one option is offered which  today is this chicken salad with fried cauliflower rice and quinoa.  Served with a little camembert cheese plate and a dried tomato bread roll, butter and  some volcanic salt from Iceland.  Usually I prefer hot dishes but this chicken quinoa salad was admittedly very tasty and  I love the dried tomato bread roll.  As for drinks, Iceland air has an impressive variety of options including various white  and red wines, little bottles of Nikola Fuyat Brutresef champagne and intriguing espresso  martini, though from a can and not freshly made.  Various beers including non-alcoholic beer and cider, various spirits, sodas, juices, tea  and coffee and what Iceland air is most famous for, their impeccable gin selection.  You can juice between 7 different gins with 2 different tonic waters on offer and suggestions  for pairings.  When it comes to beverages this is a very impressive selection especially for a 4 hour flight  on a plane with just 16 premium seats.  As we're cruising towards Keplervik let's have a look at what the inflight entertainment  system has to offer.  Iceland air uses Safran's RAFE inflight entertainment system with a variety of entertainment options  available on demand.  There are around 70 different movies and a couple of TV shows with multiple episodes  each.  Some music as well as an interactive mapping application is available too.  As saga class passengers we also get to use the plane satellite Wi-Fi.  Iceland air shows K.A. band's satellite connectivity through via set and it's fast enough to even  stream video content.  That's a really generous feature.  Our first flight is coming to an end rapidly but we still have lots to see including the  Transited Keplervik Airport, Iceland air saga lounge and one of the longest 737 max  flights in the world.  With that welcome to Keplervik International Airport our schedule transfer time here today  is 90 minutes and due to the terminal small size transiting here is really that quick.  There is no need to clear security again in either direction of travel so we only have  to pass through immigration.  I'm going to stop right here because the lounge is opposite passport control.  If there's over here in the shangan part of the terminal you'll find Iceland air saga  lounge.  With its cozy Nordic design it's a pity we don't get to spend more time in here.  You'll have access to a small buffet offering both hot and cold dishes and a variety of  alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages.  And shower rooms are available as well.  After just a couple of minutes here we'll have to continue towards our gate.  By the way if you're wondering what saga means, a saga is a type of Nordic tale composed  either in old Norse or Icelandic an important part of the country's history.  It took us only 6 minutes to transit here gate to gate including passport control.  What an efficient airport.  You can see how busy the terminal gets when all of Iceland air flights to North America  deported once.  We'll fly down to Orlando, a Bortango Foxchot India Charlie Gulf, a 2018 build Boeing 737  MAX-8 which is equipped with the exact same cabin we just encountered on our previous flight.  After an exhaustingly long wait inside the jet bridge to be finally allowed to enter  the aircraft we make it to our seat for the next 8 hours.  For F.  For this longer flight we are also given a blanket and a amenity kit in addition to the  pillow.  And we're offered some sparkling wine in a plastic cup as a pre-departure beverage.  With that we are ready for departure.  Before they begin with the service let's have a look at what the amenity kit has to offer.  We've got a toothbrush and toothpaste, a pair of ear plugs, hand cream and lip balm,  some socks, eye shades and a postcard.  It's a simple amenity kit with all the important things you'll need and I really love the design.  Once again we're starting off with a beverage of your choice any little snack.  This time some caramel popcorn.  Look at this gorgeous view over Greenland.  At this time of year our route follows the sunset almost perfectly drawing out this pretty  evening lighting for hours.  For the meal is served another hot towel.  On this longer flight two choices for the main meal service are offered either warm  lamp shanks or a cold variety of salmon.  I decided to go with the lamp shanks and doesn't that look pretty.  A variety of warm bread was offered alongside it.  For the appetizer we've got a Caesar salad with a lot of Caesar but not a lot of salad.  Some of that delicious looking warm bread with whipped butter, a scrumptious caramel chocolate  mousse topped with Oreo crumble for dessert, and the star of the meal, the lamp shanks with  mashed potatoes, baby carrots and asparagus.  Everything was served at top of tablecloth and I really liked the design of the cuplery.  Dinner service was fantastic.  Each element was high quality and very tasty.  I think Icelander could easily add a little bit of elegance by omitting the tray.  With just 16 saga class seats it could potentially be feasible to serve each element individually  especially because the crew isn't occupied with an economy class meal service as there  is none.  If you want to see what Icelander's economy class is like and how I still got a meal  there check out the economy class review covering the flights back.  Apart from it being served on a tray and maybe the salad lacking the salad part it was  a superb meal service and the lamp shanks were delicious.  During the rest of the flight I got some work done which the free in flight internet made  so comfortable and easy.  Although the tray tables of these are view enterious and drama the seats are a bit wobbly.  Before landing Icelander offered a second small meal service.  This time cold brusqueta with tomatoes, mozzarella and cured ham.  Once again very tasty but in my personal preference the bread should be a bit more toasted  especially when it's stored for extended periods of time as it loses that crispiness.  As we're starting our descent into Orlando I am left wondering how I should conclude  this video.  Obviously this is not the transatlantic business class product you'll find on basically  all other airlines but does it have to be?  After all Icelander's main business is serving Iceland and for flights between Europe  and Iceland which are 2-4 hours this is a perfectly adequate product actually better than  what you will find aboard airlines like Lufthansa and British Airways in business class.  Between North America and Iceland it's a more level playing field.  Just like WestJet in Air Canada use 737 Maxis with similar types of premium seats up front.  Same goes for Delta's flights to Minneapolis and Detroit which also CD seats up front.  However United's Boeing 757's and Delta's Boeing 767 to New York JFK both come with  lifelad seats.  Another North America specific difference is that Icelander doesn't offer lounge access  at many of their US gateways which Delta and United usually do for international flights.  Still, with the excellent quality of their catering and the business class seats being similar  or better than on most other flights to Iceland, Icelander is certainly a good choice.  Where it does fall apart a bit though is if you intend to cross the Atlantic all at once  like I did.  For that I would rather compare it to other airlines premium economy products than to business  class.  And sometimes saga class isn't even considerably more expensive than premium economy on other  airlines.  In rare cases even a bit cheaper especially for city pairs without non-stop flights and  for when you only want one transit that's not too long.  And in contrast to many other airlines premium economy class products, saga class does come  with lounge access at most airports.  The catering is far better as is the beverage selection, there's unlimited free Wi-Fi and  the seats are a bit bigger and more comfortable while the cabin of the 737 Max is smaller and  thus feels cozier, at least to me.  That might also explain why Icelander deliberately doesn't call their saga class a business class.  On flights to and from Iceland, business class is a totally appropriate description of  the product but on transatlantic flights it's simply not anywhere near what a customer  looking to book business class would expect these days.  So I would recommend Icelander to those traveling to and from Iceland wanting the comfort  of a premium class and those who want to fly in a good premium economy across the Atlantic  who don't want to fork out for the excessive business class fairs these days even when  the value for money makes sense to you.  Because keep in mind sometimes even a proper business class might be cheaper than Iceland  air across the Atlantic while other times it's not that much more expensive than premium  economy fairs.  So at the end of the day you just have to compare and see for yourself whether Icelander's  saga class makes sense for your travel plans.  With that, welcome to Orlando.  I hope you have enjoyed this review, I want to extend special thanks to Icelander for  providing the tickets for these two flights and of course to everybody who contributes  to our work through channel memberships.  Thanks to you we can further invest in our equipment, book flights and new airlines  and spend more time working on these videos.  And since we want to use your funds responsibly we also sometimes accept free flight tickets  to create these reviews at no cost to the channel.  Whether you are a channel member, a subscriber or simply stopping by for this one video, thank  you very much for watching.  I will see you again for a new video next week and until then, safe travels.  In the meantime why not check out this video too about United's Polaris business class  on a flight from Los Angeles to New York with a great seat but unfortunately catering  that doesn't come anywhere near what Icelander offers.

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Adelaide. While Sydney unveiled the impressive driverless metro extension into the CBD last week, Adelaide also celebrated the reopening of the rail line. It's the 1 km long port dog spur line to the heart of Port Adelaide. Unfortunately, I couldn't attend the opening day ceremony last Sunday as I was in Western Australia. But nonetheless, let's go and check out the new station. Now, Adelaide, the fifth largest city in Australia, once had an extensive rail network. The current Adelaide railway station, constructed in 1928, features a grand sandstone building in the neocclassical style. Until 1984, it was a hub for South Australia's regional and interstate passenger services. The station's concourse provided many facilities for long-distance travelers, such as a dining room, hairdressers, and refreshment rooms. South Australia now no longer has any regional rail services and the Sky City Casino occupies the majority of the station building. Today this massive station is home to just seven Adelaide Metro suburban lines. Seafood, Flingers, Bolair, Gula, Outer Harour, Graange, and the newly reopened Port Dock. There are two ways to travel on Adelaide's train services. At Adelaide station, you can purchase a single trip or day trip ticket from these machines. Alternatively, you can use a rechargeable metro card. It costs $5 to obtain the card, but fairs are cheaper than paper tickets, and you can load a 28-day or 14-day travel pass for unlimited travel during your selected period. Adelaide Metro operates two types of trains. The 3,3100 class diesel rail cars are the workh horses on the non-electrified network. These rail cars are based on the stainless steel shell design of the common trains used in Melbourne. The 3000 class was delivered as single units while the 3100 class arrived in twin sets. Typically, these trains run in twocar or threecar formations. From 2023, around 44 of the 70 rail cars were being converted to a hybrid system, which is quieter, uses 20% less fuel, and reduces CO2 emissions. Following the electrification of the seafood line in 2014, Adelaide Metro introduced the 4,000class electric multiple unit trains which now operate on the electrified Seafford, Flenders and Ghoul lines. These trains were also manufactured in Victoria initially by Bombardier Transportation and later by Austin. Their design shares similarities with the Vline velocity and Transper Bus trains. They almost always run in three car sets. At its peak, Adelaide Railway Station had 13 platforms and much of regional South Australia still retained daily passenger trains in the 1960s. However, following a so-called renewal in the 1980s, the station now has just nine platforms, and all of which are underground. A special extraction system is needed to remove exhaust films from the diesel rail cars. The train to port usually departs from platform 8 or 9. And since the line is not electrified, it is operated by a twocar diesel train. Stand clear. Doors closing. Welcome aboard. This is a service to Port Dock. The next stop is Bowden. Adelaide Railway Station is technically the only interchange across the city's four major train lines. About 1 kilometer from the station, the lines to the southern suburbs diverge from those heading north. And after crossing the river Torrance, my train parted ways with the Gula line. Welcome to Bowen. Welcome to Queen. The Adelaide to Port Dorkline built in 1856 was actually the first steam rail line in South Australia. The 12 km route travels almost parallel to Port Road and has 10 stations. Welcome to Woodville. Change here for services to Graange. Woodville is interchange station with a 5.5 km long spur line to Graange. Unlike the Adelaide to Port Dock route which was built by the South Australian government, the Grange line was a private venture constructed in 1882 to encourage development between Woodville and the coast. The line extended to Henley Beach in 1894, but was cut back to Graange in 1957. with fewer passengers on board. Now, let me show you the interior of the diesel rail cars. The seats are arranged in a two to configuration, and since they aren't reversible like those in Sydney, only half of them face the direction of travel. Near the doors, there are dedicated wheelchair spaces, priority seating, and even USB charging ports. Each carriage also features a ticket machine for passengers who boarded at a station without ticket selling facilities, allowing them to purchase a ticket or add value to their metro card. A small number of the 30,000 class rail cars were retrofitted to be more bike friendly. One side of the carriage retains the twin seats and the other side has been fitted with side facing seats. This gives the carriage more standing room and allows more bikes to fit on board. Welcome to Albertton. Change here for services to Outer Harbor. Albertton is the last station where we share tracks with the Outer Harbor trains. The next stop is Port Dock. This train will terminate here. We are now traveling on the newly reestablished 1 km line to Port Dock Station. Port Adelaide played an important role in Adelaide's early years, serving as a city's main supply and communication link with the rest of the world. This rail line was built to transport goods and passengers between the city and the port. In 1868, a railway from Dry Creek was extended directly into Port Dock Station. And in 1878, the line from the city was extended to Seur. The original station was quite an impressive structure. It had a two-story building, a tower, and a large curved roof over the two side platforms. By the early 20th century, the station had become too congested. It resulted in a vi duct and bridge being constructed across the port river in 1916. This diverted trains to Summer and Outer Harbor via a new station on Commercial Road, which we now know as Port Adelaide Railway Station. It soon replaced Port Dock at the town's main railway station. As a result, the Port Dock line became a spur line and the station subsequently fell into disuse and was closed in 1981. Welcome to Port Dock. This train will terminate here. Who would have thought that 40 years later in 2022, the state government committed $51 million to rebuild the station and the railway line? Welcome to the new Port Dock Station. It is located adjacent to the former Goodsyard which now houses the National Railway Museum. The new bus interchange in front of the museum offers various bus connections to the city Osborne and Tree Plaza. There have been mixed reviews about this resurrected station. Port Adelaide Station on Commercial Road is only 800 m from here and is directly next to Port Adelaide Plaza Shopping Center where most locals are more likely to go. Some argue that the money spent on this project could have been better used elsewhere. While I do agree with these points, it's still great to see Adelaide reopening a train line, even though it's just 1 km long. The suburban rail map from the 1970s shows a much broader network in the northern suburbs compared to today. I hope that reopening the port dock line is a first step toward reestablishing and extending more train lines in South Australia. It would be great to see regular passenger trains returning to Adelaide Hills, Victor Harour, Murray Bridge, Port Augusta and the Barasa Valley in the coming decades. Thank you so much for watching. If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more train and flight reviews. See you all in my next video.

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Chatswood in Sydney's north. Today, the long-awaited Sydney Metro City & Southwest line is finally opening to the public. This line will greatly reduce travel times between Chatswood and the city, double rail capacity across Sydney Harbour, and bring world-class driverless metro trains to the CBD. So, let's hop onboard and explore the stations on this exciting new line! Sydney Metro is Australia's first fully automated rapid transit system, designed to complement the existing suburban rail network. Three lines are being planned. The first segment, from Tallawong to Chatswood, opened in 2019. This initial stretch covers 36 km of twin tracks and includes 13 stations. As the line only serves the northwestern part of the city, the metro's full benefits are yet to be realised. The extension from Chatswood to Sydenham via the CBD will revolutionise urban travel, providing fast and reliable turn-up-and-go services across the city. This new 15.5 km extension has eight stations. Until yesterday, Chatswood was the eastern terminus of the metro. Travellers heading to the city had to transfer to Sydney Trains on the adjacent platform. The metro trains operate in 6-car sets, running every 4 minutes during weekday peak times, every 7 minutes during inter-peak periods, and every 10 minutes at other times.  All station platforms can accommodate 8-car sets, and the signalling system is designed to support 2-minute intervals between trains, both of which will be implemented as demand increases. Furthermore, stations along the metro lines are installed with platform screen doors—the first of their kind in Australia. These doors prevent people and objects from coming too close to the platform edge, allowing trains to enter and exit stations more quickly. Sydney Metro operates a fleet of Metropolis trains manufactured by Alstom in India. These trains use Alstom's Urbalis 400 communications-based train control signalling system, enabling fully automatic operation at all times, including door closing, obstacle detection, and emergency management.  Each train can accommodate up to 1,100 passengers, including 378 side-facing 'bench-style' seats, with designated seating for priority passengers and those with special needs. Seats in accessible spaces can fold up to make room for prams and wheelchairs. A status light above each door glows white when the doors are fully closed, green when fully open, and flashes red when the doors are opening or closing. This is an all stops service to Sydenham, the next stop is Crows Nest. This stop is Crows Nest. Our first stop is Crows Nest Station, located about 25 metres beneath Pacific Highway in the residential area of Crows Nest. It's roughly 600 metres southeast of St Leonards Railway Station. This stunning public art is created by female artist Esther Stewart. The work aims to bring a splash of colour to people's daily commute. This stop is Victoria Cross, alight for North Sydney CBD. Doors will open on the right. Victoria Cross Station is situated in the heart of North Sydney's business district beneath Miller St. It's approximately 800 metres north of North Sydney Railway Station. This station is built inside Australia's largest rail cavern at 265 metres long, 25 metres wide and 20 metres high. The next stop is Barangaroo. We are now crossing under Sydney Harbour, with the tunnel's deepest point reaching 40 metres below the surface. The metro's top service speed is 100 km/h, and thanks to the new tracks and larger station gaps compared to the existing train line, it can maintain this speed for most of the journey. This stop is Barangaroo. Alight for Darling Harbour and Walsh Bay. Change for F3 Parramatta River and F4 Pyrmont Bay Ferry Services. Doors will open on the right. This stop is Barangaroo. The first station in the CBD is Barangaroo, located 25 metres below ground. At the station entrance, you'll find an artwork titled 'In Time We Shall', which pays tribute to the traditional custodians of the Sydney basin and symbolises trees as a powerful representation of life, culture, and connection. This station serves Millers Point, Walsh Bay, and Barangaroo, while also improving pedestrian access to the northern part of the city and The Rocks. Barangaroo Ferry Wharf is just a few hundred metres away. This stop is Martin Place. Martin Place is the first interchange station on this new metro line. It provides Northwest commuters with a direct rail link to the commercial and financial hub of the city for the first time. An underground walkway connects the new metro station with the existing T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra Line trains and nearby bus services. The 40-metre-high atrium provides natural light that reaches down to the metro platforms. This stop is Gadigal. Alight for Hyde Park, Town Hall and QVB. Doors will open on the right. Gadigal station is strategically located beneath Pitt Street, serving the retail areas on George and Pitt Streets. Previously known as Pitt Street Station, its new name, Gadigal, honours the original Aboriginal inhabitants of the City of Sydney. Being just 100 metres from Town Hall Station, Gadigal Station helps alleviate congestion there and offers interchange access to other public transport options, including light rail and buses. Please stand clear, doors closing. This is an all stops service to Sydenham, the next stop is Central. Travelling from Chatswood to Central on the existing train line takes 26 minutes with 8 stops. The metro reduces this journey to just 16 minutes with only 5 stops. Central is the largest station in Australia, serving as a key interchange for suburban, intercity, and regional rail services, as well as buses, coaches, and light rail. The metro platforms, numbered 26 and 27, are directly beneath platforms 13 and 14. They can be accessed via Central Walk, a new underground concourse that opened in 2023. These escalators, measuring 45 metres in length, are the longest in the Southern Hemisphere, surpassing the 30-metre escalators at Melbourne's Parliament Station and the 35-metre escalators at Perth's Airport Central Station. Please stand clear, doors closing. Although the trains are driverless, they are far from "brainless." The entire metro system is closely monitored from a control centre in Rouse Hill, where an engineer can manually take control if any issues arise. Millions of commuters use similar networks daily in cities like Paris, Singapore, Dubai, and Hong Kong. And without a cab, passengers can even enjoy a driver's view from the front or rear of the train. This stop is Waterloo, alight for South Eveleigh. Doors will open on the right. The new metro station at Waterloo, situated between Redfern and Green Square, will ease pressure on these two stations. While the station was being built below ground, the Waterloo Metro Quarter revitalisation project was being developed above ground. Construction began in late 2020 and is expected to finish by 2026, aligning with the new airport's opening. Lastly, a 24 km underground metro line from Westmead to the city is being planned, which will double the rail capacity between Parramatta and Sydney CBD. It has a target opening year of 2032, transforming Sydney for generations to come. reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Darwin! Today, I'm flying to Kununurra and then Broome on Australia's newest airline, Nexus Airlines. Launched in July 2023, it connects many regional Western Australia towns without needing to fly through Perth. I've heard they serve really good ice cream on board. Let's go and find out! Darwin, the capital of the Northern Territory, has a population of around 140,000. The city has a tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons. Darwin's proximity to Asia brings strong Asian influences, especially evident in its vibrant food scene and bustling night markets. If you're visiting during the dry season, be sure to go to the Mindil Beach Sunset Market. It operates every Thursday and Sunday from April to October and has over 200 specialty stores and food vendors. You can find cuisines from literally around the globe. My favourite dishes are the crocodile burger and the seafood paella. Beyond the food and artwork, another reason the market is so popular is its location next to the beach, where the sunset is truly stunning. Make sure to stay for another 20 minutes after the sun goes down, not for the potato spirals, but to enjoy the magnificent hues of the sunset. Darwin Airport is the northern gateway to Australia, offering direct international flights from several South East Asian ports. Jetstar flies to Denpasar in just 2 hours and 40 minutes, while Qantas operates its shortest international route from Darwin to Dili, with a scheduled flight time of only 1 hour and 25 minutes. The terminal has changed quite a bit since my last visit in 2022. They have relocated the security screening point and upgraded the check-in area. The departure board shows the check-in open times for each airline. If you're flying with Qantas, Virgin, Jetstar, Airnorth, or Singapore Airlines, you can use one of the self-service kiosks to print your boarding pass and luggage tag, then drop off your bags yourself. Good afternoon, this is an announcement for all passengers flying with Nexus Airlines on flight GD213 to Kununurra and Broome, your service for check-in is open on the ground floor. For Nexus, I had to go to a staffed counter, which is located at one of the luggage drop-off machines. Check-in opened exactly 90 minutes before departure, and each passenger can check two pieces of luggage with a combined weight of 23 kg. Both domestic and international flights share a single terminal at Darwin Airport. The departure level features floor-to-ceiling windows, providing a great view of the apron and the runway. There are several dining options, including a bar, a restaurant, a café, and a fast food outlet. Virgin Australia used to have a lounge here, but it closed in 2020. The Qantas Club is accessible to eligible passengers on Qantas, Jetstar, and Qantas codeshare flights operated by Airnorth. I chose a table by the window and intended to have lunch at the Northern Common Tap House and Kitchen, which, according to its menu, should be open for 22 hours a day. However, I waited for half an hour—it was 11:42 AM—with no staff in sight, I ended up eating at Red Rooster instead. The fast food from there isn't really that budget-friendly! "Connect 212, runway 11, cleared to land." "Runway 11, cleared to land, Connect 212." The state of Western Australia occupies roughly a third of the land area of the Australian continent. It is massive. Qantas, Virgin, and Rex operate only out of Perth, meaning if you want to fly between towns in the northern part of the state, you would usually have to take a 2-hour flight to Perth first, then another 2-hour flight back up north. Nexus Airlines found a niche in the market, its slogan is "connecting us."  Apart from chartered routes, it flies 'milk run' style routes like Darwin to Broome via Kununurra, Broome to Geraldton via Port Hedland and Karratha, as well as Geraldton to Perth and Perth to Kalgoorlie. So, for example, if you want to fly from Port Hedland to Broome, instead of taking 8 hours and 25 minutes with a transit in Perth, Nexus can get you there in just an hour. Nexus holds a monopoly on many of its routes in Western Australia, but it faces competition from Airnorth on the Darwin-Kununurra-Broome route. Established in 1978, Airnorth is Australia's second longest-running airline, and is based in Darwin, making it well-known among Northern Territory locals. Nexus has strategically placed advertisements throughout Darwin Airport, from the luggage carousels to the check-in area and near the boarding gates, aiming to boost its visibility and appeal. Their ads have certainly caught my attention, and I'm excited to experience their service today! Boarding started on time, 30 minutes before departure. Nexus commenced operations on 10 July 2023, just over a year ago. They currently operate a fleet of 5 next-generation Dash 8 Q400 aircraft, all previously used by Air Baltic. Known for having the lowest fuel consumption per passenger seat of any turboprop in the industry while maintaining jet-like speed, I think these are the perfect aircraft for Nexus. On some flights, Air Baltic designated the front few rows of economy class seats as European Business Class. I believe a moveable curtain divider was used to seperate business and economy class. I'm surprised Nexus has kept these curtains. The Dash 8 has a total of 21 rows and 76 seats, configured in a 2-2 layout. There is no row 13. I picked 16A, a window seat on the left side of the aircraft. While Nexus does not let you select seats online, I emailed their reservation team after booking my ticket, and they were happy to assign me the seat I requested. On behalf of our captain Mike and first officer Lachie, we'd like to welcome you aboard Nexus Airlines flight to Broome via Kununurra. proudly operated by your Western Australia based crew. We really appreciate you choosing to fly with us today, and we look forward to making your journey once you remember. Darwin Ground, Connect 213, request pushback. Connect 213, Darwin Ground, pushback approved, tail East. Pushback approved, tail East, Connect 213. Ground, Connect 213 with information Lima, request taxi B2. Connect 213, taxi to holding point B2. Taxi holding point B2, Connect 213. Connect 213, line up runway 11. Line up 11, Connect 213. Connect 213, start heading 106, runway 11, cleared for take off. Fly heading 106, runway 11, cleared for take off, Connect 213. Connect 213, Darwin Approach, identified. Turn right heading 180. Right heading 180, Connect 213. And Connect 213, turn right heading 270. Right heading 270, Connect 213. Connect 213, climb to FL220, contact Brisbane Centre 129.85. FL220, 129.85, G'day Connect 213. Apart from my friend who failed to board today, there were only 20 passengers on this flight. The seat has a width of 17 inches and a pitch of roughly 32 inches, providing ample legroom. Despite being 14 years old, this aircraft is the cleanest I've ever seen. Everything looks spotless. In the seat pocket, there's a safety card and a sickness bag. Overhead, there are reading lights and air nozzles. As anticipated, the plane does not have WiFi or inflight entertainment. Shortly after the seatbelt sign was turned off, the crew began serving snacks. For this one-hour flight, I received a scone, a piece of fruit, and a hot tea with a biscuit. Nexus held a drawing competition in Geraldton and Broome primary schools last December, and selected 13 winning designs to print on cups used for in-flight service. I think this is a brilliant idea as it recognises the students' achievements and makes these cups great souvenirs for Nexus passengers. The scone was quite warm and came with butter and jam. There's a button on the side of the armrest that allows the seat to recline slightly. Ladies and Gentlemen, from the flight deck, very good afternoon, first officer speaking. Just an update on our progress, we're currently 180km to the northwest of Kununurra. There's some military training going on to the south of Darwin today so they have rerouted us slightly further west of our normal arrival plan adds couple extra minutes for us in the air today, we'll be shortly commencing our descent into Kununurra. The one-hour flight passed quickly. Interestingly, due to the 90-minute time difference between the Northern Territory and Western Australia, our scheduled arrival time is earlier than the departure time from Darwin. Before the seatbelt sign was illuminated again, the crew presented us with a basket of lollies. We are scheduled to stop here for 20 minutes. Those continuing to Broome were asked to remain onboard. Thankfully, the air conditioning was left on. The aircraft is currently being refuelled, ensure your seatbelt is unfastened, and the aisle remains clear of any obstructions. Please avoid moving around the cabin, or using the toilet at this time. Your Nexus team really appreciates you choosing to flying with us today, and we look forward to making your journey once you remember. The safety onboard card in your seat pocket, illustrates the brace position and other important information which could help you in the unlikely event of an emergency. In addition to Darwin and Broome, Airnorth and Virgin Australia also provide direct connections from Kununurra to Perth. The scenery on takeoff is truly breathtaking. Kununurra is the gateway to the East Kimberly Region, located 45km from the Northern Territory border. It's home to some of Western Australia's most stunning natural attractions, including World Heritage-listed Purnululu National Park and its iconic Bungle Bungle Range. We'll shortly commence our inflight service so settle back and let Chloe and myself look after you on your Nexus flight today. Water plays a central role in most of the area's attractions. There are countless gorges and waterfalls, several big tidal rivers, numerous smaller streams and creeks, Lake Kununurra, and, of course, the vast expanse of Lake Argyle. During this 90-minute flight, I was served a tart sourced from Oasis Bakery in Broome. It has a rich and creamy texture that I really enjoy. For those preferring something savoury instead, there were sweet chilli & sour cream or sour cream & chives chips. As for drinks, there was complimentary tea, coffee, water, Sprite, Coke, and Coke Zero. I was pleasantly surprised to find that they even had ice cubes on board. Throughout the remainder of the flight, I studied the safety card, grabbed another Mentos, and continued to admire the stunning landscape of the Kimberley region. We're currently 180km to the northeast of Broome, and our cruising altitude 24,000ft... The Dash 8 has one toilet situation at the front of the aircraft, next to the cockpit door. It turned out to be more spacious than I expected and was equipped with all the standard amenities, including hand wash and paper towels. Despite lacking WiFi or other inflight entertainment, the three-hour journey from Darwin to Broome passed quickly. Broome is a beach resort town in the Kimberley region. Along its Indian Ocean coastline, the 22km-long Cable Beach provides a dramatic backdrop for sunset camel rides. On sunny days, the ocean sparkles in vivid blue, contrasting beautifully with the soft, white sands. Although I missed out on their ice cream, my experience with Nexus Airlines was wonderful. It feels like a boutique airline to me. I appreciate their concept of serving pastries and fruit as refreshments, which not only supports local businesses but also offers passengers something different to enjoy. I'm tired of the typical sandwiches or cheese and crackers served by other airlines. The plane was clean and quiet, the seats had good legroom, and the crew were friendly and efficient. What's more, the pricing on this route is quite competitive. I paid $360 from Darwin to Broome for two people. I would certainly recommend trying this airline if you plan to visit Western Australia in the future. Broome Airport is the regional hub for northwestern Western Australia. Qantas and Virgin have multiple daily flights from Perth, and direct services are available from Sydney and Melbourne with Qantas. Recently, Jetstar Asia launched a seasonal flight from Singapore.  Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. See you all in my next video!
