chapters.title: Qantas International First Class Lounge - Melbourne

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Canberra! I'm about to fly to Melbourne, then catch Qantas flight QF9 to Perth. This flight departs from the international terminal. In this video, I'm excited to show you the Qantas International First Class Lounge in Melbourne and the Premium Economy Class on the Boeing 787 aircraft. Let's go! My flight from Canberra to Melbourne is booked through Qantas as well. It's flight QF1275, departing at 8:45 am.  Upon checking in, I was notified that I had been upgraded to business class. This is my first time getting a free upgrade from them. The aircraft taking me to Melbourne is an Airbus A220. Qantas has ordered 29 of them to replace its aging Boeing 717 fleet. This particular one, painted in Aboriginal art, is the first A220 that Qantas received. Some of us like to call it the broccoli. I love this livery. Boarding commenced 20 minutes before departure.  I travelled on the inaugural A220 service in March this year. If you would like to know more about the economy class on this plane, please feel free to check out that video. The A220 can accomodate 137 passengers. At the front are ten business class seats in a staggered 2-2 configuration. I was assigned 2F, a window seat on the right side of the aircraft. Each seat has a pitch of 37 inches and a width of 20 inches, it’s comparable to the Qantas B737 business seats and with a more modern look. There are no power plugs in business class, but there's a 60W USB-C port behind the seat-back, enough to power a laptop. Furthermore, there is a wireless charging pad and another set of USB charging ports underneath the central console. Like the B717 it replaces, there is no seat-back TV screen. Instead, there is a device holder for your mobile phone or tablet. You can download the Qantas Entertainment app and stream movies and TV shows on your device. Alternatively, you can browse the internet using the free high-speed Wi-Fi. For this hour-long flight, there's one meal option offered in business class: mushroom frittata with sausages, tomatoes and more mushrooms on the side, accompanied by banana bread and blueberry yoghurt. This is an interesting meal-choice because I know many of my friends don't like mushrooms. The frittata and sausages were slightly salty, but I still enjoyed them. The weather in Melbourne is nowhere near as sunny as Canberra. After a 20-minute hold due to air traffic delays, we landed at Melbourne Tullamarine Airport 40 minutes behind schedule. Welcome to Melbourne! QantasLink would like to acknowledge the traditional custodians of the airport's land the Wurundjeri people, and pay our respect to Elders past and present. Melbourne Airport has 4 terminals. Qantas domestic flights use Terminal 1, and all international flights depart from Terminal 2. Until July 2024, QF9 is a Melbourne to London service with a stopover in Perth. Whether travelling to Perth or London, you must check in at the international terminal. Unlike Sydney and Brisbane, all of the terminals here are connected. It was a short 5-minute walk from my A220 gate to the international departures area. Check-in for each Qantas flight opens strictly at 4 hours before departure. Qantas and Emirates Platinum, oneworld Emerald, and those travelling in first class can use the dedicated First Class check-in suite. There's a separate kerbside entrance to minimise walking. All other passengers can use check-in Bay A. Those travelling to Perth can use either a passport or an Australian driver's license. The staff will put a 'D' sticker on your boarding pass to show that you are a domestic passenger. At immigration, you must go to a staffed counter where the border force officer will verify your photo ID and put a departure stamp on your boarding pass. Voila! Despite only travelling to Perth, I'm now inside the duty-free area. The Melbourne to Perth leg of QF9 has always been a particularly popular choice for Platinum Frequent Flyers heading west, and I'm about to show you why. Qantas has two lounges at this terminal. A premium economy class ticket does not grant you access to any lounge, but you can use the business lounge if you are a Qantas Club member, have a general lounge pass or hold Qantas Gold status. Near gates 9 and 11 are a pair of escalators leading up to level 3, where you'll find the entry to the Qantas International First Class lounge on the left. This lounge is accessible to Emirates and Qantas Platinum, oneworld Emerald, and First Class passengers on a oneworld or Emirates flight. This lounge sits at arguably the best location in the terminal, with floor-to-ceiling windows giving you a sweeping view of the apron and the runway. The lounge space is split into spa, work, leisure, and dining areas. Behind the nooks on the far left are a few work desks, with printers conveniently located behind them. There are two private office suites available on a first-come, first-served basis. The rest of the lounge seating is divided into several partially partitioned areas. Some are equipped with a TV, giving me a feeling of sitting in someone's lounge room. The most iconic feature of the lounge is the two old-school split-flap departure boards. But with all codeshare flights being shown as well, the board can only display a few flights at a time. The main reason many platinum travellers, including myself, love flying QF9 to the west is this 50-seat restaurant, offering à la carte dining. The tables near the windows are the first to be taken. When multiple flights depart around the same time, the space can fill up quickly. If you can't get a table, the staff can deliver the food anywhere you want inside this lounge. Breakfast is served until 11 am, followed by all-day dining until the lounge closes. The menu is designed by celebrity chef Neil Perry and changes every three months, though some of his signature dishes like the salt and pepper squid, Pavlova, cheeseburger, and the club sandwich would never disappear from the menu. In terms of beverages, there are a few cocktails, four white wines, five red wines, and beers to choose from. If you are a platinum one or a Chairman's Lounge member, they may reserve some vintage drops for you. In the past 18 months, I have been to the Qantas first lounge approximately ten times. I have always had a good experience, and these are the four dishes that I like the most. To start, I ordered the staple: salt and pepper squid. The squid is typically crispy on the outside and tender on the inside. The green chilli sauce adds a zesty, mildly spicy kick, while the aioli provides a creamy, garlicky finish. Disappointingly, the squid was a bit underdone today, it did not taste crispy at all. Here is a picture of what the dish normally looks like. The coating should look more golden. For my drink, I ordered the Pear Royale cocktail. Usually, the cocktails come with some garnish. This time, my drink looked a bit bare, but it tasted quite good. In my opinion, the Gua bao is one of Neil Perry's finest Asian-inspired dishes. On a good day, the soft, pillowy bao bun cradles succulent braised pork. Each bite is a delightful combination of savoury, spicy, and tangy elements. Unfortunately, I could barely taste the pork in this serving, it was so small. The grilled snapper is placed on a bed of what I believe to be hulled millet. It's fluffy like rice and creamy like mashed potatoes. The celery leaf salsa and spring onions helped eliminate the snapper's fishy taste, and the pine nuts added some nutty flavour. Thankfully, I enjoyed this dish. A trip to the first lounge is not complete without trying the Pavlova. Despite its simple appearance, the combination of mascarpone, ice cream, seasonal fruit, and meringues makes it the perfect dessert. The dining room started getting busy from 11:30 am, and by 12:30 pm, every table was taken. Once I finished eating, I moved to the lounging area to free up my table for those waiting. Power plugs are somewhat limited throughout the lounge, they’re mostly situated against the walls and thus a bit out of reach for many seats. If you're still thirsty or hungry after your meal, there's a mini-bar stocked with wines, beers, juice, soft drinks, tea, coffee, as well as snacks and fruits. Qantas does not have nap rooms in its lounges. However, some of the leather seats near the windows are reclinable, and I found them comfortable enough to doze off for a little bit. Behind these doors is the Day Spa. Travellers in first class can expect a call from a lounge manager the day before their flight to organise a slot for a 20-minute treatment. All other passengers can book a slot at the lounge reception on a first-come, first-served basis. The spa is extremely popular, if you miss out, you can still use one of these private shower suites to freshen up before your flight. Each suite is equipped with a toothbrush, shaving kit, and a hairdryer. The shower water is big and hot. Overall, I believe my not-so-good dining experience was a rare occurrence. There are only two Qantas First Lounges in Australia. Together with Sydney, the calm atmosphere, personalised service, à la carte dining, and spa facilities make them the best airport lounges in the country, offering a sanctuary within the bustling terminal. Before heading to the gate, let me quickly show you the Qantas business lounge. The business lounge is on level one and can be accessed via these escalators descending below the main departure floor. This lounge is open to virtually all lounge-worthy passengers travelling on a Oneworld, Jetstar, or Emirates flight. It can accommodate up to 350 people at once, and Qantas is currently expanding its footprint by 30%. Some frequent flyers affectionately refer to it as "the dungeon" due to its location, aged interior, and lack of natural light. The food options are slightly superior to those in a domestic Qantas Club, there’s a hot dish and a salad. The mini-bar is pretty-well stocked. And shower facilities are available too. While this lounge is suitable for a brief visit, I don't think it's a place you'd want to spend an extended period of time. My flight is departing from gate 18, it’s one of the furthest gates from immigration, requiring about a 12-minute walk. Boarding began 40 minutes before departure with separate lines for priority and general boarding. QF9 is operated by a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, the newest long-haul aircraft type in the Qantas fleet.  It features a 3-class layout, with 42 business class seats in a 1-2-1 configuration. There are 8 rows in the forward cabin and another three rows behind door 2. The premium economy class are arranged in a 2-3-2 layout. I chose seat 23A, a window seat in the last row. With the bulkhead behind, it allows me to recline freely. The crew had already placed a bottle of water, a menu, a large firm cotton pillow, and a 100% wool blanket on each seat. With only four rows, this mini-cabin feels quite private. However, the downside is that there is no dedicated toilet. The nearest one for me is in the economy class section behind, it is spacious and stocked with hand wash, paper cups, and paper towels. Shortly after settling in, the crew offered me a choice of water or sparkling wine. As the premium economy section is in the middle of the aircraft, my window view is mostly blocked by the wing. Both premium economy and business are fully booked today. Qantas first revealed these next-generation seats in 2017. Let’s now take a look at the seat's features. At the front is a 13.3-inch high-definition touchscreen. The seat has a pitch of 38 inches, which is 1 inch more than the business class seat on the A220. My favourite feature is the combined leg rest and foot net, which provides several ways to support the lower body. Once I slip my feet into the netting below, it feels extremely comfortable. The seat pocket above stores the safety card, inflight magazine, and a pair of noise-cancelling headphones. This is the lever I used to lower the leg rest. There's a USB port, a small device pocket, and a personal electronic device holder below the entertainment screen. There's a universal power plug shared between every two seats. USB-C cables were not widely adopted in 2017, so there's only a USB-A charging port under the central console. Lastly, below the console, there's a bottle holder. Most seats have a width of 20.5 inches, except for the E seats in the middle, which are 22.8 inches wide. The headrest is adjustable and can be integrated with the ergonomic pillow. This is such a clever design. The Boeing 787 windows can be tinted using the control button below them. I'm glad the crew did not lock them on my flight, so I had full control over my window's brightness. Like the business seats on the A220, the tray table is hidden inside the armrest. It is quite large and stable. The meal service from Melbourne to Perth follows Qantas' long-haul international standard. In premium economy, there's typically a snack and drink service soon after take-off, followed by a meal. It has been 50 minutes since we left Melbourne, and the crew has started serving dinner, so I assume they just skipped the aperitivo. The dinner is a three-course meal. I have to say the menu rarely changes, for the main course, it's always either a plant-based option, a salad, or a roast chicken dish. The drink selection is excellent, nearly identical to the wine list in business class. The crew serves the meals according to passengers' frequent flyer status to ensure high-tier frequent flyers don't miss out on their desired choice. Here is my meal, there's so much food! This seems equivalent to the standard of a domestic business class meal. All three courses were presented on the same tray. The entrée is a Moroccan roasted vegetable salad mainly consisting of cauliflower, green peas and pumpkin. The flavours were good, except it was once again extremely salty. Thankfully, the roast chicken wasn't very salty, it was actually pretty flavourful and succulent. I loved it and found it very filling. I don't believe this is a lamington but rather a three-layered cheesecake. It tasted pretty nice. In general, aside from the very salty salad, I was satisfied with the portion, taste, and quality of this premium economy class meal. After clearing my table, the crew offered tea and coffee, and I requested a cup of hot chocolate. With about 90 minutes to go, let's look at the inflight entertainment. This is the best seat-back screen on the Qantas fleet—it is crisp and clear. The system comes in several languages. It is easy to use and stocked with 2,500 hours of movies and TV shows, updated monthly. While the selections aren't as extensive as Emirates, Cathay, or Turkish Airlines, they are adequate for a long-haul flight. There's also a 60-second video presenting all the features of the premium economy class seat for first-time travellers. The noise-cancelling headphones are the same as those in business class. They are not top-notch, but they do the job. If you're not fond of staring at a screen, there's a monthly published inflight magazine in the seat pocket. It presents the latest travel news, suggestions on where to stay, must-try food experiences, and a bunch of ads. The Boeing 787 currently does not have inflight Wi-Fi, but Qantas plans to roll it out progressively from the end of this year, and it will be fast and free for all passengers. Lastly, I attempted to nap by resting against the headrest, which I found quite comfortable. In summary, premium economy offers an enhanced product compared to economy, with a wider seat, better legroom, and meals comparable to domestic business class. Currently, a one-way flight from Melbourne to Perth in economy is $376, premium economy is $1,316, and business class is $1,780. No, it's not cheap at all, but if you purchase an economy sale fare and bid for an upgrade, premium economy costs just 10,900 points, and business class is 27,200 points. In my view, bidding for premium economy provides the best value. The seat is better than the business class seat on a Boeing 737, yet it costs only 40% of the points. Unfortunately, from 11 July, QF9 will no longer depart from Melbourne. However, if you want to experience the international premium economy product on a domestic service, you can still book such flights between Sydney and Perth. There were two cabin crews serving the premium economy cabin, they always addressed me by my last name. Apart from skipping the appertivo, their service was as expected: professional and enthusiastic. Welcome to Perth, Qantas would like to acknowledge the traditional custodians of the airport's land, and pay our respect to Elders past and present. Just a reminder for those customers finishing their journey here in Perth, please ensure you take your boarding pass that has the orange sticker on it as you'll need it to clear customs.  Welcome to Perth! My flight departed 8 minutes late, yet we landed 25 minutes ahead of schedule. After disembarking, those continuing to London are directed to the international transit area, while those concluding their journey in Perth are directed to the immigration. Here, border force officials ensured that the name on our boarding pass matched our photo ID before allowing us to exit the terminal through the international arrivals hall. Qantas uses Terminals 3 and 4 at Perth Airport. The newly opened High Wycombe train line does not have a stop here the nearest Redcliffe station is a 10-minute walk away, or you can catch TransPerth bus 292 to get there. Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. See you all in my next video!

yt_comments.author: @hanjiongmiao6067
yt_comments.text: As a Chinese avgeek growing up in Shanghai, it’s great to hear you enjoyed your flight on China Eastern. After all, it is the airline I grew up flying. About the livery, they do used to have a nicer looking old livery which had already been completely phased out favoring the more “modern looking ” white one. Few notes about their product, about the Wi-Fi, you are actually suppose to enter a access code purchased online as a economy passenger (or something like that), free access code is only given to businesses and first class. The game section had apparently been disabled for cost cutting reasons. The USB charging port also often don’t work on their 777 so be aware!

yt_comments.author: @bembs0256
yt_comments.text: I flew China Eastern Airlines last month from Jakarta to Shanghai on a A330-200. It was a pretty good flight. We had a slight delay, but they managed to land in Shanghai on time. The crew was kind and helpful (they managed to find my lost left earbuds! 😂) Also, the food was FANTASTIC! One of the best in-flight meals I’ve ever tasted, after Thai Airways and Garuda Indonesia! The only drawback was the IFE. Yes, the system was pretty dated, and the movie selections were basic. Also, they DIDN’T provide us with headphones! I thought they forgot to provide headphones on our flight to Shanghai, but no, they also didn’t provide headphones on our return flight to Jakarta! 😓 Also, I saw a flight attendant walking back and forth with a camera attached on her chest. Although it didn’t really bother me, but yeah, it was quite odd. 🤔 Overall, it was a pretty good flight. Not the best flight I’ve ever had, but considering its cheap price, heck, I would fly with them again (but this time, PLEASE don’t forget the headphones)!

yt_comments.author: @actuallyfims
yt_comments.text: Took for the first time with China Eastern a month ago from Singapore to Seoul with a layover at Shanghai. My expectation going into this was low but everything exceeded my expectations. Price was very cheap at 380SGD return flight and comparing with Singapore's budget airline Scoot which was selling at 500SGD although a direct flight, China Eastern was far more worth it. The price includes 2x 23KG check in, full meal service on all the flights totaling to 4, in-flight entertainment although i agree the content is lacking but wasn't a big deal as i slept thru out the entire flight. Legroom was enough on the B737 while big enough on the A330, the A350 has a slightly larger legroom. Food was good as well.

yt_comments.author: @anthonywalsh2164
yt_comments.text: Very similar service and IFE to China Southern, though the cabin is nicer in MU, very boring in CZ. Also the transit and airport experience in PVG are remarkably similar to those in CAN.

Al Safwa First Lounge - Private Room

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Doha. This may look like a hotel room, but I'm actually inside Qatar Airways' flagship First Class lounge at Hamad International Airport! Tonight, I'll be flying to Hong Kong on one of their Boeing 777s equipped with first-class seats. I'm curious to find out how good Qatar's First Class is compared to their award-winning Q Suite business class. I arrived in Doha 6 hours ago after flying in their Qsuite from Cairo. I had a fantastic time. My flight to Hong Kong is scheduled to leave at 8:25 am the following day. Since I'm travelling in first class, I decided to stay at the airport and relax in the lounge. Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to Doha, the state of Qatar, your gateway to the world! Doha's Hamad International Airport is constantly ranked as the best airport in the world. It is incredibly clean, and the single-terminal design makes it easy to navigate. The terminal resembles the shape of Hong Kong International Airport with shops and lounges divided into North and South sections. The southern duty-free area has roughly 100 shops selling everything from watches, jewellery, wines, cosmetics, books, electronics, food, clothes, and even cars. It has possibly the highest concentration of ultra-high-end shopping I've seen at any airport. Being the airline's home airport, Qatar Airways has a number of lounges here. You can use one of these kiosks to find your way. For departing passengers, there are Silver, Gold, and Platinum lounges for corresponding Qatar, oneworld, and Virgin Australia frequent flyers. The two Al Mourjan Business Lounges are for oneworld passengers with full-fare business class tickets. Lastly, the Al Safwa First Class Lounge is an exclusive retreat for Oneworld first-class passengers and Qatar Privilege Club Platinum members flying in business class. For transit passengers, the entrance to the Al Safwa Lounge is located on level 3. A Qatar Airways representative is stationed at the bottom of the escalator to verify your eligibility before allowing you to ascend. "Al Safwa" translates to "Elite" in Arabic. This is likely my first and only time using this luxurious lounge. As you enter, you may feel as if you're inside a museum. The lounge is indeed modelled after Doha's Museum of Islamic Art. And you can find a showcase of Islamic fine art installations and artefacts loaned from the museum. The centre of the lounge is a crossroads leading to different facilities. From here, you can appreciate the lounge's unimaginably high ceilings, elegant sandstone walls, and simple, minimalistic layout. Any of the walkways is probably larger than the size of most other first-class lounges in the world. The facilities include a state-of-the-art business centre, spa, nap rooms, duty-free shops, parents' room, prayer room, gaming room, and even a small cinema. The highlight of this entire lounge is certainly this stunning water feature, which flows gracefully from the ceiling into the centre of the fountain. With so many amenities on offer, the lounge seating seems almost secondary. It's spread throughout the space, so you definitely won't have any trouble finding a vacant seat. The best option for solo travellers is these semi-enclosed cubicles near the water feature. They are equipped with charging ports, chairs comfortable enough for a nap, and a great sense of privacy. Behind this double door is an "outdoor" terrace, which I think is a great place for those who wish to have a loud conversation with their friends or make phone calls. The calm and tranquillity of this lounge are a stark contrast to the bustling airport terminal below, it felt quite special to have the opportunity to visit this space. After briefly touring the lounge's layout, let's explore the food options. There are two types of dining. To the left of the service desk is a grab-and-go buffet area where you can find salads, freshly made sushi, and other cold bites. The main dining room, located behind the water feature, can accommodate up to 250 people at once. Before COVID, the bar was stocked with Krug and other vintage Champagnes. While this is no longer the case, the selections remain impressive, including quality red and white wines, beers, spirits, cocktails, and more. As I made my way to the dining area, I was greeted at the large brass podium and shown to a table by the window. The menu can be accessed by scanning the QR code on your phone, and the staff will return to take your order. The first-class lounge operates 24/7. Breakfast is served from 5 to 10:30 am, followed by all-day dining from 11 am to 4:30 am the next day. Additionally, there's afternoon tea between 3 and 5 pm. The menu is updated monthly. I began with the chicken chowder, as I always enjoy having soup as an appetiser. It resembled an Asian-style chicken and corn soup and tasted quite pleasant. As for beverages, aside from alcohol, they have teas, coffees, juices, smoothies, soft drinks, and mocktails. For the main course, I chose the Wagyu beef striploin. It was absolutely beautiful,  the steak was cooked exactly to my preference of medium, and it was juicy and tender. Since I wasn't very hungry, I skipped dessert. In general, although the menu isn't the most extensive I've seen, I found the food quite good. It's best to come with an empty belly. For those with a long layover, the lounge has nap rooms on a first-come, first-served basis. These rooms are free for 6 hours, with an option to extend for another 6 hours for 450 Qatari Riyal. Given that there are only 12 rooms in the entire lounge, they tend to fill up quickly during rush hours. My room looks like a single room at a hotel with a comfortable bed, TV, and ensuite bathroom. You can find all the standard amenities like a dental kit, shaving pack, hairdryer, and several body products. Before going to sleep, my sixth sense told me to check my flight on my phone. Since both Qantas and Qatar are members of the oneworld alliance, I could input my flight details into the Qantas app as well. It was 9 pm, and the app showed that my 8:25 flight the next morning was cancelled. Meanwhile, my selected seat, 2A, had disappeared on Qatar's app. A quick check of the flight's seat map revealed that there had been an aircraft change, and the new plane no longer had a first-class cabin. I immediately went to the service desk, and after several phone calls with different departments and a lengthy wait, their solution was to put me in business class. Unsatisfied with this arrangement, I began looking for alternative flights myself. I then found another Qatar flight departing in 4 hours, at 1:50 am, which still had a first-class cabin. After more phone calls and waiting, I was finally rebooked onto that flight, enabling me to continue with this first-class review video. Throughout the entire flight change process, I did not receive any in-app or email notifications from Qatar. If I had not checked the app before my nap, I would have only found out about this change at boarding, potentially facing a downgrade without knowing. After sorting out my ticket and taking a brief nap, I have less than an hour before boarding my new flight. The Al Safwa lounge is situated on the south side of the terminal, while my flight departs from gate C53 on the north side. To save time and effort, Hamad International Airport operates a 772m-long, futuristic cable liner. The journey takes approximately 90 seconds and is remarkably quiet and smooth. A notable feature of the north side terminal is the Orchard, an indoor tropical garden spanning around 10,000 square meters. This area, opened in late 2022, boasts a curved glass roof and is filled with greenery sourced from sustainable forests in southeast Asia. Hamad International Airport currently has around 41 contact gates and 65 remote stands, which means passengers on many flights are required to use a shuttle bus to reach their aircraft. C53 is a remote gate. Boarding commenced roughly an hour before departure. I was instructed to wait for the dedicated business and first-class bus after the economy-class passengers had boarded. However, as I wanted to film the empty cabin, I boarded the bus with the economy class passengers. The aircraft taking me to Hong Kong is a Boeing 777-300ER. But not all seats on Qatar's 777s are the same. In business class, some feature Qatar's award-winning Qsuites, while others have mini pods, also known as "dinosaur seats" due to their older design. Moreover, Qatar leased two former Virgin Australia Boeing 777s and maintained their super diamond seats. And my aircraft today is one of the four planes leased from Cathay Pacific. Hello how are you doing, may I please escort you to your seat? Qatar has retained Cathay's original interior. The business class is installed with the Safran Cirrus II seats in a 1-2-1 layout. The first-class section is at the front of the plane and consists of six seats spread across two rows in a 1-1-1 configuration. Cathay last refreshed them in 2014, it's evident that they have an older design. I chose seat 2A, as it's the most private out of all six. The seat has a width of 36 inches and is, in fact, still the widest first-class seat in the world to this day. There are no overhead compartments in first class, making the cabin a bit more spacious. Instead, there's a closet to the side of the seat, large enough to store a full-size carry-on. For the customers who have just joined us, welcome on board Qatar Airways, as a member of the oneworld alliance... As soon as I settled in, I was offered a drink of my choice, a wet towel, a menu, and an amenity bag. Hello, would you like to have Arabic coffee with dates? Mr Ding, would you like to try an Arabic coffee? There are only three passengers in first class this morning. With the curtains behind me closed, it feels like I'm on a private jet. Not much has changed since Cathay Pacific last flew the aircraft, except for the seat upholstery and the entertainment system. You can push a button to slide the TV screen sideways so it can be directly in front of you. Each first-class seat occupies roughly the space of four windows, providing plenty of legroom. In fact, the ottoman can double as a buddy seat, allowing you to dine face-to-face with your travel companion if you'd like. The tray table is hidden inside the console below the window and is one of the largest I've seen. A USB-A charging port and a universal power plug are oddly positioned near the ottoman. On the left side of my seat, there's a TV remote with Qatar's branding and a 4.3-inch LCD seat control pad still in Cathay Pacific's logo. In front of them is an enclosed storage compartment large enough to store headphones. Two adjustable reading lights are on either side of the seat, providing ample lighting even when the cabin light is fully dimmed. Underneath the TV, there's a shelf stocked with a bottle of water and noise-cancelling headphones. Shortly after takeoff, the crew served me some mixed nuts, and I requested a glass of bubbly. At the same time, they inquired if I would like to order something to eat. Qatar offers dine-on-demand service in business and first class, which means you can order anything on the menu at any time. On selected flights, you can also pre-order a meal online from 14 days to 24 hours before departure. This is the pre-order menu on my original 8:25 am flight. I have to say the selections are pretty underwhelming for first class, so I didn't bother to order anything. For this 8-hour flight, the crew recommended that I have a late-night meal now and breakfast before arrival. I am really glad that I didn't pre-order anything, as the onboard menu features the signature Caviar Service, and I totally don't want to miss that! For drinks, the options are similar to those at the Al Safwa lounge but with less variety. Qatar prints its wine selections on a separate menu and only presents it to non-Muslim passengers. Once again, the Krug champagne is missing, but there is still a great range of higher-end alcoholic drinks. I adore Qatar's table setup, the fake candlelight makes it especially romantic. The caviar was served with traditional accompaniments. This was my first time trying caviar, so I apologise if I didn't eat it correctly. The caviar has a briny, buttery, and slightly fishy taste, and the tiny, jewel-like eggs popped in my mouth instantly, releasing a burst of flavour that lingers on my palate. The simple accompaniments, like the blinis and crème fraîche, really allowed the caviar's flavours to shine. I enjoyed the experience. It's just 3 am in Doha, and we've only been in the air for 60 minutes, yet it's already sunrise! After clearing my table, the crew offered to make the bed for me. 36 inches equals 91.4 cm. You can see how wide it is. When fully flat, the seat is 81 inches, or 205 cm long. It's essentially the size of a single bed. For a more restful sleep, Qatar provides pyjamas and slippers. In 2022, they partnered with the French fragrance brand Diptyque to offer amenity kits to long-haul premium cabin passengers, tailored for both male and female travellers. My super low-key male kit includes socks, earplugs, eyeshades, lip balm, body lotion, face cream, and even a fragrance. There are two lavatories for the six first-class passengers, both situated at the front of the cabin. They are spacious inside and are stocked with dental kits, shaving kits, mouthwash, and some Diptyque products. I also changed into the pyjamas provided. They felt soft and premium. Now that I am all set, it's time for me to have some rest.  I had an uninterrupted 4-hour sleep. This is the most comfortable bed I've slept on in the sky. Since I was awake, the crew offered me a drink. I asked for an espresso with a cookie. That shot of coffee was absolutely necessary. I felt refreshed and ready to explore the entertainment system. The TV screen is 18.5 inches in size, which is petite for first class. It's actually 3 inches smaller than Qatar's own Qsuite business class. It is touch-sensitive but isn't the most responsive one I've used. The award-winning Oryx One system provides over 3,000 entertainment options, with plenty of movies, TV box sets, and games to choose from. There's even a dedicated section that introduces Qatar Airways to first-time flyers. When lying down, the screen can be controlled using the handset. When you choose a movie to watch, it automatically plays on the main screen. The aircraft is equipped with Wi-Fi, and even in first class, I still had to pay for it. It was reasonably priced at US$10 for the entire flight, and the connection speed was fast. I uploaded a video to my Instagram story within a minute and could instantly play YouTube videos without any delays. If you choose not to pay for internet access, you can still use it to check the weather forecast and view the inflight menu on your device. We are less than two hours from landing, and I requested a glass of mixed fruit smoothie, ordered breakfast, and was given a wet towel to freshen up. To begin, I had the seasonal fresh fruits. They all tasted fresh and sweet. The pastries in the basket were all warm. I noticed that Asian dishes always make a strong appearance on both Qatar's lounge menu and onboard menu. Therefore, for the main course, I opted to try the wok-fried noodles with teriyaki chicken. I have to say, the chicken was a little dry; I believe adding some sauce would improve it. The noodles were quite authentic, with plenty of chillies and spring onions. It was a great dish to help me stay awake. After changing back into my day clothes in the lavatory, I found that the crew had already cleaned up my table, tidied my seat, and provided another wet towel and some mints. An hour before landing, I received one last wet towel and some luxury Swiss chocolate. In summary, the flight was excellent. The most memorable parts of the journey for me were the Al Safwa lounge experience and the caviar service on board. While the seat, compared to the Qsuite, is dated and lacks an enclosed door, the bed is much softer, the relatively small first-class section allows the crew to provide a more personal service, and sitting in the second row made me feel quite secluded. I found Cairo to be a great departure point for those searching for affordable business class flights. I was able to find flights such as Gulf Air to Singapore via Bahrain for AU$1200, Oman Air to Denpasar via Muscat and Kuala Lumpur for AU$1400, and Royal Jordanian to Sydney via Amman and Bangkok for AU$2200. I booked my flights just three days before departure, and based on the exchange rate at that time, it cost me around AU$2200 to travel from Cairo to Hong Kong in first class. I believe it was an amazing deal. Unfortunately, the price has since increased to AU$6500 for the same journey. Welcome to Hong Kong, the local time here is 3:13pm. Thank you for choosing to fly with Qatar Airways and the oneworld alliance. It's been a pleasure taking care of you today. Qatar Airways, going places together! Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. See you all in my next video!

yt_comments.author: @TedsCoasterChannel
yt_comments.text: I flew on this exact same plane from MUC to JFK last September, also in the upper deck (98K). It was by far my best economy experience to date. Although the hard product was a bit dated, especially the IFE, the service was incredible, offering hot towels on multiple occasions during the flight and being absolutely attentive all the time. I didn’t really expect much from Lufthansa but they really delivered!

yt_comments.author: @K4Ediamond
yt_comments.text: I completely agree with you. I just flew LH on MUC-DEN and was surprised by the improved service. I would recommend taking the A350 for a modern hard product. I’ve only flown the A380 on British Airways ORD-LHR, and its IFEs were probably even more outdated than this. But it does have mood lighting.

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Egypt. Again! This time I'm here to film a flight review. Today I'll be flying with Qatar Airways from Cairo to Doha. The flight is currently scheduled to have Qsuites, however Qatar is famous for their last-minute aircraft swaps. So Let's hope for the best and I'm heading to the airport now! This is my third time coming to Egypt. While I find the constant harassment from the police, street vendors, taxi drivers, and others unpleasant, I do enjoy standing in front of the pyramids, admiring their magnificence, and watching the sunset over Cairo and Giza city from my hotel balcony. Since 2020, Cairo International Airport has overtaken O.R. Tambo International Airport in Johannesburg and become the busiest airport in Africa. There are direct buses between the city and the airport, but I find that using Uber is the safest and most hassle-free way, especially with a suitcase. I left my hotel during non-rush hour, and the 20 km journey took 40 minutes, costing me 201 Egyptian Pounds. Cairo Airport has four terminals. Terminal 1 caters mainly to low-cost airlines and is linked to other terminals by a mini metro. Terminal 3 is used by the country's flag carrier, Egyptair, and its fellow Star Alliance member airlines. And Terminal 2 serves Skyteam, OneWorld, and Gulf carriers. Additionally, there is a seasonal flight terminal for some Hajj flights. Qatar Airways operates out of Terminal 2. To enter the terminal, you'll need to show the police at the entry a valid ticket, and then go through a security check. Due to security reasons, Cairo Airport does not have luggage storage facilities, so my advice is to arrive here no earlier than 3 hours before departure. Qatar is part of the Oneworld Alliance. There are three lanes at check-in: one for economy, another for those who have completed online check-in, and a third for first-class or status holders. The entire process was quite efficient. Once you obtain the boarding pass, simply head upstairs for immigration and a proper aviation security check. Terminal 2 was reopened in 2016 after a six-year closure for complete renovation. It is now the newest terminal at the airport. It looks modern and clean, with many duty-free shops and a food village offering various dining options. Taking the escalators upstairs, you will find several more dining outlets, including a McDonald's, a museum (which requires an entrance fee), and airline lounges. Emirates and Saudia both operate multiple flights to Cairo each day and have their own lounges. Qatar Airways, along with most other airlines, uses the contracted Ahlein Premium Lounge. Strangely, the path from the reception to the lounge entry involves a bit of a walk, including going through a narrow, claustrophobic corridor. However, once you arrive, it feels like stumbling upon an oasis in the middle of the desert. The 152-seat lounge looks brand new and is designed entirely to Western standards. It's spacious, with floor-to-ceiling windows, cozy couches, and all seats are equipped with power points and USB charging ports. There's also a dedicated dining area, a smoking room, and a children's playroom. If you want a bit more privacy, there are multiple VIP rooms available to hire from US$10 per hour. According to the lounge's official website, there's a fully equipped, state-of-the-art kitchen with a full-time executive chef, providing high-end restaurant-quality food for its passengers. From what I see, there are hot snacks, different types of bread, cakes, soup, and hot dishes like meatballs, lasagna and butter chicken. Furthermore, there are salads and sandwiches. The lounge does not serve alcohol, but there's a self-service minibar stocked with plenty of soft drinks and water. This is the food I got from the buffet, and it tastes as good as it looks. The toilets here are quite clean, and there are two shower rooms, but they weren't available during my visit, and the staff mentioned that even when they are open, there would be an additional cost to use them. Overall, the lounge offers comfortable seats and nice food. But if you are looking for alcohol or a shower, you will be disappointed. The lounge provides a great view of Terminal 2's apron. Just before I left, look what I saw: the big three Gulf carriers parked next to one another. Currently, Etihad operates three daily flights to Cairo using only A320 or A321 narrow-body aircraft. Both Qatar and Emirates fly four times a day. Emirates uses the A380 on three of its flights, while Qatar uses a mixture of A320, A330, A350, B777, and B787 on this route. It's a mixed bag with constant last-minute aircraft swaps. Qatar only has Qsuites on selected A350 and B777 aircraft, really fortunately, my flight today is on an Airbus A350-1000, which is equipped with Qsuites. Qatar brands most of its Middle Eastern business class routes as first class, regardless of the aircraft type. For example, you can fly from Doha to Bahrain on an A320, and while the seat and service on board are the same as business class, your boarding pass will still indicate first class. I suppose this gives Qatar's Middle Eastern customers the privilege of accessing the first class lounge when departing from Doha. Qatar currently has two seating configurations on its A350-1000. At the time of filming, this aircraft had been delivered to Qatar only a few weeks ago. Instead of the usual 12 rows of Qsuite seats, it has only six rows. This change adds 91 more economy class seats, making it ideal for high-demand leisure destinations like Bali and Cairo. The Qsuites are arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration with forward-facing and rear-facing seats alternating in rows. The E and F seats are referred to as honeymoon seats, allowing couples to sleep side-by-side in a double bed. When you book the E, F, D, and G seats together, known as the quad, you can lower the dividers in the centre section, creating a mini-cabin of four seats. As soon as I settled in, the crew offered me a drink of my choice, a menu, and a hot or cold towel, followed by a cup of Arabic coffee and dates. As a first-time Qsuite traveller, I appreciate this short video showing me the seat's features. Cairo Airport has 3 parallel runways. This afternoon, we took off from runway 05C. Now, let's take a closer look at the Qsuite. At the front is a 21.5-inch high-definition touchscreen. Since the plane is still climbing, the sliding door cannot be closed yet. Next to the screen, there's a counter, and under it, is a shelf for small items like a charging mobile phone. Below the shelf, there's a set of seat control buttons, along with a Do Not Disturb button and a reading light button. Then, there's a credit card reader, a headphone jack, a universal power point, a USB-A charging port, and a touch-sensitive TV remote, all within easy reach. Under this console, I find enough floor space to put my camera bag. The tray table is hidden underneath the TV and is big and stable. The Qsuite seat has a width of 21.5 inches and can convert into a 79-inch fully flat bed, there's plenty of legroom. The armrest closer to the aisle is actually a small side compartment where you can find noise-canceling headphones, a bottle of water, and I use it to store my cable bag and passport holder. The Qsuite has a lot of storage space. Next to my seat, there's a coat hook and an adjustable reading light with several brightness levels. Once the door is closed, the 52-inch-high wall makes the Qsuite incredibly private. Being here in person, I now understand why everyone loves the Qsuite: this is a truly revolutionary design and the best business-class seat in the sky. About 15 minutes after takeoff, the crew served me some warm nuts and a Pineapple Margarita mocktail. At the same time, they asked about my meal preference. Qatar offers dine-on-demand service in business and first class, which means you can order your meal at any time you want. The scheduled flight time to Doha is just 3 hours and 5 minutes, so I requested to have my meal whenever it's ready. Even though this is a short flight, Qatar still provides a full three-course meal with several choices. For drinks, there's a comprehensive selection of mocktails, juices, soft drinks, tea, coffee, and hot chocolate. As Qatar is a Muslim country, the airline prints the wine list on a separate menu and only presents it to non-Muslim passengers. As expected, there's a wide variety of premium champagne, wines, and spirits, and the crew can make many classic cocktails too. This is again, the best business-class wine list I've seen in the sky. Twenty minutes after placing my order, the appetiser arrived. This is a restaurant in the sky, the scallops were beautifully presented. They were accompanied by a freshly baked trio of bread, another drink of my choice, olive oil, and butter. The paprika-seasoned scallops had a golden-brown exterior and a succulent taste, and the pomegranate seeds and cherry tomatoes added a refreshing touch to the dish. For the main course, I decided to try a local Qatari dish created by Culinary Artist Chef Aisha Al Tamimi. Machboos is a rice dish, the rice is cooked with a blend of spices, giving it a rich flavour and vibrant colour. The dish was generously topped with large, succulent prawns. Daqoos is a spicy tomato sauce that added another tangy and flavourful element. Like Emirates and Etihad, Qatar Airways relies heavily on transit passengers. Over 70% of its passengers have never left the airport in Doha. I believe that introducing such local dishes on the plane provides passengers with an opportunity to get to know Qatar as a country rather than just an airline. For dessert, as I was pretty full,  I opted for the healthier option of mixed berries with rose water syrup. There are two lavatories designated for Qsuite passengers on this aircraft, located at the front of the plane. The one on the left has a window and is spacious. It is stocked with infused facial water, hand lotion, and dental kits can be found in the drawers. Most airlines these days have touch sensitive seatback screens on wide-body aircraft. In business class, there's typically a hand-held remote for easier control while lying down. Qatar offers a third way to control the screen: by scanning the QR code on your phone, you can use your own device as a remote, allowing you to navigate the system without touching any surface. The 21.5-inch screen is large yet very crisp, having 11 languages. The award-winning Oryx One provides over 3,000 entertainment options, including plenty of movies and TV box sets to choose from. The A350-1000 is installed with three high-resolution onboard cameras, which is especially handy for passengers not seated near a window. The hand-held remote is the size of a mobile phone and can work completely independently with the TV screen. I can watch a movie on the small screen while checking out the flight path on the main screen. The provided headsets do a great job with noise cancellation. The flight from Cairo to Doha is way too short for me to fully enjoy every feature of the Qsuite, we are now only 50 minutes from landing. Let me quickly try the lie-flat seat. The footwell is not too narrow; I can still move my feet around. The bed is quite comfortable and long, measuring 79 inches or 200 cm in length. The velvet blanket feels luxuriously soft and warm. Sadly, I won't be able to take a nap as my time in this fantastic Qsuite is coming to an end. Just before the seatbelt sign was turned on, the crew handed me some luxury Swiss chocolate and a wet towel. The aircraft is equipped with high-speed wifi, the price is affordable, but I didn't get time to use it. The Qsuite was first launched in 2017, propelling Qatar's Business Class product to rival many airlines' First Class products. Its innovative features such as sliding privacy doors, on-demand dining, double beds and the ability to convert middle seats into quad configurations have re-defined Business Class travel. The design is impeccable. Some may be deterred by the rearward-facing seats, but personally, I found them just as comfortable as sitting forward. Qatar's soft product is also outstanding. The distance between Cairo and Doha is similar to flying Qantas from Sydney to Auckland. Yet Qatar offers a complete fine dining experience with an exceptional beverage selection. The meal I enjoyed was fresh and delicious. Putting politics aside, I would no doubt love to fly with Qatar again. Both Egyptair and Qatar Airways fly direct between Cairo and Doha. Egyptair's business class is AU$766 one way, while Qatar is AU$1,043. If you could score a Qsuite, the extra money is totally worth it. Welcome to Hamad International Airport in Doha, home to one of the cleanest, most modern, and most beautiful airport terminals in the world. The Al Safwa First Class lounge is one of the best airport lounges I've ever visited. Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. I'll show you more about this airport and the lounge in my next video!

yt_comments.author: @jckyu
yt_comments.text: I flew on Air China's 747-400 when I went back to China last year, from Beijing Capital to Shenzhen Bao'an (PEK-SZX). This route is among China's busiest, but that day only 110 passengers were onboard. The business class was fairly crowded, but in economy, Air China was literally ferrying chairs - cushy vintage airplane seats with a boxy shape that reminded me of Pan Am's 747s, which I have only seen in online pictures. The business class seats are angle-flat and exactly the same as Asiana's, as shown in this video. I was fortunate to book myself in business class on the upper deck, with my friend and I each occupying a window seat. The view from the upper deck was truly amazing; I've never seen the ramp from such a tall angle. The inflight meal, a mediocre Japanese-style rice bowl, was unremarkable, but the cabin crew was stellar. They seemed to know a lot of aviation geeks are flying this route and were quite welcoming to us, two young students who are obviously different from the other business people on the plane, who were either taking a nap or doing paperwork, while we were unsettled in our seats, eager to explore the rest of the cabin. So, the flight attendants invited us to tour the first-class section on the lower deck, where Air China has swivel-style seats, quite similar to American Airlines’ first-class product on their 777s. We also toured the galley area, where we saw the cassette-based IFE system. Sadly, the economy class movie screen has been retrofitted, using LCD TVs rather than CRT projectors. The cabin has lots of interesting details, such as a fixture on the wall that is a Chinese drawing on one side, and a mirror when flipped to the other side. Some research revealed that Air China is using these B744s as backups for Xi’s "Air Force One", and that’s the reason why they are still flying. The last time the plane I was on (B-2447) was used for governmental tasks was flying Kim Jong Un to Singapore, phew. Of course, the airplane will be remodeled for these tasks. Another interesting aspect of my flight was that my friend and I estimated the cost per seat using fuel burn information and found it to be even higher than what we paid for our tickets (about $350 per person). This confirmed our suspicion that Air China wasn't expecting these 747s to generate revenue, but rather they were in operation for political reasons.

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to my home Adelaide. Tomorrow I'll be heading to Melbourne where I'll catch Quantis's inaugural A220 flight to Canra. This aircraft is set to revolutionize regional travel in Australia. I'm excited to be one of the first passengers to experience it. Let's go. I booked the earliest flight out of Adelaide this morning. Arriving in Melbourne at 7:45 a.m., which will give me about 2 hours to connect to my A220 flight. The journey was smooth and we touched down in Melbourne on time. Melbourne airport has four terminals. All domestic Quantis and Quantis Link flights depart from terminal one. The terminal has undergone a significant upgrade of its retail and other general facilities. Some of the dining outlets have reopened, including a very stylish hungry jacks. The central food court is installed with floor toseeiling windows, which are perfect for plane spotting. Quantis operates three lounges at this terminal. They all share the same entrance. Upon taking the escalators up, the Quantis Club is situated on the right hand side, welcoming Quantis Club members, Quantis Gold and One World Sapphire members. [snorts] The invitation only chairman's lounge is discreetly located behind the doors marked private. And the business lounge is on the left, open to business class passengers, Quantis platinum and above and one world emerald members. The business lounge features floor toseeiling windows along its entire length providing sweeping views of the apron. From here, I could clearly see my aircraft. This lounge can accommodate up to 350 people. There's a range of seating options, including benches for working, booths for dining, and other seats for relaxing. The dark luxurious tones and sophisticated finishes reflect the chic urban feel of Melbourne. For those needing to freshen up, there are several private shower suites stocked with organic shower products and a variety of toiletries. The breakfast buffet is available until around 11 to 11:30 a.m. The food is on the basic side. There are usually baked beans, scrambled eggs, sausages, yogurts, fruits, deli meats, salads, and bread. One highlight for me is a fruit juice machine, as I enjoy making myself a glass of carrot juice. In the heart of the lounge, there's a bar serving barista style coffee throughout the day, as well as tap and bottled beer, spirits, and Australian wines from midday onwards. Overall, as many would agree, this is a best domestic business lounge in Australia. After over two months of crew training, today marks the first day that Quantis puts its A220 into revenue service. Quantis has ordered 29 A220-300 aircraft and has received two so far. The first A220 features a striking livery design and is the sixth aircraft to join Quantis' flying art series which has showcased Aboriginal art since 1995. The aircraft is named after an artwork that tells the dreaming story of two sisters journeying across remote Australia, covering vast distances to find their way home. I had been really hoping to fly on this aircraft today, but unfortunately this second A220 that Quantis received painted in the regular Quantis link livery will be the one that flies me to CRA. Boarding for Quantis domestic flights typically begins 20 minutes before departure. I headed to the gate early to see if Quantis held any special ceremony. Well, aside from some aviation enthusiasts taking photos of the plane, there wasn't much else happening. Hello everyone. We now like to invite our business customers Quantis and Em one platinum and gold together with one more camera. Fantastic. Thank you. Hello there. Welcome. This Quantis Link A220 has a total of 137 seats. At the front are 10 business class car seats in a 22 configuration with three rows on the right side of the cabin and two on the left side. Each seat has a pitch of 37 in and a width of 23.9 in, which is quite comparable to the Quantis Bone 737 business seats, but with a more modern touch. The economy class is arranged in a 32 configuration. All standard seats have a pitch of 30 in. Due to one fewer row of business car seats on the left side, Quantis utilized the additional space to create extra leg room seats in rows 4 to9 on that side of the cabin. I chose seat 9A. This extra leg room seat is complimentary for platinum one and chairman's lounge members, while for everyone else it is $30. In return, my seat had a pitch of 34 in. Welcome on board. It's great to have you with us. Additionally, seats 4 D, 4E, 4 F, as well as the seats in row 12 are extra leg room seats, too. To celebrate this inaugural service, everyone received a special gift bag upon boarding. Today, we're on a historic flight. It's our first inaugural flight of this particular aircraft servicing Quantis Ning 220. We have 29 of these aircraft on order which are gradually replacing our aging Boeing 717 fleet. We hope enjoy your flight with us today. So please sit back, relax, let us take care of you as you enjoy your place in history making Quantis Link the very first aircraft and airline to fly the A220 in Australia. Good morning and welcome on board. The A220s will be replacing the aging Boeing 717s in the Quantis Link fleet. With a range of up to 6,390 km, they are capable of flying non-stop between any two destinations in Australia. The A220 is a clean sheet design bringing together state-of-the-art aerodynamics, advanced materials, and the latest generation technologies. It has the largest windows of any single aisle aircraft, providing a superb view of the scenery outside. Now, let's take a more detailed look at my seat. All economy class seats are 18 in wide. My height is 6'1. The extra leg room allows me to fully stretch out my legs. The seat can recline 5 in and a sixway adjustable headrest provides great neck support. At the back of the seat, there's a drop- down tablet holder with an anti-slip mat, perfect for streaming videos on your personal device. Next to it are both USBC and USBA ports to keep your electronic devices charged. There's also a universal power plug shared between every two seats. Quantis has chosen not to install seatback screens in both business and economy class. Instead, they offer free highspeed inflight Wi-Fi. To connect, simply select Quantis free Wi-Fi in settings and you'll be connected after watching a short ad. The Wi-Fi speed is fast enough for streaming Netflix and watching YouTube videos. Alternatively, you can stream a selection of movies and TV shows provided by Quantis by using the Quantis Entertainment app on a device. The app offers over 2,500 hours of content to choose from. If you don't have an electronic device, you can still enjoy your flight by browsing through the monthly published Quantis magazine. The flight time to CRA is around 45 minutes. I received a small snack along with a choice of tea, coffee, water, juice, and soft drinks. If your flight departs after 12:00 p.m. or is over 2 and 1 half hours long and departs after 9:00 a.m., wine and beer are also available at no extra cost. The Airbus A220 has three toilets, one at the front for business class passengers, and there's another two at the back of the aircraft. As expected, the toilet is modern and quite spacious. I found a vacant standard seat toward the back of the aircraft. While the leg room isn't as generous as mine, it's certainly tolerable for a short flight like this. Hello everyone, the captain switched on the fastener seat belts under preparation for landing as we are also experiencing some mild turbulence. It's now time for your flight attendant to take their seats. All customers and crew must now be seated with seat belts firmly fastened. Shortly after the snack service, it's already time for landing. In general, the A220 is a fantastic aircraft to fly on. It features the same three two configured economy seats as the Boeing 717, meaning there are fewer dreadful middle seats than the Boeing 737. The A220's cabin is lined with special insulation and sound deadening materials, making it much quieter than the previous generation aircraft. There are currently four airlines offering direct flights between Melbourne and CRA. Without checked baggage, the lowest economy fair I could find with Jet Star is $77. Virgin's light fair is $99. Choice fair is $119. Rex with checked baggage is $115 and Quantis is $169. Whether it's worth paying the extra money to fly with Quantis is a personal decision, but I thoroughly enjoyed this flight and can't really fault anything. On behalf of all of us here at Quantis Link and One World, we like to thank you for choosing to fly with us and being part of this historic inaugural flight of Quantis Link A220 Melbourne to CRA. article_quotes.text: From its inception, KrisWorld has been designed to cater to diverse passenger preferences, offering a vast selection of entertainment options, including movies, TV shows, music, games, and more.
"With KrisWorld, customers have access to 22 video channels, 12 audio channels, 10 popular video games, real-time news, information on popular SIA destinations and a personal in-seat telephone.
WISEMEN is a major enhancement of KrisWorld being the first in-flight entertainment system to offer both video and audio on demand.
This includes the latest Hollywood, Bollywood, and international films, TV series, live programming, and a broad selection of music genres.
The system now features high-definition touchscreens with intuitive user interfaces, making it easy for passengers to navigate the extensive content library.
Passengers can stay connected during their flight with in-seat power outlets, USB ports, and Wi-Fi available on most flights.

Posts By Sumit Singh Technological Innovations Inflight connectivity Singapore Airlines has been a pioneer in inflight connectivity, launching its inflight internet service in 2005 through Connexion by Boeing.
The latest Panasonic eX3 systems introduced in 2012 further improved inflight connectivity, allowing passengers to make phone calls, send text messages, and access the internet for a fee.

article_quotes.text: Additionally, Thales will install the AVANT Up IFE System on Air India’s 11 new Airbus and Boeing aircraft with deliveries to commence in 2025.
Thales’ AVANT Up features Optiq , 4K QLED HDR displays for high-quality outputs.
The Optiq system features in-screen USB-A and USB-C high-speed charging ports and is the only display with two Bluetooth connections and built-in Wi-Fi.
With Optiq passengers can pair their wireless headphones or other devices to the display while also charging their phones and laptops so they can arrive at their destination recharged and relaxed.
This is paired with 3D mapping and Thales’ Select User Interface.
Partnering with Thales for its top-of-the-class AVANT Up inflight entertainment systems is a step in the direction of our transformation programme.

On larger displays, there is some HD content – but it can be a struggle to have suppliers deliver content at the high resolutions needed to play this – as well as the storage servers on the aircraft to deliver this content.
It’ll be interesting to see how Air India addresses this with their suppliers to deliver HDR and 4K content to the seat – and what its requirements will be.

Air India, India’s leading global airline with the largest international network in the country and the most non-stop routes connecting India with global destinations, has selected Thales’ AVANT Up inflight entertainment (IFE) solution.
Additionally, Thales will install AVANT Up IFE on Air India’s 11 new Airbus and Boeing aircraft with deliveries to commence in 2025.
AVANT Up offers tremendous possibilities for integrating a wide range of services and applications, such as an interactive 3D map and immersive route-based programming.
Thales’ AVANT Up features Optiq, 4K QLED HDR displays designed to provide the best viewing experience in the air with unrivalled picture quality.
Optiq features in-screen USB-A and USB-C high speed charging ports and is the only display with two Bluetooth connections and built-in Wi-Fi.
With Optiq passengers can pair their wireless headphone or other devices to the display while also charging their phones and laptops so they can arrive at their destination recharged and relaxed.
Partnering with Thales for its top-of-the-class AVANT Up inflight entertainment systems is a step in the direction of our transformation programme.
