reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Yerevan, Armenia. Tonight I’m going to catch a cross border train from Yerevan to Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia. I have never been on an international train before, I don’t know what to expect, but I think it’s gonna be an interesting ride! Let’s go! Armenia is a landlocked country located in the South Caucasus region of Eurasia. It shares borders with Georgia to the north, Azerbaijan to the east, Iran to the south, and Turkey to the west. The capital and the largest city of Armenia is Yerevan. Armenia was part of the Soviet Union from 1922 until its independence in 1991. The Yerevan Metro currently consists of a single line that runs for 13.4 kilometres (8.3 miles) and has ten stations. It was the first metro system built in the Soviet Union outside of Russia and began operating in 1981. From Republic Square, located in the heart of the city, the most efficient way to reach Yerevan Railway Station is by taking the metro for two stops. Upon arrival, the metro exit conveniently leads directly to the station. Unfortunately, filming inside the metro stations is prohibited. Therefore I wasn’t able to show much of the experience. Yerevan Station was built in the early 1950s to serve as a hub for train travel throughout Armenia and provide connections to neighbouring countries. The large and impressive building reflects the architectural style of the Soviet era and it remains under the ownership and maintenance of Russian Railways to this day. The expansive main hall has a restaurant, a rail museum, waiting rooms, and ticket offices. To purchase a ticket to Tbilisi, you can come to this ticket counter. My train, number 372, operates every two days. It’s worth noting that tickets can sometimes sell out, so I purchased mine on the official Armenian Railways website a few weeks ago to secure my spot. Armenia’s intercity, commuter, and freight rail transport is exclusively operated by South Caucasus Railway, a company that is 100% owned by Russian Railways. The country’s rail network spans approximately 780 km of tracks, all in the 1,520 mm Russian gauge. Good evening! When I arrived at the station an hour before the train’s departure, it was already on the platform. The carriages look brand new don’t they? Initially, South Caucasus Railway used old Soviet-era carriages on this service, but in June 2021, they were replaced by these state-of-the-art smart air-conditioned carriages imported from Russia. The entire railway line to Tbilisi is electrified. Tonight, the train is being pulled by the VL10 electric locomotive, introduced in the 1960s. The VL10s are renowned for their reliability and durability, especially in extreme weather conditions. They were extensively used throughout the Soviet Union. The initials VL stand for Vladimir Lenin, after whom the class is named. Boarding for my train commenced 45 minutes before departure, each carriage has a conductor who checks passengers’ tickets and travel documents. Tonight’s train consists of 4 carriages with 3 different travel classes. I booked myself a 2-bed First Class Spalny Vagon, which is the most expensive option on board. Each cabin has a lockable sliding door, and I will show you more about it later. The next class down is the four-bed 2nd class compartment Купейный. Each cabin features four berths, with the two lower berths convertible into seats during the day. There are retractable ladders to assist passengers in climbing up to the upper berths. In front of the window is a large table with built-in cup holders. Under the table, there are four power sockets available. Each 2nd class compartment also has a lockable sliding door. The third class on the train is open-plan sleepers, known as Плацкарт. While it is the most economical option, everyone still gets a bed, power sockets, USB ports, air conditioning, reading lights, and overhead storage space. When travelling in second and third class, passengers can pay a bit extra to opt for the lower berth. The hallways are monitored by CCTV cameras for added security, and every carriage has two toilets. Returning to the first class section, I noticed a high-definition touchscreen in the centre of the carriage displaying information on the onboard facilities and the train’s schedule. Despite indicating the presence of a vending machine on the screen, I was unable to locate one. Nonetheless, as the train does not have a buffet car, I highly recommend that you have dinner in the city before boarding. On one end of my carriage, there is a mini bar equipped with a cold and hot water dispenser. We departed from Yerevan on time at 9:30 pm and are expected to reach Tbilisi at 7:35 am the next day, completing the 370-kilometre journey in 10 hours and 5 minutes. The lack of customs facilities at the train stations in both cities makes the trip take much longer than it should, as the train has to stop for approximately 40 minutes at the final station in Armenia and the initial station in Georgia. Each first-class carriage has nine private cabins, accommodating a maximum of 18 passengers. The toilets in each carriage are identical, with a green WC sign indicating the toilet is vacant and turning red when occupied. The toilet on the left is spacious and modern, with a baby changing table. The other toilet is equipped with a shower, however, shampoo and body wash are not provided, only some leftover soap is available. Therefore, I would recommend you to bring your own toiletries if you plan to shower during the trip. Finally, let me show you my first-class cabin. Each cabin door is equipped with a hotel-style key card, allowing passengers to lock the door when leaving the cabin. However, the conductor did not distribute key cards to any passengers, and the door remained unlocked for the entire trip. Fortunately, the door can still be locked from the inside, so it’s not a very big deal. The first-class cabin is the same size as the 4-berth second-class compartment, but with only two beds, it feels much more spacious. There is a TV above the sliding door. Sadly I was unable to figure out how to use it. Above the TV is a storage space for small suitcases or backpacks. If you have a larger bag, you can store it under the bed. My 78cm suitcase fit perfectly. As expected, there are four power sockets located below the table. First-class tickets come with complimentary snacks, including a pack of biscuits, coffee sticks, strawberry milk sticks, a bottle of spring water, and sparkling water. A first-class ticket comes with one single bed, so as a solo traveller, I bought two tickets to have the whole cabin to myself. The table is the same in all three travel classes and can be moved to an upright position to create more space. As you can see, the cabin is currently configured for daytime use, with a reading light and a headphone jack situated at each end of the seat. I assume the remaining buttons on the panel are for adjusting the TV channels and the volume. Besides the cabin door, there’s a button for calling the train guard, light switches, and an emergency stop button. Beddings are supplied in all three classes, but first-class passengers receive extra amenities such as slippers, a toiletry kit including dental care products, a comb, a soap, a shower cap, and a sanitary bag. The current temperature outside is around 5 degrees Celsius. There are heaters throughout the train. The temperature on board is centrally controlled, and I found it to be quite warm. The good news is that the window in each cabin can be opened, which is excellent for getting a breath of fresh air. The train is equipped with Wi-Fi, although I was unable to connect to it. So this is what my first-class cabin looks like. I love the tall ceiling and the modern facilities. I’m also very pleased with the twin bed setup instead of the bunk bed arrangement that is common on many overnight trains worldwide. This layout made it easier for everyone to access the bed and created an impression of having more space in the cabin. Yerevan isn’t a large city, the city lights faded away just 15 minutes after the train departed. It’s already 10:30 pm, and we’ll reach the border in five hours, so I’ve decided to make the bed. The seat can be folded down like this, and voila, it’s now a single bed. The bedding packet includes a hand towel, two sheets, and a pillowcase. Now this looks more like a single cabin with a bed on one side and a chair on the other, which is perfect for me!! Even though blankets were not provided, the cabin temperature was warm enough, I didn’t really need one. The bed is a bit narrow, but it is long and quite comfortable. There are 13 stops between Yerevan and Tbilisi, with most being brief except for the stop in Gyumri. Being the second largest city in Armenia, Gyumri is located just 16 km from Turkey. Historically, there was a railway connection from Kars in Turkey to Gyumri, but this was closed in the 1990s due to political tensions. The train will stop here for 20 minutes, and passengers are allowed to smoke on the platform. After three more hours, we arrived at Ayrum, the last station in Armenia. Once the train stopped, 5 Armenian border police boarded the carriage, each carrying a portable computer for scanning passports. They flipped through every page of my passport but didn’t ask any questions. Within 30 seconds, they put an exit stamp on an empty page and allowed me to continue my journey. There was no bag search, and the whole process was quite efficient. In the meantime, I also managed to figure out how to turn on the TV. Although everything is in Russian, I believe the TV is capable of receiving satellite signals for various channels. However, after trying for 20 minutes, I could not find a working channel and eventually gave up. Maybe I’m just not tech-savvy enough for this. We stopped at Ayrum for 40 minutes, Georgia is only 20 minutes away! We have finally reached the actual land border! Goodbye Armenia, and hello Georgia! This is the busiest border crossing between the two countries, located on the M6 highway connecting Tbilisi to Yerevan. The crossing is open 24/7 and is used by thousands of people and hundreds of vehicles daily. Three minutes after crossing into Georgia, we arrived at Sadakhlo Station, where the Georgian police boarded the train and conducted random checks of passengers’ luggage, mainly looking for excessive alcohol and cigarettes, and then we were all asked to bring our travel documents and go to the offices on the platform for passport checks. The process of entering Georgia is much more complex than exiting Armenia. The police asked various questions regarding the purpose and duration of the visit. The train was scheduled to stop here for 40 minutes, but some passengers experienced delays in processing their documents, and several individuals were forced to leave the train and were sent back to Armenia. As a result, the departure time was delayed from 5:30 am until 6:10 am. It takes only two hours to get to Tbilisi from the border, and I fell back to sleep until the conductor knocked on my cabin door half an hour before arrival. Along with the wake-up call, she also collected the bed sheet. The descent into Tbilisi is very scenic. This train is a popular choice for tourists and locals who wish to avoid lengthy bus rides or expensive airfares between the two cities. Despite being unable to figure out the TV, having no functioning Wi-Fi, not receiving a swipe card, and the conductor’s limited English skills, I appreciate the modern facilities in my first-class cabin. On the other hand, having the border crossing between 3:30 am and 5:30 am gave me only four hours of sleep during the journey, leaving me sleepy for the rest of the day. It would be ideal to have immigration facilities at both Yerevan and Tbilisi stations, similar to the Eurostar, to enable passengers to enjoy uninterrupted rest during the trip. Nonetheless, this was an unforgettable experience for me. Welcome to Tbilisi Station, the hub for Georgian Railway. From here, you can board a train to the stunning coastal city of Batumi on the Black Sea, as well as to Yerevan and Baku, the respective capitals of Armenia and Azerbaijan. Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more train and flight reviews. See you all in my next video!

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Kuala Lumpur international airport. I've been to Malaysia quite a few times in the past, but I never get to fly with Malaysia Airlines. This morning, thanks to Oman Air, I'm finally going to fly with them to Bali Denpasar on an A330 aircraft. Hopefully, it'll be a great experience. Let's go! Welcome to Malaysia! I arrived here 12 hours ago after flying with Oman Air. As I booked both the Oman Air and the Malaysia Airlines flight under the same PNR, my bag was through-checked from Muscat to Bali. This allowed me to stay within the transit area and skip the immigration. Kuala Lumpur International Airport is Malaysia's main international airport, situated roughly 45 kilometres south of the city. It served more than 62 million passengers in 2019, making it the 21st busiest airport globally. The airport has two terminals, terminal 2, also known as KLIA 2 is a purpose-built terminal for budget airlines. It's the hub for Air Asia and Air Asia X. The main terminal building, also known as KLIA main or KLIA 1, along with a satellite terminal, handles most of the airport's domestic and international flights. It's the primary hub for Malaysia Airlines. As you can see, the satellite building offers a variety of amenities, including restaurants, cafes, duty-free shops, lounges, and prayer rooms. To move between the main terminal and the satellite building, passengers can ride the aero train. The satellite building also houses a transit hotel named Sama Sama Express KLIA. Due to the confusing signage, it took me a bit of time to find it. It's actually situated just before Gate C5. The hotel has 80 rooms, each with a private bathroom and a king-sized bed. My room was impeccably clean, and most importantly, it boasted a fantastic view of the apron. You can book the room for 6, 9 or 12 hours. My 12-hour stay cost me 386 Malaysian ringgit. The price is reasonable. Malaysia Airlines is a member of the Oneworld Alliance, its international flagship lounge is called the Golden Lounge Satellite, located above the aero train platforms. This lounge complex is shared between first-class and business-class passengers, with the entry to the first-class lounge on the right and the business-class lounge on the left. Flying in business class tomorrow gives me access to the business lounge. Being a Qantas Platinum Frequent Flyer with Oneworld Emerald status, I have access to the first-class lounge as well. Although not overly spacious, the lounge features plenty of comfortable seating and stunning apron views during the day. The self-serve counter provides alcoholic beverages, soft drinks, water, coffee, and tea.  Other amenities include toilets, prayer rooms, a napping area, and individual shower suites. There's no food available in the main seating area, instead, there's a small restaurant offering a la carte dining. Featuring only 13 tables in this room, the space fills up quickly. During my visit, I had to wait for half an hour before finally securing a table. While the menu is not the most extensive, it stills offer several options for each course. To start, I opted for their signature OX Tail soup, and I must say, it was worth my half-hour wait to get in here. The broth was rich and flavourful, and the meat on the ox tail was tender. Malaysians are known for their skill in cooking chicken, it is a staple protein in Malaysian cuisine. For my main course I chose the boneless roasted chicken, which had crispy skin and moist meat. Both the chicken and the noodles below were complemented by the tangy and slightly spicy mustard sauce,  this is another flavourful dish. The chicken alone was already very filling, so I decided to skip the dessert. In general, what I appreciate about the first-class lounge is its peaceful atmosphere and the a la carte menu that showcases local Malaysian cuisine. Now, let's take a look at the business class lounge. Passengers with a business class ticket from any Oneworld airline and Oneworld Sapphire tiered frequent flyers flying in Economy can enter this lounge free of charge. This place is much larger than the first-class lounge. I was particularly impressed by the food selections here. While it may not offer the fine-dining experience of the first-class lounge next door, the buffet is expansive and varied. The menu changes seasonally. It typically features local Malaysian dishes such as Nasi Lemak, Chicken Satay, Curry Laksa, and Beef Rendang, and international options like salads, sandwiches, soups and pasta dishes. In addition, there's an assortment of cakes, pastries, and fresh fruit. After a few hours of decent sleep, I checked out of my hotel room and returned to the Golden Lounge for a quick breakfast before my flight. I went directly to the business lounge this time, as it had a more comprehensive food selection. Although it was busier than the previous night, I was still able to find an empty table. By the way, the business lounge also has napping rooms, prayer rooms, and showers. As of November 2022, Malaysia Airlines has a fleet of 69 aircraft comprising of 42 Boeing 737-800, 6 A350-900, 15 A330-300, and 6 A330-200. At the time of filming, the airline operates three daily flights between Kuala Lumpur and Denpasar, utilising a combination of Boeing 737 and A330 aircraft. Similar to Singapore Changi Airport, security screening is carried out at the boarding gate, so please make sure you allocate sufficient time for boarding. My flight this morning is operated by an Airbus A330-300, which features 27 business class and 263 economy class seats. Malaysia Airlines uses Thompson Aero's Vantage model business seats on their a330 and a350s. They are arranged in a combination of 1-2-2 and 1-2-1 configurations. The seats on the right-hand side of the cabin are all single, those in the middle are double, and those on the left are a mix of single and double seats. Additionally, there are two rows of 2-4-2 configured extra-legroom economy class seats behind the business cabin before door 2. I particularly like this seat design as it caters to both solo travellers and couples. For this flight, I selected seat 6K, which is a throne seat. There is a lot more surface space around my seat compared to the double seats behind. Once I had taken my seat, the cabin crew offered me a glass of juice and a cold towel. Moments later, the cabin manager walked to every seat and greeted everyone by their last names. There are two lavatories assigned for the 27 business passengers. Despite the short flight, each lavatory is stocked with body and hand lotion, eau de toilette and toothpicks. Kuala Lumpur International Airport has 3 runways, and today we'll be using the east runway. Now let's take a closer look at my seat. I noticed a coat hook situated beside the entertainment screen. There are several storage places surrounding the seat, including a spacious area under the window enough to fit my camera bag and the provided blanket. On the opposite side of my seat, there's a hidden compartment with a vanity mirror. There are two control panels for adjusting the seat's position, activating the massage function and turning on the overhead reading light. Adjacent to the armrest, there's a USB-port, a headphone jack, a remote for the entertainment screen, and an adjustable reading light. A universal power socket and the safety card holder are positioned near my leg. The seat has a width of 20 inches, which is on the narrower side, and the pitch is 43 inches. Overall, while Malaysia Airlines' Vantage-based seats are not the most luxurious option on the market, they do offer all the features that a business traveller would anticipate. The product ticked all my boxes. Shortly after takeoff, the crew commenced lunch service. A menu was handed to me when the plane was on the ground. There are three choices for the main course, and I opted for the Nasi Lemak. As of 2020, the estimated Muslim population in Malaysia is 63.5%. Although there aren't any alcoholic beverages listed on the menu, a bottle of red, white and champagne were displayed on the drink trolley. Accompanying the main course were a selection of pastries, including crustless white toast, croissant, and banana cake. The champagne served onboard was produced by Philipponnat, it has a retail price of $82 per bottle in Australia. Nasi Lemak is often considered the national dish of Malaysia, it is a popular meal enjoyed at any time of the day. The dish typically comes with cucumber slices, a hard-boiled egg, fried anchovies, and roasted peanuts. The proteins in this dish can be varied, but chicken, beef, and prawns are typically the most common options. A spicy chilli paste known as sambal is added to enhance the dish's flavour. The prawns are big and tasted fresh and succulent. However, the highlight of the meal was undoubtedly the sambal, which boasted a perfect blend of spicy, sweet, and savoury flavours. Pairing the rice with this sauce was simply delectable. Instead of using the boiled egg, Malaysia Airlines used the omelette, which was nothing special. In general I was absolutely delighted with this dish, I have no doubt that this is the most delicious Nasi Lemak one could have in the air! Let's have a look at the inflight entertainment system. In the pocket below, there is a very basic noise-cancelling headphone. The 16" HD screen is a touchscreen, and you can also control it with the remote. The system is available in both English and Malay and offers a decent selection of movies, including recent releases, and TV shows. And of course, you can check out the flight path as well. We are currently just 57 minutes from Denpasar, and the plane will begin its descent in less than 20 minutes. As expected, each seat can be converted into a fully-flat bed. The bed length is 76 inches, which should be long enough for most people. The biggest drawback of my "throne" seat is its narrow foot nook compared to other business class seats, resulting in limited space for foot movement while lying down. Despite this, this bed is still relatively comfortable for those flying long-haul. In summary, this flight was fantastic. While their business class seats may not be the latest and the greatest, from ample storage space and power outlets to a comfortable lie-flat bed and direct aisle access, the seat still has everything I needed. What impressed me the most, however, was Malaysia Airlines' exceptional soft product. The crew members were all friendly, professional, and energetic, with smiles on their faces throughout the flight. And let's not forget about the Golden Lounge in Kuala Lumpur, which is undoubtedly one of the best airport lounges in Southeast Asia. Thank you for joining me on this flight to Denpasar, Indonesia. I hope you found this review informative and enjoyable. If you did, please give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. In my next video, I'll be in Yerevan, Armenia, taking a journey on a state-of-the-art Russian-built night train from Armenia across to Georgia. Stay tuned and see you then!

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Muscat, the capital of Oman. Today I’m going to fly with Oman Air to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. This airline is expected to officially join the oneworld alliance in 2024 and I’ve read good things about them on the internet. But what are they really like? Let’s go and find out together! Oman is a middle-eastern country located in the southeastern coast of the Arabian Peninsula. It’s known for its diverse landscapes, including stunning coastlines, rugged mountains, and vast deserts. The capital city Muscat is renowned for its historic landmarks, vibrant markets, and beautiful architecture. The Omani people are also known to be one of the most welcoming people in the world. Muscat International Airport is the main airport serving Muscat. It’s the hub of the nation’s flag carrier Oman Air, which offers flights to destinations throughout the Middle East, Asia, Europe, and Africa. The airport has undergone several expansions and renovations since its establishment in 1973. In 2018, a new state-of-the-art passenger terminal was opened to increase the airport’s capacity and enhance the passenger experience. It covers a space of 580,000 sqm and features 45 boarding gates. The luxurious experience of flying in Oman Air’s business or first class commences as soon as you step foot in the airport. Located on the departures level, there is a specialised entry for business and first class passengers, which leads to Oman Air’s dedicated check-in area. Upon entering, a porter immediately offered to take care of my suitcase, and I was directed to one of the empty check-in counters. The process was fast, smooth, and straightforward. Today, I am flying with Oman Air to Kuala Lumpur and then continuing on to Denpasar with Malaysia Airlines. I received my boarding pass for both flights, and my bag was also through-checked. After obtaining my boarding pass, I proceeded through the private immigration and security line, where the wait was minimal. Once airside, the terminal is divided into three concourses: A, B, and C, with a large central section for duty-free shops and restaurants. The airport’s layout is similar to Hamad International Airport in Doha, Qatar, but on a smaller scale. There are ample signs throughout the terminal to assist travellers in finding their gates. Above the main departure level, you can find a transit hotel and several lounges. Among them is Oman Air’s flagship first and business class lounge. Beyond the impressive golden metal doors lies the joint lounge complex, with the entrance to the business class lounge on the left and the first class lounge on the right. Adjacent to the reception desk, you’ll find a model of Oman Air’s latest addition to its fleet, the Boeing 787-9. Additionally, there is a sign that lists all of the features at this lounge. This place is massive, it has the capacity to accommodate 500 people across the span of two levels. Starting in 2024, I believe OneWorld Emerald and Sapphire tiered frequent flyers flying in Economy should be at least eligible to use the business class lounge. Oman Air is among the few Middle Eastern airlines that serve alcohol on board, and their lounge is no exception.  The bar offers an extensive selection of wines and spirits to cater to passengers’ preferences. The lounge also features a terrace that extends beyond the floor-to-ceiling windows, providing a stunning view of the airfield. However, the outdoor area is not accessible to passengers. There are two main dining areas with mirrored layouts. While heading towards the bar, I caught a glimpse of the first dining area, and here’s the second one. It is currently closed as it only opens when the first dining area is filled to capacity. Deeper into the lounge, you will find toilets, shower facilities, and a prayer room. Additionally, there is a sleeping room that features several day beds separated by curtains, allowing travellers to catch a quick nap. I particularly admire this feature, and I hope that Qantas will consider incorporating it into its international lounges in the future. The upper level of the lounge features a spa section. In terms of the facilities, this is definitely one of the best lounges I’ve ever visited. It’s spacious, modern, clean, relaxing and well-equipped with everything I need. With my quick tour complete, I’m excited to head to the main dining area for a quick breakfast before boarding! The food and beverage selection was nothing short of remarkable. Let’s start with the drinks section, the semi-circular buffet features self-service coffee machines, various teas, authentic Omani coffee, soft drinks and water. On the opposite end of the buffet, there’s an array of refreshing juices. When it comes to food, the options are abundant, ranging from fruits, cheeses, cold cuts, cakes, cereals, and bread. There are several hot dishes as well, including the omelette, fried noodles, and meat. Overall I was truly impressed with the variety and quality of the food here. As of February 2023, Oman Air operates a fleet of 50 aircraft, ranging from Boeing 737-800, -900ER, and Max 8 to Boeing 787-8,-9 and Airbus A330-300 and -200. All aircraft feature business and Economy, with first class service being only available on selected A330-300 and Boeing 787-9, and Oman Air is planning to gradually phase out first class entirely. Boarding for my flight to Kuala Lumpur commenced an hour before departure, the aircraft operating this flight is an Airbus A330-200. There are 4 of them in the fleet. Each is equipped with 30 Collins Aerospace Apex business suites and 196 economy-class seats. The seats in business are in a 2-2-2 configuration, they’re Oman Air’s newest product. There are 5 rows in total, the forward cabin has three rows, and there are another 2 rows behind door 2. I picked seat 12K, which is in the last row in the forward cabin. I’m usually not a fan of the 2-2-2 configured business class due to the lack of privacy and the lack of direct aisle access for window seats. However, on this aircraft, each window seat is installed slightly ahead of the aisle seat, allowing for a direct path to the aisle. Additionally, there’s a partition that goes up between the two seats, creating a mini-suite for the window seat. Within a few moments of taking my seat, the cabin crew presented me with a choice of cold or hot towel followed by a choice of lemon mint or orange juice. After just five minutes, they returned with some dates and Omani coffee. With such excellent service, I knew it was going to be a wonderful flight! Muscat Airport has two runways, but only one of them is currently operational. Today, we will be taking off from the new runway, then make a U-turn and head east towards Kuala Lumpur. Sitting on the right-hand side of the plane will give me a bird’s eye view of the airport and Muscat City. Let’s take a closer look at the features of the business class seat. There are no overhead storage bins in the middle of the cabin, creating a more spacious feeling. There is ample space under the ottoman to store a backpack. The seat has a pitch of 82 inches and a width of 22 inches, providing plenty of legroom. There are two additional exposed storage areas for personal belongings, as well as a magazine holder with a wine list, a remote for the entertainment screen,  two USB ports, one headphone jack, and a universal power plug under the central armrest. The tray-table is hidden inside the armrest. And the other armrest has buttons to control the seat’s recline, leg rest position, and massage function. As anticipated, the seat can be transformed into a fully-flat bed that spans 77.5 inches in length. On the ottoman, the crew has placed a seat cover, a blanket and a pair of noise-cancelling headphones. The headphones work fine, but nothing special. Oman Air is not a dry airline, from the wine list, you can see it offers champagne, red and white wines, dessert wine and other alcoholic beverages. It’s nice to see that a South Australian wine has made to the list. Not long after the seat-belt sign was turned off, the crew served me some mixed cold nuts. I requested a glass of coke, and the crew also suggested a glass of the Champagne Lallier Blanc de Blancs, which retails for $75 a bottle in Australia. The 17-inch entertainment screen is controlled solely by this touch-sensitive remote. The screen is clear and well-positioned. The system comes in both Arabic and English. You can check out the forward and downward view of the aircraft fed live by the two exterior cameras, look at the flight path powered by GeoFusion, play games, purchase duty-free items and choose from a wide selection of movies and TV shows. With so many options, I have plenty to keep me entertained throughout the flight. There are three lavatories exclusively for the 30 business class passengers. The amenities include a hand cream, perfume, cologne and dental kits. What I like the most though, is that there’s a window here! This truly makes it a “loo with a view” and I love it! About 90 minutes after take off at 10:40 Oman time, the crew started serving lunch. Theoretically, I should be able to check out the menu from the entertainment screen, but it didn’t work on my flight. I was informed by the crew that there are four choices for the appetiser and three for the main course. I really like the thoughtful design of the plate and the shape of the salt and pepper shakers, which reflect Oman’s mountainous and rugged terrain. From my memory, the appetiser menu included four options: fruit, yogurt, scallops, and Arabic mezze. I was disappointed to discover that the scallop dish only had a single seared scallop along with some tender fish chunks. Nevertheless, the flavours of the seafood were delicately enhanced by a blend of herbs and spices, and I still found the dish satisfying. For the main course, passengers can choose from chicken kofta, fish with yellow rice and vegetarian. The fish dish appears to be a traditional Omani dish, and although the crew was unsure of the specific type of fish, they believe it may be emperor fish. The portion size was quite generous, the fish was fresh, and the rice had absorbed the flavourful sauce from the fish above. Overall the whole main course was healthy, colourful and tasty. The lunch is just two course, dessert was not offered, I didn’t mind it as the filling main course left me little room for anything else. We are now just 4 hours from Kuala Lumpur. While individual amenity kit was not offered,  I was pleased that the bedding was still provided on this day flight, so I could take a conformable nap. I’m sure the crew would be more than happy to set up the bed for me, I noticed that other passengers were doing it themselves so I did the same. Being situated away from the aisle, the window seat provides a heightened sense of privacy. Once the seat is fully reclined, you have the option to either sit up to watch a movie or lie down for a nap. I found both positions to be comfortable. Additionally, there is a reading light located above the headphone hook for those who prefer to do some light reading. The entertainment screen, remote screen, and the light above the ottoman can all be turned off for a more restful sleep. Approximately 90 minutes before landing, there was a small snack service. It includes some freshly cut fruits with cookies and a cup of tea. The idea of serving fruit is perfect, they’re not greasy, not too filling but refreshing. There’s a 4h time difference between Muscat and Kuala Lumpur, it’s already 8pm in Malaysia. Oman Air’s hard product, from dedicated check-in and massive lounge to modern business suites and comfortable beds, is on par with other major Gulf and Asian carriers. The cabin crew are some of the best I’ve ever encountered. They’re friendly, professional, and accommodating. With Oman Air joining the OneWorld alliance in 2024, I would definitely fly with them again in the future. I actually flew on their B737-800 from Cairo to Muscat yesterday and I will be flying on Malaysia Airline’s A330-300 to Bali tomorrow. I booked all three flights on Oman Air’s official website, and these business-class flights cost me just $1300.  Welcome to Kuala Lumpur International Airport! The hub of Malaysia Airlines, a member of the OneWorld Alliance. Thank you so much for watching, if you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. My flight to Bali is leaving in 13 hours, I decided not to go through immigration, instead, I booked a room at the transit hotel, and as a Qantas platinum frequent flyer, I spent a few hours at Malaysia Airline’s flagship Golden Lounge. Please stay tuned for my next video, where I'll show you more about these experiences. See you there!

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Egypt, a country famous for its ancient civilisation and the monuments of the majestic pharaohs. Today I’m going to catch an overnight train from Cairo to Aswan, it will travel along the beautiful Nile Valley and arrive at the historical city of Aswan tomorrow morning. I’m sure this is gonna be quite a memorable trip, I cannot wait, let’s go! Egypt is undoubtedly on many people’s travel lists! The country links Northeast Africa with the Middle East and has a population of over 100 million. The Giza Pyramids are probably one of the most famous and recognisable landmarks in the world. They are a testament to the incredible achievements of the ancient Egyptians and their enduring legacy. The capital city, Cairo, is a bustling metropolis with a rich history, vibrant culture, and a diverse population. Located on the banks of the Nile River, the Greater Cairo Region is home to over 20 million people, it’s the biggest and most densely populated city in Africa. It is well-known for its notoriously bad traffic, particularly during peak hours. Therefore, it is crucial to plan trips accordingly and account for extra time to reach destinations. The main train station of Cairo is called Ramses Railway Station. The name is derived from the Ancient Egyptian Pharaoh Ramses II. The current building was erected in 1892 and has undergone several renovations over the years, with the most recent one completed in 2017. The easiest way to get here is by taking Cairo metro line 1 or 2 and alighting at Al-Shohadaa Station. To purchase a train ticket, you can book online at the official Egyptian National Railways website or at the ticket offices at most major stations. Starting from December 2022, foreign travellers are required to pay higher fares than the locals. My train to Aswan tonight is operated by a private company called Watania Sleeping Trains. I bought my ticket on their official website. Alternatively, you may make reservations at their Ramses Station office. Depending on the demand, the company operates up to three trains in both directions between Cairo and Aswan every night. Usually, it is not necessary to book tickets well in advance. In early 2011, Ramses station was fully upgraded and air-conditioned, with new marble flooring across the station. The main waiting hall is spacious and impressive, with a vaulted ceiling and large, ornate chandeliers hanging from above. It is also home to a number of shops and food vendors, selling everything from souvenirs and snacks to newspapers and magazines. If you take the escalators upstairs, there’s a cafe with views of the platforms. Ramses Station has 28 tracks in total with a combination of dead-end and through platforms. The numbers are assigned from right to left. Platforms 1-7 are dead-end platforms, with platforms 1-4 located under the train shed. Northbound express trains to Alexandria usually use these platforms. Services to southern Egypt, including Luxor and Aswan, normally leave from the four through platforms numbered 8-11. Alongside platform 11, there are more dead-end platforms, which are used by northbound ordinary trains. It’s worth noting that a new railway hub is currently under construction in Greater Cairo, it is expected to be three times bigger than Ramses Station, and it should open very soon. At the moment, all intercity and long-distance trains in Egypt are hauled by diesel locomotives. The country is planning to introduce high-speed trains in the near future, with a planned speed of up to 250 km/h. The current passenger rolling stock is varied, with a mix of modern and older trains serving different routes. However, most trains are equipped with basic amenities, such as toilets, and comfortable seating. Good evening. My train to Aswan is scheduled to depart at 7:45 pm. To find out which platform your train is departing from, just check the information board. It’s displayed in both Arabic and English. A ticket is required to enter the platform. Ramses Station is very busy, trains only stop here for 5-10 minutes, so there’s no need to arrive too early. The through platforms are connected by an underground tunnel. Along each platform, there are shops selling snacks and beverages. Here it comes! The train arrived 5 minutes before its scheduled departure time. You can see there are a few armed military personnel in the power van, presumably they’re here to ensure the security onboard. There are also a large number of uniformed and plainclothes policemen patrolling each platform. Behind the power van, there are 12 air-conditioned sleeping cars and a lounge car. They were built in East Germany in the 1980s, but the interior of most carriages has been refurbished. Boarding was extremely efficient. There’s a dedicated attendant for each carriage, so they could check everyone’s ticket quickly. The locomotive used on this service is an ES30ACi double-cab diesel-electric locomotive built by General Electric in the US. It is specifically designed to operate in the hot and dusty environment in Egypt. Welcome aboard! Each carriage has ten sleeping compartments, and each has two bunk beds. For foreigners, the price of each cabin is 160 USD for two people or 120 USD for one person. If you’re travelling solo and don’t mind sharing the cabin with a stranger of the same gender, you can pay for one bed for 80 USD. We left Ramses Station at 7:50 pm, 5 minutes behind schedule. Soon after departure, the carriage attendant greeted everyone individually and showed me the features of the room. Each cabin door can be locked from the inside. Next to the door, there are controls to adjust the volume of the PA system, the room temperature, and the cabin’s brightness. Above the door, there is space to put a large suitcase. The upper berth was already made when I boarded the train, and the lower berth is currently set up as three comfortable seats. Since the cabin is designed to accommodate just two people, you can flip down the back of the middle seat to make it a table. This is a brilliant design! In addition, you can find two detachable tables if you don’t want to twist your body when sitting and eating. Below the window, there is a rubbish bin, next to it, there is a hidden washbasin equipped with soap, two cup holders, a power plug, and a mirror. Although it says that the power is for shavers only, I was able charge my camera and phone throughout the journey. Next to the washbasin, you can find a cloth hanger and a door. This is a connecting door between the adjacent pairs of compartments, allowing a group of four to move between rooms without having to go into the hallway. After crossing the Nile River, we entered the city of Giza. Giza Station is 30 minutes from Ramses station by train. It is a major transportation hub for commuters and travellers in Giza and southwest Cairo. The station is well-connected to the rest of the country’s rail network. Besides the private cabin, my ticket also includes an airline-style economy-class meal for dinner and breakfast. When booking the ticket online, I was asked to choose from chicken, meat, vegetarian, light meal, and fish. I selected meat, so tonight, my meal consists of a beef dish with bread, salad, boiled vegetables, rice and a chocolate cake for dessert. The beef was tender and flavourful, it tasted slightly spicy, there was plenty of sauce in the dish. The vegetables and salad looked fresh. Overall, enjoyed this meal, the portion was excellent. The paper below the meal containers is a drink menu. The drinks are not complimentary. You can purchase from the carriage attendant. A can of coke for 15 Egyptian pounds, the price is pretty fair. Apart from the ten sleeping compartments, one end of the carriage is the office for the attendant, and the other end has two unisex toilets. There’s no shower on this train. The toilets look pretty clean by Egyptian standard. There’s running water, toilet paper, hand wash, paper towels, and a hand dryer. All the human waste is dumped straight on the track. Therefore, passengers are not allowed to use the toilet when the train approaches a station. The lounge car is situated roughly in the centre of the train. After dinner, everyone is heading that way. Although there were many locals waiting on the platform, from what I see now, the whole train is mostly booked by foreign tourists. I anticipated finding a kitchen offering late-night snacks with booth-style seating at the club lounge. But to my surprise, it’s comprised of rotatable chairs and a bar. There’s no food available and the drink menu is identical to the one I saw on my meal tray. The lounge car opens all night, it was really busy so I didn’t stay for very long. The distance between Cairo and Aswan by rail is approximately 880 km. As a VIP express service, my train will only stop at 13 stations and arrive at the destination at 9:25 tomorrow morning. It’s bedtime. I have decided to sleep on the upper berth so that I can still use the seats below to put my belongings there. The ladder is stored under the seats, and it didn’t take me too much effort to get up here. The sheet looks relatively clean, the bed is wide, and there’s a blanket to keep me warm. The mattress isn’t very thick but it should be okay for the night. Up here, there’s a small reading light with a train attendant call button, a little pocket, and a cup holder. The light switches are within my arm’s reach. I forgot to switch off the mirror light. Otherwise, the cabin could be completely dark. Good morning! I slept alright, but during the night, even after adjusting the cabin temperature to the warmest possible setting, I still felt cold under the blanket. I’m glad that I packed a jacket with me I decided to fold up the upper berth so I can have more space while sitting down. The train is currently running 40 minutes behind schedule. The next stop is Luxor. This historical city is a popular tourist destination, often referred to as the world’s largest outdoor museum as it contains numerous ancient Egyptian monuments and ruins, including the famous Luxor Temple, the Karnak Temple Complex, and the Valley of the Kings. Luxor Station has several platforms and serves a range of local and express trains to Aswan, Cairo, and Alexandria. Although a significant portion of Egypt is dominated by the desert, the country’s long and slender Nile River Valley region is renowned for its fertile land. Fed by the Nile River and its tributaries, the region boasts rich agricultural lands that have sustained the population for thousands of years. The entire rail line from Cairo to Aswan runs along the Nile River. Seeing that I was already awake, the carriage attendant promptly served me breakfast along with a complimentary cup of tea or coffee. The breakfast consisted of a variety of bread and spreads, and I especially loved the cheeses. The guava juice was too sweet for my liking. But again, by Egyptian standards, I was pretty satisfied with what they offered. After breakfast, I decided to relax in the club lounge and bought another tea for 10 Egyptian pounds. The lounge is a lot quieter now, the chairs are comfortable. Sitting here allows me to enjoy the scenery from both sides of the train. The rail line is a lot busier than I thought, there are at least 50 trains a day travelling between Cairo and Aswan. We are almost in Aswan, and here are my thoughts about this journey. My private cabin was relatively clean, the bed was comfortable, the food was delicious, the scenery was beautiful, and my carriage attendant was super friendly and lovely. The train departs from the centre of Cairo and terminates in the centre of Aswan, it was very convenient. I enjoyed my journey. In comparison, flying from Cairo to Aswan with Egyptair costs around 80 USD in economy and 110 USD in business. I actually flew business class on my way back to Cairo, and I suggest you do the same so you can experience both modes of travel Tipping is fairly common in Egypt, but it’s not mandatory, at the end of the trip, I gave my carriage attendant 50 EGP before getting off. The train arrived Aswan an hour behind schedule, which was expected as Egyptian trains don’t usually run on time. Aswan is located in the far south of Egypt, near the border with Sudan. This is the south-most railway station in the country, serving as the terminus of the local and long-distance trains from Cairo and Alexandria. Welcome to Aswan! The city is renowned for its beautiful natural scenery, ancient monuments, and bustling markets.  It is the gateway of many famous attractions. There are a variety of Nile River cruises available as well, offering a range of amenities and activities, such as onboard dining, entertainment, and excursions to nearby temples and sites. Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more train and flight reviews. For my next video, I will take you to Oman and fly on Oman Air’s Airbus A330-200 business class from Muscat to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. See you there!

reviews.transcript_full: Hey all, here OS reviews. During the holiday season, I did a little bit of traveling. For the first time, I tried a carrier called Iceland Air connecting over to Europe. And that's because Iceland Air offered some discounts that made it one of the more cost effective options to get from the US to Europe. oftent times with roundtrip tickets, that is getting there and then getting back costing around $300 to $400 USD, which is considered quite good for international travel on a flight that takes around 7 hours give and take. And so I was actually quite surprised because this was an economy ticket. But I found myself staring at a pretty recently renovated screen in front of me when sitting down. And that's because later on I discovered that Iceland Air actually partnered with Panasonic to kind of refurbish their planes which are based on the Airbus A321 Neo long flight with the newer Panasonic Estroa in-flight entertainment system. They now have 13in 4K OLED displays for accessing videos that you can watch, playing back some mini games, listening to music to help the time pass by a little bit more quickly. It actually felt very modern because of the inky vibrant contrast of the OLED panels as well as having a matte layer on top of the display to further reduce glare and reflections coupled with relatively slim bezels on the side of the screen just made the entire experience. The content seemed to fill up even more space. And all of this was flanked by an LED light strip beneath the display itself, which can be further tilted up and down to give you some more adjustability depending on how far back you want to recline the seat. So, these large 4K HDR certified OLED panels are not only extremely sharp, but furthermore, if you are in business class, it comes with an even larger 16-in panel, but again, across the board, they are all 4K resolution OLED displays. Now, I have a couple of thoughts around this. I wanted to briefly point out and that is of course OLED and AMOLED displays have a potential or higher likelihood of burn-in over time. That is if it's sitting on a static image like this for example hours and hours on a higher brightness level there can be some ghosting or residue image left on there which is typically not found on LCD screens despite those having inferior contrast. Now, of course, this being pretty much brand new, when I was looking at this flight and display, there were no signs of burn-in yet, but really only time will tell further down the line in a couple of more months or years whether this will become more of something to be cautious of. So, it is a rather interesting decision from them. But again, perhaps being optimistic, Panasonic perhaps built in some different software enhancements, refresh the screen every once in a while, or just limit the in-flight entertainment systems to not always be on maximum brightness, of course, can further help elongate the lifespan of those displays. But at the moment, of course, I can't complain because I got to see it when it was pristine. And it was definitely very immersive, almost eyepopping in terms of the brightness as well as the richness of colors on a panel that would typically be reserved for higherend monitors or home cinema TVs versus it being on a form of public transit. But at least we are seeing some gradual improvements there. Now, as a geek at heart, obviously I was excited to see this newer in-flight entertainment system, check out the new UI as well as the carousel of apps and features that it could deliver. But on the other hand, if I'm being more practical in terms of the seat overall, of course, there can be additional enhancements that perhaps are going to be more useful to an average user, like adding in a little bit more leg room to make the seats feel a little more spacious or add more padding to make the seat softer. I think that arguably matters more overall when it comes to the experience versus having a cuttingedge OLED 4K screen in front of you. But ultimately, I'll take something over nothing. And this is at least one step in the right direction. So some other attributes of these newer Astrovia systems include having Bluetooth connectivity built on in. Not too surprising because it's likely based on a version of Android OS. And so what struck me is now I could connect wireless headphones directly onto the in-flight entertainment panels even in economy class. This was not something I was able to do before and oftent times with outdated planes you had to plug in a headphone jack and not only a 3.5 millimeter headphone jack but an airplane adapter splits it into that dualprong connector which is sometimes hard to even find a compatible adapter for if you're using your own headphones or you're stuck with rather crappy sounding headphones that the airlines give you that don't have really&c or anything like that. And now finally, you can use your own standard Bluetooth wireless headsets, AirPods, larger headphones with active noise cancellation, all wirelessly via Bluetooth. The audio experience is also supported with spatial audio effects as well. So, it gives you a little bit more of separation as you are listening to movie soundtracks. There's a couple of different EQ effects basically that you can play around with and click to turn on or off. I wouldn't say the effect is as strong as spatial audio on iPhones that does actual head tracking, but it is better than nothing and you can kind of play around with it. reviews.transcript_full: There are often a few things we can enjoy to pass the time while crossing the world at subsonic speeds over 30,000 ft above sea level on a commercial airliner. On the long flights, after enjoying a meal and drinks, we then decide what we want to do for the rest of the time. Some will take a short nap or just go to sleep or start to read a book or magazine. Those sitting in the window seats can enjoy the window views. Then there's the option to watch a movie or listen to music on the seatback screen or our own device. Since the first commercial flights, keeping passengers occupied while infight has been a question airline operators have asked themselves. One answer has been to provide audio and video systems referred to as infight entertainment or if to provide content such as movies and music to enjoy while on board. Today, these systems have been advanced to allow passengers to go beyond movies and music to play video games, see outside views of the aircraft, or get the flight status and connecting flight information on their own seat. if systems have come a long way from the early projection screens to show the very first inflight movies to the vast content libraries available on HD seatback screens today. So in this video, we'll take a look at the history of inflight entertainment systems and how airlines have made improvements to these systems that not only we enjoy inflight but have empowered passengers and enhanced the overall travel experience. Far from the modern IF systems we enjoy today, the very first infight video was shown on a short fight over the skies of Chicago in the early 1920s. In the August 22, 1921 issue of Aerial Age magazine, history's first aerial movie show took place aboard an 11 seat Felixto F5 flying boat named the Santa Maria as part of Chicago's Pageant of Progress trade show. The short film shown was named Howdy Chicago, which was a local production to promote the city. According to the account on aerial age, the film was shown on a plane while flying 90 mph 2,000 ft above the city of Chicago. A dey suitcase projection machine was fastened in a position and connected with an electrical flight socket. The film was viewed on a projection screen towards the front of the cabin and it was switched on by a projectionist who pressed the button to start it. This was the first known experiment in showing a flight on board an aircraft. Though the technology at the time was limited, it was described as a success. An account from the article said, quote, "Before the flight, it was feared that the vibration of the giant hydroplane as it shot through at 90 mph would seriously interfere with the screening, but it did not." This historic flight demonstrated the practicability of movie entertainment for transatlantic aerial commuters in the days to come. The success of the film screening on the promotional flights around Chicago opened up the ideas for those in aviation and how to show films on board. This would lead to the very first featurelength movie film being shown a few years later aboard a Imperial Airways flight. On April 6th, 1925, the very first movie shown on an airplane, The Lost World, was promoted by Imperial Airways with its flights as being quote the world's first aircraft cinema. Following the first movie showings aboard the Imperial Airways flights, airlines would experiment using radio signals from the ground for live broadcasts and performances from singers. Fast forward to the 1960s and jet aircraft then started to fly faster, higher, and for longer distances than the previous generation of planes. The aviation industry had to adjust some challenges to show movies on planes, such as getting the reels on board. The other challenge was to find a projector that could withstand turbulence yet be light enough not to add extra weight onto the aircraft. These challenges would be solved by cinema owner named Dave Flexer. Flexer would start a company named Infight Motion Pictures, a company that would lead to the rise of regular film showings on flights, but also served as the foundation for systems that the aviation industry would improve on later. After an investment of $1 million, Flexer and his company would develop a 16mm film system with a 25-in reel mounted horizontally to maximize space. Passengers would view the film on a projector at the front of the cabin. Using the new system, Transorld Airways showed the movie by Love Possessed to firstclass passengers on board a Boeing 707 in 1961. TWWA's main rival Pan-American would then follow and a year later Pakistan International Airways became the first international airline to introduce inflight movies with the same new system. The ability to show films on board aircraft presented an opportunity for airlines to show another type of film before a flight inflight safety videos. Provided the aircraft had the required video and sound systems, the US FAA from 1984 allowed for these pre-recorded videos to be shown replacing the standard live demonstrations performed by flight attendants. Airlines such as TWWA, Panama, and Northwest began showing their own inflight safety videos to passengers using the onboard screens. The aviation industry would continue to experiment with new media technologies that were introduced in the 1970s and 1980s such as videotapes, closed circuit television, and overhead screens. The one airline, Northwest Airlines, would make infight entertainment become more personal with the introduction of individual seatback screens in the late 1980s. During this time, Arn Stevenson, a businessman involved in aviation components, wanted to put a small liquid crystal display LCD TV screen for each airplane seat. This would lead to the founding of a new company, Airvision, and the company would partner with Philips for the screens. Warner Brothers would provide the content for this new IF system. And in June 1988, Northwest Airlines began trials using the new IF system on its flights between Detroit and Tokyo. Airvision's if was the world's first with personal if screens. The Boeing 747 on Northwest Detroit Tokyo flights had 116 of the 6.9 cm seatback screens installed on which passengers could watch video content on six channels. These six channels showed movies, news, documentaries, music videos, and cartoons on a fixed schedule. Both Northwest and Warner Brothers surveyed the passengers, and the result was 70% preferred the personal screens to the overhead screens. Following Northwest, British Airways and Quantis would launch their own trials of Airvision's IP system on board their aircraft. From six channels offered on the Northwest Airlines 747s, these IP systems would expand with far bigger libraries and CPC screens going beyond movies and music to offer passengers the ability to play video games, listen to podcasts, watch live TV, see the inflight map, and even communicate with their fellow passengers. Among the biggest libraries of content that airline passengers can enjoy today comes from Emirates ICE system. Widely regarded as the world's largest with 6,500 channels of audio video on demand content. It is one of the well- reggarded IF systems along with Qatar Airways Orics, Singapore Airlines Chrisworld and Cafe Pacific's own system. Of the audio video on demand IF systems today, Singapore Airlines Chris World is widely regarded as the first to allow passengers to pause, rewind, and fast forward movies or music. After launching Chrisworld in 1995 with 32 audio and video channels and 10 video games, it launched the new system called Wisemen 3000 in September of 1997. First introduced to first and business class passengers, it was then rolled out to economy class passengers in 2001. In addition to the media control options, it also featured news text displays and destination information. While Chris World is the longest active prior to the Singapore's Wisemen 3000, Swiss Air had launched its own audio video on demand system earlier in the year 1997 with its own system powered by interactive flight technologies. Similar to Wisemen 3000, it also let passengers watch pay-per-view movies and take gaming on an airplane to another level with infight gambling. However, that system was cited as a factor in the crash of Swiss Air Flight 111. Prior to the crash, Swiss Air complained that the electric boxes under the seat would get too warm and hard drives installed failed regularly. Following the crash, Swiss Air removed the IFT system from aircraft with them and it was never used again. Well into the 2000s and the rise of the internet, airlines, including the budget airlines, have expanded the streaming the very same content on their IF systems beyond the seatback screen, but rather onto the passenger's very own device. This has led to the rise of the bring your own device model, providing inflight entertainment. Airlines now make decisions on whether to install seatback entertainment screens or skip it in favor of providing Wi-Fi and content through passengers own devices. To install modern seatback screens, the cost can vary depending on aircraft. Whether it's a small narrow body jet or a wide body such as the 8380, a typical individual seatback installation can cost between $10,000 to $15,000 per seat. Along with the installation of wirings, servers, power systems, insec controls, airlines also have to invest heavily in both the hardware and software along with the maintenance after installation. Combined those costs can be far higher than offering a Wi-Fi system minus the seatback screens. Adopting the bring your own device model, airlines, especially budget airlines, can focus on modifying the seats to offer maybe a device holder and charging ports. With these choices, airlines may have fleets with mixed entertainment systems. Their narrow body jets used on short hall flights may have just bring your own device systems, while widebody jets used on medium and long haul flights featuring both Wi-Fi and seatback screens. Whether aircraft are equipped with seatback screens or not, more aircraft are now featuring seatback charging ports as passengers increasingly bring their own devices on board. Passengers can also use their own audio devices such as Bluetooth enabled earphones to enjoy the content. Compared to the IF systems of the past, modern seatback and wireless systems also provide passengers more flight information. Passengers can view the current flight status information and the exact location of the aircraft on interactive maps. External cameras installed on select aircraft such as the Airbus A380, A350, and 7 intended for pilots to navigate on the ground. allows for passengers to view things that they would normally not get during takeoff and landing. In addition to getting the estimated arrival time, passengers can also access connecting flight information and airport terminal maps at key airline hubs through the same if systems. While some aircraft lets passengers enjoy external views to the IF, one airline has allowed passengers to actually listen into the conversations between the pilots and air traffic controllers United. There is no official history of Channel 9 and it's not really mentioned by the airline, though it history goes back to the 1980s. There are videos on YouTube that do feature passengers listening in onto the pilot ATC conversations on channel line, but on board the pilot in the command has the final decision on whether the passengers can listen into it. Today, it can be found on United Seatback screens listed as from the flight deck. In recent years, there has been an increased interest from airlines and the traveling public for infight Wi-Fi access. On a casual poll on the Fights in Asia X page, when asked which is more important on a flight, having infight Wi-Fi or an in-flight entertainment screen, over 70% of the over 180 people voted for the Wi-Fi. In a larger poll of over 11,000 passengers by Viasat, 81% of those surveys said that being able to connect is more important for them. Among the headline internet providers has been SpaceX's Starlink, which has seen a growing list of major airlines selecting Starlink to provide free high-speed internet access on board. Starlink is one company that addresses an interest from passengers and airlines for great internet access on board flights, which the 2023 VISAT survey also reported 48% of passengers want the reassurance of free and reliable internet on board an aircraft. Having this feature is an important and will influence booking decisions as 83% of respondents in the VISAT survey said that they would select an airline if they offered quality Wi-Fi experience. With more surveys showing similar sentiments and a growing number of airlines introducing free onboard internet, it is becoming clear having free high-speed internet access is becoming an important factor when selecting which airline to fly with. Going forward, the basic amenities most airlines will offer to each passengers will be free internet access and charging ports. Budget airlines and those with aircraft operating shorter flights will likely take the route of bring your own device, while bigger full service carriers may choose the hybrid model that allows connections between passengers devices and the seatback screen. Regardless, there are opportunities for budget and full service carriers to incorporate personal greetings and allow passengers to enhance their infight experience by using it for meal orders, showing food and beverage options, reading materials, or communicating with the flight attendants. Airlines could further experiment with technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality, but the successes of those technologies will depend heavily on the ability for passengers to enjoy these activities in the limited space on the plane. even in the premium seats and the needed equipment can safely be installed on the aircraft. That said, modern IF have come a long way from the simple projector showing how Chicago. We now have more options when it comes to the types of content and games to keep us occupied as airlines push the boundaries of flight. We are no longer just limited to the personal screen, but can enjoy and control the same content and connect to the internet on our own devices. With the internet, if systems expanded what can be enjoyed in a flight beyond the seatback screen. That's all for now, though I do want to hear your thoughts. Which airline has your favorite inflight entertainment system? As inflight Wi-Fi becomes more common, which is more important, the internet access or having an I screen? And how do you see the future of inflight entertainment? I definitely would love to hear your thoughts again, but in the meantime, this has been another edition of Flights in Asia, highlighting the news and updates from the aviation and travel scene in the Asia Pacific. Thank you for watching and have a great day.

reviews.transcript_full: In my previous video, I briefly reviewed the Business Class of An India's Airbus A319  aircraft, which you can see by clicking on the video now or clicking the link in the description  box.  In this video, I will show you the details of the in-flight entertainment system available  on their Airbus fleet for domestic sectors.  The Business Class VTV is 10.6 inches in size and is touchscreen.  The IFE starts in the map mode wherein it toggles between the flight details screen,  the airline logo screen and the map screen in three different zoom levels.  Touching the mode button on the screen brings you to the video mode where 6 movie channels  are displayed.  This unfortunately is a non-Award system which I believe is a norm for short-haul flights  these days.  The on-screen touch controls give you an option of changing channels, volume and brightness  of the screen.  Touching the mode button again will switch off the video and take you to the audio mode  with the wide variety of audio channels choose from.  Press mode again and the map screen appears along with the music playing in the background.  There is also an option to change the aspect ratio of the screen if you are not a big fan  of 16s to 9.  All this can also be controlled by the hard button controls on your armrest.  The IFE kept me busy on a 3 hour flight from day to day and the movie is that being played  with a tradition.  Overall I would rate the IFE 4 out of 5 for short-haul flights.  It would have been a perfect 5, 100 been an Award system just how they have on their long  haul-buying aircraft.  Please leave a comment below and do check out the other videos.  Also don't forget to subscribe.  Thank you.

In terms of choices for airlines watching interior upgrade budgets at present , “you could just do the seat-end.
“You’re probably taking the cabin out, you’re probably changing the seats out anyway — you don’t have to … but you probably are — in that particular case, seat-ends only.

That’s all part of the sculpted precise design that we put together, and we did that because it then strips weight out.” Astrova was unveiled at the Aircraft Interiors Expo, sized here for premium seat implementations.

Most airlines still have just a handful of 4K movies on board.
And there’s an impressive amount of power to go round: Astrova can provide 67W of juice over USB-C, enabling fast-charging of devices — even the larger, power-hungry ones like tablets and laptops.

article_quotes.text: Bluetooth Pairing goes mainstream For several years in the middle of the last decade the idea of Bluetooth pairing for headphones on in-seat IFE systems was considered impossible.
Today, new IFE installations include Bluetooth more and more.
Bluetooth pairing is, at this point, table stakes for a modern embedded IFE solution.

Imagine where internet and seat-back merge, and then bringing partners on board to be the gateway of that intersection, to be traffic managers and to ensure that the experience we are delivering at that intersection meets or exceeds what our customers would expect on the ground.

It delivers what the airline wants. – David Thomas, Apios Chief Product Officer Similar to a ChromeCast or AppleTV, passengers will be able to connect to the screen on the seatback to display their own content.

The connection is driven via a QR code on the screen and a unique Wi-Fi SSID for that seat, making it easy for the passenger at that seat while simultaneously reducing the opportunities to abuse the system.
It also allows for offline casting (e.g. a plane with no inflight connectivity link), assuming the app supports it.

reviews.transcript_full: hello everyone i'm luis thanks for joining me today at amphenol's pasadena technical center here in pasadena california i am a product specialist for amphenol pcd which is headquartered in beverly massachusetts amphenol pcd offers a wide variety of products and solutions for military and aerospace applications to customers around the world the amphenol pasadena technical center exists with the intention to provide support to our west coast customers one of the latest additions to the apcd product line offerings is the ife systems products if you have ever traveled on an airplane you probably quickly realize that the trip is more enjoyable when you have something to distract you whether it is music a movie or playing poker on the screen in front of you all these forms of entertainment stem from the same core concept making the passengers experience as enjoyable as possible in today's times we usually expect to see a digital screen in front of us and a usb charging port near us when we are in an airplane there is a screen there must also be an audio jack to connect your headphones these services all belong to a part of the commercial aerospace industry known as ife and c so what is ifenc the acronym stands for in-flight entertainment and connectivity this encompasses the whole passenger experience including the display used to watch movies the headphones provided by the airline food and drinks as well as the cabin network system that allows you to connect to the aircraft's wi-fi network ifvnc can be broken into two major groups one group consists of passenger facing components including the display unit audio jacks the passenger electronic device charging ports remote controls and any device that the passenger can see and touch the other group consists of system components which includes modems servers routers and wireless access points the passengers do not directly interface with the system components but they are very critical in making the passenger components function the ife systems products at amphenol pcd are passenger facing components that integrate with the ife and are designed to enhance the passenger experience the idea behind in-flight entertainment after all is of course in the name itself to provide entertainment to passengers but the engineering that goes into the passenger facing components attacks problems from a higher point of view one of the biggest problems we face when traveling is undesired noise the noise begins from the minute the aircraft takes off to the minute it lands that's the entire trip undesired background noise results in passengers exiting the aircraft at the end of their flight feeling unrested and probably frustrated this makes traveling a painful and tiring process when in reality the goal is to make traveling enjoyable easy and refreshing so how do we attack that problem well you offer a product that cancels out the undesired noise of course so introducing our active noise canceling jacks let us start with a little bit of background how does noise canceling technology work you start by understanding how noise works how sound works think of reviews.title: United’s latest jets will offer Bluetooth for in-flight entertainment
reviews.transcript_excerpt: with these screens will finally make it a reality.…

captions.text: with these screens will finally make it a reality.

reviews.transcript_full: reported today in the verge. United's latest jets will offer Bluetooth for inflight entertainment.  United Airlines is adding a long awaited feature to the inflight entertainment seatback  screens of its new Boeing 737 MAX-8 jets, support for Bluetooth headphones. The company is  making the upgrade as part of United Next, a new plan to expand and modernize its fleet  with what it says are larger, fuel-efficient jets and a more comfortable inflight experience.  I haven't flown in the last two years, for reasons that are hopefully obvious, but the  thing that grinds most of my past flying experience to a halt is dealing with the bizarre  Tuporong Daudi OJax airplanes used for inflight audio. Having headphones with a 3.5mm  Zordio jack isn't hard, but it doesn't reflect the Bluetooth audio lifestyle, Apple,  and plenty of other tech companies have slowly forced me to adopt. I don't like the wireless  audio freak I've become, but it happened, which makes United's upgrades so exciting,  as demoed in the tweets below from aviation writer Jason Rabinovitz. The main attraction  of it United's new interior is the new at Panasonic Caroseat Back-Eye System. It finally offers  one of the overall most requested passenger items, Bluetooth audio. Narrow-body aircraft  with these screens will finally make it a reality.  Hashtagpacsexpick.twitter.com slash TDO04G4 by 7C. Adding seatback screens made a huge  difference in how tolerable flying is, but it's been held up by lagging audio support  that the Verge has even written a guide to getting around. And this isn't a problem  unique to United. Other airlines like Delta or JetBlue have been offering seatback screens  for years, but have also saddled flyers with analog audio. United just might be one of the  first airlines to start the next wave of in-flight entertainment improvements, hopefully.  However, there's room for things to go a bit sideways. As part of its upgrades, United's  new 737 Max8 jets offer 10 or 13-inch in-flight entertainment screens on the backs of all seats,  which might mean a lot of people trying to connect to Bluetooth at once. That could cause  interference, and might also make the process of connecting your headphones more of a chore if  you're having to hunt through multiple devices trying to pair in the same menu. United currently  only offers Bluetooth on its Max8 jets which it says should start flying this summer.  The company didn't share how it plans to address issues with Bluetooth, but said it's still  studying the technology. I can't rightfully claim that Bluetooth is as meaningful a change  as more a grimoire safer flights, but for an airline industry hoarding cash to make it through  the pandemic and looking to entice frequent flyers to earn their miles again, any snazzy new feature  can't hurt.For more on this story, visit the news article link.
